title: RPT-European Factors to Watch-Shares set to continue bounce on U.S. optimism
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)               

LONDON, March 26 (Reuters) - European stocks were seen rising at the open on Wednesday, buoyed by increasing signs of life in the U.S. economy, with a key index set to continue a rally off a one-week closing low back towards multi-year highs.               

At 0720 GMT, futures for the Euro STOXX 50, Britain's FTSE 100 , Germany's DAX and France's CAC were 0.3-0.5 percent higher.               

Stock markets in Europe were broadly expected to track gains made in Asian and U.S. trade, where buoyant U.S. consumer confidence and house prices helped to fuel gains.               

The two reports were the latest in a series of positive data releases from the United States, supporting the view that bad weather rather than inherent economic weakness affected weaker reports earlier this year.               

"Concerns around the three C's (cold, Crimea, China) are dropping off as the effect of the US winter subsides, the Crimean conflict is no longer affecting markets and China has seen stimulation bets ramping up," Evan Lucas, market strategist at IG, said in a note.               

"This will mean markets will continue to push higher in the short term, with the US and China currently driving most market reactions; and signs of stability or growth will be equity and commodity supportive."               

Growing bets that China will act to stimulate its economy and an increased resilience to uncertainty over relations between Russia and the West over Crimea helped to support European equity markets on Tuesday.               

The pan-European FTSEurofirst 300 rose 1.3 percent in the previous session, bouncing off a one-week closing low set at the start of the week.               

The index remains 3 percent off its closing high in February, however, which was its highest close since May 2008.               

Economic confidence in Europe also held up despite ongoing concerns about Russian intervention in Ukraine, with market research group GfK finding that German consumer morale held steady at its highest reading since January 2007.               

The reading comes on the back of comments from European Central Bank President Mario Draghi and Bundesbank President Jens Weidmann that stimulus from the euro zone's central bank was not out of the question as the euro zone still battles with deflationary pressures.               

The unexpected intervention from Weidmann, whose Bundesbank had previously expressed scepticism about such measures, also helped to boost European shares on Tuesday.               

"While talk is cheap, the ECB will ultimately need to back its words with credible measures, with the standard toolbox running on empty," Anatoli Annenkov, senior European economist at Societe Generale, said in a note.

title: European Morning Briefing: Stocks Seen Higher; Focus on Ukraine, China
text:
SNAPSHOT:

========

European bourses seen higher, bunds and gilts mixed; euro, oil mixed, spot gold up slightly

-Shell Gas To Focus On Larger Projects As It Cuts Spending

-Barclays, China Development Bank Ink New Pact

-Deutsche Banker Who Committed Suicide Anxious Amid Probes

-Facebook to Acquire Virtual Reality Company for $2 Billion

-Left Alliance Quits Finland Government Over Austerity Measures

-WATCH FOR: German, Italian consumer confidence; ECB's Draghi, France's Hollande meet; U.S. durable goods, services PMI, weekly oil data

EUROPEAN OUTLOOK & U.S./ASIAN SUMMARIES:

========

Investors hoping for stimulus from China and the eurozone, are looking for slightly higher stock markets in Europe, with bunds and gilts mixed, while watching for developments around Ukraine to unfold.

President Barack Obama will meet European allies and NATO officials in Brussels on Wednesday, following a session in The Hague at which members of the Group of Seven leading nations adopted a formal statement condemning Russia's intervention and annexation of the Crimea region of Ukraine.

The future of natural gas supply in central Europe will be discussed at a conference Wednesday, while the U.S. and the Czech Republic will cement their ties in nuclear energy.

Officials from Europe's gas sector, wary of potential disruptions to deliveries of Russian gas after Russia's recent annexation of Crimea, will meet in Prague to discuss how the sector should best position itself given the uncertain outlook.

Stocks rallied across Asia on Wednesday, tracking gains in U.S. shares after consumer confidence in the world's largest economy rose to an over six-year high. However, traders say the gains could be fleeting as the focus turns to local factors.

Wall Street futures were slightly higher, with Treasurys hardly changed, as the euro and oil futures traded little changed, while spot gold edged higher.

STOCKS:

======

Stock markets may start higher on hopes for stimulus measures from China and the eurozone after European Central Bank officials offered dovish views.

Ahead of the opening, IG has called the FTSE up 17 at 6621, the DAX up 43 at 9381, and the CAC up 21 at 4365.

"The comments sound somewhat more open-minded to the idea of additional policy action from the ECB," said Ken Wattret, co-head of European market economics at BNP Paribas.

As for China, "the market has shifted focus away from growth concerns and toward possible policy steps by Chinese authorities to stem the economic weakness," said analysts at Barclays.

"The bets are growing that further stimulus measures across Europe and China will be introduced over the coming months," noted IG strategist Evan Lucas.

U.S. stock futures were higher Wednesday, after benchmarks rose Tuesday, breaking a two-session slide in choppy trading that saw the market's recent highflying names swerve between gains and losses.

Some market watchers said the abrupt weakness in highflying stocks appeared to be the work of long-term investors booking profits before the end of the first quarter. Others said the selloff in strong-performing stocks represents an ominous signal that investors are girding for additional market declines.

"When you start to see momentum leadership reverse, it is usually the first stage of some type of risk-off mode," said Mike O'Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading Institutional Services. Recent selling in biotech has "filtered through all the momentum stocks as well," Mr. O'Rourke said, including internet stocks. "There is no compelling reason to be aggressive right now."

On the data front, traders will look for U.S. durable goods data figures due at 1230 GMT. "We expect durable goods orders to increase m-o-m by 1.0 percent in February, versus a decline of 1.0 percent in January," Handelsbanken said. "The ISM manufacturing's new order component, which is a leading indicator of durable goods orders, was on strong 54.5 in February," it noted.

FOREX:

======

The euro was mixed against major currencies in Asia after a slew of policy makers from the European Central Bank and the European Commission decried the strength of the common currency and offered measures to stem the risk of deflation.

"People keep trying to buy dollars, but they get frustrated because it keeps snapping back on them," said Brad Bechtel, managing director at Faros Trading. He added that trading flows may ramp up as month-end and quarter-end buying takes place.

BONDS:

=====

Bunds may start mixed as investors get the latest readings of consumer confidence in embattled Italy and flourishing Germany amid speculation about monetary policy.

Setting a negative deposit rate to guard against excessively low inflation is an option for the European Central Bank, said Finland's central bank governor Erkki Liikanen, the latest indication that officials are willing to provide fresh stimulus to protect a fragile economic recovery.

U.S. Treasurys were little changed Wednesday, after government bonds on Tuesday edged higher as a round of mixed U.S. economic releases deflated concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates sooner than expected.

A $32 billion sale of two-year notes also saw strong demand.

The selling in short-dated bonds is "overdone in the short term," said Charles Comiskey, head of Treasury trading at Bank of Nova Scotia in New York. "The timing for the first rate hike from the Fed depends on upcoming economic data."

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Charles Plosser said the time to think about raising short-term interest rates may well have arrived.

In Japan Wednesday, government bonds edged higher as the fiscal year approaches its close.

ENERGY:

=======

Oil prices were little changed amid a range of U.S. and international factors, including continued geopolitical tensions over the Ukraine and cleanup efforts from an oil spill in a major U.S. shipping channel.

"Oil is just fluctuating in response to myriad items here," analyst Jim Ritterbusch said.

Analysts are expecting another increase in domestic oil inventories in data to be released Wednesday by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, with a consensus estimate of 2.8 million barrels, according to a survey of analysts by The Wall Street Journal. Crude stockpiles have risen as refineries have reduced operations during spring maintenance season.

Nymex crude was unchanged at $99.28, while Brent was off 2 cents at $106.97.

METALS:

======

Base metals could be rangebound as they look for cues, but expectations of stimulus measures from the Chinese government could help to provide a floor for prices. The market is "most likely already pricing in this slower growth," in China, the world's biggest consumer of industrial metals, Walter de Wet, analyst at Standard Bank, said in a report. He expected China's economic growth to slow over the next three years and said the current slump in growth momentum was cyclical.

LME 3-month copper was up $5.75 at $6,577/ton.

Gold edged higher in Asia with modest physical demand helping to underpin prices. "Better physical demand suggests there may be a turn in momentum in the coming days," ANZ said in a report. Spot gold prices have slipped about 5.6% from its six-month high this month as geopolitical tensions in Ukraine eased and U.S. Federal Reserve's stance suggested the central bank may start raising the interest rate sooner than the market expects. Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Charles Plosser said the time to think about raising short-term interest rates may well have arrived.

Spot gold was at $1,313.90/oz, up $2.80.

title: MORNING BID: EUROPE-A daily note from our Economics/Politics Editor
text:
LONDON, March 25 (Reuters) - G7 leaders didn't move the dial far last night, telling Russia it faced more damaging sanctions if it took any further action to destabilize Ukraine.

They will also shun Russia's G8 summit in June and meet "à sept" in Brussels, marking the first time since Moscow joined the group in 1998 that it will have been shut out of the annual summit.

There were some other interesting pointers. For one, the G7 agreed their energy ministers would work together to reduce dependence on Russian oil and gas. Could this lead to the United States exporting shale gas to Europe in the long-run?

A committee of U.S. lawmakers will hear testimony on Tuesday from those who favour loosening restrictions on gas exports.

Sanctions imposed so far may be limited but they are hitting investment and Russia's currency and stock market. The economy is barely growing and the government said yesterday it now expected net capital outflows of up to $70 billion in the first quarter of the year.

The G7 leaders remain in The Hague for day two of a nuclear security summit and the EU leaders plus Barack Obama will reconvene in Brussels on Wednesday for the annual EU/U.S. summit.

But the big moment of the day could come from the IMF which is due to wind up its work in Kiev and is expected to offer an economic reform and aid programme soon.

Aid for Kiev will also hurt Putin.

The U.S. and EU would row in behind any IMF package, helping Ukraine meet its debt obligations and begin the process of rebuilding. The EU has signed the political elements of an "association agreement" with Kiev, promising closer ties that will help draw it more closely into the heart of Europe.

That is precisely what Putin was trying to avoid.

Remaining Ukrainian troops are being withdrawn from Crimea, the last step in cementing Russia's control of the region. Russian intervention in eastern or southern Ukraine would be the trigger for additional sanctions, as would violence in Crimea.

Having also been in the Hague, Chinese President Xi Jinping will begin a three-day state visit to France. The bilateral focus will be on business and trade deals. But Xi is also a big player in the Ukraine crisis whether he likes it or not.

Beijing has stayed studiously to one side of the Ukraine crisis, as is its wont, and Moscow still has high hopes of a huge natural gas supply deal with China that is apparently close after years of negotiations.

China has said sanctions are not the way forward but it abstained on a U.N. Security Council resolution, which Russia vetoed, that declared the Crimea referendum on joining Russia was invalid. Xi called for a political solution on Monday but did not harden Beijing's position towards Moscow.

Germany's Ifo index will be the main event for the macro markets after its March PMI survey showed solid expansion but at a slightly slower rate than in February. The Ifo is expected to hold steadyish at a high level although German business lobbies are starting to warn about the threat to them from tough sanctions on Ukraine.

Germany's finance ministry will release its monthly report and both European Central Bank President Mario Draghi and Bundesbank chief Jens Weidmann are making speeches.

Hungary's central bank - full of government appointees - appears not to have sated its appetite for interest rate cuts despite having lowered them month in, month out since late 2012.

A Reuters poll of economists found most expect a further 10 basis points reduction today, taking rates down to 2.6 percent although some think it will hold for the first time in over 18 months. Further cuts could increase the risk of a sell-off in Hungarian assets given the U.S. Federal Reserve's steady reduction of its money creation.

Nigeria's central bank, on the other hand, is expected to leave rates at 12 percent today to support its currency at its first meeting since President Jonathan suspended Central Bank Governor Lamido Sanusi, a monetary-policy hawk, last month. It could even hike.

Arab leaders meet in Kuwait, the first high-level political meeting since Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain withdrew their ambassadors from Qatar in a dispute about Doha's involvement in the region, such as its support for the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt.

Saudi Arabia designated the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group shortly afterwards. Kuwait is attempting to mediate.

We will also be watching for news of more Gulf aid to Egypt and there are differences over Syrian and Iran too. (Editing by Jon Boyle)

A likely cut in Hungary's benchmark interest rate to a new record low and comments from Slovakia's policy maker on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank will be in focus Tuesday.

Magyar Nemzeti Bank is expected to cut interest rates for the 20th consecutive time to boost fragile economic growth. Hungary's central bank is forecast to cut its main rate 0.1 percentage point to 2.60%, according to 15 of 18 economists polled by The Wall Street Journal.

The MNB is also due to release its latest forecasts for inflation and economic growth.

"Despite the euro-forint rising above 313 several times since the beginning of March, [governing party] Fidesz's polling numbers do not seem affected by currency weakness," said UniCredit economist Dan Bucsa in a note to clients Monday, referring to parliamentary elections in April.

Also Tuesday, Jozef Makuch, an ECB interest rate setter, is likely to comment on possible measures the ECB could take to help the euro area's economic recovery, after it cut its headline interest rate by half in November to 0.25%.

Mr. Makuch, who is also governor of the National Bank of Slovakia, will speak at a conference to present the bank's latest economic growth and inflation outlook for this small euro-area country of 5 million people.

Unlike other countries that share the euro, Slovakia has avoided falling into recession since 2009 following the onset of the global financial crisis.

In Prague, Czech lawmakers are scheduled to vote on a bill sponsored by legislators behind the ruling coalition government to boost the country's defense spending to 1.3% of gross domestic product as of 2015, from 1.08% now. The motion to raise defense spending reflects the country's heightened security concerns in the wake of events in Ukraine and Crimea, the lawmakers behind the bill say.

title: EUR/USD May Face Pressure After G-7 Agrees to Exclude Russia, Increase Sanctions -- Market Talk
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

2154 GMT [Dow Jones] The EUR may face pressure in Asia after news leaders of the world's largest economies agreed to effectively remove Russia from the Group of Eight nations in response to Moscow's military intervention in Ukraine. The leaders, meeting in emergency session, also agreed that they would begin to exert punitive sanctions on Russia's energy, banking, finance and arms industries unless Moscow dialed back plans to seize the Crimea region from Ukraine. While the EUR/USD gained overnight, the possibility of further sanctions could drag it down, says Stuart Ive, senior client advisor at OM Financial in Wellington. "Anything along those lines may see the EUR dip down, mainly because central Europe receives the majority of its oil supplies from Russia and the euro zone has very strong economic links with Russia. Any sanctions will weigh on the EUR," he says. The EUR/USD is at 1.3836 mid-morning in New Zealand. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com @FarroHoward)

2152 GMT [Dow Jones] AUD/USD's rise to a 3 1/2-month high of 0.9150 last night was driven more by U.S. dollar weakness and flows, rather than a "bad news is good news" view that China data is sufficiently weak that it will elicit a strong policy response, says NAB's Co-Head of FX Strategy, Ray Attrill. "Flows-wise, we note that repatriation flows by local asset managers look to be offering support for the currency at present, alongside ongoing offshore asset manager interest in Australian assets, and suspected corporate demand," he adds. Focus turns to a speech by RBA deputy governor Phil Lowe at an ASIC forum at 0445 GMT, followed by German IFO business conditions data, U.S. data on new home sales, house prices, consumer confidence and the Richmond Fed's manufacturing survey overnight. On a closing basis, AUD/USD remains below potentially strong resistance from its 200-day moving average at 0.9138. Any negative catalysts could trigger a dip toward uptrend line support near 0.9000 on a technical basis. AUD/USD last 0.9133. (david.rogers@wsj.com)

17:31 EDT - BMO Capital says real housing prices in Canada since 1980 have averaged 2.7% growth a year, "amazingly close" to average real GDP growth over that time. By one measure, Toronto's great real estate bubble of the '80s hit its apex 25 years ago, BMO says. Adjusted for inflation and seasonality, average home prices topped out in February '89, and didn't bottom out until more than seven years later with an after-inflation drop of 38%. "But, notably, even a first-time buyer at the very peak of that episode has still seen an annualized price gain of nearly 1% after inflation," BMO says. "Real prices more than doubled in a four-year period from 1985 to 1989, while it took 18 years to double this time," firm adds. (don.curren@wsj.com @dbcurren)

2112 GMT [Dow Jones] Asian stock markets may open slightly lower after some profit-taking in U.S. markets, Philip Hunter, a broker at First NZ Capital in Wellington, says. "There has been some weakness in stocks that have run pretty hard and we might see some consolidation in Asian markets," he says. He says sentiment may also still be weighed by weaker-than-expected China data from Monday. In New Zealand, the NZX-50 is down 0.4% at 5100.886 early but Hunter expects light trading due to a dearth of drivers. Investors will be watching for results from Fonterra Cooperative Group (FCG.NZ) and Synlait (SML.NZ) later in the week. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com @FarroHoward)

17:00 EDT - The latest position reports show US dealers' Treasurys inventory up a slight $4.3B for the week ended March 12. That was the same week Treasurys held at the NY Fed for foreign accounts dropped a record $105B. The lack of pick-up in dealer inventory is yet another sign that the drop in custody holdings did not represent selling. Instead, it corroborates what many believe is a government -- perhaps Russia -- deciding to shift it Treasurys holdings to a custodian outside the US. One popular custodian destination lately has been Belgium, as suggested in recent TIC data. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

1942 GMT [Dow Jones] The AUD/USD's "remarkable buoyancy"--the pair gained strongly overnight despite a disappointing data release out of China--is attributable to investors believing the Chinese data tone has become negative enough to warrant a policy response from Beijing, BNZ FX Strategist Raiko Shareef says. "This 'bad news is good' dynamic for risk assets harks back to days of crises past," he says. Scheduled remarks from RBA Deputy Governor Phil Lowe in Hong Kong may push the pair around as "with the AUD/USD bumping up against its 200-day moving average, the RBA will no doubt be tempted to talk it lower." The pair is at 0.9128 early in New Zealand. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com @FarroHoward)

1927 GMT [Dow Jones] The NZD/USD remains well supported early in New Zealand trading as markets digest weaker-than-expected HSBC China PMI, German PMI and the U.S. Markit PMI, say ANZ Bank. The pair is at 0.8538. "Domestic factors will ensure NZD/USD will remain strong on slow global growth," it says. The USD was also weighed after San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President John Williams, in an interview with the Washington Post posted on the newspaper's website Monday, said last week's Fed statement--seen by some as signaling a more hawkish Fed--didn't constitute a policy shift. Looking ahead, markets will now focus on U.S. consumer confidence and the Richmond Fed to provide direction later in the global trading day. ANZ Bank tips a short-term range of 0.8520 to 0.8620 for the NZD/USD. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com @FarroHoward)

15:20 EDT - The Australian Dollar strengthened against the US dollar despite discouraging factory numbers from China, touching $0.9151 at one point, its highest since December 11. As an export-driven economy that relies heavily on China, Australia is affected by a slowdown in demand from its trading partner. Yet, traders say today's weak manufacturing gauge actually fueled expectations that China's policymakers may opt to stimulate the economy sooner. That turned around to boost AUD, lifting it above its 200-day moving average at $0.9139. AUD/USD last up 0.5% at $0.9127. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

13:35 EDT - Economists at the San Francisco Fed find potential losses incurred by the Fed due to rising rates are "very likely to be manageable." The team bases its analysis on the $1.6T of Treasury securities owned by the Fed at the end of 2012, accounting for nearly 60% of the Fed's portfolio then. "The likelihood that the Treasury portfolio's value will fall below its face value and incur a financial loss by the end of 2015 is less than 5%," they say. As for the income the central bank remits to the Treasury, the study finds only a 5% chance the Fed will have no investment income to pass to the agency from 2016-8. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

However, they say, if they're proven correct, they'd still enter fresh long dollar trades should the greenback slip. title: Offshore Russian stocks attract premium in jittery markets
text:
LONDON, March 19 (Reuters) - Offshore Russian stocks are trading at a high premium to onshore stocks, brokers and analysts said on Wednesday, as traders worry about access to domestic Russian markets.

The higher price for offshore stocks - global (GDR) or American (ADR) depositary receipts - compared with the locally listed stocks mirrors the premium investors have been paying for offshore derivative contracts in the rouble currency.

With the possibility of increased sanctions on Russia and weakness in the country's economy due to tensions with the west over Crimea, market participants fear Russia could shut down foreign access to markets and make it harder to remove roubles from the country.

This concern has seen rouble-listed stocks in Moscow trade at a discount of as much as 20 percent to the GDR/ADR market.

"There is a dislocation in the market, it's not normal," said Joseph Dayan, managing director of brokerage BCS Financial Group. "It's to do with the geopolitical issues."

GDRs are denominated in hard currencies such as dollars or euros and usually entitle the holder to several shares in a company. There is a large market for Russian GDR/ADRs listed in London or New York and sold independently of the local shares.

The GDRs have traditionally traded at a premium to onshore stocks, investors say, due to the relative ease of access to offshore markets. But reform of Russia's local markets has seen that premium shrink in recent years.

President Vladimir Putin's assertions of Russia's rights to intervene in Ukraine and make Crimea part of Russia are expected to cause net capital outflows in the first quarter to $50-$70 billion, compared with $63 billion for the whole of 2013.

The central bank will not impose capital controls to defend the rouble, the bank told Reuters this week.

But there is still longer-term uncertainty, investors said.

"People have generally taken that at face value, but the situation is fluid, that stance could change if other factors change," said Collin Crownover, head of currency management at State Street Global Advisers.

Sberbank's stock in Moscow normally trades at the same price as the London-listed GDR and is currently trading at a 3 percent discount. Traders said that discount deepened to as much as 7 percent a week ago, before Crimea voted to join Russia.

Investors have become a little less anxious, however, after reassurances by President Vladimir Putin this week that Russia does not need further division of Ukraine.

The price discrepancies between the two markets could make the local stocks a buy, analysts at Bank of America-Merrill Lynch said in a note:

"Existing and rising spreads between local (stocks) and GDR/ADRs may offer considerable opportunities if there is... stabilisation in the political situation." (Additional reporting by Jason Bush in Moscow and Neal Kimberley in London; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

title: European Morning Briefing: Markets on Pause Before Fed's Verdict
text:
SNAPSHOT:

========

European bourses, bunds and gilts seen mixed; euro, oil lower, spot gold higher

-Japan's Trade Gap Narrows

-Speedy Traders Face U.S. Scrutiny

-BOE's Carney: Welcome Move By China to Widen Yuan Trading Band

-BOE's Carney: U.K. Economy to be Buffeted by Global Forces

-White House Spokesman's Advice: Don't Invest in Russian Stocks

-MPS Foundation Launches Sale of Monte dei Paschi Stake

-Insurer Allianz Pays Compensation to Malaysia Airlines

-Oracle Profit Rises, but Disappoints Wall Street

WATCH FOR: U.K. unemployment data, Bank of England meeting minutes, Chancellor Osborne's budget statement; U.S. oil data, Federal Reserve decisions

EUROPEAN OUTLOOK & U.S./ASIAN SUMMARIES:

========

European stock markets, along with bunds and gilts, may start mixed as attention shifts to the U.S. Federal Reserve's meeting announcements, followed by a press conference by Fed Chairwoman Janet Yellen.

The Fed is expected to announce a further cut of 10 billion dollars per month in its bond-buying program. But despite jitters in stock markets last week and some weather-affected economic data, investors doubt the Fed will shift from that path.

Investors will also continue to keep an eye on Ukraine and on Russia's reactions to sanctions imposed by the U.S. and the EU. Although investors were relieved after President Vladimir Putin addressed the Russian parliament Tuesday and indicated he had no further designs on Ukraine territories, any signs that tensions are escalating will put a damper on risk appetite.

Chinese stocks moved lower, as property developers continued to weigh on the market, while the rest of Asia was softer ahead of the conclusion of Federal Reserve's policy meeting.

Wall Street futures were lower, with Treasurys nudging higher, as the euro and oil trader slightly lower, and spot gold higher.

STOCKS:

======

Investors will see a mixed European opening with the focus on the Federal Reserve after Russian President Vladimir Putin turned down the volume a bit.

Ahead of the opening, IG has called the FTSE down 5 at 6600, the DAX flat at 9242, and the CAC off 8 at 4305.

"Putin's speech didn't indicate he is looking for an escalation of the crisis. All the focus was on Crimea rather than any further areas of Ukraine," said Guillaume Tresca, emerging-market strategist at Crédit Agricole.

With Mr. Putin largely steering clear of inflammatory rhetoric in response to the sanctions, markets are likely to turn their immediate focus to other issues, including the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, Mr. Tresca said.

Even so, investors remain nervous.

"I don't really see this as a de-escalation. The situation is still a very tense one," said François Savary, who helps oversee roughly $10 billion of assets as chief investment officer at Swiss bank Reyl.

Mr. Savary thinks European stocks have the potential to rise further as the economy improves, but avoids buying while the Ukraine situation remains so uncertain. Reyl reduced its exposure to stocks last week, he said.

U.S. stock futures were lower Wednesday after markets rallied for a second straight session Tuesday, bringing the S&P 500 within a fraction of another record.

Traders said concerns over Russia's intervention in Ukraine remain in the background.

Jim Russell, senior equity strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management, which oversees about $115 billion, said he has seem some flows into domestic equity mutual funds. Those flows may not be heavy, but given the light volumes and a lack of selling, it may be having an "outsize impact on the market," Mr. Russell said.

FOREX:

======

The euro was lower in Asia as traders wait to compare the Federal Reserve's stance against that of the European Central Bank.

The resilience of the euro is impressive, noted Brian Martin, senior European strategist at ANZ. The ability to engineer a "permanent" depreciation in the euro is difficult at present, Martin said. "We feel that current statements on the exchange rate are aimed more at trying to slow the euro's rise rather than reverse it," Martin said.

The dollar fell against the yen amid soft sentiment toward the U.S. currency.

"In general, markets are content to wait for the FOMC before making a move," said Brad Bechtel, managing director at Faros Trading.

The Federal Open Market Committee is expected to keep interest rates unchanged and to announce an additional $10 billion monthly reduction to its bond purchases. Investors also expect confirmation that the recent soft patch in the U.S. economy has been a temporary setback caused by extreme winter weather.

"All of that would be positive for the dollar," said Omer Esiner, chief market analyst at Commonwealth Foreign Exchange Inc.

BONDS:

=====

Bunds may start mixed with a lack of focal points in the euro zone, leaving investors to spotlight the Federal Reserve's meeting in the presumed absence of a flare-up in the Ukraine situation.

In the U.K., gilts may also start mixed with unemployment data on tap. The unemployment rate is expected to remain steady at 7.2% while another sharp fall in monthly jobless claims is expected of 25,000, noted Michael Hewson, chief market analyst at CMC Markets UK.

The U.K. will also issue its budget statement. Chancellor George Osborne has said it will keep a strong focus on austerity but will also include measures to support business investment and exports, long-term soft-spots in the economy.

Treasury prices were slightly higher Wednesday, after markets traded slightly higher as investors awaited the Fed's monetary-policy decision.

Prices eased from prior highs after Mr. Putin said Moscow has no intentions to partition Ukraine.

On Wednesday, the Fed will announce its policy decision and Ms. Yellen will hold a news conference.

"The market is put in a range now as they are waiting for the decision Yellen will make at the FOMC," said Millan L. Mulraine, deputy head of U.S. research and strategy at TD Securities. "This is a new Fed with a new slate of players. As an investor, you wouldn't want necessarily to prejudge that until you have more clarity on where Yellen wants to take the Fed."

The Fed's decision could add pressure on short-term yields by pushing the market's expectation for the firs rate increase further out. Therefore, the Treasury yield curve will steepen.

Some investors said there is a possibility that Ms. Yellen takes a more pro-growth approach at the meeting, for example, by reducing the pace of tapering.

"Just looking from the domestic perspective, I wouldn't rule that out," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist at Prudential Fixed Income, referring to the recent softness in economic data.

In Japan Wednesday, government bonds edged higher ahead of the Fed.

ENERGY:

=======

Crude-oil futures drifted lower in Asia after settling higher Tuesday on reports of the Seaway pipeline expanding capacity by May-June. "U.S. inflation figures, which were broadly in line with expectations and positive housing data, helped WTI close the Brent discount to $7/bbl," ANZ said. "Putin's signing of a treaty to annex Crimea also supported oil markets a little. However, the general consensus is that neither Russia nor Europe can afford to cut energy ties," the bank noted. The closely watched survey from the U.S. EIA is due later Wednesday. U.S. oil inventories are projected to have increased by 2.3 million barrels, on average, in the week ended March 14, according to a Wall Street Journal survey. The API said late Tuesday that its own data for last week showed crude stocks rose by 5.9 million barrels.

Nymex crude was down 28 cents at $99.42/bbl, and Brent crude was down 19 cents at $106.60/bbl.

METALS:

======

Gold edged higher in Asia with attention remaining fixed on the outcome of the Fed's meeting. With the geopolitical issue in Ukraine returning to a "high simmer from last Friday's boil" the temperature has lowered enough to take the edge off the fear, Peter Hug, global trading director at Kitco Metals, said in a report. "Metals tend to be an advance trigger trade against upcoming events, but many times after the perception becomes reality, the hedge wanes because the event can be quantified," he said.

Spot gold was at $1,357.90/oz, up $2.40.

Copper looks set to remain rangebound as traders reassess risks in China after news Chinese property developer Zhejiang Xingrun was unable to repay almost $600 million in loans. "The knock-on impact stemming from China, allowing various small privately held companies to default, is hard to gauge, but will likely see a re-appraisal of risk by Chinese investors and banks," Leon Westgate, an analyst with Standard Bank, said in a report.

LME 3-month copper was little changed at $6,483/ton.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Russian stocks track emerging equities higher, rouble back in red
text:
LONDON, March 18 (Reuters) - Russia's rouble fell on Tuesday from the previous session's two-week highs on fears of fresh economic sanctions and a further military standoff, though Moscow equities firmed in line with other emerging markets.

Equities were generally stronger across emerging markets, lifted by big gains in Indian and Korea, while Russian shares extended the 3.6 percent rise posted on Monday after Western sanctions were seen as milder than expected.

But Moscow's defiant move towards formally annexing the Crimea region is keeping alive tensions with the West. President Vladimir Putin is expected to back absorbing the territory into Russia when he addresses parliament later in the day.

HSBC strategist Murat Toprak said investors would scan Putin's speech for clues as to whether military intervention was likely for the rest of Ukraine. The rouble weakened 0.6 percent against the dollar.

"The Crimea election is a done deal, the market wants to know if there is any intention to go beyond Crimea. This is one of the concerns of the market," Toprak said.

Fears the West will respond with fresh, more stringent sanctions are reflected in the offshore rouble forwards, which continue to trade at a rare premium to onshore contracts on fears that future local settlements could prove difficult.

In neighbouring Ukraine, the hryvnia fell more than 4 percent to the dollar. Investors are waiting to see the result of an IMF mission to Kiev which concludes on Friday. Currency flexibility is one of the IMF's demands.

"What happens to hryvnia depends on whether the central bank is intervening and given the level of their FX reserves I'd expect that authorities would not stand in the way of the currency," said RBS analyst Tatiana Orlova.

"On the basis of fundamentals, hryvnia should move to 11 or 12 per dollar."

While broader emerging markets have been boosted by better economic data from many countries, including the so-called Fragile Five, gains were seen capped by Chinese developments.

The yuan traded almost at one-year lows to the dollar after the central bank's weekend move to widen its trading band, indicating it was willing to tolerate more currency volatility. Traders expect more weakness as the economy loses steam.

"The China backdrop is not very supportive - all these uncertainties about potential bankruptcies - this is a market concern, it's not very positive for emerging markets," Toprak said, referring to recent corporate difficulties.

Chinese stocks ended flat but MSCI's emerging markets index rose 0.2 percent, buoyed by gains in Seoul which posted the biggest one-day rise in two weeks and in Mumbai where foreign buyers pushed shares to record highs before elections.

Overseas funds have bought a net $1.6 billion worth of Indian shares in the past 20 sessions, while Goldman Sachs upped its recommendation on Indian shares to overweight.

Turkish equities were a quarter point higher but the lira fell 0.4 percent ahead of a central bank meeting that is expected to leave interest rates unchanged. The bank jacked up all its interest rates by 250-500 basis points at the end of January to protect the lira.

title: EXCLUSIVE- Central bank  says Russia will not impose capital controls
text:
* Central bank says policies provide financial stability

* Finance ministry would oppose capital controls

* Capital fight expected at $50-$70 billion in first quarter

By Oksana Kobzeva and Lidia Kelly

MOSCOW, March 18 (Reuters) - Russia will not impose capital controls, the central bank said on Tuesday, easing concerns that restrictions could be introduced to stem capital flight that has accelerated since the Ukrainian region of Crimea was seized by Russian forces.

President Vladimir Putin's assertions of Russia's rights to intervene in Ukraine and make Crimea part of Russia are expected to cause net capital outflows in the first quarter to $50-$70 billion, compared with $63 billion in the whole of last year.

Limiting money flows, once considered a damaging constraint on open markets, has been more accepted in the aftermath of the 2008-2009 financial crisis as a tool sometimes needed to manage financial stability.

But the Russian central bank said its current monetary policy is strong enough to provide financial stability and the issue of capital controls is not on the table.

"The Bank of Russia is not considering at this time the possibility of introducing measures that would restrict the movement of the capital," the bank told Reuters in an emailed statement.

"Actions taken by the Bank of Russia in the framework of exchange rate policy help contain excessive exchange rate fluctuations, and as such prevent the emergence of risks to financial stability."

The central bank, which has been gradually allowing the rouble to float more freely, had to halt the process earlier this month and start defending the currency, which has lost more than a tenth of its value this year.

Introducing restrictions on money flows would reduce Russians' demand for foreign currency, but it would also raise borrowing costs for the state and corporations alike.

The finance ministry has spent the past few years building up the country's debt by successfully raising billions in foreign borrowing. This year's plans envisage another $7 billion worth of Eurobonds.

"If such an idea (capital controls) were to be discussed, the finance ministry would be against it," Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Moiseev, responsible for financial markets, told Reuters on Tuesday.

POLITICAL DECISION

The Russian rouble has been weakening since the start of the year, along with the Turkish lira and other emerging market currencies. But Russia's declaration in early March of its right to intervene in Ukraine has accelerated the rouble's fall, costing the central bank more than $20 billion in interventions to defend it.

"When any central bank intervenes heavily in the forex market, selling its reserves, one wonders how long it is going to continue its policy. One of the alternatives to not spending reserves is capital controls," said Alexander Morozov, chief Russia economist at HSBC in Moscow.

Russia's gold and foreign currency reserves, the world's fifth-largest, stand at $494 billion, giving the central bank some room to manoeuvre.

But Morozov, who also said there is no need for now for any capital restrictions, reckons there is also a political reason behind the stance of monetary officials.

Russia introduced capital account liberalisation only in 2006, spending years to repair the damage caused by the financial chaos after the fall of the Soviet Union in the 1990s.

"It was done to make the Russian economy open as an OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) economy and it's still one of the more paramount political objectives of the Russian political leadership," Morozov said.

"Any stepping back would be like an admission of failure, so it's a political issue."

MONETARY POLICY

Morozov and other economists in Russia also believe that there is no economic reason to introduce capital controls.

In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, the central bank went through $200 billion of its reserves, but without having to introduce capital controls.

On March 3, after Russia's parliament backed possible military action in Ukraine, the central bank was forced abruptly to raise its key lending rate by 150 basis points to stem capital flight. It also said it would make daily decisions on regulating the rouble's exchange rate, increasing its scope to make forex market interventions.

The central bank believes these moves are sufficient for now.

The policy, based on "an assessment of the current situation on the currency market, allows (the bank) to respond quickly to sudden changes in the situation," the bank said in its statement.

Analysts say that central bank will keep employing more conventional monetary policy for the time being.

"Unless capital outflows stabilise, further rate hikes are possible," said Neil Shearing, chief emerging market economist at Capital Economics in London. (Additional reporting by Darya Korsunskaya; Writing by Lidia Kelly; Editing by Jason Bush and Giles Elgood)

US STOCKS: 

U.S. stocks rallied for a second-straight session Tuesday, bringing the S&P 500 within a fraction of another record high.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 102 points, or 0.6%, to 16349. Microsoft and Pfizer paced gains in 26 of the Dow's 30 components.

The S&P 500 index advanced 13 points, or 0.7%, to 1872 and the Nasdaq Composite Index gained 50 points, or 1.2%, to 4330.

The technology, health care and energy sectors led the advance.

The S&P 500 has gained 1.7% in two sessions, and is just 0.3% away from its March 7 record closing high of 1878.04, which was the sixth record close of the year. Meanwhile, the Dow has gained 283 points, or 1.8%, this week, to trade 1.4% below its Dec. 31 record close 16576.77.

Traders say there was no single piece of news driving the market higher. They say concerns over Russia's intervention in Ukraine remain in the background, but investors believe over the long term, it will end up as a nonevent. If recent upbeat economic data were providing the boost, they would expect a rise in bond yields, but yields are down.

And with volumes light, they aren't seeing a big increase in buying, even by those who may have been selling as the market fell last week.

Jim Russell, senior equity strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management, which oversees about $115 billion, said he has seem some flows into domestic equity mutual funds. Those flows may not be heavy, but given the light volumes and a lack of selling, it may be having an "outsize impact on the market," Mr. Russell said.

On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a treaty formally annexing Ukraine's Crimea region after Crimeans voted overwhelmingly over the weekend to join Russia, as expected. But fears of escalating tensions were soothed after Mr. Putin said that while Crimea must be under Russian sovereignty, "we don't want a partition of Ukraine," and would defend Russia's interests by "diplomatic and legal means."

On the economic front, housing starts for February slipped 0.2% to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 907,000, just above expectations of 905,000. Building permits grew 7.7%, exceeding forecasts of a 1.1% increase. The consumer-price index for February rose 0.1% on the month, and by 0.1% if food and energy are excluded, with both measures matching expectations.

In corporate news, Hertz Global Holdings rose 0.2%, erasing earlier losses, as the company's plan to spin off its equipment-rental business overshadowed fourth-quarter earnings and revenue that missed expectations.

Apple advanced 0.9% after the company updated its low-price iPad offering, adding a handful of new capabilities but keeping the price at $399.

Dow component American Express tacked on 0.4% after saying late Monday it will sell half its corporate-travel business for $900 million to a group of investors including Certares and funds managed by BlackRock and Qatar Holdings. 


 
WORLD FOREX: 

The dollar fell against the ruble after a further advance by Russia into Ukraine seemed unlikely, while the Australian dollar strengthened after its central bank suggested rates would remain steady for some time.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday signed a treaty to annex Ukraine's Crimea region, where voters had chosen to rejoin Russia in a Sunday referendum, but indicated there were no plans for a further push into Ukraine. The West has objected to the annexation and has imposed sanctions on senior officials.

The dollar fell to 36.2344 rubles from 36.2865 rubles late Monday.

The sanctions imposed by the U.S. and European Union, including asset freezes and travel bans on officials from Russia and Ukraine, were "relatively weak," said RBC Capital Markets senior currency strategist Sue Trinh in a note.

Meanwhile, the Australian dollar rose to 91.27 U.S. cents from 90.89 U.S. cents. The Reserve Bank of Australia released minutes of its March meeting, which showed expectations for interest rates to remain steady for a while.

Concerns about the pace of growth in China, which is Australia's largest trading partner, had led to expectations that the RBA could cut rates further, said Chris Tevere, a senior currency strategist at Forex.com. "The most recent employment data out of Australia...coupled with the RBA's minutes have led to the realization that maybe the rate cuts that were priced in should be priced out," he said.

U.S. data released Tuesday showed a dip in housing starts in February, a rise in building permits to the highest rate since October, and a 0.1% increase in consumer prices last month.

The ICE dollar index, a gauge of the currency's strength, rose to 79.38 from 79.363. The WSJ Dollar Index, an alternate measure that pits the dollar against more rivals, edged down to 73.01 from 73.07.

Investors are looking ahead to Wednesday's conclusion of the first Federal Reserve meeting led by Chairwoman Janet Yellen. The central bank's guidance on the future path of interest rates should be in focus, with some expecting a reduced emphasis on the unemployment rate. The Fed is widely expected to continue reducing its monetary stimulus at the meeting and will issue new economic projections.

The euro was at $1.3931 from late Monday's $1.3927. The shared currency earlier Tuesday fell below $1.39 after a survey on German sentiment missed expectations. The ZEW indicator of economic sentiment dropped 9.1 points to 46.6, lower than expectations of a 52 reading.

The greenback fell against the Japanese yen, buying Y101.42 versus Y101.71 late Monday. The British pound was at $1.6591 from $1.6593. 


 
US TREASURYS: 

Treasury prices traded slightly higher on Tuesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's monetary-policy decision.

Prices eased from overnight highs after Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow has no intentions to partition Ukraine.

The benchmark 10-year note added 5/32 in price to yield 2.679%, according to Tradeweb. The 30-year bond was up 2/32 in price to yield 3.625%. Bond prices rise when yields fall.

The Federal Open Market Committee kicked off its two-day meeting Tuesday, the first one under Chairwoman Janet Yellen. On Wednesday, the Fed will announce its policy decision and Ms. Yellen will hold a news conference.

"The market is put in a range now as they are waiting for the decision Yellen will make at the FOMC," said Millan L. Mulraine, deputy head of U.S. research and strategy at TD Securities. "This is a new Fed with a new slate of players. As an investor, you wouldn't want necessarily to prejudge that until you have more clarity on where Yellen wants to take the Fed."

The Fed is expected to announce another $10 billion cut to its bond-buying program and officially step away from the 6.5% jobless threshold for raising the federal funds target rate. The decision could add pressure on short-term yields by pushing the market's expectation for the first rate increase further out. Therefore, the Treasury yield curve will steepen.

Some investors said there is a possibility that Ms. Yellen takes a more pro-growth approach at the meeting, for example, by reducing the pace of tapering.

"Just looking from the domestic perspective, I wouldn't rule that out," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist at Prudential Fixed Income, referring to the recent softness in economic data.

In Russia, Mr. Putin signed a treaty formally annexing the breakaway Ukrainian region of Crimea, but sought to reassure Ukrainians by signaling that Moscow isn't planning to send its troops further into Ukraine. The latest move by Mr. Putin eased some fears and sapped demand for safe-haven Treasurys.

On the economic front, U.S. consumer prices rose 0.1% in February from a month earlier, the Labor Department said Tuesday. But on a year-over-year basis, prices were up 1.1% from a year earlier, the weakest 12-month gain since October and far below the Fed's 2% target for annual inflation.

"We expected subdued data, but this is more subdued than we expected," said Kathy Jones, a fixed-income strategist with Charles Schwab. "It is telling us there is still a long way to reach the 2% target." 


 
EUROPEAN STOCKS: 

European stocks extended their rally into a second day Tuesday, with investors interpreting a speech by Russian President Vladimir Putin as a step back from further confrontation with Ukraine.

Mr. Putin signed a treaty to annex the breakaway Ukrainian region of Crimea, but otherwise sounded a more conciliatory tone than many investors had expected. He said Russia isn't seeking "a partition of Ukraine" and would defend the interests of Russian speakers in the country by "diplomatic and legal means."

European shares, which had fallen as investors awaited the speech, rallied sharply, and were followed higher by U.S. markets. The Stoxx Europe 600 index closed 0.6% higher.

In Russia, the RTS index climbed 4.2%, while the ruble bounced back from steep losses earlier in the day.

"Putin's speech didn't indicate he is looking for an escalation of the crisis. All the focus was on Crimea rather than any further areas of Ukraine," said Guillaume Tresca, emerging-market strategist at Crédit Agricole.

With Mr. Putin largely steering clear of inflammatory rhetoric in response to the sanctions, markets are likely to turn their immediate focus to other issues, including the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, Mr. Tresca said.

Even so, investors remain nervous.

"I don't really see this as a de-escalation. The situation is still a very tense one," said François Savary, who helps oversee roughly $10 billion of assets as chief investment officer at Swiss bank Reyl.

Mr. Savary thinks European stocks have the potential to rise further as the economy improves, but isn't buying while the Ukraine situation remains so uncertain. Reyl reduced its exposure to stocks last week, he said.

All major European indexes picked up from early losses, with Germany's DAX up 0.7% and London's FTSE 100 gaining 0.6%.

Among individual stocks, shares of Intesa Sanpaolo SpA rose 3.2% in Milan, BNP Paribas SA was up 1.8% in Paris and Banco Santander SA added 1.3% in Madrid.

Shares of Metro AG picked up 3.8% after the German retailer said it has pushed back plans for an initial public offering of its Russian Cash & Carry business due to the political uncertainty in Russia and Ukraine. 


 
ASIAN STOCKS: 

Asian stocks rose Tuesday, with Japan supported by a softer yen, while declining Chinese property companies were the focus in Hong Kong and Shanghai.

The region took its lead from the U.S., where stocks finished higher on Monday, after Wall Street shrugged off a referendum in Ukraine's Crimea region showing that the vast majority of voters wanted to secede and join Russia.

"The conflict is far from over. But markets don't regard the situation as critical," said Kengo Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Mizuho Securities.

The improved sentiment was most evident in Japan. Early weakness in the yen had a knock-on effect on Japanese stocks, with the Nikkei up 0.9% at 14411.27--putting the market on a recovery track from its 6.2% slump last week, its worst weekly performance since June last year.

In China, the Shanghai Composite rose less than 0.1% to 2025.20, as declines in developers weighed on the market. Data showed that gains in property prices in 70 Chinese cities continued to moderate in February after slowing in January for the first time in a year. News that a property developer in a small city in eastern China was unable to pay almost $400 million in debt also weighed on the sector.

China Vanke Co. fell 2.1% in Shenzhen, while China Overseas Land & Investment fell 1.3%.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index however gained 0.5% to 21583.50 due to a strong showing by one of its largest constituents. Tencent Holdings jumped 5.2% after the internet giant cashed out of its investment in ChinaVision Media for a total of 1 billion Hong Kong dollars ($129 million).

South Korea's Kospi was up 0.7% at 1940.21, and Singapore's Straits Times Index was up 0.05% at 3093.84. 


 
NEW ZEALAND STOCKS: 

The NZX-50 closed 0.9%, or 47.6 points, higher at 5135.66 as the market benefited from global strength, with risk sentiment improving during the U.S. trading session, Craig Investment Partners broker Belinda Stanley said.

Governments seeking to further narrow their budget deficits should ensure spending cuts don't reduce support for vulnerable groups and further increase poverty and income inequality, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development says.

Iran and six major powers begin on Tuesday a fresh round of high-level nuclear talks, the first since tensions erupted within the six-power group over Ukraine.

The Government said hundreds of National Guard and police were deployed before dawn to take control of the key site of antigovernment protests.

Prosecutors in the terror trial of Osama bin Laden's son-in-law asked a judge to block supporting testimony by alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheik Mohammed.

A 12% drop in the value of Colombia's currency against the dollar in the last year has been a boon to its exports.

Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi insisted Monday that Rome has no intention of asking to breach the fiscal rules set down for the euro area in Maastricht more than 20 years ago.

title: FOREX -Yen nurses losses, euro edges up as Ukraine anxiety ebbs for now
text:
* Yen continues to lose safe-haven glow               

* Focus on Putin speech later in session               

* U.S. CPI, housing-related data awaited               

By Shinichi Saoshiro               

TOKYO, March 18 (Reuters) - The safe-haven yen stayed below a recent peak against the dollar and the euro stood firm on Tuesday as anxiety over the Ukraine crisis ebbed for the time being.               

Economic sanctions imposed by the United States and the European Union against Russia following Crimea's weekend vote to join Moscow were seen as too modest to dramatically escalate near-term tensions over the former Soviet republics - reducing demand for flight-to-safety currencies such as the yen and the Swiss franc.               

The dollar held steady at 101.76 yen, staying above a recent trough near 101.20 yen hit on Friday. The dollar gained some support against the yen after U.S. Treasury yields rose on Monday as safety demand for government debt receded.               

The euro edged up 0.1 percent to $1.3934, within reach of a 2-1/2-year high around $1.3967 hit on Thursday on diminished expectations of easing by the European Central Bank.               

Against the yen, the euro edged up 0.1 percent to about 141.79 yen.               

After Sunday's referendum in Crimea in which an overwhelming majority of voters chose to join Russia, the United States and the European Union on Monday imposed personal sanctions on Russian and Crimean officials involved in the seizure of Crimea from Ukraine.               

"In immediate focus is Russian president Putin's speech later today. If he plays down an immediate annexation of Crimea by Russia, the dollar could gain further ground on unwinding of risk aversion," said Masafumi Yamamoto, chief strategist at Praevidentia Strategy in Tokyo.               

"But an expression of desire for a swift annexation and retaliation against sanctions placed by the European Union and the United States will rekindle economic fears, driving U.S. government bond yields lower and weighing on the dollar," he said.                              

PUTIN SPEECH               

President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday will address a special joint session of Russia's State Duma, or parliament, which could take a decision on annexation of the majority ethnic-Russian region.               

With Crimea seemingly set to split from Ukraine, market players are watching eastern Ukraine and the possibility of Moscow's involvement in the region with a large population of Russian speakers.               

With Russia's armed forces holding war games near the border and Moscow threatening to intervene to halt violence against Russians in Ukraine, some fear Putin will not stop at Crimea and may try to grab more territory in the east and south.               

Market players said any re-emergence of tensions would support the yen and Swiss franc.               

One possible resistance level for the dollar against the yen now lies around 102.30 yen, said Philip Wee, senior currency economist for DBS Bank in Singapore.               

The dollar's 20-day moving average now lies roughly around 102.30 yen, while the 100-day moving average comes in slightly above that level, around 102.38 yen.               

Against the Swiss franc, the dollar traded at 0.8729. The dollar had hit a 2-1/2-year low of 0.8698 against the Swiss franc last week on trading platform EBS, but has since pulled up from that trough as investor risk aversion ebbed.               

The dollar index, a measure of the greenback's value against six major currencies, was at 79.355, clinging above a four-month low of 79.268 hit last week.

title: MORNING BID: EUROPE-A daily note from our Economics/Politics Editor
text:
(A daily view of what's eye-catching in Europe from EMEA Economics & Politics Editor Mike Peacock. The views expressed are his own.)

LONDON, March 14 (Reuters) - U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will meet in London on Friday, a last chance by the look of it to make diplomatic headway before Sunday's Crimean referendum on joining Russia, which the West says is illegal.

Kerry said he would present "a series of options that are appropriate in order to try to respect the people of Ukraine, international law, and the interests of all concerned" and that sanctions would be imposed against Moscow if the referendum went ahead.

A full NATO meeting will take place in Brussels with the Russian and Ukrainian ambassadors invited. There is no sign yet of Vladimir Putin coming to the negotiating table.

Following Washington's lead, the European Union has agreed on a framework for sanctions against Russia, including travel restrictions and asset freezes, which goes further than many expected. The list of targeted individuals is still being worked on but will be ready for the bloc's foreign ministers to look at on Monday.

Germany had been cautious about imposing anything too tough but now agrees actions will be taken next week unless diplomatic progress is made - signalled by a notably uncompromising speech by Angela Merkel on Thursday in which she warned Moscow risked massive political and economic damage.

Moves are also accelerating to shore up the new government in Kiev. An International Monetary Fund team will begin formal negotiations with Ukrainian authorities about an economic reform programme and aim to complete it by March 21.

Interesting that one of the more thoughtful voices in Russia - that of former finance minister Alexei Kudrin - said the country could face economic stagnation and capital outflows of $50 billion a month if tough sanctions are imposed. Kudrin remains an adviser to Putin.

Russian markets took a bath last week as the situation in Crimea escalated but have since steadied. This morning stocks in Russian utilities, steelmakers and banks have fallen sharply with the main share index down 5 percent.

Russia's central bank holds a regular policy meeting having been forced to yank up interest rates by 1-1/2 points last week in order to try and defend the rouble and stave off market chaos. It also blew the thick end of $12 billion of its reserves trying to put a floor under the currency.

The rate hike is intended as a temporary step but with few expecting strong downward pressure on the rouble to abate quickly it is unlikely to be reversed soon.

The central bank's efforts to adhere to a more orthodox inflation-fighting mandate, progress it has made in building a reputation for steady economic management, and plans to allow the rouble to float more freely risk being utterly derailed by Putin's intervention in Ukraine.

Longer-term, the crisis has also focused minds in the EU and spurred efforts to end decades of dependence on Russian gas by developing the bloc's own energy supplies and pushing for greater access to U.S. supplies. That will come up at next week's summit of EU leaders. It's a long-term project but could be a hammer blow to the Russian economy if it succeeds.

Spain's Treasury will publish the contents of a fiscal reform proposal presented to it by a committee of experts on Thursday. The government has already promised income tax cuts for 2015, an election year, though it has also said they will initially be revenue-neutral.

It seems Mariano Rajoy is prepared to take a big electoral gamble - shifting the tax burden from jobs to consumption by lowering the burden on businesses but pushing up consumption taxes such as VAT.

The strategy would probably boost exports further, and help create jobs, but it could also hit domestic demand. Spanish retail sales fell at their fastest rate in four months in December, adding to evidence that a tentative recovery has yet to be supported by depressed consumer demand.

(Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: Russia capital flight $45-50 bln this year, full year may be $130 bln -Goldman
text:
LONDON, March 13 (Reuters) - Capital flight from Russia has risen sharply since the start of this year to $45-$50 billion, Goldman Sachs said on Thursday, predicting full-year outflows could be as much as $130 billion, or double 2013 levels.

Goldman says its calculations show capital outflows have jumped 60 percent from year-ago levels as the economy slows and the threat of Western sanctions bites. It also slashed its forecast for Russian economic growth this year to 1 percent.

Western powers are considering imposing sanctions on Moscow in response to its military intervention in neighbouring Ukraine, especially if the Crimea region votes this weekend in a referendum to secede from Ukraine and join Russia.

"The Achilles heel of the Russian economy remains the flow abroad of Russian capital following any shock. We would also think that any sanctions or even the threat of sanctions will be ultimately targeted at these flows," Goldman analysts Clemens Grafe and Andrew Matheny said in a note.

"Most of these flows, in our view, are driven by Russian capital outflows rather than lower foreign inflows."

Grafe and Matheny calculate that total net private capital outflows amounted to $45-50 billion in the year to date, or more than a 10th of Russia's economic output in the first 2014 quarter. The outflows also represent a big jump over the $28 billion that left the country in the first three months of 2013, they said.

Their models indicate total capital outflows for the year of $130 billion.

If confirmed, the data indicates growing pressure on the Russian economy which is already showing its slowest growth since 2008. Official data shows capital flight was $62.7 billion in 2013, with outflows totalling $420 billion since 2008.

Goldman based its capital flight calculations on estimates of a $25 billion current account surplus in the first three months of the year and around $30 billion in foreign exchange interventions by the central bank.

"If we are right in our estimate of net private capital flows, pressure on the central bank's FX reserves will continue all year," the analysts said.

Goldman also is the latest investment bank to cut economic growth forecasts, predicting the economy will grow 1 percent this year. Citi this week also cut its 2013 growth estimates to 1 percent.

"Recent events including an even sharper than we had forecasted depreciation in the rouble, an even more aggressive reduction in public sector wage growth and, most importantly, a sharp shock to confidence on the back of the heightened political tensions ... require a significant change in our forecasts," Goldman told clients.

They added however that given the fluidity of the Ukraine situation and possible policy responses, the margin of errors in all the forecasts remained large.

title: PREVIEW-Ukraine tensions to keep Russian  central bank  on guard
text:
MOSCOW, March 12 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank will probably keep key policy rates on hold at its regular meeting on Friday, economists say, but any escalation of tensions over Ukraine could prompt a further tightening in monetary policy.

The Russian Central Bank has had to hike interest rates to defend the rouble and stem capital flight since President Vladimir Putin said he had the right to intervene to protect the rights of ethnic Russians in Ukraine.

Russian forces' seizure of Crimea has been bloodless so far, but it has cost Moscow dearly. The central bank has spent at least $13 billion on defending the rouble and Russian equities have tumbled, knocking $60 billion off the MICEX index.

The tightening of the one-week repo rate, by 150 basis points to 7 percent, interrupts the central bank's long-promised shift towards inflation targeting and risks tipping the Russian economy into recession in order to ensure temporary financial market stability.

Sunday's referendum in Crimea, on whether the region should join Russia, carries additional risks of a further rate hike.

But "if the situation remains more or less stable, like now, the central bank is unlikely to change anything (rates)," said Dmitry Polevoy, an economist at ING Bank.

The risk of the West imposing sanctions or of Crimea voting in favour of joining Russia are likely to encourage investors to ditch Russian assets, with economists predicting as much as $100-$150 billion in capital will flee Russia this year.

"For the time being, we think monetary policy will be under manual control, dominated by the need to stabilise the rouble," Jacob Nell and Alina Slyusarchuk, economists at Morgan Stanley, wrote in a note.

"If tensions escalate, and foreign currency demand rises again, more tightening is possible. If tensions ease, we think the central bank will initially hold rates, but increase the rouble's flexibility again."

Just a couple of weeks ago, analysts saw the central bank keeping its monetary policy unchanged until the fourth quarter, worrying about risks to inflation.

VICTIMS OF FINANCIAL MARKET STABILITY

Panic on the market, forcing repeated currency interventions and rate rises, has shunted worries about the stagnating economy to the sidelines.

Although many economists say the central bank had no option but to raise borrowing costs and douse the rouble's volatility, such moves are doomed to backfire.

"Raising (benchmark) rates can translate into increased lending rates, which increases the risks of recession," said Alexander Morozov, chief economist for Russia at HSBC in Moscow.

The central bank's latest forecast from mid-February envisages Russia's gross domestic product (GDP) expanding by 1.5-1.8 percent this year.

"In the first and second quarter we can easily see negative GDP data," said Vladimir Kolychev, an economist at VTB Capital, who reckons the central bank will spend the next three months defending the rouble before tensions ease.

Ivan Tchakarov, an economist at Citi in Moscow, cut his GDP forecast for this year to 1 percent from previous 2.6 percent.

"The central bank was right, in our view, to hike rates ... but this will also come at the cost of stronger headwinds to growth even if the central bank fully unwinds the hike by year-end," he said in a note.

A weaker rouble will push up the prices of imported goods, alarming Putin's inflation-conscious electorate.

"It makes the goal of 5 percent (inflation at the end of the year) difficult to achieve," HSBC's Morozov said.

The central bank says recent moves to defend the rouble have not changed its commitment to shifting its chief monetary tool to inflation targeting and away from controlling the exchange rate by 2015.

But economists are not so sure.

"If Russia annexes Crimea ... then we can forget about inflation targeting," ING's Polevoy said. (Reporting by Oksana Kobzeva and Lidia Kelly; Writing by Lidia Kelly; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)
