title: European Morning Briefing: Markets Seen Lower Ahead of U.S. Jobs Data
text:
SNAPSHOT:

========

European bourses seen lower, bunds and gilts mixed; euro little changed, spot gold lower, oil up

-Crimea Sets Secession Vote as Crisis Escalates

-Ukraine's PM Urges Russia to Start Talks, Reject Crimea's Referendum

-U.S., EU Impose Sanctions against Russia

-BOE Governor to Respond in Parliament to Forex Market Charges -Report

-Schneider Electric Revives Plans to Sell CST Unit -Report

-Total SA Explores Sale of its TotalGaz Subsidiary -Report

-Cerberus, Safeway Reach $9 Billion Deal

-Fed's Dudley Upbeat on Economy

WATCH FOR: Germany industrial output; U.S. trade data, labor data

EUROPEAN OUTLOOK & U.S./ASIAN SUMMARIES:

========

Investors will shift their radar to the U.S. jobs numbers, hoping a strong number can keep the rally in stocks going. Stock markets may start lower and premium government bonds mixed ahead of the data.

Asian markets were mixed on Friday. While the crisis in Ukraine is still to be resolved, investors are focused on economic fundamentals, with confidence boosted by upbeat comments on the eurozone from the European Central Bank (ECB), while Wall Street saw another record close.

President Barack Obama laid down a tough challenge to Moscow's support for a referendum in Ukraine's Crimea on joining Russia. "The proposed referendum on the future of Crimea would violate the Ukrainian constitution and violate international law," Mr. Obama said.

The U.S. Treasury formally warned banks Thursday to watch out for transactions by ousted Ukraine President Viktor Yanukovych and his relatives and associates, citing sanctions by Canadian and European officials.

Wall Street futures and Treasurys were little changed Friday, with the euro barely moved, spot gold higher and oil higher.

STOCKS:

======

As the Ukraine crisis festers in the background, European markets were likely to start slightly lower ahead of the U.S. payrolls.

Ahead of the opening, IG has called the FTSE down 8 at 6780, the DAX off 15 at 9527, and the CAC off 4 at 4413.

Wall Street futures were little changed Friday, after the S&P 500 index closed at a record high after an upbeat reading on weekly jobless claims, while weakness in shares of drug makers helped push the Nasdaq Composite lower.

Market participants appeared to be selling some strong performers ahead of the government's February employment report due Friday, according to Rick Fier, director of equity trading at Conifer Securities.

The S&P 500 has rallied 5.8% over the past month despite a string of lackluster reports on U.S. manufacturing and housing. Each of the past two monthly jobs reports have missed forecasts, and many have pinned the recent poor economic performance on the cold weather.

Friday's payrolls report is eagerly awaited. Economists expect nonfarm payrolls increased by 152,000 in February, versus 113,000 in January. The unemployment rate is expected to tick down one-tenth of one percent to 6.5%. One component, government jobs, will be watched to see if the protracted wave of layoffs of civil servants is letting up. In January, 29,000 government jobs were eliminated.

Joseph Quinlan, chief market strategist for U.S. Trust, said that stocks have been rising in recent weeks because investors anticipate a "strong snapback in growth" after winter ends, particularly from consumers. Stocks are likely to rise should Friday's jobs report come in close to expectations, but investors will likely brush off a disappointing report and attribute any softness to the weather, he said.

FOREX:

======

The euro was little changed in Asia, following its rally to its highest level against the dollar this year, after the European Central Bank decided to leave monetary policy and interest rates unchanged.

"On current information, they seem pretty far away from easing," said Jens Nordvig, head of fixed income research Americas and global head of currency strategy at Nomura Securities.

The yen struggled, particularly against the euro and the dollar, following upbeat jobless claims data in the U.S. and the results of the ECB meeting.

A broad expectation remains that U.S. data should improve as the weather warms and the drag and uncertainty surrounding the "weather effect" on the numbers dissipate, according to Richard Cochinos, head of Americas G-10 FX strategy at Citigroup.

"For now, better U.S. data means higher risk appetite--and potentially underperformance of the dollar (against) the New Zealand dollar and the euro," Mr. Cochinos wrote in a research report. "A broadly stronger dollar would come later in the month when U.S. data accelerates and the strength of U.S. outperformance becomes clear."

BONDS:

=====

Bunds may start mixed as investors focus on U.S. jobs data after the European Central Bank's unexciting stance.

"In the end, the ECB's March policy meeting seems a bit of a damp squib with no move on interest rates or liquidity, and no strong indication that it feels action is necessary as things stand," said Howard Archer, chief U.K. and European economist at IHS Global Insight in emailed comments.

German industrial production is seen rising by 0.7% on the month, according to a Dow Jones poll of analysts.

Treasury bonds were flat Friday after markets dropped Thursday as better-than-expected data on weekly jobless claims buoyed sentiment and weakened demand for government debt. The claims data fueled a whisper figure of up to 185,000 for payrolls Friday.

Treasury bonds took an additional hit as selling of German government bonds, another major safe-haven market, spilled over, traders said. ECB President Mario Draghi suggested the central bank would take its time before adding more stimulus amid signs of improvement in the euro zone's economy.

As for U.S. payrolls Friday, "A number that is higher than expected could do some real damage to the Treasury market," said Alex Manzara, vice president of rate futures at brokerage R.J. O'Brien & Associates in Chicago.

New York Fed President William Dudley said recent economic weakness hasn't changed his upbeat expectations for the economy and isn't enough to alter the central bank's plan to reduce bond purchases.

ENERGY:

=======

Crude-oil futures extended gains in Asia. "Looking ahead, we expect markets to ebb and flow on geopolitical news, but increasingly factor physical indicators," ANZ said. "With northern hemisphere refineries starting to transition to summer fuels in the coming weeks, we expect slightly weaker performance across both benchmarks," the bank said. The U.S. labor market report due later Friday will also provide cues for oil prices. "Payrolls are on tap and markets have been giving every piece of lousy data a free pass to the Bahamas," DBS said.

Nymex crude was up 14 cents at $101.70/bbl, and Brent crude was up 16 cents at $108.26/bbl.

METALS:

======

Gold prices were moving sideways in tight ranges in Asia ahead of U.S. jobs data. A weak figure could suggest that economic recovery remains fragile and underpin gold, which is considered a safe-haven asset. Spot gold prices rose 1.2% overnight after U.S. President Barack Obama said that Crimea's referendum on seceding from Ukraine to join Russia is illegal. He added that the U.S. and EU are united against Russia's intervention in Ukraine.

Spot gold was at $1,349.51, down $1.31.

Base metals could remain rangebound as traders wait for the payrolls. While weak jobs data could weigh on prices, an upbeat figure could improve market sentiment about demand.

LME 3-month copper was $20 higher at $7,050.

0206 GMT [Dow Jones] China shares are higher with petroleum and petrochemical companies leading gains on hopes that Beijing will push forward state-owned enterprise reforms in the sector, say analysts. The Shanghai Composite Index is up 0.8% at 2075.22 and is tipped to face immediate resistance at 2100. "Bleak economic growth outlook and concerns over bond default risks may rein in the upside in the stock market," says Huang Cendong, an analyst with Sinolink. Among actives, Sinopec (600028.SH) jumped 5.2% to CNY5.49 and PetroChina (601857.SH) is 2.7% higher to CNY7.88. Metal firms rise on the back of stronger metal prices in the global market; Inner Mongolia Baotou Steel Rare-Earth (Group) Hi-Tech (600111.SH) gains 2.7% to CNY21.35 and Chalco (601600.SH) climbs 2.1% to CNY3.37. The Shenzhen Composite Index is up 0.5% at 1111.29. (amy.li@dowjones.com)

0206 GMT [Dow Jones] Consumer price inflation in China likely softened in February, economists say. The CPI likely rose just 2.0% on year--down from 2.5% in January, according to the median forecast of 13 economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal. That remains easily within the maximum tolerance of 3.5% announced by Premier Li Keqiang on Wednesday. "A relatively warm winter should have kept food prices and overall CPI growth soft," UBS economist Tao Wang says. Meanwhile, the producer price index, which tracks factory-gate prices, may also have taken a turn south. The PPI likely dropped by 1.8% on year in February compared with 1.6% the month before, according to the same survey. (richard.silk@dowjones.com)

0204 GMT [Dow Jones] BMD crude palm oil is off to a bullish start at MYR2,890-MYR2,900/ton after finding support near the MRY2,800/ton zone Thursday. Support also comes from soyoil, which posted strong gains of nearly 2% overnight, says Malaysia's AmFutures. "(BMD CPO) is backed fundamentally by anticipations of slower productions and diminishing stockpiles amid dry weather in the plantation states," notes another Kuala Lumpur-based brokerage. Benchmark May CPO settled 1.2% higher at MYR2,867/ton Thursday. (huileng.tan@dowjones.com)

0201 GMT [Dow Jones] A lesson many countries learned from the Asian financial crisis is that foreign capital can evaporate overnight. As a result, they have amassed foreign exchange reserves as shock absorbers against sudden capital outflows. But not all are so well-prepared for another crisis. Goldman Sachs says that within emerging markets, Turkey, South Africa and Indonesia are most vulnerable to a foreign-exchange crisis. By comparing a country's reserves against its projected external financing needs, the U.S. bank finds that many Asian countries like China, Thailand and South Korea are relatively safe. SNAPSHOT

Better-than-expected jobless-claims data helped U.S. stocks finish mostly higher, while pushing Treasurys lower. The euro gained against the dollar and the yen after the European Central Bank stood pat on policy and rates. Gold and oil ended up on escalating tensions between Russia and the West.

OPENING CALL

Friday is deadline day for Chinese solar-equipment maker Chaori Solar to pay interest on its debt. Market watchers will be paying close attention to whether the government steps in with funds or lets the firm become the first default in China's fast-growing corporate-bond market. Also in focus is February trade data from Taiwan for signs of whether the recovery in the U.S. and Europe starts to show up in the form of better exports from the island, which is a major cog in the electronics production chain.

EQUITIES

The S&P 500 index closed at a record high after an upbeat reading on weekly jobless claims, while weakness in shares of drug makers helped push the Nasdaq Composite lower.

Market participants appeared to be selling some strong performers ahead of the government's February employment report due Friday, according to Rick Fier, director of equity trading at Conifer Securities.

The S&P 500 has rallied 5.8% over the past month despite a string of lackluster reports on U.S. manufacturing and housing. Each of the past two monthly jobs reports have missed forecasts, and many have pinned the recent poor economic performance on the cold weather.

Friday's payrolls report is eagerly awaited. Economists expect nonfarm payrolls increased by 152,000 in February, versus 113,000 in January. The unemployment rate is expected to tick down one-tenth of one percent to 6.5%.

Joseph Quinlan, chief market strategist for U.S. Trust, said that stocks have been rising in recent weeks because investors anticipate a "strong snapback in growth" after winter ends, particularly from consumers. Stocks are likely to rise should Friday's jobs report come in close to expectations, but investors will likely brush off a disappointing report and attribute any softness to the weather, he said.

In corporate news, office-supplies retailer Staples slumped 15% after missing fiscal fourth-quarter earnings and revenue estimates. The company said it plans to close 225 stores by the end of 2015 as part of a plan to cut costs by $500 million. Declines also weighed on Office Depot, which slid 5.7%.

Costco Wholesale shed 2.8% after reporting fiscal second-quarter earnings and sales that fell short of forecasts. Lower overseas profits and weak results from nonfood merchandise categories weighed on the results.

Pandora Media declined 5.6% even after reporting an increase last month in listener hours and a boost to its market share.

In Asian trading Thursday, Japan led most stock markets higher, with the Nikkei surging to a five-week high after the government revealed a plan to diversify the portfolio of its giant pension fund.

FOREX

The euro strengthened against major currencies, rallying to its highest level against the dollar this year, after the European Central Bank decided to leave monetary policy and interest rates unchanged.

The yen struggled, particularly against the euro and the dollar, following upbeat jobless claims data in the U.S. and the results of the ECB meeting. Both drove the value of the Japanese currency lower.

The dollar advanced against the yen as the U.S. labor market showed progress. The Labor Department reported that initial claims for jobless benefits fell 26,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000 during the week ended March 1, the lowest level since November.

The number came in below forecasts of 335,000 and showed a job market improving despite persistent severe weather. The number arrived before Friday's jobs number, which the Federal Reserve watches closely to determine to what degree the economy is recovering.

The Fed has linked its bond-buying program to the health of the U.S. economy. As it has shown signs of improvement, the central bank decided to make measured cuts to its bond purchases. The Fed's program has weighed on the dollar, so the cuts in bond purchases have given the greenback a boost.

There is a broad expectation that U.S. data should improve as the weather warms and the drag and uncertainty surrounding the "weather effect" on the numbers dissipate, according to Richard Cochinos, head of Americas G-10 FX strategy at Citigroup.

"For now, better U.S. data means higher risk appetite--and potentially underperformance of the dollar [against] the New Zealand dollar and the euro," Mr. Cochinos wrote in a research report. "A broadly stronger dollar would come later in the month when U.S. data accelerates and the strength of U.S. outperformance becomes clear."

BONDS

Treasury bonds dropped after better-than-expected data on weekly jobless claims buoyed sentiment and weakened demand for haven government debt.

Treasury bonds took an additional hit as selling of German government bonds, another major safe-haven market, spilled over, traders said.

The selling was driven by comments from European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, who suggested the central bank would take its time before adding more stimulus amid signs of improvement in the euro zone's economy. Mr. Draghi disappointed some investors who expected him to signal further easing measures as soon as April.

The Labor Department reported that the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell last week by a bigger-than-forecast 26,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000 in the week ended March 1, the lowest level since November.

The data come ahead of Friday's nonfarm-payrolls report. Economists expect the economy to have added 152,000 jobs last month, more than the 113,000 added in January. The unemployment rate is seen falling to 6.5% from 6.6% a month ago. The monthly nonfarm-payrolls release is one of the main reports influencing the Federal Reserve's interest-rate policy outlook.

"A number that is higher than expected could do some real damage to the Treasury market," said Alex Manzara, vice president of rate futures at brokerage R.J. O'Brien & Associates in Chicago.

COMMODITIES

Gold prices rose while palladium set a fresh 11-month high after tensions between Russia and the West escalated.

Gold prices have been steadily climbing in recent weeks, as a series of geopolitical flare-ups stoked investor demand for wealth-preserving assets. Some traders view gold as a haven because it is a widely accepted reserve asset without links to a particular government or country.

U.S. President Barrack Obama said that Crimea's referendum on seceding from Ukraine to join Russia is illegal and added that the U.S. and European Union are united against Russia's "intervention" in Ukraine.

Russian troops entered Ukraine's Crimea region late last week, escalating the conflict between the former Soviet state and the West.

"Gold's catching a bid any time there's instability," said Adam Klopfenstein, a senior market strategist with Archer Financial Services Inc. "People are going to want to gravitate toward safe-havens like gold anytime questions about the Ukrainian situation re-emerge," he said.

Palladium futures rocketed to their highest level since April 1 after the U.S. paved the way for sanctions against Russia.

Crude-oil futures rose for the first time in three days as concerns over the political situation in Crimea were rekindled.

title: WRAPUP 1-EU weighs Russia sanctions as Ukraine diplomacy falters
text:
* Divided EU to warn, not sanction Russia at summit

* Moscow says OSCE, NATO efforts not helpful

* Kerry, Lavrov to meet again in Rome

* U.N. envoy surrounded, forced to leave Crimea

* Rouble weakens despite central bank intervention

By Luke Baker and Elizabeth Piper

BRUSSELS/MOSCOW, March 6 (Reuters) - European Union leaders were set to warn but not sanction Russia on Thursday over its military intervention in Ukraine after Moscow rebuffed Western diplomatic efforts to persuade it to pull forces in Crimea back to their bases.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov refused to meet his new Ukrainian counterpart or to launch a "contact group" to seek a solution to the crisis at talks in Paris on Wednesday despite intensive cajoling by U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry. The two men will meet again in Rome on Thursday.

Tension remained high in Ukraine's southern Crimea region, where a senior United Nations envoy was surrounded by a pro-Russian crowd, threatened and forced to get back on his plane and leave the country.

An emergency EU summit in Brussels is unlikely to adopt more than symbolic measures against Russia, Europe's biggest gas supplier, because neither industrial powerhouse Germany or financial centre Britain are keen to start down that road.

The United States has said it is ready to impose sanctions such as visa bans, asset freezes on individual Russian officials and restrictions on business ties within days rather than weeks.

Russia's rouble currency weakened further on Thursday despite central bank intervention due to what analysts at VTB Capital called a political risk premium.

The European Commission announced an aid package of up to 11 billion euros for Ukraine in the next couple of years provided it reaches an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, entailing painful reforms like ending gas subsidies.

Diplomats said that at most, the 28-nation EU would condemn Russia's so far bloodless seizure of Ukraine's Black Sea province and suspend talks with Moscow on visa liberalisation and economic cooperation, while threatening further measures.

But they will hold back from further reaching steps both in hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to ease tensions in Ukraine and out of fear of a tit-for-tat trade war with Russia, a major economic partner of Europe.

France has a deal to sell warships to Russia that it is so far not prepared to cancel, London's banks have profited from facilitating Russian investment, and German companies have $22 billion invested in Russia.

The crisis began in November when Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich, under strong Russian pressure, turned his back on a far reaching trade deal with the EU and accepted a $15 billion bailout from Moscow. That prompted three months of street protests leading to the overthrow of Yanukovich on Feb. 22.

ILLEGITIMATE

Moscow denounced the events as an illegitimate coup and refused to recognise the new Ukrainian authorities.

But Russia kept the door ajar for more diplomacy on its own terms, announcing on Thursday a meeting of former Soviet states in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), including Ukraine, for April 4 and saying it would be preceded by contacts between Russian and Ukrainian diplomats.

Lavrov said attempts by Western countries to take action over the Ukraine crisis via democracy watchdog OSCE and the NATO military alliance were not helping cooperation and dialogue.

"I want to very briefly say that we had a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry on the situation in Ukraine in relation to the actions that our partners are trying to take via the OSCE, the NATO-Russia council and other international organisations - action that does not help create an atmosphere for dialogue and constructive cooperation," he said in a statement issued by the ministry on Thursday.

In a day of high-stakes diplomacy in Paris, he refused to talk to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Deshchitsya, whose new government is not recognised by Moscow.

As he left the French Foreign Ministry, Lavrov was asked if he had met his Ukrainian counterpart. "Who is that?" the Russian minister asked.

He stuck to President Vladimir Putin's line - ridiculed by the West - that Moscow does not command the troops without national insignia which have taken control of Crimea, besieging Ukrainian forces, and hence cannot order them back to bases.

But Western diplomats said there was still hope that once Lavrov had reported back to Putin, Russia will accept the idea of a "contact group" involving both Moscow and Kiev as well as the United States and European powers to seek a solution.

The European Union formally announced it had frozen the assets of ousted Ukrainian president Yanukovich and 17 other officials, including former prime minister Mykola Azarov, suspected of human rights violations and misuse of state funds.

"RUSSIA! RUSSIA!"

U.N. special envoy Robert Serry had to abandon a mission to Crimea after being stopped by armed men and besieged inside a cafe by a hostile crowd shouting "Russia! Russia!" The Dutch diplomat flew to Istanbul after the incident.

In eastern Ukraine, a pro-Russian crowd in Donetsk, Yanukovich's home town, recaptured the regional administration building they had occupied before being ejected by police. But police loyal to the new authorities in Kiev raised the Ukrainian flag over the building again on Thursday.

Putin has said Russia reserves the right to intervene militarily in other areas of Ukraine if Russian interests or the lives of Russians are in danger.

Dropping diplomatic niceties on Wednesday, the U.S. State Department published a "fact sheet" entitled "President Putin's Fiction: 10 False Claims about Ukraine."

"As Russia spins a false narrative to justify its illegal actions in Ukraine, the world has not seen such startling Russian fiction since Dostoyevsky wrote, 'The formula "two plus two equals five" is not without its attractions,'" the State Department said in the document. (Writing by Paul Taylor; editing by Anna Willard)

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Assets firmer but some lose ground after Crimea vote
text:
(Adds afternoon retreat, fresh Hungarian bond sale figure)
    * Hungary sells more bonds than planned, yields fall
    * Tension over Ukraine, Romanian domestic politics eased
    * Crimean vote trims CEE asset gains, hits shares
    * Serbian central bank keeps rates on hold

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, March 6 (Reuters) - Central European markets
mostly firmed up on Thursday as diplomatic efforts to cool the
crisis in Ukraine supported riskier assets, and Hungary sold
more bonds than planned at an auction. 
    Most regional currencies and stocks continued to recover
from jitters caused by the situation in neighbouring Ukraine,
the second hit to the region this year from developments in
other emerging economies.
    "Near-term price action remains largely a function of the
uncertain geopolitical outlook," Raiffeisen said in a note,
adding that sentiment was also improved by Wednesday's data
confirming an economic pick-up in Hungary and Romania.
    European Union leaders were set to warn but not sanction
Russia on Thursday over its intervention in Ukraine, after
Moscow rebuffed a diplomatic push for it to pull its forces in
Crimea back to their bases. 
    With fear of a war to the east receding, Hungary's bond
auctions attracted healthy demand. It sold 85.4 billion forints
worth of three-, five- and 10-year bonds - 50 percent more than
planned.
    Hungary's three-year bond yields were down 6 basis points
from Wednesday at 4.7 percent. The bonds were sold at 4.66
percent at the auctions, their lowest level since January.
Long-term bonds gave up their gains, however.
    Traders said investors were scrambling to cover short
positions built in recent weeks, betting for yield rises.
    "Demand was particularly high for short-end bonds," one
Budapest-based trader said. "Some people may buy based on
increasingly dovish central bank comments, like in Poland, and
the European Central bank may also loosen conditions somehow."
    Polish bonds firmed slightly. They surged on Wednesday after
the central bank cut inflation forecasts and said it would keep
rates flat at least until the fourth quarter of this year.
 
    The zloty and the forint dipped against
the euro after Crimea's parliament voted to join Russia. But by
late trade they had gained 0.3 percent, helped by the euro's
 surge as the European Central Bank signalled no need for
new economic stimulus.
    The region's equities fell after the Crimean news, however.
Shares in OTP Bank and drug maker Richter -
Hungarian firms that have business in Russia and Ukraine - fell
2 and 2.4 percent, respectively, dragging Budapest's main index
 almost 1 percent lower. The main indices in other
regional capitals rose 0.4-0.7 percent.    

    ROMANIAN POLITICS HELP NOW
    Romanian assets got local backing from easing domestic
political tensions on Wednesday.
    President Traian Basescu ratified a review of a 4 billion 
euro aid deal with the IMF, ending a weeks-long standoff, and
endorsed a newly formed coalition government just days after he
threatened to block its creation. 
    The leu was flat, but Romania's five-year bond
yield dropped to 4.9 percent from 4.97 percent in the previous
session, and 5.05 percent three days ago.
    The government sold 700 million lei worth of Treasury bonds
due in June 2017, as planned. Last month Romania
failed to sell debt at three tenders as the political standoff
and escalating violence in Ukraine weighed on assets.
    Serbia's central bank kept its benchmark rate on
hold at 9.5 percent for a third month running on Thursday, as
expected, amid uncertainty over a mid-March election, pressure
on the dinar and a pick-up in inflation.
    The dinar firmed up a shade. The bank has been
buying the dinar in the market for weeks to protect it from
contagion from abroad and pre-election uncertainty over fiscal
policies.

title: CORRECTED-Rouble weakens as Ukraine concerns weigh
text:
(Corrects figures in paragraph 4 on scale of Tuesday's intervention, changes headline and lead)

MOSCOW, March 6 (Reuters) - The rouble opened down against the dollar on Thursday as concerns about the Ukraine crisis continued to weigh.

Moscow stock indexes saw fragile gains, tracking a reprieve in Asian markets after diplomatic efforts seemed to slightly moderate the crisis over Russia's military intervention in Ukraine.

At 0635 GMT, the rouble was down 0.3 percent against the dollar at 36.15 and down 0.2 percent versus the broadly weaker euro at 49.63, indicating that investors nonetheless remained worried about the possibility of Russia launching an overt invasion of Ukraine.

Data showed on Thursday that the central bank spent just over $300 million of its gold and foreign exchange reserves on Tuesday, despite the rouble's firming that day, after spending $11.3 billion on Monday to keep the currency from falling too fast.

The central bank releases its intervention data with a two-day delay.

Analysts at VTB Capital reckon that the rouble is about 8.0-8.5 percent behind the emerging markets average index so far this year, and that Ukraine's political crisis has accounted for 2.0-3.0 percentage points of that.

"Now that is fading away, but we are not quite sure that the premium for political risks will disappear completely in the near term," the analysts wrote in a morning note.

title: UPDATE 1-Poland says to leave rates flat until end of third quarter
text:
* Central bank extends rates guidance by three months

* Move was partly to reassure markets rattled by Ukraine

* Governor says don't assume rates will rise in Q4

* Says Ukraine crisis showed benefits of euro membership   (Adds quotes, market reaction)

By Karolina Slowikowska and Christian Lowe

March 5 (Reuters) - Poland said on Wednesday it would keep interest rates flat at least until the fourth quarter of this year, three months longer than its previous guidance, and said the need to reassure markets rattled by the Ukraine crisis influenced its decision.

Central bank governor Marek Belka said that fresh projections showed the recovery in Poland, eastern Europe's biggest economy, was robust and that inflation was low, so there was no pressure to change rates from their 2.50 percent level.

But he said Russia's intervention in Ukraine's Crimea Peninsula -- which unleashed a wave of market jitters around eastern Europe, including in Poland -- had persuaded the bank's rate-setters to act sooner than it might otherwise have done to extend the forward guidance on rates.

That decision surprised the market, and yields on Polish 10-year bonds fell by 17 basis points to their lowest point in three months. The zloty was unchanged.

"The situation in Ukraine sped up our decision to show that we do not see risks for the Polish economy, at least in the sphere of monetary policy," Belka told a news conference.

"We wanted to express our confidence in the fundamentals of the Polish economy, and thus in the stability of the zloty."

The bank earlier had left rates unchanged, as expected, and released new projections for inflation and gross domestic product (GDP) growth. It had said this month's projections would be decisive in determining its stance on rates.

The new forecasts put GDP growth for this year at between 2.9 and 4.2 percent, up from the previous projection of between 2.0-3.9 percent. Inflation was projected to be in the 0.8-1.4 percent range this year, lower than previously forecast.

RATE HIKES NOT A DONE DEAL

Many in the market anticipate that the next rate move once the forward guidance expires will be an increase, to ensure the improving economy does not overheat. Analysts polled by Reuters expected the hikes would come in the fourth quarter

But Belka cautioned against assuming that was a done deal, saying rates could stay flat for longer.

"One should not expect that as soon as the third quarter ends, the (rate-setting) Council will take up its pick axes and spades and get down to work," he said.

Belka said he did not expect any major lasting impact on the Polish economy from the events in Ukraine. Both Ukraine and Russia are major trading partners for Poland, leaving Warsaw vulnerable if sanctions are imposed.

Belka said Ukraine and its repercussions could in theory knock a fraction of one percent off GDP growth, but the economy was sufficiently robust that the effects would not be more pronounced.

If exports to Russia and Ukraine drop, causing a surplus of goods in the domestic market, that could have the effect of slowing inflation.

In another echo from the crisis in Ukraine, Poland's neighbour to the east, Belka said events there had made him more positive on the benefits of Poland joining the euro single currency.

Belka, who has previously said he backs Polish accession but at a cautious pace, said political instability underlined the value of being in a big economic bloc.   (Additional reporting by Marcin Goettig, Marcin Goclowski and Michal Janusz)

title: UPDATE 1-Russian stocks fall back as Ukraine weighs, rouble buoyed by cbank comments
text:
* Russian stocks dip as Ukraine talks continue

* Ukraine crisis expected to weigh on stocks in March

* Central bank says rouble undervalued, cites strong trade data

By Jason Bush and Zlata Garasyuta

MOSCOW, March 5 (Reuters) - Russian shares retreated on Wednesday, halting the previous day's rebound, as diplomatic efforts to ease the crisis in Ukraine showed little sign of providing a breakthrough.

The rouble nevertheless strengthened after the central bank said it regarded the currency as undervalued.

Shares fell 2 percent early in the day, recovered in the afternoon but slipped back slightly in late trade.

At 1445 GMT the rouble-denominated MICEX index was down 0.4 percent at 1,351 points and the dollar-denominated RTS was 0.2 percent lower at 1,182 points.

After plummeting by 10-12 percent on Monday on nervousness after Russia's intervention in the Crimea region of Ukraine, the stock indexes had rebounded by 5-6 percent on Tuesday.

Probusinessbank trader Evgeny Volkov, however, described the rebound as "purely technical".

"Unfortunately the market will probably try to return to the levels reached on Monday. The rhetoric of the U.S. remains hostile and foreign capital is leaving," he said.

Investors are reducing their exposure to Russia due to uncertainty about how the situation in Ukraine will play out. The United States has warned it could impose sanctions on Russia, which could hit Russia's already slowing economy.

Diplomatic efforts to end the armed stand-off in Crimea continued on Wednesday, with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov due to meet his U.S. counterpart John Kerry in Paris.

A spokesman for German Chancellor Angela Merkel said that Germany continued to view the situation in Ukraine as "alarming" and "unacceptable".

"Players in the Russian market will most probably adopt a waiting position, but the dead-end situation around Ukraine will limit purchases," said Sergei Suvarov, head analyst at Russian Standard. "The market is very speculative and the ball is in the court of hedge funds."

Although concerns about Ukraine weighed on the market, it was supported by positive developments in other global markets, with Wall Street hitting new record highs on Tuesday.

"But let's look the truth in the face: our market won't be a good object for investments this month," Andrei Vernikov, analyst at Zerich Capital, said in a note.

He said the Russian market "will not soar" at least until March 30, when pro-Russian authorities in the Ukrainian region of Crimea have announced that they intend to hold a referendum on the region's status.

However, the rouble, which plunged to a record low against the dollar on Monday, forcing heavy intervention by the central bank to prop it up, strengthened for a second day on Wednesday and was boosted by bullish comments from central bank governor Elvira Nabiullina.

Nabiullina said she saw no fundamental reasons for the weakening of the rouble, saying the central bank considered it to be undervalued given Russia's rising current account and trade surpluses in the first two months of this year.

She also reiterated the bank's 5 percent inflation forecast by year-end, and its commitment to shift to an inflation- targeting policy regime, planned from next year.

At 1445 GMT the rouble was up 0.1 percent at 36.02 against the dollar, and was 0.2 percent stronger versus the euro at 49.45.

It was also up 0.2 percent against the dollar-euro basket , at 42.06.

"In the last three months the rouble in relation to the dollar has definitely lost practically all connection with fundamental factors," commented Investcafe analyst Timur Nigmatullin in a note.

The rouble has shed 9 percent against the dollar this year.

The central bank said on Wednesday it had spent the equivalent of $11.4 billion in foreign currency reserves on Monday to support the rouble, stemming a sell-off caused by the escalation of the Ukraine crisis.

"It is too early to talk about a stabilisation of the situation, as the tone of statements from American and European officials isn't weakening," ING economist Dmitry Polevoy said.

"In these conditions the rouble could easily move (down) further, especially in advance of the referendum date in Crimea and in the absence of obvious ways out of the crisis."

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Polish bonds surge,  central bank  plays down Ukraine impact
text:
* Polish 10-year yield at 4-month low after cbank cuts CPI
forecast
    * Forint firms as data shows pick-up in Hungary growth
    * Leu surges as Romanian president ends IMF deal stand-off
    * Richter shares fall, reminder of risks over Ukraine

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, March 5 (Reuters) - Polish government bonds surged
on Wednesday after the country's central bank cut its inflation
forecast and said the zloty could weather any turbulence caused
by the crisis in Ukraine.
    Other Central European assets firmed for a second straight
day, helped by data confirming economic growth in the region as
local factors overshadowed events in neighbouring Ukraine for
the first time in over two weeks.
    Poland's 10-year bond yield, which moves
inversely to prices, fell 17 basis points to 4.18 percent, its
lowest level in four months. The zloty was flat.
    The Polish central bank kept rates on hold as expected and
extended its guidance for keeping its key interest rate at a
record low 2.5 percent at least until September, instead of
June.
    The bank cut inflation forecasts for this year and its
governor Marek Belka said the zloty could resist
contagion effects from neighbouring Ukraine where the crisis
would have a marginal impact on Poland's economic growth.
    "The inflation projection is very positive, there's no
pressure whatsoever, reaching the inflation target is only
planned in 2016. This shows that there's a good period for bonds
ahead of us," said Pekao SA analyst Arkadiusz Urbanski.
    Elsewhere, the leu surged half a percent versus
the euro after Romania's president signed the review of an IMF
aid agreement seen as key to Romania's economic credibility.
 
    The Hungarian forint firmed 0.3 percent.
    Hungarian bonds extended Tuesday's gains posted after
Russian President Vladimir Putin said he saw no need for now to
use military force in Ukraine after Russia intervened in the
Crimea region.
    Analysts said spillover effects from Ukraine and other
volatile emerging markets remained a risk. A Reuters poll,
however, forecast that the region's economic recovery could help
the forint and the zloty firm 3.5 percent against the euro in
the next 12 months. 
    Shares of Hungarian drug maker Gedeon Richter,
which has significant sales in both Ukraine and Russia, plunged
6 percent in a reminder of contagion risks from the crisis.
    Richter's Chief Executive Erik Bogsch warned that the firm
expected its first-quarter operating profit margin to plumb
record lows due to the fall in the value of the Russian rouble,
as Russia is the company's biggest market.      
    
    MORE SWINGS POSSIBLE
    Further market jitters are still possible as contagion risks
from other emerging economies linger, some traders warned.
    "Most market players look more optimistic than me at the
moment," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said.
    "I will be right in the end, but that is thin comfort if
before that I have to close my positions," he said.
    Hungarian assets have been particularly vulnerable despite
the country's big trade surplus. It is the most indebted state
in the region and some investors also fret that it may have cut
interest rates too low given the contagion risks.
    Investors have been withdrawing capital from emerging
economies for months as a cutback in U.S. monetary stimulus has
triggered risk aversion.
    Hungary's central bank has cut its base rate to 2.7 percent
from a peak of 7 percent in 2012. Its last cut in February
defied wobbles in emerging markets, and even though the bank
indicated caution, it did not rule out further monetary easing.
    The forint hit a two-year low against the euro last month.
On Monday, the bank's deputy governor Adam Balog called the
forint's recent moves a "smaller turbulence", caused by global
factors rather than the rate cuts. 
    "The market understands, feels and has priced in that the
current forint levels are fine to the central bank, and that
they will not try to calm down markets, only if the forint falls
beyond 320," one Budapest-based currency dealer said.
    "I can easily imagine now that they will continue to cut
rates," the dealer said.

title: Should Investors Start Loving Russia? -- Money Talks
text:
The ruble and Russian equities had taken a considerable beating well before Ukraine's political crisis erupted. But the selling gathered pace when the shooting in Kiev started. And then, when it seemed that Russia was invading Crimea, Ukraine's militarily sensitive and ethnically Russia southern province, the markets plunged. Russia's RTS dollar-denominated equity index nosedived 12% in a day.

Just under three years ago, the index was trading at a little more than 2100. By the time it bottomed on Monday, the RTS was only just over 1100--around a 48% tumble. Of course, emerging market equities have generally taken a beating lately. Indeed, Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed equity market weakness on the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to trim its bond-buying program. Even so, Russia has seriously underperformed other markets. The MSCI emerging markets index is down 9.7% over the past year. The MSCI Russia index is down 23.9% during the same period.

The ruble has routinely hit new lows. In the spring of 2011, a dollar was worth 28 rubles. By the start of this year it was 33. At one point on Monday, it was nearly 37.

For a time, Russia's monetary authorities treated the ruble with benign neglect. Its depreciation was seen as broadly helpful in making the country more competitive at a time when economic growth had started to flag. But the recent declines had become so precipitous that on Monday, the Russian central bank raised its key interest rate by 1.5 percentage points to 7% in order to defend the currency.

The negative stories are still there. Ukraine's internal politics haven't been resolved and Russia's involvement complicates things. Civil war is still a possibility. Russian military intervention in Ukraine's ethnic-Russian regions could trigger sanctions from the West. That's not to mention Russia's own long-term problems of a sclerotic economy, corruption, lack of corporate transparency and increasingly autocratic politics.

But in the near term, adventurous investors might well find attractive propositions.

"At these prices, you don't have to take a very optimistic view of Russia's future to see some potential bargains," according to Stephanie Flanders, J.P. Morgan Asset Management's chief European market strategist.

Oil prices have rallied sharply since the start of the year. Given that Russia is a major producer, higher prices should boost government finances and shore up the country's current account surplus. This also makes the ruble less of a losing proposition. With lower currency risk, Russia's interest rate spread becomes attractive again, which should draw in capital.

Meanwhile, valuation multiples look attractive--with equities trading at 3.9 times earnings and 0.6 times book value, they've only been cheaper at the worst points of the 2008 financial crisis, according to Morgan Stanley.

Some of that bargain hunting seemed to kick in on Tuesday, with both Russia's currency and equities bouncing sharply. By early afternoon, the RTS index was up more than 6% on the day.

This is an opinion column by Alen Mattich, who has been a columnist for Dow Jones for more than a decade. Write to him at alen.mattich@dowjones.com or on Twitter @AlenMattich

title: Russian Markets Shudder Under Threat Of Sanctions
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 3/4/14) 
   By Greg White, Laurence Norman and Andrey Ostroukh 

MOSCOW -- A Russian weakness was exposed in its confrontation with the West over Ukraine, as its currency hit a record low and its stock market plunged in the face of U.S. and European warnings of sanctions.

President Barack Obama said the U.S. is looking at economic and diplomatic measures to isolate Moscow, which he said is "on the wrong side of history" as well as international law with its occupation of the Crimea region of Ukraine. Further military moves into the country, he warned, "will be a costly proposition for Russia."

The Kremlin has dismissed any sanctions as inappropriate and showed no sign of backing down under the pressure, which so far has been primarily in the form of tough talk.

European foreign ministers backed off any immediate action on sanctions Monday, despite what some called the gravest threat to European stability since the end of the Cold War.

The U.S. State Department said that punitive measures are likely if Moscow does not temper its military intervention in Ukraine, but wouldn't give details. Spokeswoman Jennifer Psaki indicated they would go beyond things like visa freezes to measures with economic bite.

The developments highlighted the West's limited options for deterring a Russia determined to reassert its influence in a neighbor with which it shares centuries of common history and culture as well as myriad economic ties.

Russian troops occupying the Crimean peninsula in southern Ukraine tightened their control, raising pressure on the few Ukrainian military units based there, but stopping short of violence. The Kremlin drew up plans for urgent financial aid to its new clients in the predominantly Russia-speaking region, and even ordered preparations for building a massive bridge to link it directly to Russia.

Ukraine's prime minister admitted that his government has little near-term hope of regaining control of the region.

President Vladimir Putin on Monday visited massive military maneuvers under way outside St. Petersburg, arriving in a helicopter to view tanks and paratroopers in live-fire exercises.

The Russian central bank sharply raised interest rates Monday to help stem the ruble's slide, which could push Russia's already sputtering economy into recession if the hike lasts for long.

But the impact would be eased thanks to high oil prices -- they rose Monday on the turmoil -- which would mean the Kremlin's coffers would likely remain flush with rubles needed to shore up public support. Russia is one of the world's biggest energy exporters.

European Central Bank President Mario Draghi said the direct impact of the Ukraine crisis on the continent's economy would be relatively limited. Still, he added, "the geopolitical dimensions" of the crisis could have effects that "go beyond the actual links."

Some tremors were already being felt: U.S. wheat futures surged 4.6% as traders fretted that the escalating crisis will slow grain exports from Ukraine, a major producer.

Rising tensions are clouding sales forecasts and investment plans for global corporate giants such as Renault SA and PepsiCo Inc. that are exposed to Russia's market.

Shares in European banks with operations in Russia or Ukraine, including Italy's UniCredit SpA and France's Societe Generale SA, got clobbered as markets across Europe were rattled. The Stoxx Europe 600 index fell 2.3%, and countries with closer economic ties to Russia suffered more. Germany's benchmark DAX dropped 3.4%. Poland's main stock index fell 5.2%.

In Brussels, European foreign ministers condemned what the European Union foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton called Russia's "act of aggression" in Crimea.

The ministers said that "in the absence of de-escalating steps by Russia," the EU would consider suspending talks with Russia on easing visa procedures and on a trade and economic agreement.

The warning was an attempt to strike a balance, refraining from hasty action that would foreclose Russia's ability to save face, while simultaneously signaling that the EU wouldn't hold off for long.

So far, the pressure on Moscow has been limited mainly to stern rhetoric and canceled meetings, including preparations for the Group of Eight summit in Sochi, Russia, in June. The White House said it won't send a presidential delegation to the Paralympic Games in Sochi either.

In Europe, at least, there appears to be little appetite for broader sanctions that would upend trade with Russia.

France, for instance, is on schedule to deliver the first of two Mistral carriers, valued at 1.4 billion euros ($1.9 billion), to the Russian Navy by the end of the year, according to DCNS, the French firm building the high-tech amphibious assault ships.

Asked Monday whether Moscow's incursion was forcing Paris to rethink its trade ties, French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said: "We're not there. For the moment, we are trying to stop Russia's mobilization in Ukraine and establish a dialogue."

Diplomats said that Germany argued strongly in the meeting for Europe to move cautiously and to ensure that channels of communication were kept open to the Kremlin.

Along with Russian stocks, which fell about 10%, the shares of Western companies like Renault, Danish brewer Carlsberg A/S and British oil giant BP PLC also fell on fears their big Russian investments would suffer as tensions over Ukraine grow.

Russia is PepsiCo's second-largest market by revenue after the U.S. The Purchase, N.Y.-based snack and beverage giant has billions of dollars of assets in the country. It declined to comment on Monday.

Entanglements between Russia and Europe go much further than with U.S. companies. Europe is a major buyer of Russian natural gas; Russia is a strong market for German goods; energy companies in Italy, the U.K. and elsewhere have major investments in Russia.

The ties make punishing Russia practically difficult because of the divisions within Europe between those close to Russia and those with less to lose.

But Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, a London-based think tank, warned against exaggerating Russia's economic leverage over Europe.

Cutting off gas supplies to Europe via Ukraine -- a perennial Russian threat -- would do plenty of damage to Russia too, he said. "We need (Russia), and it needs us."

title: RPT- FOREX -Euro rises versus yen as geopolitical risk fears ebb
text:
* Russian news agencies say Putin orders troops in military exercise back to base

* Euro edges higher on the reports, yen extends earlier losses

* No news on movement of Russian forces in Crimea (Repeats to additional subscribers)

By Masayuki Kitano

SINGAPORE, March 4 (Reuters) - The euro rose against the yen on Tuesday following reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered troops who took part in military exercises in central and western Russia to return to base.

The euro rose to intraday highs versus both the yen and the dollar after the reports by Russian news agencies, which quoted the Kremlin spokesman.

Moscow had denied that the exercises, which began last week and ended on schedule, had anything to do with events in Ukraine, where Putin has said he has the right to deploy troops to protect Russian compatriots. There was no news of Russian troop movements in Crimea.

The euro rose 0.1 percent to $1.3752, after rising to about $1.3767 at one point. Against the yen, the euro gained 0.4 percent to 139.96 yen, having risen to as high as 140.35 yen at one point.

The safe-haven yen slipped broadly, helping the dollar rise 0.3 percent to 101.75 yen. The greenback pulled away from a one-month low of 101.20 yen that had been set on Monday.

"There is some unwinding of long positions in the yen and long positions in the Swiss franc, but it's hard to tell at this point if the trend has changed," said Satoshi Okagawa, senior global markets analyst for Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation in Singapore.

Risk sentiment has been hit of late by the crisis over Russian military intervention in Ukraine, boosting safe haven currencies such as the yen and the Swiss franc.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's forces have tightened their grip on the Russian-speaking Crimea region, a move described by U.S. President Barack Obama as a violation of international law and of Ukraine's sovereignty.

The dollar could extend its recent fall against the yen if risk sentiment worsens further, although the yen's gains could be limited by speculation that the Bank of Japan might eventually step up its monetary stimulus, said Sim Moh Siong, FX strategist for Bank of Singapore.

"I think in the back of the market's mind...is always the backstop, in terms of BOJ," Sim said.

Many market participants expect the BOJ to take further easing steps at some point to achieve its 2 percent inflation target, although expectations for the central bank to act soon have faded recently as BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda remains doggedly positive that the economy is improving.

"If the Ukraine situation escalates, and that leads to a global risk-off, and perhaps higher oil prices as well...Japanese policymakers would have to reassess the economic impact on Japan and that may prompt a policy response," he added.

The Russian military intervention on the Crimean peninsula has rattled oil markets, with U.S. crude rising to its highest settlement price in 5-1/2 months on Monday.

Trading in the Australian dollar was somewhat choppy after the Reserve Bank of Australia kept interest rates steady at a record low of 2.50 percent, as widely expected, and reiterated that the most prudent course for policy was likely a period of stability.

The Aussie dollar rose to around $0.8970 or so right after the RBA decision, but later faltered when the RBA said in its post-meeting statement that the Australian dollar's exchange rate remains high by historical standards.

The Australian dollar was last steady on the day at $0.8936 , staying above a one-month low of $0.8891 that had been set on Monday. (Additional reporting by Ian Chua in Sydney)

title: METALS-London copper near 3 month low; more losses eyed on Russia
text:
SYDNEY, March 4 (Reuters) - London copper steadied on Tuesday, holding not far off three-month lows touched the day before as widespread risk aversion tainted sentiment already damaged by signs of shrinking manufacturing growth in top metals user China.                              

FUNDAMENTALS               

* Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange  was flat at $6,970 a tonne by 0720 GMT, from the previous session when it fell to a three-month low of $6,944 a tonne.               

* The most-traded May copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange fell by 0.4 percent to 48,790 yuan ($7,900) a tonne, having descended to a new seven-month trough in overnight trade.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Assets rebound, Ukraine crisis still a threat
text:
(Adds bonds, updates markets)
    * Markets bounce back as Ukraine/Russia tension eases
    * Return of wobbles remains a threat, Ukraine is main factor
watched
    * Romania, Serbia market interventions have not eroded
reserves

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, March 4 (Reuters) - Central European assets
rebounded on Tuesday after President Vladimir Putin said Russia
saw no need to use military force in Ukraine for now. 
    Putin's comments, and an earlier order for Russian troops
involved in a military exercise near the border with Ukraine to
return to base, were seen as an attempt to ease East-West
tension and fears of war in the former Soviet republic.
    That helped lift stocks and currencies in the European
Union's emerging east, which had tumbled as Russian assets were
hit by panic-selling on Monday.
    Shares in Hungary's OTP bank, which has some 140
branches in Ukraine, led gains, firming 5.8 percent after the
previous day's plunge of 10 percent to 18-month lows.
    But the situation in Ukraine is still "a time bomb" for
central and east European markets, one Budapest-based currency
dealer said, with investors eyeing the risk that Kiev will
default on debt as well as the possibility of military conflict.
 
    "Clearly the Ukrainian issue moves everything in the region
now," the dealer added.    
    Moscow's forces remain in control of Crimea, seized
bloodlessly after Russia's ally Viktor Yanukovich was ousted as
Ukrainian president last month. In his first comments on the
crisis, Putin said all options could be used to protect
compatriots who were living in "terror" in Ukraine.
 
    The turmoil in Ukraine has been a fresh blow to emerging
markets, many of which have already had to hike interest rates
and defend their currencies this year as investors fret about
U.S. stimulus withdrawal and Chinese economic growth. 
    Exports from the EU's eastern states to Ukraine are around
only 1-2 percent of their foreign sales, but a debt default or
war could have an impact in the region's markets.
    Central European states' economic fundamentals are
relatively strong but investors have tended to sell emerging
market assets indiscriminately this year. 
    Trading on Tuesday was thin and the tone still jittery but
Hungary's forint and Poland's zloty regained
some of the ground lost the day before, firming 0.7 and 0.3
percent against the euro, respectively.
    One Budapest-based trader said local banks had bought
Hungarian government debt, mainly long-term paper yielding more
than 5 percent - a big pick up from the central bank's 2.7
percent two-week deposit rate.
    "Foreigners bought the papers, too, and there was a rebound
in Poland," the trader said. "We will see now if there are
sanctions against Russia and what their response will be. In my
view the Ukrainian story is not over yet."
    
    RISK CHANNELS
    The forint is seen as vulnerable to contagion from other
emerging markets because Hungary is the region's most indebted
state and its interest rates are low following a long series of
cuts. The country is also due to hold elections in April.
    Firms with business interests in Ukraine, such as Hungarian
drug maker Richter and Poland's PKO BP, could
also be hurt by more financial turbulence or war there.
    Some investors also believe Romanian rate cuts have been too
deep given contagion risks. The country's central bank has had
to intervene to prop up the leu following a split in
the government last month, before which the currency of the EU's
second poorest member had been stable for several months.
    Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ponta won a confidence vote
in parliament late on Tuesday, which gave him a new mandate to
push through IMF-backed reforms. 
    Prior to the vote, the leu had gained 0.2 percent
in illiquid late trade, after earlier failing to benefit from
the improved regional mood.
    Serbia's central bank has also stepped up interventions to
defend the dinar as the country prepares for early elections on
March 16, though as with Romania its foreign currency reserves
remain healthy.
    The bank is expected to keep rates on hold on Thursday given
uncertainty pending a mid-March election, pressure on the dinar
and a pickup in inflation. 
    The dinar firmed 0.1 percent against the euro on
Tuesday. The central bank had spent 50 million euros in the
market on Monday to defend the currency, the same amount raised
by the Serbian debt agency in a Treasury bill auction.
    Poland's central bank is also expected to leave its
benchmark interest rate unchanged at its monthly meeting on
Wednesday and to start raising late this year.

title: UPDATE 3-Russian stocks, rouble rebound as Putin breaks silence on Ukraine
text:
* Russian stocks up more than 5 pct

* Sentiment lifted as Moscow orders troops back to base

* Putin slams "coup" but plays down invasion threat

* Investors wary of economic effect of Ukraine crisis

By Jason Bush and Zlata Garasyuta

MOSCOW, March 4 (Reuters) - Russian assets rebounded on Tuesday as President Vladimir Putin said he would only use force in neighbouring Ukraine as a last resort.

The mood on the markets was calmer after panic selling on Monday when escalating tensions between Ukraine and Russia sent Moscow's main stock indexes plummeting and forced the central bank to unexpectedly raise interest rates - by a hefty 150 basis points - and burn its way through as much as $12 billion of reserves to prop up the rouble.

By 1400 GMT on Tuesday the rouble-denominated MICEX share index had rebounded 5.2 percent to 1,356 points, while the dollar-denominated RTS index was up 6.1 percent at 1,184 points. The indexes have yet to fully recover Monday's more than 10 percent declines.

"From morning today we've seen good demand for liquid shares from foreign hedge-funds and also long-only funds. Oddly enough American investors are also buying," said Andrei Yarnikh, equity salesman at UBS.

"It looks like Western countries aren't so intent on introducing sanctions against Russia, and the threat of bringing (Russian) troops into Ukraine has also lessened."

Markets were cheered initially when Putin ordered the end of large-scale military exercises in Russia, and gained a further boost after his comments at a press conference, his first on the crisis.

Putin slammed Western powers for backing what he called an "armed seizure of power" in Ukraine, but also emphasised that he saw no immediate need for Russian military intervention, which he described as a "last resort".

He also said Russia was willing to work with Western states and the International Monetary Fund on financial assistance for Ukraine, and cooperate with the new authorities in Kiev although Russia does not regard them as legitimate.

"People are bored of expecting a bad scenario in Ukraine and have started to believe that there will be no military scenario and a confrontation of the Ukrainian army with Russia won't happen," said Oleg Dushin, senior analyst at Zerich Capital Management.

"The fear that Russian troops might go into, say, Kharkiv (in eastern Ukraine), isn't now on the agenda. You could say that the question of a Third World War has been removed," he said.

The rouble also rebounded, after sliding 2 percent on Monday. At 0930 GMT it was up 1.2 percent to 36.10 against the dollar and was up 0.8 percent at 49.75 versus the euro.

Against the dollar-euro basket it was up 1 percent at 42.20.

"Many in the market took Putin's speech as an attempt to reverse gear in the conflict, or tried to convince themselves of this," said a forex trader at a large Russian bank, who cautioned that "it isn't over yet".

COOLER HEADS

In a note to investors, Mattias Westman, founding partner of Prosperity Capital Management, a major portfolio investor in Russia, said "a series of bad decisions has been made by all sides in this situation" in Ukraine, but that cooler heads were now expected to prevail.

"The situation, in the last day or so, appears to have stopped escalating and different parties appear to be trying to find a peaceful solution," he said.

Investors, however, continued to be wary about the economic implications of Russia's involvement in the Ukraine crisis.

The United States said on Monday that Russia had violated international law with its military intervention in Ukraine and that it would look at a series of economic and diplomatic sanctions to isolate Moscow.

The Russian economy was showing signs of slowing before the crisis, with manufacturing activity shrinking for a fourth month in a row in February.

A salesman at a Russian investment company said institutional investors still expected a wave of outflows from Russia and the region this week.

He said "the market is pricing a completely different valuation range for Russia as a consequence of recent events" because of the increased risk caused by Putin's unpredictability and economic difficulties that Russia may experience for an extended period.

"When the further development of events becomes more-or-less clear then it would be worth taking a look at murdered liquid Russian stocks," said Vladislav Silaev, trader at Alfa Capital.

Russia's finance ministry announced on Tuesday it was suspending purchases of foreign currency on the domestic market to replenish its Reserve Fund because of high volatility on financial markets.

The purchases, equivalent to 3.5 billion roubles ($95.7 million) a day over three months, had been one of the factors weighing on the rouble.

The central bank announced on Tuesday it had moved the rouble's floating corridor by an unusually large 35 kopecks to 35.75-42.75 against the basket the previous day.

On Monday, the bank said it was increasing the intervention threshold to move the corridor by 5 kopecks to $1.5 billion from $350 million, and that it would revise its intervention parameters on a daily basis.

title: Grand Central: Evans vs. Taylor -- War of the Fed Policy Rules -- WSJ Blog
text:
The Wall Street Journal's Daily Report on Global Central Banks for Tuesday, March 4

.

Highlights 


   -- Da Costa's Take: Evans vs. Taylor - War of the Fed Policy Rules 
 
 
   -- ECB Watching Ukraine Crisis Closely: Draghi 
 
 
   -- Crimea Conflict Makes Poland Rethink Euro, Central Banker Says 
 
 
   -- China Central Bank Guides Short-Term Rates Higher 
 
 
   -- BOJ Economist Says Tax Hike Won't Derail Recovery 

DA COSTA'S TAKE

The idea that the Federal Reserve would commit to keeping interest rates near zero until unemployment fell to at least 6.5% became known as the Evans Rule, because it was first advocated by Chicago Fed President Charles Evans. Now, as the jobless rate hovers just around that level, Mr. Evans appears to be trying take his rule-making inclinations a step further.

In a speech Friday, Mr. Evans defended what he called a "goal-oriented monetary policy strategy." In short, the Fed must clearly lay out the economic objectives it intends to target -- lower unemployment and 2% inflation -- and then proceed to take measures to get there.

That's already the central bank's prevailing approach. But with talk of interest rate increases appearing in Fed policy debates, Mr. Evans seems to want to preempt any moves toward rate hikes. Mr. Evans' case was aimed at countering the views of Stanford University professor John Taylor, famous for his 1993 "Taylor Rule," which prescribes how central banks should adjust short-term interest rates according to several economic variables.

Mr. Taylor has recently argued the U.S. central bank has gone too far with its aggressive efforts to spur economic growth, including holding short-term interest rates near zero and buying bonds to lower long-term rates. At a hearing last month following Fed Chairwoman Janet Yellen's congressional testimony, he said "there is little evidence that the policy has helped economic growth or job growth."

Mr. Evans takes issue with this reading. He says the Fed's aggressive support for the economy has helped sustain the recovery and it should continue. He notes unemployment exceeds levels the Fed sees as consistent with full employment while inflation has long been falling short of the central bank's 2% target.

"For me, there is a problem with simplistic approaches. Simple Taylor rules fail the strategic principle to express policy intentions clearly, " Mr. Evans said. The severity of the financial crisis renders mechanistic approaches even less relevant, argued Mr. Evans. "The rule completely breaks down during the Great Recession and its aftermath."

title: Russia Halts Buying of Foreign  Currency  Due to Market Volatility
text:
MOSCOW--Russia's finance ministry said Tuesday it had halted the buying of foreign currencies for the reserve fund due to increased financial market volatility, which should ease downside pressure on the ruble.

The finance ministry started buying 3.5 billion rubles ($95.9 million) of foreign currencies on the open market on Feb. 20 to stash the extra revenues from oil and gas exports in the rainy-day reserve fund.

The finance ministry's decision to buy foreign currency worth 212.2 billion rubles by the end of May had a negative impact on the ruble in February despite the ministry's claim that its purchases won't have an impact on the exchange rate.

On Monday, the ruble plummeted to its new lows against the dollar and the euro due to heavy selloff triggered by threats of sanctions from the West in response to Moscow's decision to send troops to Ukraine.

The central bank had to change its intervention mechanism to stop the ruble from falling and sold more than $10.5 billion from its gold and forex reserves, the world's fourth largest. The central bank has also unexpectedly raised interest rates by 1.5 percentage points to ease downside pressure on the ruble.

The finance ministry said it has bought foreign currencies worth 38 billion rubles for the reserve fund so far this year.

text:

WATCH FOR: EU PPI; U.S. API oil data; U.K. construction PMI

UKRAINE:

========

Markets in Asia were able to recover as the situation in Ukraine hadn't deteriorated significantly and stocks had already sold-off in the previous session.

European foreign ministers backed off any immediate sanctions on Russia on Monday but warned the bloc was ready to act within days if Moscow didn't reverse course.

In a statement, the ministers said that "in the absence of de-escalating steps by Russia," the EU would consider suspending talks with Russia on easing visa procedures and on a future trade and economic agreement. The bloc would also consider further targeted measures, they said.

Britain is preparing to rule out trade sanctions against Russia amid fears that the Ukraine crisis could derail the global economic recovery, The Daily Telegraph reported Tuesday, citing a government document.

But the U.S. said it will suspend talks with Russia aimed at boosting trade and investment and it is drawing closer to imposing economic or political sanctions against Russia.

European Council President Herman Van Rompuy confirmed he had summoned EU heads of government to meet in Brussels on Thursday. Officials said the bloc could start to adopt targeted measures then if the situation in Ukraine wasn't calmer. The U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry will be in Kiev Tuesday and an International Monetary Fund delegation will also be there to meet with Ukraine's interim government and to discuss security and financial issues.

EUROPEAN OUTLOOK & U.S./ASIAN SUMMARIES:

========

European stock markets may start higher, with bunds and gilts mixed, as the Ukraine crisis simmers.

Most Asian markets edged higher on Tuesday, as stocks picked themselves up from a selloff in the previous session sparked by concerns over the situation in Ukraine.

Another sign of easing tension in the market was a softer yen--a safe-haven asset that is typical bought in times of turmoil.

"The immediate and likely largest impact from the risk-off sentiment due to the crisis in the Ukraine may have already passed," said Norihiro Fujito, senior investment strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.

Wall Street futures were higher, with Treasurys little changed, the euro and spot gold a bit lower, and oil mixed.

STOCKS:

======

Markets may rebound slightly as investors monitor capital flows among asset classes in Europe.

Ahead of the opening, IG has called the FTSE up 17 at 6725, the DAX up 6 at 9365, and the CAC up 14 at 4305.

"Why Europe's response is being watched is due to commodity trades with Russia, and unlike its G-7 counterparts in the U.S. and Canada, Europe has a trickier path to tread," noted Evan Lucas, strategist at IG.

"The U.S. as expected has acted in accordance with its standard response to these kinds of events. It has cancelled travel for diplomats, threatened sanctions on trade and banking; it has even kicked Russia out of the G-8. But Europe has yet to really push Russia on its current military program."

Wall Street futures were slightly higher Tuesday, after all three major U.S. stock indexes posted their biggest one-day declines in a month.

But the brunt of market pain was felt by Russia. The country's Micex stock index tumbled 11%, while the Russian ruble plummeted to a record low against the dollar and euro.

Investors in the U.S. said they were taking a cautious approach to events in the region. "Most people are of the mind-set that we have to wait and see how this plays out over the next day or two before doing anything with their portfolios," said Joseph Spinelli, head of cash equity trading for the Americas at Deutsche Bank. "The belief that it won't escalate to full-on military action seems to be the prevailing wisdom," he said.

Susan Bao, co-manager of J.P. Morgan's U.S. Equity Fund, which oversees about $10 billion said, "beyond the obvious risk of military conflict the most obvious risk for investors are...that Western countries impose economic sanctions on Russia."

But Ms. Bao said she remains optimistic on the U.S. economic recovery and is keeping an eye on declines in U.S. stocks for opportunities to add to her portfolio.

FOREX:

======

The dollar edged higher in Asia against the euro and other rivals as the Ukraine situation simmered.

"At this point, seems like there is very little that the U.S. and EU can do to dissuade Russia from taking this sort of action," said Win Thin, global head of emerging-market currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman. "I don't think this is going to go away or get resolved any time soon," he added.

But investors also responded to an uptick in manufacturing data last month as a signal that the U.S. economy is improving, which boosts the dollar.

The numbers begin to point to a decreasing "climate effect" on the economy, as they were collected during months where the U.S. experienced bouts of severe weather.

Investors will watch closely employment numbers released later this week, including weekly jobless claims on Thursday and the employment situation for February on Friday.

As Russia's military secured the Crimean peninsula, its currency hit a record low and its stock market plunged in the face of U.S. and European warnings of sanctions over the incursion into Ukraine.

BONDS:

=====

Bunds and gilts may start mixed as improving economic data were largely cancelled out by the political jitters.

The European Central Bank policy-setting meeting is due Thursday, and economists were speculating whether the bank will act following five months of inflation below 1%.

International Monetary Fund chief Christine Lagarde on Monday warned that a longer period with low inflation bears the risk of derailing the euro zone's already fragile economy. To fight this, she urged the ECB to launch "even further accommodative policies and targeted measures."

On the supply side, Austria and the U.K. have operations on tap for Tuesday.

U.S. Treasurys were little changed Tuesday, after markets rallied as the crisis in Ukraine deepened, unsettling global financial markets and triggering strong bidding for safe-haven assets.

The market was "completely geopolitical-driven," said Todd Hedtke, vice president for investment management at the U.S. division of Allianz Investment Management, which manages about $100 billion in assets. "A lot of capital is flowing into Treasurys and other U.S. markets, as the U.S. right now is probably the strongest developed market," he said.

Some analysts also noted the latest economic reports show the U.S. economy is emerging from the winter blues, keeping a lid on Treasurys' gains.

ENERGY:

=======

Nymex futures turned mixed in Asia after settling on Monday at their highest level this year. The API Weekly Statistical Bulletin due later today will indicate the status of U.S. oil stockpiles. Morgan Stanley said oil balances in the U.S. Gulf Coast remain surprisingly tight. The crisis in Ukraine remains in focus for Brent crude, which has risen for two straight sessions although some market participants said concerns of supply disruptions are overblown.

Nymex crude was down 1 cents at $104.91/bbl, while Brent was up 8 cents at $111.28/bbl.

METALS:

======

Base metals traders in Asia were waiting for more news on the crisis in Ukraine and on demand from China. Soft economic data from China along with its sliding currency has hit metals price recently. "If you can't count on demand from China what else is there to prop up copper prices," Barclays analyst Nicholas Snowdon said.

LME three-month copper was down $42 at $6,968.

Gold traders faced a similar scenario. "Looking beyond the geopolitical haze, Chinese physical demand remains largely absent, suggesting the current round of gains may retrace should the tension in the Ukraine ease," ANZ said in a report.

Spot gold was at $1,350.55/oz, off 6 cents.
