KIEV, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Ukrainian hryvnia <UAH=> extended losses on Tuesday, hitting a fresh six-month low against the dollar and prompting the central bank to intervene by selling about $100 million on the market.

The hryvnia hit 7.953 against the dollar at 1120 GMT, its lowest level since early April and compared with 7.950 at the previous day's close.

The central bank then offered to sell dollars at 7.9440 <NBU01> and sold "about $100 million", a source at the central bank told Reuters.

The Ukrainian currency has been weakening since early September after the country's current account deficit surged to $563 million, its highest this year, and after central bank First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov, who was closely involved in exchange rate policy, resigned on Sept. 1 and was replaced by Serhiy Arbuzov, seen as a close ally of President Viktor Yanukovich.

Some analysts say the hryvnia's decline -- still relatively small compared with gains made since presidential elections in January -- goes against fundamentals as the country's balance of payments, supported by metals exports, remains healthy.

U.S. economist Nouriel Roubini told a conference in Kiev on Tuesday that, overall, the hryvnia "remains slightly undervalued", adding that "appreciation could actually help with reducing inflation" which more than doubled to 2.9 pct in September.

Some analysts say the currency's gradual depreciation is being driven by speculative buying of dollars.

"The hryvnia remains under pressure from the cash market, as companies and households have been showing interest in buying dollars since August," said a dealer at a Western bank in Kiev.

"The central bank is not in a rush to slow down the process, assuming that a weaker hryvnia will have a positive effect on the economy."

A number of emerging market economies are managing exchange rates to avoid fast appreciation against the weakening dollar and maintain economic competitiveness.

The dealer also said that Ukraine's central bank avoided heavy intervention as that would prompt dollar holders to postpone converting the greenback into the hryvnia as they expected a more favourable exchange rate in the future.

Another local dealer said foreign investors could be selling Ukrainian treasury bills to take profits.

"The yields of T-bills are about to bottom out," he said.

Ukraine's T-bills maturing on Nov. 23, 2011 <UA62012=PFT> yielded 9.05 percent on Tuesday as their price rose 0.15 percent from the previous day's close on the PFTS exchange.

Ukraine's central bank said this week the net influx of foreign currency into the country had exceeded $5 billion so far this year. But it said the flow of foreign currency remained volatile as it was dominated by export revenues and loans.  KIEV, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday to support the weakening hryvnia <UAH=> as foreign investor buying of local bonds, which had underpinned the currency dried up, dealers said.

 The central bank offered to sell dollars at 7.9350 hryvnias <NBU01> per dollar as the currency weakened to 7.9400 per dollar, according to Reuters data, matching a multi-month low touched earlier in September after a central bank reshuffle.

 "Everybody is buying (dollars)," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Kiev. "Many banks are buying enormous volumes (of foreign currency)."

 She said the hryvnia had been previously supported by foreign investors who were buying so-called VAT bonds -- special government bonds issued to exporters to settle value-added tax reimbursement arrears. [ID:nLDE67U1YY]

 But as most of the bonds had now changed hands, foreigners' demand for the hryvnia had fallen.

 "Looking forward, I see (the dollar) only going up," the dealer said.

 The hryvnia started weakening against the dollar in early September after a reshuffle at the central bank prompted concerns of a policy shift. [ID:nLDE68519F]

 The central bank has since said it saw the hryvnia staying roughly stable until the end of this year and the exchange rate would not fall below 8.0 hryvnias per dollar.

 But analysts expect more volatility ahead due to Ukraine's pledge to allow more exchange rate flexibility under a deal with the International Monetary Fund and due to political factors such as mayoral and local council elections on Oct. 31.   (Writing by Olzhas Auyezov; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: UPDATE 3- Ukraine  c.bank sees hryvnia roughly stable
text:

* Adjusts intervention rate

* But sees little appreciation potential in the long run (Adds c.bank comment)

KIEV, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank, seeking to clarify its policy towards the hryvnia <UAH=> exchange rate following a slew of mixed signals, said on Thursday the currency would remain broadly stable against the dollar.

The bank, which has stepped in this week to support the hryvnia in a series of interventions, said its chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh's earlier comments suggesting future depreciation had been misunderstood.

Stelmakh said on Wednesday that the currency, which now trades at about 7.92 per dollar, would probably slip to 7.98-8.0 to the dollar by the end of 2010. [ID:nLDE6871AF]

But his senior advisor Valery Lytvytsky told Reuters on Thursday the figure was a floor for possible devaluation rather than a forecast of the exchange rate.

"Volodymyr Stelmakh has said (the hryvnia) would not go lower than that but that does not mean it cannot perform better and it can perform better," Lytvytsky said.

Separately, the Ukrainsky Novyny news agency quoted Stelmakh as telling a meeting of government officials and regional governors on Thursday: "The (exchange) rate ... will be stable. (...) Of course, we do not foresee a large appreciation."

Stelmakh did not say what time frame he was referring to but made his comments in a speech covering the bank's outlook for the next year.

"I think the central bank is trying to send the right signal to the market," said Renaissance Capital analyst Anastasia Golovach. "They are saying they will allow more hryvnia volatility and I think this is good for the economy."

Allowing greater exchange rate flexibility is one of the terms of Ukraine's $15 billion deal with the International Monetary Fund agreed in July.

On Thursday, the central bank offered to sell dollars at 7.9200 hryvnias per dollar <NBU01>, down from 7.9269, the rate it had used on Tuesday and Wednesday to support the hryvnia <UAH=> which has been volatile since Sept. 1.

The bank has sold $133 million on the interbank market so far this week.

"The dollar is weakening (against the hryvnia), the quotes are still close to where the central bank is selling but we may go even lower," said a dealer at a large Ukrainian bank.

The hryvnia rose to 7.9150 per dollar on Thursday from 7.9265 at the end of the previous session, according to Reuters data, recovering further from a five-month low of 7.94 hit earlier in the week.

The hryvnia's steady appreciation during the summer came to a halt after a central bank reshuffle on Sept. 1 when Stelmakh's first deputy Anatoly Shapovalov replaced by younger banker Serhiy Arbuzov and prompted speculation of a change in the bank's stance towards the currency.

The devaluation, although very small compared to overall gains since February, has drawn analysts' attention as a potential signal of a longer-term shift. [ID:nLDE68519F] (Reporting by Natalya Zinets, writing by Olzhas Auyezov; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: UPDATE 2- Ukraine  c.bank  intervenes  as hryvnia hits 2-mth low
text:
* Hryvnia hits 2-month low vs dollar at 7.914

* Central bank offers to sell dollars at 7.9082

* Investors worried c.bank may be less keen on appreciation

* Monthly Naftogaz dollar purchases add pressure

(Recasts with c.bank intervention)

By Natalia Zinets and Olzhas Auyezov

KIEV, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened to defend the hryvnia <UAH=> on Friday, two days after the replacement of a central bank official prompted selling pressure that was spurred by state firm Naftogaz buying dollars.

The intervention helped steady the hryvnia at 7.914 per dollar according to Reuters data, its weakest since early July. That puts the hryvnia on track for its biggest weekly slump since April with losses of 0.4 percent.

The sharp move prompted the central bank to update its dedicated Reuters page for the first time since Tuesday <NBU01>, indicating it was ready to sell dollars at 7.9082 hryvnias.

A trader at a Western bank in Ukraine confirmed the interventions had taken place.

The sell off began after the central bank's First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov, who was closely involved with exchange rate decision-making, resigned on Wednesday to be replaced by Serhiy Arbuzov, a banker with no prior central bank experience.

Arbuzov is seen as an ally of President Valdimir Yanukovich and investors are concerned that he may be less keen on a stronger hryvnia, which hurts powerful exporters such as steelmaker Metinvest.

"It is highly likely the NBU will put more effort in preventing the hryvnia from strengthening excessively as the business entities that support the current president mostly represent large exporters and are not interested in hryvnia strengthening," Alexander Pecherytsyn, analyst at ING, said in a research note.

Investors who had previously bet on a stronger hryvnia "were probably frightened that the change of deputy governor at the central bank could be followed by a shift in currency policy," said a dealer at a major bank.

"They started to buy foreign currency, which added to demand from Naftogaz."

The Ukrainian gas giant needs the dollars to pay for gas purchases from Russia's Gazprom . For July's imports, it owes around $780 million, although Prime Minister Mykola Azarov said on Friday the country would like to renegotiate its contracts to pay less in the future. [ID:nLDE6820TB]

"I think the growing demand (for dollars) is the work of Naftogaz, which traditionally needs to pay for imported gas by the seventh of the month," said one market participant.

Ukraine's current account, which moved into deficit in July, may also keep downward pressure on the hryvnia, said Irina Piantkovskaya, economist at Troika Dialog in Kiev.

STABILITY TO COME?

Credit derivatives traded on Ukraine jumped to $9.0 billion in gross notional volumes in the week to Aug 27, up more than 40-fold from $211 million the week before, according to the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC).

However, analysts said the surge in volumes reflected a rise in investor appetite for Ukraine's debt following the resumption of financing from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) last month and resulting credit ratings upgrades.

Five-year Ukraine credit default swaps (CDS) <UAGV5YUSAC=MP> nudged higher this week following the central bank reshuffle, but the cost of insuring the country's sovereign debt has fallen to below 600 bps since late August. [ID:nLDE6820PG]

At the start of the week, the central bank had actually offered to buy foreign currency, last setting the intervention level at 7.8889 per dollar on Aug. 31, weaker than the previous day's close of 7.8850.

"The central bank gave a signal for the hryvnia's weakening," said a chief dealer at a Western bank in Kiev.

A trader at a local bank said Friday's round of interventions would likely bridge the short-term dollar supply gap and help the hryvnia to stabilise.

"The central bank simply sold dollars to Naftogaz. I don't see any reasons for swift market movements," the trader said.

ING said in the medium term it did not expect the reshuffle to affect the central bank's policy, although the bank does not expect any more hryvnia appreciation this year.

Arbuzov's appointment comes as Ukraine's government moves towards boosting the power of Yanukovich, pledging to reverse curbs on presidential authority passed under his predecessor. [ID:nLDE6811U7] (Additional reporting by Andrey Ostroukh and Vladimir Soldatkin in Moscow and Sebastian Tong in London; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Bulgaria, Hungary CDS rise on debt worries
text:
* Bulgaria, Hungary CDS rise on debt worries

* Global emerging stocks, debt spreads improve slightly

* Ukraine increases FX flexibility as IMF arrives in Kiev

* Dubai holds investor roadshow, bond seen unlikely

By Carolyn Cohn

LONDON, June 10 (Reuters) - The cost of insuring Bulgarian and Hungarian debt against default rose again on Thursday as the debt and deficit position of emerging European economies remained in focus.

Hungarian assets slumped last week on comments that Hungary might suffer a Greek-style debt crisis, while the European Commission has queried changes in Bulgarian deficit statistics.

Concern about Hungary sent global markets briefly into panic, given existing worries about the debt of peripheral euro zone countries like Greece.

"The correction in risky assets will last a bit longer due to technical reasons as well as fundamental concerns about possible contagion of problems in the euro zone area," said James Lord, emerging FX strategist at Morgan Stanley.

"Bulgaria is yet another example of the prevailing market concerns over fiscal sustainability. The question marks over the reliability of Bulgaria's fiscal accounts are obviously not good news and are part of the wider trend across Europe, whether developed or emerging."

A surge in Chinese exports provided support for global emerging markets on Thursday, however, although trading ranges were generally subdued ahead of the European Central Bank's interest rate announcement at 1145 GMT, expected to result in steady rates of 1 percent.

Benchmark emerging equities <.MSCIEF> rose 0.3 percent and emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> tightened by 3 basis point to 335 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

Non-resident bids above 50 percent for a Spanish three-year bond auction also provided some relief. [ID:nLDE6590T9]

Emerging market currencies mostly rose, led by a near-1 percent rise in the rand <ZAR=>, with FX flows to South Africa helped by the World Cup which kicks off on Friday.

DEFICIT FOCUS

Hungary's five-year credit default swaps rose 11 basis points to 351 bps, although the forint steadied against the euro <EURHUF=> and stocks climbed 0.5 percent <.BUX>, as investors mulled the government's deficit-cutting plan released this week.

The Hungarian government's commitment to its 2010 budget deficit goal is "moderately encouraging" but details are lacking and medium-term deficit aims must be clarified, ratings agency Fitch said on Wednesday. [ID:nLDE6581OT]

Focus has moved onto Bulgaria, after the European Commission this week demanded Bulgaria explain why it abruptly raised its 2010 budget deficit forecast. [ID:nLDE65827G]

Bulgaria's five-year credit default swaps rose 10 basis points to 373.4 bps, according to CDS monitor CMA DataVision, close to 11-month highs hit this week.

Ukraine's five-year CDS rose to 660.5 bps from 656.1, as a mission from the IMF arrived in Kiev this week.

Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich on Wednesday assured the IMF that his country was on track to meet its budget deficit targets as it seeks a fresh $19 billion loan. [ID:nLDE65820X]

The IMF also wants more exchange rate flexibility, and Ukraine's central bank on Wednesday adjusted its forex intervention rate for the third consecutive day, after keeping the rate unchanged for almost two months.

Emerging debt issuance has dried up due to ballooning spreads in the past few weeks, but Dubai is meeting investors this week.

Dubai has been shut out of international capital markets since state-owned Dubai World declared a standstill on debt payments in November.

"With current risk aversion towards debt markets and further debt restructurings among local quasi-sovereign entities, we see the possibility of a new debt issue rather limited in the short term," Commerzbank emerging credit analyst Nuria Jorba said in a client note.

(Additional reporting by Sujata Rao; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Conflict with  Ukraine  sinks the ruble again
text:
The military intervention in Ukraine, which Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered in February 2022, and subsequent Western sanctions against Russia are shaking the ruble. The Russian currency depreciated sharply after the "special military operation," as Russia calls it, but over the months and with the intervention of the Russian monetary authorities it recovered. This summer it depreciated again and on August 14 it broke the barrier of 100 units per dollar.

The Central Bank of Russia explains the weakening of the ruble by the imbalance in the trade balance, i.e. between export and import operations. The value of exports, it has noted, has fallen by a third since the second half of 2022.

December 2022, major Western countries imposed a $60 cap on the price of Russian oil, the country's main source of foreign exchange. Western sanctions significantly reduced revenues from hydrocarbon exports. Natural gas costs ten times less than last year.

But the fall also seems to be influenced by the political and military developments surrounding the current conflict. In fact, the ruble has been depreciating steadily since the end of June, following the failed armed rebellion of the Russian mercenaries of the Wagner Group, led by St. Petersburg businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin.

For the time being, the Central Bank of Russia sees no risk to financial and economic stability. But experts and observers believe that the Russian state will have to take measures to strengthen the national currency.

In an opinion piece for the Tass news agency, Maxim Oreshkin, Putin's economic advisor, blamed the ruble's more than 30% drop in 2023 on the Central Bank's policies.

"The main source of the weakening of the ruble and accelerating inflation is a soft monetary policy. The central bank has all the tools to normalize the situation in the near future and ensure that interest rates are reduced to sustainable levels," wrote Oreshkin.

The advisor assures that the Kremlin wants a strong ruble. "A weak ruble complicates the structural transformation of the economy and negatively affects the real incomes of the population," he said.

Before the war against Ukraine broke out, one dollar exchanged for about 75 rubles. One euro, for about 85 rubles. This Monday, August 14, the drop is already over 101 rubles to the dollar, 111 to the euro.

Last year the fall was greater and reached 120 rubles per dollar on March 11, 2022. But the Russian currency recovered in the following months thanks to capital controls and increased export revenues.

Alexei Antonov, head of investment advisors at Alor Broker, explains to the RBK newspaper that for this period of decline to end it is necessary either for imports to stop falling or for the monetary authorities to take decisive steps. "Before those factors come about, we do not rule out the exchange rate reaching 115-120 rubles to the dollar," he warns.

Last week the central bank halted the Finance Ministry's foreign exchange purchases in an attempt to thereby reduce volatility. But the effect was limited and did not translate into significant support for the Russian currency.

To stem its slide, Russia could reintroduce tighter capital controls. Another option could be to raise interest rates, but that would limit the potential for economic growth and would mean higher government borrowing rates at a time when it has to continue to fund its military activity in Ukraine.

title: This is Russia living the Kremlin's alternate reality
text:
"We have to erase those symbols, the V and the Z, and whoever sticks them on our vehicles should be put in jail. A totalitarian regime is never as firm as it was before it collapsed." Over the past year Russian citizens have suffered the consequences of the Kremlin's intervention in Ukraine. Hundreds of thousands fled Russia to avoid being mobilized. Those who stayed behind live in a bearable parallel reality following government measures that have so far prevented economic collapse. And those who protest are repressed. In Russia, allegations like the above against the Kremlin can only be heard in court, during trials against activists, opponents or simple citizens accused of discrediting the armed forces.

The above words were uttered by journalist Maria Ponomarenko last week in her last word before judges in Barnaul (Altai krai) who sentenced her to six years in prison for a post she published on Telegram on March 17, 2022 saying that Russian forces had shelled the Mariupol theater, where hundreds of civilians had taken refuge. The Russian Defense Ministry had denied having anything to do with it and blamed the shelling on Ukrainian "nationalists."

The law against "fake news" about the army and the crackdown has reduced opposition to almost zero.Vladimir Putin signed the law against spreading "false news" about the army shortly after sending troops to Ukraine. Since then that rule, which can punish the offender with up to 15 years in prison, has conditioned Russian opposition to the Kremlin's plans in Ukraine and reduced it to almost zero.

Pavel Chikov, head of the Agora NGO, counted 180 criminal charges brought in this case as of December. This week, Alexander Bastrikin, head of the Russian Investigative Committee under the Kremlin, told the Tass news agency that to date "152 criminal cases have been opened, in which 136 people were prosecuted. Fifty-three criminal cases have been brought to court, 16 sentences have already been handed down."

It has affected both prominent political opposition figures (Ilya Yashin, sentenced to 8.5 years in prison) and activists (artist Sasha Skochilenko may spend 10 years in prison if convicted for changing supermarket price tags in St. Petersburg to peace messages) or simple citizens (in Arkhangelsk, university student Olesia Krivtsova is under house arrest for a message on Instagram about the explosion of the Crimean bridge in October). To citizens who have stayed in Russia and others who have left the country: recently well-known journalists Alexander Nevzarov and Veronika Belotserkhovskaya have been sentenced in absentia to 9 years in prison.

All these cases are an unmistakable message to those who in the first months of the special military operation , the euphemism used officially in Russia, were ready to show their faces and demonstrate. "From the very beginning we carried out protests against the war as an organization. In accordance with the new laws that reduce freedom, we were forced to stop carrying them out," explained Oleg Orlov, of the historical outlawed NGO Memorial, winner of the Nobel Peace Prize 2022, to La Vanguardia a few months ago.

Today only a vague memory remains of protests that the enormous police repression ended up blurring. From time to time, one can still see in Moscow a green ribbon that someone forgot to hang in a window or on a tree branch. Few know that for a few days it was used as a symbol of a resistance that today is totally silent.

Silent are also the few spontaneous signs of rejection, as when anonymous citizens left flowers next to a statue of the Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka after a Russian attack on the city of Dnipro this January. And the police continue to arrest anyone who still dares to step forward. According to the NGO OVD-Info, more than 19,500 people have been arrested since February 24, 2022 for demonstrating against the war and military mobilization.

The IMF forecasts that Russia will grow by 0.3% in 2023 and the government believes it will emerge from recession this year.Every once in a while little glimmers of hope appear. Grigory Yavlinsky, founder of the liberal Yabloko, the only opposition party still active, wrote a few weeks ago an article in the magazine Novaya Rasskaz-Gazeta , one of the many banned or blocked media in Russia. In it, he insisted on achieving peace, the goal set by his party.

Peace "in practice can only be implemented if at least Putin, Zelenski, Biden and the leaders of the EU and NATO want to do it." But he regrets that "to date all parties intend to continue hostilities on a large scale, wrongly counting on a military victory, which in modern conditions is unattainable for anyone," wrote the veteran politician. And he ended with an emotional "Reflect! Stop!".

During the first Cold War, crossing the Iron Curtain was accompanied by a strange sensation of having arrived in a parallel world, where many things were familiar but totally different. Something similar is gradually happening in today's Russia. Except for the regions close to the Ukrainian border (Belgorod, Kursk, Bryansk), Russian cities give the impression that life goes on as if thousands of people were not dying a thousand kilometers away.

But there are disturbing signs that everything is changing. On their way to work, many Muscovites still stop by Starbucks to pick up their morning coffee or a Dunkin Donuts coffee shop to complete a quick breakfast. The problem is that they are now called Stars Coffee and Donutto. You look up and on the office building where there used to be a billboard advertising Ikea or Decathlon, now a huge Z and other patriotic messages are drawn.

After February 24, 2022, the Moscow we knew is turning into a parallel Moscow, as the authorities try not to make the changes too noticeable. It is part of the process of adapting to the sanctions and the departure of more than a thousand Western companies.

In the grocery stores there is no more Coca-Cola, Pepsi or Sprite, to name the best known. The factories of these and other brands have been sold to Russian entrepreneurs who continue to produce the same products under different names. The McDonald's chain was bought by a Russian entrepreneur and renamed Sabroso y Punto. Ikea has just announced the sale of its four factories.

Despite the war earthquake, the population that was not affected by the military mobilization in October has hardly felt a tremor. Why?

The explanation may lie in the fact that the catastrophic forecasts that many analysts and observers made about the Russian economy under the pressure of sanctions have not come true. Last March, Russian Central Bank experts expected an 8% drop in GDP, annual inflation of over 20% and an average annual rate of 110 rubles to the dollar. But none of these things happened. There was no banking crisis, because the Kremlin and the Central Bank took drastic measures to plug any holes and prevent the outflow of foreign currency from the country.

At the end of the year, Putin announced a 2.5% drop in GDP, much lower than the best forecasts of months earlier.Russia has also been helped by its main economic resource: hydrocarbon exports. Together they allowed the ruble to recover from the March slump and inflation to be contained. In the first six months of the intervention in Ukraine, Russia made a piggy bank of $158 billion from the sale of energy products, according to the Energy and Clean Air Research Center, Finland. Moscow found in Asian markets, especially China and India, an alternative to the loss of customers in Europe.

In the first months of the conflict, the sanctions hardly affected hydrocarbon exports, explained Oleg Itzhoki, a professor at the University of California in Los Angeles, in Meduza. Only the US imposed an embargo on Russian oil, but supplies there were small, while the European Union continued to buy oil and gas.

At the end of the year, Putin announced a 2.5% drop in GDP. Much lower than the best forecasts months earlier. Moreover, the IMF has predicted that this year Russia may even have growth. In January it stated that the Russian economy will grow by 0.3%, when its previous forecasts indicated a fall of 2.3%. By 2024 he forecasts growth of 2.1%. Deduction in Moscow: Russia has resisted.

With these figures Andrei Belousov, Russian deputy prime minister, said two weeks ago that Russia can emerge from recession this year 2023. And the Ministry of Economic Development said in a statement that "the Russian economy is confidently overcoming the barriers of sanctions from hostile countries."

Another reason why many Russians have not noticed the change too much is that many Western products, in theory affected by sanctions, are still coming into the country. This is due to the so-called "parallel imports" allowed by the government.

In the context of the fight against intellectual piracy, in 2002 Russia banned products from entering the country without a license or permission from the manufacturer or rights owner. That ended last year, when Moscow decided that it was no longer illegal to import through third countries - such as Kazakhstan - a long list of products, including iPhones, cars or furs.

Will Russia continue to resist and will many Russians continue to live in this sort of alternative limbo?

The situation may start to change. On December 5, the EU implemented the full embargo on Russian oil, and since this February 5, on petroleum products. Also on December 5, the G-7 "price ceiling" began to operate, which set at $60 per barrel the maximum price at which ships and insurers can transport Russian oil. As a result, the Kremlin's coffers began to feel the pressure. In January, the fiscal deficit soared and state revenues from energy sales fell by 46%.

More than 19,500 people have been arrested for protesting against the war, according to the NGO OVD-Info.Another challenge Russia will have to face is the fall in consumption, exacerbated by uncertainty. In a December report Natalia Orlova, chief economist at Alfa Bank, predicted that the economy will shrink by 6.5% in 2023 due to a slowdown in consumption, lower investment and the loss of export potential.

But forecasts are just that, forecasts sometimes influenced by our own desires. With or without them, this year Russia has definitely moved away from the West and, as in the first cold war, is already walking in parallel.

title: Ukraine finally in NATO? The US 'theory of victory
text:
In his 2015 book, Conflict in Ukraine: The Unwinding of the Post-Cold War Order, co-written with fellow international relations specialist Eugene Rumer, Rajan Menon discussed one of the possible future scenarios of the Donbas war, which began in 2014: the ceasefire, he wrote, "breaks down and the conflict in eastern Ukraine escalates again and leads to direct Russian military intervention beyond the Donetsk and Lugansk regions; Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and occupies significant parts along the right bank of the Dnieper River, possibly including Kiev, leaving a truncated independent Ukrainian state."

Despite explicitly contemplating this scenario eight years ago, Rajan Menon, professor emeritus of international relations at City College of New York, senior fellow at the Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies, Columbia University, and director of the Grand Strategy program at the Defense Priorities think tank, acknowledges that last year's full-scale invasion surprised him. By the scale of the gamble and by the scale of the response, as if we had been catapulted into one of those epic conflagrations you only read about in history books.

We spoke with Menon, who has just returned from his second visit to war-torn Ukraine, about the prospects for the conflict and the role played by the United States - the main material and diplomatic driver of the Ukrainian war effort. We asked him about Biden's plans, European defense, the roots of the Russian invasion and the role of China. From a, as he says, "realistic" and "measured" perspective. The interview has been slightly edited for clarity.

QUESTION. First of all, I'd like to clarify something about the think tank you work for, whose mission, expressed on the front page of its website, is to promote a U.S. foreign policy based on diplomacy and temperance. What is the philosophy of international relations that underlies Defense Priorities?

ANSWER. It is a center that accommodates realism and restraint. That is, a policy that understands what the vital national security interests of the United States are, but without necessarily having to intervene elsewhere in the world, stretching our capabilities too far and reducing our ability to solve our domestic problems. Part of this philosophy was born as a result of the disastrous wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. But also to solve the problems that accumulate at home. You live in New York and you see what's going on in the streets.

At the same time, if you look at places like Europe, and you add up their GDP, their technology and their population, the idea that they can't organize their own defense against Russia is simply impossible to believe. People say that's a lot of countries and how are you going to organize them. But look at what the European Union has done. Who would have thought, 20 years ago, that there would be a central bank and a common currency for most countries, or the abolition of travel restrictions. So it can be done. Only Europe doesn't have the incentive to do it, as long as the US remains its protector. And the US, even though it wants to be the protector, complains. But part of the US position in the world is because it provides security for Europe, Japan, South Korea and Australia. In other words: all the great economic power centers of the world, except China and perhaps India.

P. It's a paradoxical relationship. Presidents as different as Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden have been asking European partners for years to raise their defense spending, since only 10 of the 30 NATO members reach the agreed 2% of GDP. The United States wants Europe to defend itself so that it can devote its resources to China, to the Pacific. However, the Americans are also pressuring European nations not to do business with the Chinese, and there is a perception, especially on the left, that Washington is using the war in Ukraine to secure its political and military influence in Europe.

A. That's very interesting. The complaints about Europe date back even to the time of John F. Kennedy in the 1960s. That the Europeans were not doing enough to defend themselves and that they had to be made to do so. But at the moment when, in Europe, someone like Emmanuel Macron is talking about strategic autonomy, that's not allowed. So we want them to spend more money on defense within NATO, but we're not comfortable with them going beyond that. And we're tolerating a lot of underspending on defense. If you look at the richest country in Europe, Germany, the reports of the parliamentary committee on the armed forces paint a picture of the German military that is shocking. I have a hard time understanding it. So the U.S. complains, but then sends its secretary of state, almost as if he were a Roman proconsul visiting the provinces of the empire, and I think we like that. We like going to Japan, we like going to Korea.

Regarding competition with China, the interesting thing is to look at new industrial policies. We've always talked, in general, about how much the U.S. likes the free trade system and dislikes protectionism. But if you look at agriculture, for example, it is heavily subsidized. Not as much as the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, at least for now. But essentially, we're making adjustments to produce in the U.S. as much as possible. Joe Biden's latest law, the Inflation Reduction Act, and others, give a lot of incentives to produce here, also for foreign companies. So Europe and Japan see this and worry about job losses. In this initiative there is also the need to prevent the leakage of sensitive technologies to China. So Europe is in a difficult situation: on the one hand, the Europeans understand that these leaks have to be prevented; on the other hand, it is a protectionist policy that causes tensions. It is important to remember that the U.S. has been committed to free trade since 1945. But throughout the 19th century it was an enormously protectionist country.

P. I wanted to ask you about the reasons behind the Russian decision to invade. The realist school tends to place part of the responsibility on the US, which would have overreached itself and behaved arrogantly, getting involved in Ukraine with promises and military investments, knowing, as the former ambassador to Moscow, William Burns, now director of the CIA, said, that Ukraine for the Russians was the "most vivid of red lines". The other side, which we can call idealistic, explains the aggression as a consequence merely of Russian traumas, of their revanchism and their apocryphal understanding of Ukraine. What is your position?

A. It is a mixture. I don't quite fit into either camp. Let me briefly present the landscape of the debate. On the one hand, you have people like John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago who say that the invasion is entirely due to NATO expansion. The idea is that because the 2008 NATO summit in Bucharest opened the door to Ukraine, Russia concluded that Ukraine was going to be a NATO member. And this is a special country for Russia. They are geographically tied. Putin faced, as John says, an existential threat. On the other hand, to mention two names, you have Michael McFaul and Anne Applebaum, who say that the invasion has absolutely nothing to do with NATO expansion. That Putin wants to control as many ex-Soviet countries as possible, in particular Ukraine, whose independence he cannot accept. These two extremes end up nullifying the possibility of standing in the middle.

My position is this: from the moment NATO expansion was shuffled around in the 1990s, and then made a reality, I always thought it was a terrible idea. Because, if you put yourself in Russia's position, whether you're a leftist, liberal or conservative, and you see a Cold War alliance parading to your borders, even if the United States tells you that the Cold War is over and Russia is democratizing, and so on, the question remains: why are you moving the alliance to our borders? And the idea that this enlargement was harmless is absurd. Imagine for a moment that the U.S. loses the Cold War and the USSR places Mexico in the Warsaw Pact. We would not accept it either way. This is where I differ with Applebaum and company. I think telling the story of the invasion of Ukraine without mentioning NATO expansion makes no sense.

But I also differ with John Mearsheimer. In 2008 NATO opened the door to Ukraine, but in order to accept it, the first thing to do is to draw up a Membership Action Plan. 14 years later, Ukraine had not been given such a plan. So it was clear that, for whatever reason, the unanimity required to accept this new member did not exist. I don't buy the argument that Putin invaded a country larger than Spain because of its imminent NATO membership.

Another thing to keep in mind is that the expansion of NATO has shifted, little by little, the balance of power within the organization away from countries like Spain, France and Germany, towards countries like Poland and the Baltics, which have a very different, very complicated history with Russia, with many conflicts. So I think the harder line towards Russia, in a way, is a consequence of NATO's expansion into these countries. There is also the argument that these countries wanted to join NATO, that they kept asking for it and that's why we had to accept them. But a military alliance is not a book club. A military alliance is serious, because it involves going to war to protect the other members.

P. Be that as it may, the damage has already been done. What do you think of the Biden Administration's policy towards Ukraine after the invasion began?

A. For me, especially after going to Ukraine and seeing the incredible damage, which I don't mind having seen on television or in the newspapers before, because it is shocking, I am not opposed to providing Ukraine with the means to defend itself. But I think that difficult decisions will have to be made. For example, let's say the war evolves and the Ukrainian Army is in a position to enter Crimea, will the West be united in its support for Ukraine, or will it be considered too dangerous? Because, if Putin is left with nothing, the war could spiral out of control. We would need a deal that would leave him something, so the Crimea issue would have to be fine-tuned as a problem that would be solved by future generations. Ukraine has not been given a blank check, because it has not been given certain weapons, such as ATACMS tactical missiles or fighter jets. It is being supported, but without allowing the war to escalate. The rule is to give weapons, but not to reach Russian territory.

P. The United States was absolutely right with the prediction of invasion, and with months to spare. But it also made a mistake. It thought that Ukraine would be quickly defeated by Russia. Washington was preparing to arm a Ukrainian resistance, not to support a full-fledged war effort, as turned out to be the case. Interestingly, it was the same mistake Russia made: the notion that the Ukrainians didn't stand a chance against the Russian tank roll.

A. The Russians have made many mistakes. When Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in World War II, the Russians demonstrated an impressive capacity for sacrifice to defend their country. What did they expect would happen when they invaded Ukraine? That the Ukrainians would not defend themselves? Ukrainian soldiers told me the same thing many times: for us this is no ordinary war. If we lose this war, we lose a country. Are there any Russian soldiers who believe that, if they lose this war, they would lose Russia? No. There is an asymmetry in combat morale. That was one mistake. Another mistake has to do with the training provided by NATO to the Ukrainian Army since 2014. 60,000 Ukrainian soldiers received training and the Ukrainian armed forces have been adopting NATO military practices. In addition, they have been fighting in two separatist provinces. So the Ukrainian Army had changed a lot. I don't think Putin took it seriously. But neither did we. The CIA thought the Ukrainian resistance would collapse immediately. Honestly, I thought so too, because, if you look at any measure of power, like population, tanks, aircraft or artillery, Russia had a huge advantage. But it's not just that the Ukrainians have higher morale, it's that the Russian Army didn't turn out to be what was expected.

Ukrainian soldiers told me the same thing many times: this is no ordinary war. If we lose this war, we lose a country

. P. You have mentioned in your articles that peace negotiations, for now, are impossible, because neither Ukraine, nor Russia, have incentives to sit down and negotiate. Both believe that they can improve their position in the spring or summer, that is why neither country seriously offers to mediate between them, because they know it would fail. On the other hand, we are getting curious signals, like that anonymous White House source who told The Washington Post that, essentially, Ukraine had this spring to carry out its counter-offensives, but then American support would probably cease and they would have to sit down and talk. What do you think the United States will do? What is its next step?

A. The Washington Post article came up at an event we hosted at Defense Priorities. In my view, it has received a lot of attention precisely because it is an exception. If you read most of the statements from the Biden Administration, they don't say they will give all the aid to Ukraine all at once, but they do say they will help Ukraine get the territories back, although without mentioning to what extent [Menon is referring to the possibility of Ukraine getting the entire territory back, up to the 1991 borders, including Crimea, or the territory from before February 24, 2022]. So I wouldn't read too much into it. It's not consistent with what the administration has been saying. And, if you compare it to other articles, you'll see that those articles say the opposite. I think what it suggests, probably, is that there's a debate within the Biden administration about how far they're willing to go.

P. Certainly, but it's also true that while the Biden Administration presents a consistent message, sometimes it leaks to the media what looks like a knock on the Ukrainians. For example, when it was leaked that Biden had raised his voice to the president, Volodymir Zelensky, during a telephone conversation, and told him to show a little gratitude for the aid. A way, perhaps, to remind the Ukrainians that American aid is not unconditional.

A. It's the oldest game in Washington and I'm sure in Madrid as well. To have in the government someone with a different opinion who wants it publicized. I don't know what exactly is going on. What we have to do is look at concrete actions, and what we see is $27 billion in U.S. military assistance. And, if you add in European, it's $7 billion or $8 billion. We're talking about 40% of the Russian defense budget last year. If we had sat down to talk a year and a half ago, and asked ourselves whether there was any chance of an all-out war between Ukraine and Russia, we probably would have said no. And, if there was such a war, and we had wondered whether the US and NATO would act in unison and send some $40 billion in military aid, we would have thought it was highly unlikely because of the risk of escalation. This has been a war of surprises for me. So much so that I am very reluctant to make predictions, because I have seen things that I thought would never happen.

Now people say Putin is an expansionist and an imperialist. He is an expansionist, but he has never done anything like this. A full-scale invasion of a large country. Georgia in 2008 was very different. In Syria, it was mostly the air force. In 2014, in Donbas and Crimea, it was provinces very close to Russia. What is happening now is an extraordinary step. How do you explain it? There is a theory going around that, during the covid, Putin was reading a lot about the conquests of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and all these nationalist philosophers like Ivan Ilyin. Some kind of Russian fascist. Who knows. But I didn't expect Putin to do something like this, even when he was amassing his troops on the border. I thought it was a bullying tactic to force the US to stall NATO involvement in Ukraine. That was my view.

P. A year after the start of the full-scale war, there is a possibility that is sounding more and more in military and geopolitical circles: that of ending up with a territorially diminished Ukraine, but integrated, at last and as a reward for what it has suffered, into NATO. Or with some other security guarantee. It would also be the only way to make possible its reconstruction, which promises to be very costly, without the risk of Russia attacking again in the future. Figures of more than $300 billion are being bandied about. That is 50% more than the Ukrainian GDP in 2021.

A. Now there is even talk of a trillion [trillion] dollars. A gigantic amount.

Q. How do you see the option of a Ukraine in NATO as an outcome of this war or as a kind of compensation for the loss of territories?

A. I can certainly imagine a peace, even though Zelensky says he wants everything back, including Crimea, in which Ukraine is territorially diminished: perhaps preserving 85% of its territory [that is currently under its control], but not all of it. NATO expansion is a complicated issue, because the alliance would possibly be divided. The eastern flank, plus the United Kingdom and the United States, would say yes, after all that Russia has done, and Russia has shown its true colors, Ukraine should be admitted to NATO. The question is: would Hungary, France and Germany think the same? I am not so sure. Look at what has happened with the Turks regarding the admission of Finland and Sweden. So it is not clear that Ukraine can join.

If you are in Ukraine and you say this, they get angry, because.There it is almost a religious question. They believe that, after all that has happened, joining NATO and the European Union is a birthright. But even the EU has been very careful in its statements. Also, if Ukraine joins the EU, the EU would have to bear most of the cost of reconstruction. We are talking about an awful lot of money.

"For every artillery shell Ukraine fires, the Russians fire ten. But they can't take it, because they are too badly commanded"

Now, there is a second possibility, although the

Ukrainians refuse to mention it because they don't want anyone to think that there are better options than NATO, and that is a different security guarantee. But a security guarantee would be worthless if it doesn't include the United States. So, if you have the UK, the Baltics and the US, maybe they'll be happy with second prize. It would be interesting to see what happens. The other possibility is a neutral Ukraine, which is what the Russians will demand, and I think the Ukrainians will put up a lot of resistance.

There are many things we cannot predict. Some will depend on what happens in the next year. And I also don't exclude the possibility that the war will continue. If the Ukrainians regain a lot of territory, they will be in a position of strength, vis-à-vis Russia and vis-à-vis the West. One thing to watch in the next three months is the Russian offensive. From what we can see they are attacking all along the front, from north of Lugansk to the south, but they are not doing well. They have not been able to take Bakhmut. They have been trying to take Bathmut since the end of August. A town that before the war had 70,000 inhabitants and now has 7,000, and they can't, despite having many advantages. For every artillery shell Ukraine fires, the Russians fire ten. But they can't take it, because they are too badly commanded.

P. As you watch this war, don't you worry that we might be missing something? Ukraine has a lot of activists, young, English-speaking, charismatic, social media-savvy people who are often the fixers who guide foreign reporters and who are active on Twitter. Zelensky's government has many such profiles and has led an iron grip on content. There is no doubt that pro-Russian views have greatly diminished since 2014, and it would not be correct to speak of a divided country, especially now. But, according to the director of the Kiev Sociological Institute, Anton Hrushevsky, there were around 30% of pro-Russian voters in Ukraine at the beginning of 2022. Probably many of them changed their minds soon after, but it is still a significant number.

A. That's an excellent question. As you said, the Ukraine narrative has been very well coordinated and orchestrated by Zelensky. And I'm not saying it's propaganda, but they have a point of view. And they've been very efficient promoting it in Western countries. They use social media and they do an excellent job. So in the West there is huge support for this narrative, which is backed by the U.S. foreign policy establishment, and by major newspapers. Even the British Guardian, a reference of the left, supports it.

It is true that there have been divisions in the country. Before 2014, it was not clear that there was broad support for joining NATO. The country was divided. The west and the center were more inclined to join NATO and the EU than the east and the south. But I think the war has changed a lot of things. All this talk by Putin that the war is to protect Russian speakers from genocide is absurd. The Russian-speaking parts of Ukraine have suffered the most destruction. Look at Mariupol, for example. The war has changed a lot of things. More and more Ukrainians, even if they are Russian speakers or ethnic Russians, identify themselves as Ukrainian citizens. There is a sense of a consolidating national identity. The Ukrainian language is increasingly used in cities like Kiev. It is encouraged by the government. And resistance to joining NATO is now much lower. The problem is not in Ukraine, the problem is to see to what extent NATO is ready to open its doors.

P. Speaking of narratives, a question about the tone of the debate. I'm going to read you this that realist thinker Stephen Walt, professor of international relations at Harvard University, wrote recently in Foreign Policy: "The public debate over Ukraine has been extraordinarily vituperative, with warmongering commentators competing with each other to see who expressed the most support for Kiev, while dismissing alternative perspectives as naïve, immoral, pro-Russian, or worse." As a realist, do you recognize this sentiment?

A. Personally, I find no difficulty in expressing my views, but there is no doubt that people critical of mainstream narratives, say, John Mearsheimer or the late Stephen Cohen of Princeton, have been vilified. They've been called all sorts of things, almost treated as Putin sympathizers. And I think that's a very unfortunate thing, because you can debate someone on the assumption that, if that person disagrees with what you think, it's because they work for a foreign government. I find it in very bad taste and social media has exacerbated the problem. All you have to do is sit in front of your computer, type something without caring, and make it go viral. But people with alternative views to those of the establishment, like John Mearsheimer, have not been quiet. Is it harder for them to be heard in the mainstream media? Absolutely. When was the last time you read a piece by John in The New York Times or The Washington Post

? P. The New Yorker did two interviews with him and in both cases he got a good one.

Right, right. And the guy who did the interviews, Isaac Chotiner, is known to be a suck-up. But John is a different guy. He almost likes controversy, he loves to be in the middle of it. But yes, I think the debate has degenerated because there are so many passionate beliefs. The NATO expansion people believe that the invasion justifies their position. So when John Mearsheimer comes along and reminds us that NATO expansion would lead to war and that Ukraine would be destroyed by Putin, the insults get very harsh. And the more nuanced part of the debate is drowned out between these two extremes. Yes, I think Steve Walt is right.

P. We can't end without asking you about Taiwan. Despite the many differences, the case of Russia and Ukraine, in which a revanchist power wants to annex by force a neighboring country that it does not recognize and considers a province, has led many analysts to draw parallels with the case of China and Taiwan. To what extent do you think it is useful to conflate the two disputes?

A. Some people who show almost unconditional support for Ukraine make exactly that argument: that the current war goes beyond Ukraine because, depending on how we act, the Chinese will gauge our resolve and conclude that they may or may not attack Taiwan. I hear the same thing all the time. The credibility argument. You have to do something in this conflict because your credibility is at stake. My sense is that the Chinese are much smarter than this. They are not going to think about invading Taiwan based on what the Americans have done in Ukraine. They are going to look at the local circumstances. What capacity do we have to defeat Taiwan? What could the Americans do? Can we defeat them? If not, can we raise the cost so high as to deter them from defending Taiwan? What will be the effect on the global economy? Because this is no longer Mao's China. China is deeply connected to the global economy. An attack on Taiwan would make the markets go crazy. I think they will look at local circumstances. I don't think Ukraine is the element that will make them make a decision. But, of course, if you're someone who considers Ukraine a sacred cause, you'll conflate it with Taiwan and China. I'm not persuaded by that argument.

In his book published in 2015, Conflict in Ukraine: The Unwinding of the Post-Cold War Order, written four-handed with fellow international relations specialist Eugene Rumer, Rajan Menon shuffled through one of the possible future scenarios of the Donbas war that began in 2014: the ceasefire, he wrote, "breaks down and the conflict in eastern Ukraine escalates again and leads to direct Russian military intervention beyond the Donetsk and Lugansk regions; Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and occupies significant parts along the right bank of the Dnieper River, possibly including Kiev, leaving a truncated independent Ukrainian state."

title: EXCLUSIVE-Russia likely to buy yuan on  FX  market in 2023 - sources
text:
*

This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine

By Elena Fabrichnaya

MOSCOW, Dec 22 (Reuters) - Russia will start buying yuan on the currency market next year if oil and gas revenues meet expectations, two sources said, opening a new front in an accelerating dedollarisation drive designed to reduce its dependency on Western finance.

Western sanctions on Moscow over its actions in Ukraine have curbed its use of and access to dollars and euros, and the Chinese currency's role in Russia's economy is growing fast.

Daily yuan-rouble trading volumes on the Moscow Exchange are already exceeding dollar-rouble trades on some days, according to Refinitiv data, a trend set be to accentuated in 2023 as an oil embargo and price cap squeeze Russia's traditional export routes.

Russia stopped intervening on the FX market in February due to restrictions imposed on its use of foreign exchange reserves after it sent tens of thousands of troops into Ukraine.

Interventions will resume next year in yuan, the two sources told Reuters, provided that revenues from oil and gas exports exceed 8 trillion roubles as set out in budget plans.

"The central bank can currently now buy yuan," a banking source close to monetary authorities told Reuters. But the bank would not do so while the government continued, as now, to spend its oil and gas revenues.

"(However), if next year budget revenues from the export of oil and gas exceed 8 trillion roubles, then the central bank will buy yuan," that source added.

Under the budget rule, designed to replenish state reserves, oil and gas revenues above that figure are currently directed to the National Wealth Fund (NWF), which Finance Minister Anton Siluanov has said is equivalent to oil prices of $62-63 a barrel.

The central bank and finance ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Russia has for years adopted conservative fiscal policies and sought to run budget surpluses, but is on course for a deficit of 2% of GDP this year as Moscow ramps up spending to finance its military campaign in Ukraine.

Siluanov's ministry expects 900 billion roubles in additional hydrocarbon revenues next year, though analysts, wary of the impact of export restrictions, are sceptical.

'FRIENDLY' CURRENCY

A senior government source confirmed that FX interventions next year would be in yuan.

"We have a lot of friendly currencies. On the exchange, the Chinese yuan is the most traded currency, it is the friendliest currency so far," the source said.

Russia considers countries that have not joined in with Western sanctions as "friendly".

The banking source said the central bank's operations with yuan would be protected from sanctions and freezing. Russian government assets worth around $300 billion have been frozen since the conflict in Ukraine began.

The government source said a decision about interventions within the framework of the budget rule was needed in order to start accumulating reserves, and as soon as authorities adopted the plan, it would be announced.

At the start of this year, the yuan accounted for 17.1% of Russia's FX and gold reserves, the most recent available data. Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina last week said Russia has sufficient funds in yuan and gold.

The yuan, or renminbi, has already enjoyed a dramatic acceleration into Russia's markets and trade flows, with its share of the currency market reaching 48% in November, MOEX Group said last week, up from less than 1% at the start of the year.

Moscow Exchange, Russia's largest bourse, will expand the range of yuan instruments it offers next year, changes the exchange's head Yuri Denisov said would enable traders to hedge currency risk and increase yuan liquidity.

(Reporting by Elena Fabrichnaya; additional reporting and writing by Alexander Marrow; editing by John Stonestreet)

title: *S&PGR Affirms Czechia At 'AA-' FC; 'AA' LC; Outlook Stable
text:
14 Oct 2022 16:07 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Czechia At 'AA-' FC; 'AA' LC; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- We expect that a sharp slowdown in the eurozone, reduced Russian 
energy supplies to Europe, and high inflation will weigh on the Czech 
Republic's (Czechia's) economic activity in 2023. 
     -- We now project Czechia's inflation will average about 17% in 2022, and 
we expect the economy to stagnate in 2023. 
     -- Despite uncertainty over the evolution of the conflict in Ukraine, 
including heightened risks to Europe's energy supply, we believe Czechia's low 
government debt, solid external financial profile, and strengthening natural 
gas reserve levels provide buffers that can help mitigate these risks. 
     -- We have affirmed our unsolicited 'AA-/A-1+' foreign currency and 
'AA/A-1+' local currency ratings on the Czech Republic and maintained the 
stable outlook. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On Oct. 14, 2022, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 'AA-/A-1+' unsolicited long- 
and short-term foreign currency sovereign credit ratings and its 'AA/A-1+' 
unsolicited long- and short-term local currency sovereign credit ratings on 
the Czech Republic (Czechia). The outlook on both long-term ratings remains 
stable. The transfer and convertibility assessment is 'AA+'. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our view that the buffers provided by Czechia's 
solid government and external balance sheets, including still sizable foreign 
currency reserves, are able to mitigate the adverse macroeconomic impact 
stemming from the Russia-Ukraine conflict. 
 
Downside scenario 
The ratings could come under pressure if: 
     -- The negative impact of the conflict in Ukraine proves more severe than 
we currently expect, hurting economic output while causing budget deficits and 
government debt to soar above our current expectations. 
     -- The supply of energy to Czechia becomes meaningfully constrained, 
preventing the country from sustaining industrial production and leading to a 
much weaker medium-term growth outlook. 
     -- If the Czech National Bank (CNB)  overextends its currency market 
interventions, materially reducing its foreign currency reserves and prompting 
concerns about the credibility of the monetary regime and the effectiveness of 
its execution. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could raise the ratings if, once the effects of the conflict subside, 
Czechia's income levels improve to those of similarly rated sovereigns 
globally. 
 
RATIONALE 
The Russia-Ukraine conflict and the associated shock of stagflation is 
exerting pressure on Czechia's open and industrialized economy through 
multiple channels, such as trade, inflation, energy supply concerns, 
tightening monetary conditions, and weakening business and consumer confidence 
levels. 
 
Domestic demand has held firmly through the first half of 2022, providing 
support to the annual growth forecast, but we anticipate that very high 
inflation will eat into households' purchasing power in the second half of the 
year, thus negatively affecting private consumption and investment. 
 
We expect Czechia's full-year real GDP growth will reach 2.5% in 2022 but will 
stagnate in 2023, compared with our previous projections of 1.8% and 4.0%, 
respectively. We have also raised our annual average inflation forecast to 
16.8% in 2022 and 8.0% in 2023, reflecting global energy and food price 
pressures, a very tight labor market, supply-side bottlenecks, and loosening 
fiscal policies. 
 
Czech inflation, as measured by consumer price inflation, reached a multi-year 
high of 18% year over year in September 2022 and has prompted assertive 
monetary policy actions from the CNB . So far in 2022, the CNB  has hiked its 
policy rate four times from 3.75% at the end of 2021 to the current level of 
7%, with the policy rate kept stable over the past two central bank meetings. 
 
Additionally, the CNB  has intervened intermittently in the foreign currency 
market since March this year in support of the koruna. While the total amount 
of interventions has not been disclosed, we observe a sizable 22% decline (in 
U.S. dollar terms) in the CNB 's foreign currency reserves since March 31, 
2022, which stood at US$135.9 billion on Sept. 31, 2022. Despite this 
decrease, we note that the reserves remain very high by international 
standards, at about 47% of GDP or 8.4 months of imports. 
 
Based on our current macroeconomic assumptions, we think the Czech economy 
will maintain its resilience to the current shock. We base this view on what 
we regard as Czechia's solid economic fundamentals and the temporarily 
improving energy supply outlook on the back of government efforts to secure 
non-Russian natural gas resources, alongside its ample fiscal headroom and 
still sizable foreign currency reserve buffers. More broadly, our assessment 
of the country's strong institutional arrangements and high degree of monetary 
flexibility underpin our view of its credit quality. That said, the country 
reports lower income levels than most sovereigns rated in the 'AA' category, 
which weighs on the ratings. 
 
If the situation in Ukraine broadened to a conflict between NATO  and Russia, 
it would likely lead to substantial downside pressures to the base-case 
economic, balance-of-payments, and fiscal projections published in this 
report, with likely adverse impact on the sovereign creditworthiness. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: High inflation and falling external demand 
will hurt economic growth in 2023 
     -- We currently expect real GDP growth to stagnate in 2023, as domestic 
consumption stalls and external demand drops from a broad-based eurozone 
slowdown. 
     -- We expect energy supplies to remain sufficient through the upcoming 
winter because gas reserves stand almost 90% full, with additional security 
from a leased Dutch liquid natural gas (LNG) terminal. 
     -- The new government will introduce windfall taxation on utilities and 
banks to finance the fiscal costs related to a price cap on energy. 
 
Czechia's economic growth has shown resilience through the first half of this 
year, with year-on-year GDP growth at 3.7% in the second quarter providing a 
solid carryover into the full-year outturn. Behind the headline numbers, a 
substantial part of the strong output was attributable to solid fixed capital 
formation and households tapping into their high savings to support a 
post-pandemic consumption rebound. 
 
We expect contraction of output over the second half of the year as external 
demand and household consumption cool because of the continued increase in the 
cost of living, especially energy prices, and by a tighter monetary policy. We 
project Czechia's real economic growth will slow to 0.15% in 2023 with 
additional significant downside related to the further development of the 
conflict in Ukraine and the direct and indirect repercussions it has on the 
whole of Europe's economy. 
 
As a small and open economy, Czechia's economic development will be hit by 
lower business activity at its main European partners, particularly Germany, 
which receives over 30% of Czech goods exports. We now forecast the euro area 
will expand by just 0.3% in 2023 and Germany will post a mild full-year 
recession of 0.3% next year. 
 
Although Czechia's direct trade exposure is limited, with Ukraine, Russia, and 
Belarus representing a combined 3% of exports and imports, its heavy reliance 
on Russian gas makes it vulnerable to exogenous volatility. Specifically, 
Czechia imports 90% of gas and about 50% of oil from Russia, therefore being 
heavily reliant on energy imported from Russia. Natural gas represents 20% of 
the country's total energy mix, with coal representing 35%, oil 25%, nuclear 
17%, and minor portions of renewables making up the rest. We note that the 
Czech authorities have re-commissioned previously closed coal plants to secure 
the domestic energy supply. 
 
Energy supply concerns are very significant. Any abrupt shortages to natural 
gas or oil supplies would be felt mainly in Czechia's industrial sector and 
materially impact economic activity. Currently, Czechia's gas storage levels 
stand at about 90%, which we believe should cover the upcoming winter months. 
In addition, the authorities have leased a shared LNG terminal in the 
Netherlands that is estimated to reduce the reliance on Russian gas by up to 
one-third. 
 
In terms of oil imports, Czechia has received a temporary exemption for oil 
imports from Russia through the Druzhba pipeline until alternative sources are 
put in place. We understand that the Czech authorities are exploring 
possibilities of increasing the capacity of the Transalpine pipeline, which 
today supplies about 50% of Czechia's oil imports, to remove its dependance on 
Russian hydrocarbons. In the event of disruption to the Druzhba oil flows, we 
understand that the state's strategic oil reserves would suffice for a 90-day 
respite until alternatives sources came on stream. 
 
While event risks to energy supply remain, we do not project the current 
environment will have a permanent negative effect on the Czech economy. For 
now, the country's labor market seems hardly affected. The unemployment rate 
remains around 2.5%, one of the lowest levels in the EU. We do not anticipate 
that in the near term, and in absence of a more abrupt reduction in energy 
supplies, the cooling economic environment will result in any material 
increase in unemployment; but rather help fill the high level of vacancies. 
Furthermore, the inflow of over 400,000 Ukrainian refugees, per October 2023, 
will inevitably result in a boost to exports (Ukrainian refugees are 
statistically considered nonresidents) and government spending, as well as 
provide some relief for the very tight Czech labor market. 
 
We believe the increased inflow of additional EU funds from the next EU 
Multiannual Financing Framework 2021-2027, as well as the Next Generation EU 
Funds (NGEU), will support economic activity. Total EU fund absorption will 
likely exceed 2% of GDP this year and next, given the additional NGEU funds.
