The incumbent government, consisting of two electoral alliances with inherent 
and substantial ideological differences, has remained united and navigated 
various instances of friction throughout the past year. It has recently been 
under pressure to produce mitigating measures that alleviate cost-of-living 
pressures on households from the soaring energy prices, and in September the 
government announced a comprehensive price-capping scheme that will cost an 
estimated 2% of GDP, which the government intends to finance through windfall 
taxation imposed on utilities and banks. 
 
Overall, we view Czechia's institutional capabilities as a credit strength. 
Over the past few years, Czech governments have established a strong record of 
taking a firm pro-EU stance and pro-business policies, while generally 
maintaining fiscal prudence. Importantly, the independence and effectiveness 
of key political and economic institutions, such as the CNB , are not impeded. 
We do not anticipate any near-term challenges to this institutional setup. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: High inflation has prompted a significant 
monetary response from the CNB  in recent months 
     -- Rising energy and food prices are exacerbating already elevated 
inflation, and we expect inflation to average about 17% this year. 
     -- In response, the CNB  has hiked its policy rate to 7% currently from a 
low of 0.25% in May 2021, complemented by meaningful foreign currency market 
intervention in support of the koruna. 
     -- The government will tap into windfall revenue to help finance 
energy-related extraordinary fiscal support measures over 2022-2024. 
 
Despite additional tax revenue on the back of higher nominal economic growth, 
we expect general government deficits will remain elevated over 2022-2023. In 
September 2022, the government announced a Czech koruna 130 billion (2% of 
GDP) fiscal package, comprising predominantly a capping scheme on energy 
prices with the intention to alleviate pressures on households and small 
businesses. The majority of this scheme will be financed by using dividends 
from state companies, as well as income from planned windfall taxes on utility 
entities and banking sector and from emission allowances. The windfall tax on 
utilities will be complementary to the revenue generated from the European 
wide price cap of EUR180 per megawatt hour on wind, solar, and nuclear power 
generation. Any revenue above that will be taken by the government. 
 
We forecast Czechia's fiscal deficit at 4.4% of GDP in 2022 and expect a 
similar level for 2023. Our budgetary projections incorporate multiple revenue 
and spending-side pressures and are still subject to risks. For example, 
refugee-related spending could increase significantly as could military 
spending in light of the commitment to raise the related spending to 2% of GDP 
(1% of GDP in 2020). In addition, the indexation of wages and pensions in line 
inflation will put additional pressure on spending. Hence, we believe that the 
government's budgetary consolidation will be more gradual and delayed compared 
with our previous assessment. 
 
Czechia's relatively low stock of government debt will help the government 
digest the comparatively elevated budget deficits. We forecast the stock of 
government debt will remain stable at around 40% of GDP between 2022 and 2025. 
We project net government debt at about 33% of GDP in 2025, which ranks as one 
of the lowest in the EU. 
 
We expect the Czech government to continue to finance itself predominantly in 
the domestic market. Despite the uptick in government borrowing costs on the 
back of higher interest rates at home and abroad, the favorable maturity and 
currency composition of the debt stock will allow rising interest rates to 
only gradually re-price into the government's interest bill. The average tenor 
of the state's treasury debt is about 6.5 years and the share of foreign 
currency-denominated debt remains a modest 15% of the total. Furthermore, 
strong nominal growth will sustain government tax revenue over 2022-2023. We 
expect the share of interest payments in general government revenue to be 
broadly stable during our forecast horizon through 2025, at about 2.5%. 
 
Inflation has increased rapidly over 2022 and stood at 18.0% in September, up 
from 17.2% in August. We expect full-year a harmonized index of consumer 
prices of 16.8% for 2022. Inflation in Czechia was already elevated before the 
Ukraine conflict, partly due to its tight labor market, and reaching 10% year 
on year already in February. Inflation in the country has therefore exceeded 
that of most Central and Eastern European countries for some time. 
 
The high inflation, combined with external factors forcing many prices up, has 
created a difficult policy environment for the CNB , which has an inflation 
target of 2%. To curb inflation and anchor expectations regarding future 
inflation, the CNB  frontloaded its policy tightening to the first half of 
2022, hiking rates earlier and more rapidly than most other central banks in 
the region. Currently, the main policy rate stands at 7%, having been hiked 
four times in 2022 from 3.75% in December 2021, and compared with 0.25% in May 
2021. The CNB  has kept rates stable over the past two meetings and future rate 
hikes will likely be tied to a situation where wages shoot up materially more 
than CNB  expectations of nominal wage growth of 4.5% for this year, in line 
with the actual developments through the second quarter. 
 
In addition to rate hikes, the CNB  has intervened intermittently in the 
currency markets since March, during a period of heightened exchange rate 
volatility following the onset of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. While the total 
amount of interventions has not been disclosed, we observe a 22% decline (in 
U.S. dollar terms) in the CNB 's foreign currency reserves between March and 
September this year. We consider accentuated use of non-conventional monetary 
policy tools and the magnitude of the interventions as limiting the free 
floating nature of the koruna. That said, we maintain our assessment of the 
strong credibility of the CNB 's monetary policy regime. We expect the 
country's flexible exchange rate will help contain the build-up of external 
imbalances and, in tandem with still sizable official reserves (equivalent to 
47% of GDP), continue to serve as a buffer against external shocks. 
 
We expect the current account to swing into a sizable deficit of 4.6% of GDP 
this year, driven by a deterioration in the terms of trade. We project the 
current account to remain in deficit over the next few years, based on a 
sluggish recovery in exports, along with imports related to EU-funded 
projects. Moreover, we forecast the terms of trade will gradually improve from 
2024, which will help to narrow the current account deficit through 2025. 
 
We consider Czechia's external profile as a rating strength. We project a 
temporary dent to the country's net creditor position in 2022-2023 due to the 
reduction in public external assets, namely its foreign currency reserves, but 
we expect liquid external assets will again exceed external debt in the outer 
years of our forecast. This is because we expect capital account inflows, 
including EU  funds and net foreign direct investment, to exceed current 
account deficits over the 2024-2025, thereby curbing external leverage and 
replenishing foreign currency reserves over the next few years. Nevertheless, 
downside risks to our assessment of the external position could rise if the 
economy's external financial position increased, for example, through rising 
external leverage or rising external financing needs. 
 
The banking sector remains predominately foreign owned, profitable, 
well-capitalized, and funded by domestic deposits. In our view, it poses a 
very limited contingent liability risk for public finances, particularly in 
light of the shift from a bail-out to an effective bail-in regime for the 
majority of banks in the country. We consider that the Czech regulator 
effectively monitors commercial banks under a fairly advanced regulatory 
framework and that it has enough power and independence to enforce regulations 
and implement macroprudential policies. In our view, foreign strategic 
shareholders will remain committed to supporting their Czech subsidiaries if 
needed, thus being a backstop for Czech banks if there are material shocks. 
 
The Czech banking sector performed strongly in 2021, and we expect resilience 
in 2022. While we expect Czech banks to benefit from higher interest income on 
repricing of assets and new loans, debt repayment capacities of households and 
corporates will be tested and ultimately have an impact on credit losses in 
the next 12 months. Similarly, the Russia-Ukraine conflict will likely lead to 
a temporary increase in credit losses because of adverse secondary effects on 
the corporate sector through supply-chain bottlenecks and spikes in commodity 
prices. 
 
That said, the increase in policy rates by the CNB  will translate into higher 
margins for the banking sector and help banks maintain solid profitability, in 
our view, even in the face of recently announced windfall taxation by the 
Czech government. We assume banks to preserve sound profitability, strong 
capitalization, and self-funded natures with high liquidity buffers. Tighter 
financial conditions on capital markets have not hit Czech banks because they 
are mainly funded with loyal customers' deposits.

title: Oil prices fall to pre-Ukraine invasion levels
text:
? Financial markets resent geopolitical tensions in Asia. Electronic screen with the Hang Seng index in Hong Kong.Afp Photo Clara Zepeda Periódico La JornadaFriday, August 5, 2022, p. 24Withthe high risk of recession and galloping inflation in the European Union, driven by energy prices, the price of WTI oil fell 2.3 percent and closed at 88.5 dollars per barrel, below 90 dollars for the first time since February, the month in which Russia intervened militarily in Ukraine

.Brent, meanwhile, fell 3.18 percent to 93.7 dollars per barrel and the Mexican blend fell to 84.20 dollars, the lowest level since February 10.

Oil's losses accelerated on Wednesday after U.S. data showed crude and gasoline stockpiles rose.

Natural gas futures contracts for September lost 11 cents to 8.12 dollars, and gasoline futures expiring in the same month lost 11 cents to 2.79 dollars a gallon.

Meanwhile, the dollar registered significant weakness against its main international crosses, amid geopolitical tensions in Asia, bad economic news in Europe and awaiting employment data in

the United States.Due to the above, the peso closed Thursday with an appreciation of 0.59 percent against its US counterpart, equivalent to 12.08 cents, to end at 20.3413 units per dollar spot (wholesale). According to data from the Bank of Mexico, this is the second consecutive gain of the Mexican currency against the dollar; the peso traded between a high of 20.3910 and a low of 20.2940 units.

The dollar index, the DXY, which measures the performance of the US currency against a basket of six international currencies, registered a 0.73 percent drop to 105.597 units.

The market anticipates that 250 thousand jobs will be created in July, but a lower than expected job creation could cause greater risk aversion, as it would imply a deterioration of the labor market after two quarterly GDP contractions.

Wall Street closed mixed: the Nasdaq ended higher, with a gain of 0.41 percent, at 12,420.58 points, while the Dow Jones fell 0.26 percent to 32,726 units and the S&P 500 increased only 0.08 percent.

Meanwhile, the Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) lost 0.16% to close at 46,916.17 units, affected by the drop in the price of Banco del Bajío (2.59%), Peñoles (2.40) and Grupo México (2.05) shares.

The Bank ofEngland

on Thursday made the highest interest rate increase in 27 years, in order to counteract inflation that is expected to exceed 13 percent annually in October, when the United Kingdom will enter a recession that will last until the end of 2023.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee raised the bank rate by half a point, from 1.25 to 1.75 percent. This is the largest increase since 1995 and brings it to the highest level in 13 years.

This is the sixth consecutive increase in the rate since December last year, in order to combat rising inflation in the country, which already reached 9.4 percent annually in June, a record in 40 years and more than four times the 2 percent target set by the Bank of England, which has triggered strikes, amid the rise in the cost of living, particularly for households with fewer resources.

The central bank forecasts that inflation will reach 13.3 percent in October, the highest level since 1980, mainly due to the rise in energy prices following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

With information from Reuters and Afp

title: At least three killed in 13-missile attack in central Ukraine
text:
KeymomentsKey moments4h agoAt least 358 minors killed in Ukraine since start of conflict17h agoWhat happened in the last hours EL PAÍS offers free of charge the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine as a public service. If you want to support our journalism, subscribe.

At least three people have been killed in a Russian attack with 13 missiles on a military airfield and railroad network in Kirovograd province in central Ukraine, local governor Andriy Raikovich said Saturday. In a televised interview, Raikovich detailed that at least nine Ukrainian soldiers have been injured and that the provincial capital, Kropivnitsky, is currently without electricity due to infrastructure damage. Ukrainian authorities have also denounced a Russian missile attack on the Black Sea port of Odessa, a day after Kiev and Moscow signed two separate agreements with Turkey - with UN mediation and supervision - to resume grain exports from Ukraine. "The enemy has attacked the port of Odessa with cruise missiles. The air defense forces fired two missiles that hit the port infrastructure," the Southern Ukrainian Military Command has warned in a message on the Telegram network.

Latest videos of the invasionKey dates of the conflict: when and how it started. New publications Expansion | Ukraine asks UN to hold Russia to agreement to unblock grainTheUkrainian Foreign Ministry on Saturday asked the United Nations and Turkey to hold Russia to its commitments made yesterday with the signing of an agreement to unblock grain stored in Ukrainian ports. Kiev has denounced this Saturday a missile attack on the port of Odessa, in the south of the country.

The spokesman for the Ukrainian administration in Odessa, Serhi Bratchuk, has assured the portal New Voice of Ukraine that two other missiles were intercepted by the Ukrainian Army's air defense systems. All the projectiles were Kalibr model, used by the Russian forces, the administrator detailed. Earlier, MP Oleksiy Goncharenko had reported that there had been six explosions in the city, as well as the start of a fire in the port.

The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry has condemned the attack. "Russia has taken less than 24 hours to launch a missile attack on the port of Odessa, reneging on its promises and undermining its commitments to the UN and Turkey under the Istanbul agreement," ministry spokesman Oleg Nikolenko lamented on his Twitter account. "In case of non-compliance, Russia will bear the full responsibility for the global food crisis," he lamented. (Agencies)

Kiev denounces Russian missile attack on Odessa port, a day after signing deal to unblock Ukrainian grainUkrainehas denounced on Saturday that Russia has attacked the Black Sea port of Odessa with missiles, a day after Kiev and Moscow signed two separate agreements with Turkey - with UN mediation and supervision - to resume grain exports from Ukraine

."The enemy has attacked the port of Odessa with cruise missiles. The air defense forces fired two missiles, which hit the port's infrastructure," the Military Command of Southern Ukraine has warned in a message on the Telegram network.(Reuters)

Orbán calls for new European war strategy after 'failure' ofsanctionsHungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán said on Saturday that the European Union needs a new strategy to react to the war in Ukraine, as the sanctions adopted against Moscow "have not worked," he said in a speech in Romania. (Reuters)

Borrell: "Spain is in a very good position to help supply gas to the EU "The European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell, advocates that the European Union should prepare "as soon as possible" for a possible cut-off of Russian gas, with savings in consumption, and considers that Spain is in a "very good" position to help supply that energy from other suppliers

."We can't suddenly say, 'Oh, they've cut off our gas!' We have to take measures and those measures are savings measures, but there are measures to increase supply and Spain is in a very good position to help Europe have more gas that is not Russian gas," Borrell said in a telephone interview with Efe. The also Vice President of the European Commission responded in this way when asked about the opposition of Spain and other countries of the community club to the proposal to cut 15% of gas consumption until next spring, which was presented on Wednesday by the President of the Community Executive, Ursula von der Leyen, and which will be discussed by the countries in the extraordinary Energy Council next Tuesday in Brussels.

Borrell pointed out that 37% of the natural gas liquefaction capacities and 40% of the storage of this gas in the EU are in Spain, which long ago began to import from Algeria as opposed to other countries that "relied solely and exclusively on Russian gas".

At least three people were killed in aRussian

missile attack in central UkraineAtleast three people were killed Saturday in a Russian attack with 13 missiles in Kirovograd province in central Ukraine, local governor Andriy Raikovich said. They were two security guards at a power substation and a Ukrainian soldier, Raikovich said in a televised interview. Nine other servicemen were wounded, he added.

The provincial capital, Kropivnitsky, is currently without electricity, according to the governor. Initial reports of the attack suggest that the missiles hit a military airfield and the railroad network. (Reuters)

At least 358 minors killed in Ukraine since start of conflict, says country's prosecutor's officeTheUkrainian prosecutor's office for minors said Saturday that at least 358 children have been killed and around 683 injured in attacks by Russia since the invasion of Ukraine began in late February

.Most of the child casualties, counting killed and wounded, have been recorded in Donetsk region with 361, Kharkov with 194, the capital Kiev region with 116, Chernihiv (68), Lugansk region (54), Kherson (54), Mikolaiv (48), Zaporiyia (40), Sumy (17), and Yitomir (15).

Some 5,110 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and nearly 6,800 injured as a result of the Russian invasion, according to the latest updated balance sheet of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, published last Monday. The UN has recorded, in the same balance sheet, 346 children killed and 547 wounded since the beginning of the war.

However,both the United Nations and the Ukrainian Prosecutor's Office fear that these data are actually lower than the real figures given the difficulty of collecting information during the conflict. (EP)

Erdogan, the balancing act between Kiev and Moscow, achieves a diplomatic victory with the Ukrainian grain agreementTheagreement to unblock the export of grain from Ukraine, signed this Friday in Istanbul, has allowed the Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, to insist that the diplomatic route is the best way to stop the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. But beyond the negotiating table, the Turkish leader is scoring a victory on the international stage as a mediator. After the Russian invasion last February, and while bombs were falling on Ukrainian cities, Turkey postulated itself as mediator between the two actors: Kiev's friend and Moscow's partner. Both turn out to be, for Turkey, of paramount importance. And the conflict between the two has shown that Ankara does not want to tip the balance in favor of either. In fact, while the international community was closing in on Russia and supporting sanctions packages against the Kremlin, Turkey remained neutral and did not follow any guidelines for punishing Moscow. But neither did it forget Ukraine, to which the Turkish arms industry has sold the Bayraktar drones, of utmost importance for Kiev's military objectives and Ankara's diplomatic weapon.

Immersed in a galloping economic crisis, with the lira vanishing day by day and inflation continuing to escalate, Turkey continues to seek friends abroad and wants to assert itself on the international scene. António Guterres, UN Secretary General, has highlighted and thanked Turkey for its role in the achievement of the agreement - in the signing of which he participated - which will allow the distribution of basic foodstuffs to millions of people all over the world. Erdogan, on the other hand, has boasted about hosting the event and recalled that after four months of work -since the first meeting promoted by Ankara- the negotiations are beginning to yield positive results.

Russian troops' supply lines west of the Dnieper River are in danger, says UKInthe last 48 hours, heavy fighting has been raging in the Kherson province of southern Ukraine, where Ukrainian forces are continuing their offensive against Russian occupation, the UK Ministry of Defense highlights Saturday. Supply routes for Kremlin troops west of the Dnieper River are increasingly at risk, adds the latest British intelligence report.

Difficulties in fulfilling deal releasing Ukrainian grain: sailing around mines and distrust of RussiaTwoseparate but symmetrical agreements with Turkey - one signed by Russia and the other by Ukraine, mediated and monitored by the UN - are the hope for unlocking millions of tons of Ukrainian grain, trapped since the Russian invasion last February by the blockade of Ukrainian ports. After weeks of diplomatic negotiations, the pact signed Friday in Istanbul, which envisages an almost cinematic deployment to get the wheat out, provides for the arrival of cargo ships to Ukrainian ports through "safe channels" identified by the Kiev authorities to avoid mines in their territorial waters, guided by Ukrainian pilots, without military escort, but supervised beforehand by Turkish and UN teams to ensure they are not carrying weapons into Ukraine. Moscow has sought to downplay the role of the agreement in alleviating the food crisis aggravated by Russian aggression and its export policies. The Kremlin insists that the problem, which could escalate into a severe famine, has been caused by Western sanctions against Russia over the invasion.

The aim of the deal, which would open a path for significant volumes of commercial food exports from three key Ukrainian ports - Odessa, Chernomorsk and Yuzhny - is to enable Ukraine to export around five million tons of grain per month, a volume similar to that before the full-scale war launched by Russia five months ago, which blocked Ukrainian ports leaving tens of millions of tons of grain in silos and clogged the global supply chain. In addition, Ukrainian authorities have accused Moscow of stealing grain in the territories it has occupied - as an investigation by EL PAÍS showed - and of deliberately bombing Ukrainian fields to set them on fire and thus fuel the global crisis, with great destabilizing potential.

, an engineer next to one of the conveyor belts of the Mlybor granary, in Chernihiv, northern Ukraine, last month.Read the full story here

Putin awakens identity sentiment in UkraineUkraineis a young state that, since it gained its independence 30 years ago, coexists with a neighbor that denies its existence. This neighbor, Russia, has wanted to militarily subdue the former Soviet republic since 2014. Ukrainian national sentiment has been growing exponentially since Vladimir Putin ordered that year the annexation of Crimea and promoted the uprising of the Donbas separatists (in the east). The invasion that began last February has further boosted the population's affinity for a Ukrainian identity, both in the western provinces and in those closest to Russian culture, those in the east.

Andrew Wilson, professor of Ukrainian Studies at University College London, wrote in the latest edition of his acclaimed The ukrainians, unexpected nation (2015, Yale University Press) that Ukrainian national identity is still in the process of construction after centuries of subjection to outside powers-Poland, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, tsarist Russia and the Soviet Union. "Nations are formed by circumstances and opportunities," Wilson wrote. "Ukrainians like to talk about a 'national idea.' Concepts like 'nation' belong to the realm of political and cultural imagination," this scholar reflected. Putin, according to his thesis, has been the determining circumstance in building the new Ukrainian citizen.

Macron and Al Sisi discuss Ukraine, Middle East and IranThePresidents of France and Egypt, Emmanuel Macron and Abdelfatah al Sisi, today discussed the threat to food security created by the war in Ukraine, the situation in the Middle East and the Iranian nuclear program. The two leaders met today at the Elysee, without making statements, in their first meeting after Macron's re-election last April. The consequences of the war in Ukraine, especially the threat to international food security, were among the main issues they discussed, the Elysee said in a statement. Egypt is a grain-importing country, so it has been hit hard by the international price increases of recent months.

After Macron has recently received in Paris the Israeli prime minister and the Palestinian National Authority, the situation in the Middle East was another topic discussed. The two presidents also discussed the Iranian nuclear program, about which the director general of the UN atomic agency, Rafael Grossi, was "alarmed" this week by Tehran's recent claims about its progress towards the possibility of building nuclear weapons. Cooperation in the fight against terrorism and the situation in Libya were other topics discussed. On Libya, Macron and Al Sisi agreed to continue working to restore the unity and sovereignty of that country, neighboring Egypt, after the long period of instability and civil war it has suffered.

EFE agency reports.

Zelenski, on the agreement to export grain: "It is possible to avoid a global catastrophe, a famine that could lead to political chaos "The Ukrainian President, Volodymir Zelenski, expressed his satisfaction for the agreement reached this Friday in Istanbul, since it could unblock the export of grain from the country, stranded in the ports due to the war. "It is possible to avoid a global catastrophe, a famine that could lead to political chaos in many countries of the world, particularly in the countries that help us," he said. In his address via social networks tonight, Zelenski indicated that about 20 million tons from last year's harvest and also from this fiscal year's harvest could be exported. "These are revenues for farmers, for the entire agricultural sector and for the national budget. These are jobs," he said. "There is a possibility to reduce the severity of the food crisis caused by Russia," Zelenski stressed.

The agreement reached today will allow exporting from three Ukrainian ports - Odessa, Pivdennyi and Chornomorsk - about 22 million tons of wheat, corn and other grain stored in silos, which could not be sold due to the Russian naval blockade. Russia and Ukraine are world grain exporters and together, they sell a third of the world's wheat supply. This is the first major agreement between the two warring countries since the Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24 and is expected to ease a crisis forged by the Russian naval blockade of Ukraine and Western sanctions on Russia, which have also driven up fertilizer and energy prices.

EFE agency reports.

Ensuring pricestabilityInflation is too high. Russia's war in Ukraine has pushed up the cost of energy and agricultural products. Shortages of materials, equipment and labor resulting from the pandemic are also contributing to higher prices, which is hurting citizens and businesses across the euro zone, especially those with low incomes.

Much of this inflation is due to factors that central banks cannot control, but what we can do is ensure that inflation does not become persistent. This is what could happen if price increases spread throughout the economy and people start to expect higher inflation in the future. In such a case, wage and price spirals of the kind that have historically led to inflation spiraling out of control could be generated.

An opinion of Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank.

Lithuania reintroduces rail transit of goodsa KaliningradLithuaniaon Friday resumed allowing unrestricted transit of non-military goods by rail between Russia and its Kaliningrad enclave bordering Poland and the Baltic country. Vilnius thus complies with the protocol agreed by the European Commission, which states that sanctions only apply for goods transported by road.

Vilnius had been preventing the transit of several sanctioned goods between Russia and its enclave since June, which aroused the ire of Moscow, which accused Lithuania of breaching the treaties signed between the two countries regulating transit to and from Kaliningrad. Moscow can now return to transporting cement, timber and alcohol to its territory. The organization, which legally assists victims of political repression in Russia, said it had calculated the figure between March 4 and July 14, based on Russian Interior Ministry data. "On average, Russian police issue 35 files for discrediting the army every working day," the NGO said via its Telegram account.

The offense, which came into force in March to silence criticism of the offensive in Ukraine, carries fines of up to 100,000 rubles (€1,700) for an individual and up to 1 million rubles for a legal entity. According to the specialized NGO OVD-Info, about 200 people who have denounced the intervention in Ukraine were prosecuted in Russia in criminal cases, which carry very harsh prison sentences. On July 8, a Moscow city councilor, Alexei Gorinov, was sentenced to seven years in prison for "spreading false information" about the Russian military after publicly condemning the attack on Ukraine.

US announces new $270 million military package to UkraineThePentagon on Friday announced a new $270 million military aid package to Ukraine. Of that figure, $100 million will be earmarked for the purchase of an additional 580 Phoenix Ghost drones. This class of unmanned vehicles can fly for six hours and is designed for ground targets with unreinforced armor. More than a hundred Phoenix Ghost drones were sent to Ukraine last April for use in the battle for the Donbas region. In addition, four more HIMARS multiple missile launcher systems will be sent, bringing the total delivered to Ukraine to 20.

Pentagon spokesman John Kirby said that the U.S. Defense Department is conducting "preliminary explorations" into the possibility of delivering fighter jets to Ukraine, an option so far ruled out by Washington in view of the possibility of an escalation of the direct conflict by Russia. However, he has indicated, if it were to happen, "it would not be executed in the short term."

title: The problem with the current Russian sanctions regime
text:
Five months have passed since Europe and the United States imposed harsh economic and financial sanctions on Russia, a G20 country that was the world's 11th largest economy on the eve of its invasion of Ukraine. Although the sanctions have been gradually tightened in the intervening months, the debate over their effectiveness, the broader implications of the war for global markets and the global economy, and what the West's next steps should be, is intense.

On the first question, while the sanctions have been less effective than Europe and the United States expected, they are also proving more onerous than the Kremlin claims. Russia's Central Bank expects GDP to contract by 8-10% this year, while other forecasts predict a larger drop, along with more lasting damage to growth potential. Imports and exports have been severely disrupted, and foreign investment inflows have come to a virtual halt. Shortages are multiplying, pushing inflation up. At this point, the country no longer has a properly functioning foreign exchange market.

The sanctions would have been much tougher if the West had not opted for a carve-out of the Russian energy sector, and if many more countries had joined the United States and Europe in the effort. Since that did not happen, Russia has not felt as much pressure as it would have. Moreover, it has been able to continue to trade through various side and back doors that are likely to become increasingly important as long as the sanctions regime, as currently designed, continues.

However, it is only a matter of time before the Russian economy takes a bigger hit. Inventories of imported goods - including many critical technological and industrial inputs - are declining rapidly, and many sectors are becoming less resilient. The cumulative damage to the Russian economy will be significant and long-lasting, a fact that has not yet been fully captured by consensus medium-term forecasts.

The second issue concerns the overall effects of the war and the sanctions regime. Most observers agree that the Russian invasion has increased not only energy but also food insecurity, highlighting the consequences of the disruption of Ukrainian agricultural exports. However, there remains much debate about the West's use of the nuclear economic sanctions option: the restrictions imposed on the Russian central bank and on Russia's use of the international payments system.

These curbs are far more intrusive than the usual combination of restrictions on sanctioned government and private sector trade and financial transactions by individuals. However, because they are not subject to internationally agreed standards, guidelines or controls, they fall outside the purview of the relevant global governance bodies, such as the Bank for International Settlements, the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization.

In times of war, this kind of oversight might seem like a detail. But some worry that sanctions could significantly reduce the role of the dollar as the world's reserve currency and the role of the U.S. financial system as the main global intermediary for other countries' savings and investments. After all, there is no doubt that a growing number of countries now feel more vulnerable to the reach of U.S. sanctions.

But it is impossible to replace something with nothing, which means that there will be no significant loss of the dollar or U.S. financial primacy in the foreseeable future. Rather, the sanctions will give further impetus to the gradual process of global economic fragmentation, which was also fueled a few years ago by the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration. More countries now have even more reason to seek greater financial resilience and inherently inefficient forms of self-insurance.

This brings us to the third debate. With no end to the war in sight, what should the West do next? Fearing the implications for energy prices and gas supplies to Europe, many in the West are tempted to call for a moratorium on any new sanctions, or even to make further exceptions. Others, however, favor additional measures to hold Russia accountable for its indiscriminate attacks on the Ukrainian civilian population.

In any case, maintaining the current sanctions regime is not without its problems, due to the dual objectives of pressuring Russia and limiting economic disruption in Europe. Moreover, as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen recently said, it gives the feeling that Russia is "blackmailing" Europe with the threat of disrupting gas supplies at any time. No wonder the Commission is urging member countries to reduce consumption by 15%.

With the current sanctions regime, the West risks falling between two horses. While easing sanctions could help alleviate concerns about Europe's economic prospects, this option is not viable given the atrocities being committed by Russian forces in Ukraine. But if the West is serious about pressuring Russia through truly crippling economic and financial sanctions, it needs to make a U-turn and remove the energy cuts.

Doing so would undoubtedly have a serious short-term economic impact on European economies and the rest of the world, amplifying the "small fires everywhere" syndrome I warned about in May. It is therefore critical that governments use the fiscal space available to them to provide targeted support to vulnerable segments of the population, as well as to fragile countries; and multilateral agencies should support developing countries through aid and a more operational debt relief framework. If done well, this option would yield better results in the medium and long term than the current strategy.

If pursued, it risks the worst of all possible worlds. It is not enough to deter Russia from continuing its illegal war; it is fueling further fragmentation of the international monetary system; and it is not even protecting Europe from a winter gas disruption.

title: Euro traded below the dollar for the first time in two decades
text:
? The EU currency fell to its worst level due to fears of economic recession in Europe and uncertainty in the supply of Russian gas.Photo Ap Clara Zepeda Periódico La JornadaThursday, July 14, 2022, p. 17Theeuro broke the one dollar level for the first time in two decades, falling to 0.9998 dollars, before recovering to trade at 1.0061. This is the worst level for the continent's currency since December 2002. The situation could worsen if the energy price shock triggered by the conflict in Ukraine pushes the bloc into a protracted economic crisis.

This comes as fears of an economic recession in Europe are growing in the markets, against a backdrop of high inflation and increasing uncertainty about the continuity of Russian gas supplies.

Gone are the years when the euro was so strong (1.6 times the dollar during the 2008 global financial crisis) that many Europeans went on vacation to the United States because of the low prices in hotels and food, and returned home with suitcases full of electronics and clothes. But now the situation is completely different, with Europe suffering the economic consequences of the war in Ukraine and the decision of the European Central Bank (ECB) to maintain interest rates.

Thus, there is concern that this crisis could cause a recession with unsuspected consequences, a shadow that intensified on Monday with the reduction of Russian gas supplies and the concern that inflation will continue to rise.

According to analysts, the EU currency has lost ground against the U.S. currency since 2021, but this was accentuated after Russia's intervention in Ukraine, taking into account the low economic growth in the euro zone and a less restrictive central bank, which has also caused distrust in the euro.

title: Ukraine  raises rates to 25% in first  central bank intervention  since Russian invasion
text:
The board of the National Bank of Ukraine has decided on Thursday to raise the benchmark interest rate to 25% per annum from the 10% at which it had kept the price of money anchored since before the start of the Russian invasion at the end of last February.

The institution has explained that its decision is aimed at protecting households' hryvnia income and savings, increasing the attractiveness of assets denominated in the Ukrainian currency, reducing pressure on the foreign exchange market and thus improving the institution's ability to maintain exchange rate stability and curb inflationary processes during the war.

"The development of inflation requires the National Bank of Ukraine to return to active interest rate policy to prevent further deterioration of inflation expectations and dollarization of the economy," the institution has noted.

Thus, it has pointed out that, after considering several scenarios, it decided to increase the rate by 15 percentage points, thinking that a slight increase "would not have had a significant influence on the financial and economic system", as the monetary transmission mechanism has a limited effect in wartime, while it would have given rise to expectations of further rate hikes, in addition to the fact that, to revive interest in hryvnia assets, their yield must exceed the expected inflation rates.

Separately, the National Bank of Ukraine has reported an increase in the scope of its foreign exchange interventions in defense of the country's currency, noting that it raised foreign exchange sales from a monthly average of $2 billion (€1.87 billion) in March-April to $3.4 billion (€3.18 billion) in May.

The governor of the National Bank of Ukraine, Kyrylo Shevchenko, has defended the bank's decision not to take any monetary policy measures so far as he believes that due to "strong psychological pressure caused by the war,changing rates would not be enough to stabilize expectations and accumulate and hold assets in hryvnias."

To this end, in the first months of the war, the bank directed its monetary policy measures primarily to ensuring the uninterrupted functioning of the banking system and payments in the economy.

title: UPDATE 2-Putin hikes Russian pensions, plays down Ukraine impact on economy
text:
(Adds Siluanov estimate of cost of measures, paragraph 13)

LONDON, May 25 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin ordered 10% rises on Wednesday in pensions and the minimum wage to cushion Russians from inflation, but denied the country's economic problems were all linked to the war in Ukraine.

With annual inflation near 18% last month, the Kremlin leader acknowledged that 2022 would be a "difficult" year for the Russian economy.

"When I say 'difficult', it doesn't mean all these difficulties are connected to the special military operation," Putin told a televised meeting of the State Council in Moscow.

"Because in countries that aren't conducting any operations - say, overseas, in North America, in Europe - inflation is comparable and, if you look at the structure of their economies, even more than ours."

His comments ignored the fact that rising inflation in Western economies is in part a direct consequence of Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven up prices for energy and food around the world.

The pension increase comes into effect from June 1, while the minimum wage hike kicks in on July 1. Analysts said the steps would not prevent a sharp fall in real incomes.

Putin -- whose approval rating has jumped more than 10 points since the start of the Ukraine campaign to 82%, according to the independent Levada Centre's April poll -- pledged in March to reduce poverty and inequality this year despite crippling Western sanctions and high inflation.

The Russian economy has been rocked by an unprecedented barrage of Western sanctions imposed over his decision to send troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, with consumer prices soaring and foreign companies quitting Russia en masse as trade becomes near-impossible.

The Research and Expert Review Institute of the bank VEB said the increase in social payments would slow but not prevent a decline in Russians' real incomes, wages and pensions - after inflation is taken into account.

Even with a 10% increase in the minimum wage and retirement pensions, VEB expects Russians' real disposable incomes to fall by 7.5% and real wages to drop nearly 6% this year. VEB also expects poverty to rise to 12.6% this year from 11% in 2021.

Russia's minimum wage currently stands at 13,890 roubles ($250) a month, while the average retirement pension amounts to 18,521 roubles per month.

The increase in wages and pensions may add to the inflation pressures that the central bank tried to cap with an emergency rate hike to 20% in late February, as the rouble's foreign exchange value plunged. It has cut its rate twice since then as the rouble has recovered.

Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said the measures would cost the federal budget around 600 billion roubles ($10.5 billion) this year and about 1 trillion roubles in 2023.

On Thursday, the central bank is set to hold an out-of-schedule policy meeting, where analysts expect it to slash the benchmark interest rate from 14% back towards the 9.5% where it stood before the intervention in Ukraine.

(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Mark Trevelyan and Kevin Liffey)

Italy proposes at the United Nations a gradual plan to achieve peace in UkraineItalian Chancellor Luigi Di Maio presented the plan at the UN. Photo: EFE/Georg Wendt...

Italy, through its Chancellor Luigi Di Maio, delivered to UN Secretary General António Guterres a four-step plan to restore peace in Ukraine.

In its first point, the plan drawn up by the Italian Foreign Ministry foresees a ceasefire, which "should be accompanied by mechanisms of supervision and demilitarization of the front line", the Italian newspaper La Repubblica published in its digital version. The second point is the neutrality of Ukraine, which has to be backed by an international political "guarantee" and will be discussed within the framework of a peace conference.

The territorial issue, which envisages the status of the Crimean peninsula and the Donbas region, constitutes the third section of the Italian plan, while the last part proposes to elaborate a new multilateral agreement on peace and security in Europe.

More Ukrainian soldiers surrendered at Mariupol steelworksUkrainian soldiers who have surrendered were sent to a prison campon. Photo: Russian Defense Ministry press service via AP.

Russia announced Thursday that a total of 1,730 Ukrainian servicemen who were entrenched at the Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol surrendered this week, following a battle that has become emblematic in this war that has been raging for nearly three months.

About 1,000 fighters were taken to a prison camp on Ukrainian soil under Russian control in the Donetsk region. Read more

Ten civilians were killed and seven others wounded in two towns in Ukraine's Donetsk region, part of the Donbas, in shelling by the Russian military in recent hours, the head of the regional military administration, Pavlo Kyrylenko, told Interfax Ukraine on Thursday.

"On May 18 the Russians killed ten civilians in the Donbas, seven in Lyman and three in Bakhmut. Among the dead were two children. Another seven people were wounded today," Kyrylenko said, adding that "it is impossible to establish the exact number of victims in the occupied towns of Mariupol and Volnovakha."

Russia will reopen Ukrainian ports only if sanctions are liftedRussia will reopen access to Ukrainian ports, whose blockade threatens to provoke a global food crisis, only if Western countries lift sanctions against Russian exports

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko told the Interfax agency that the first cause of the food crisis is "the sanctions imposed on Russia by the United States and the European Union, which hinder freedom of trade, particularly in foodstuffs such as wheat, feritilizers and others."

"Therefore, if our partners want a solution, it is necessary to solve the problems connected with the lifting of restrictions imposed on Russian exports," the deputy foreign minister added.

Prosecutor's office demands life imprisonment for Russian soldier tried for war crimesThe Ukrainian prosecutor's office asked for a life sentence for the Russian soldier on trial for shooting a 62-year-old man in the head through his car window in Sumy, a village in northeastern Ukraine.

Private Vadim Shishimarin, during the trial against him, testified that he acted on orders from a superior who insisted that the man, who was talking on a cell phone, might be divulging his location to others.

19.05.2022

George Bush wanted to condemn Russia, but confused the war in Ukraine with the one in IraqFormer President George W. Bush made a mistake in condemning Russia. Photo: Reuters/Kevin Lamarque/file photo.

Former U.S. President George Bush made an unusual "gaffe" that is sure to haunt him for a while: he called the Russian invasion of Iraq "totally unjustified and brutal," although he quickly rectified himself and said he was talking about Ukraine.

In a speech on Wednesday, Bush, 75, seemed to realize what he had said and after correcting himself quietly added "Iraq too," which drew laughter from the audience. Read more

Parliament calls for special court for Russian crimes in Ukraine The European Parliament on Thursday came out in favor of establishing a special international tribunal to try the "crime of aggression perpetrated against Ukraine by the political leadership and military commanders of Russia and its allies."

MEPs believe that since the International Criminal Court has no jurisdiction over the crime of aggression in this situation (because neither Ukraine nor the Russian Federation has ratified the Rome Statute), "this lacuna should be addressed by setting up a special international tribunal."

The deputies called on the European institutions "to support the creation without delay of an appropriate legal basis (...) to enable the establishment of this tribunal" and to provide "all the human and budgetary resources and administrative, investigative and logistical support necessary for the establishment of this tribunal."

19.05.2022

UK sanctions major Russian airlines Aeroflot is one of the airlines sanctioned by the UK. Photo credit: Reuters/Maxim Shemetov/File image.

The British government announcedon Thursday imposed new sanctions against major Russian airlines, including Aeroflot, banning them from reselling their slots in retaliation for the invasion of Ukraine.

Aeroflot, Ural Airlines and Rossiya Airlines will not be allowed to sell their slots - which they are no longer allowed to use at British airports - estimated at £50 million ($62 million), it said in a statement.

The UK had already closed its airspace to Russian aircraft shortly after the invasion of Ukraine on February 24, as well as its ports to Russian ships, and had banned the export of goods and technology to the Russian air sector.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (Cicr) began registering prisoners of war evacuated from the Azovstal steel mill, including the wounded, at the request of both sides, the Committee said in a note detailing that it has so far registered "hundreds" of them.The registration operation began on Tuesday and continued today. The recognition process includes a module with personal data, such as date of birth and next of kin.? "This information allows Cicr to follow those who have been captured and help them to remain in contact with their families," the note states. The question remains as to where the Ukrainian prisoners are taken once they have been registered.

The first soldier on trial in Ukraine for war crimes asked for "forgiveness" Thursday before a Kiev court as he detailed how he killed a civilian at the start of the Russian invasion.

"I know you won't be able to forgive me, but I ask for forgiveness anyway," 21-year-old Russian sergeant Vadim Shishimarin told the wife of the 62-year-old man he admitted killing in northeastern Ukraine on February 28.

Russia is ready to resume negotiations with Ukraine if Kiev expresses its readiness to do so, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko said Thursday.

"It was not us who interrupted the negotiation process, it was paused by our Ukrainian partners. As soon as they express readiness to return to the negotiating table, we will naturally respond in the affirmative," he told the Russian press, quoted by the Interfax agency.

According to the Russian top diplomat, "the important thing is that there is something to talk about". The day before the Kremlin stated that at the moment negotiations between Moscow and Kiev are completely stopped due to Ukraine's "absolute unwillingness".

In a speech to a group of young Turks, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan accused the two Nordic nations, especially Sweden, of being a "hotbed of terror, the home of terror''. The video of the conversation was made public on Thursday.

Erdogan's objections stem from Turkey's complaints that Stockholm, and to a lesser extent Helsinki, would support the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, and an armed group in Syria that Ankara considers an extension of the PKK. It also accuses them of harboring followers of U.S.-based Muslim cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom the country blames for being behind a 2016 coup attempt.

Turkey's yes is crucial for Sweden and Finland's membership in the military alliance because the decision must be unanimous. Each of its 30 members can veto the entry of other candidates.

- Russia digs in in southern Ukraine and prepares for a long war.

- Ukrainian surrender at the Azovstal steelworks (Mariupol).

22:10 Biden to sign additional $100 million in Ukraine security assistance U.S. President Joe Biden may sign $100 million in military aid to Ukraine today, Thursday, including additional artillery munitions and counter-artillery battery radars. This is a new request as part of a series of transfers to help Kyiv repel Russia's invasion, according to two sources briefed on the matter

21:40 Call between U.S. and Russian Chiefs of General Staff on Ukraine Russia's Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov and Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Mark Milley held a phone call, RIA news agency has reported Thursday, citing the Russian Defense Ministry. They discussed issues of "mutual interest," including Ukraine, the cited agency said. 21:10 G7 finance ministers want to help Ukraine financially The finance ministers of the G7 countries, the world's most industrialized, want to help Ukraine financially to ensure its ability to make payments in the wake of the direct consequences of the Ukrainian war. Germany's Finance Minister, the liberal Christian Lindner, said today, Thursday, that his country will help Ukraine with 1 billion euros after deliberating with his G7 counterparts at the Petersberg Hotel in Königswinter, outside Bonn.

20:39 At least 12 killed in Russian shelling of Severodonetsk At least 12 people were killed and 40 others wounded today Thursday in Russian shelling of the eastern Ukrainian city of Severodonetsk, which is almost surrounded by Moscow forces, the regional governor said this evening. On the second day of the trial, Sgt. Vadim Chichimarine, 21, came face to face with the widow of Oleksandr Chelipov, a 62-year-old civilian he admitted to shooting dead on Feb. 28 in northeastern Ukraine. 19:46 BRICS support negotiations with Ukraine and sending UN aid The foreign ministers of the BRICS forum countries (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) today supported "negotiations between Russia and Ukraine". Also the UN efforts to send humanitarian aid to the latter country. This was expressed in a joint statement after the virtual meeting held by the five ministers of the group, where they also discussed "their concerns about the humanitarian situation in and around Ukraine".

19:38 First Russian soldier on trial for war crimes "asks for forgiveness" The Russian soldier at the center of the first organized war crimes trial in Ukraine "asked for forgiveness" Thursday from the widow of the Ukrainian civilian he killed, in a moving exchange in a Kiev court. 19:29 Feijóo condemns Putin's "warlike excesses" in a meeting with the leader of the Belarusian opposition The national president of the Popular Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, on Thursday conveyed to the leader of the Belarusian democratic opposition, Svetlana Tijanóvskaya, the support and firm commitment of the PP to democracy, freedom and peace in the countries around the former Soviet Union. The representative was expelled from her country since August 2020 for political reasons. "I have conveyed to her our commitment to democracy, peace and freedom, as well as our condemnation of Putin's war excesses and our support for those who suffer the cruelty of war," Feijóo said on Twitter.

19:20 Scholz is confident that Sweden and Finland will join NATO German Chancellor Olaf Scholz said today that he is confident that Sweden and Finland will succeed in joining the NATO defense alliance and that Germany is doing everything possible to make it happen. At a press conference with his Dutch counterpart, he reiterated that Germany took a good look at the Nordic countries' offers and said he had the impression that many other countries shared his view. "If you identify a general will, then it is that Sweden and Finland should quickly become members, so I am confident that the many efforts being made to enable a joint decision will succeed," he said.

19:11 McDonald's finds buyer for its Russian restaurants McDonald's has started the process of selling its restaurants in Russia after more than 30 years in the country. The Chicago-based burger giant has secured Alexander Govor, who operates 25 restaurants in Siberia, agreed to buy 850 Russian McDonald's restaurants and operate them under a new name. And is that the company said Monday that it would leave Russia after the invasion of Ukraine. The sale agreement is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close within a few weeks, McDonald's said.

19:02 G7 countries commit $18.4 billion in funds for Ukraine: draft The Group of Seven (G7) industrialized nations have committed $18.4 billion in transfers and loans to help Ukraine meet its immediate financial needs, according to a draft communique accessed by Reuters on Thursday. "We have mobilized $18.4 billion of budget support, including $9.2 billion of recent commitments in the run-up to the Petersberg meeting, to help Ukraine close its financing gap and continue to ensure the delivery of basic services to the Ukrainian people," the text said.

18:52 U.S. aims to arm Ukraine with anti-ship missiles The White House is working to put advanced anti-ship missiles in the hands of Ukrainian fighters to help defeat Russia's naval blockade. These are reports from officials to Reuters. Ukraine has made no secret that it wants more advanced U.S. capabilities beyond its current inventory of artillery, Javelin and Stinger missiles, and other weapons. Kyiv's list, for example, includes missiles that could draw the Russian navy away from its Black Sea ports, allowing it to restart shipments of grain and other agricultural products around the world.

18:43 Russia vows to take all of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk A senior Kremlin official said Thursday that Russia intends to take all of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk regions, according to Bloomberg reports.

18:38 Azovstal counts down the hours before falling into the hands of the Russian Army The Azovstal steel mill is a clear symbol of Ukraine's resistance to Russia's military campaign. But now it is counting down the hours before it falls completely into the hands of the enemy Army, which continues to shell the plant to force the last fighters to surrender after the departure of 771 other fighters from the plant. In all, 1,730 Azovstal defenders surrendered in the last three days in the port city of Mariupol, according to Russian military spokesman Major General Igor Konashenkov.

18:29 Biden to sign additional $100 million in Ukraine security assistance U.S. President Joe Biden may sign $100 million in military aid to Ukraine today, Thursday, including additional artillery ammunition and counter-artillery battery radars. It is a new request as part of a series of transfers to help Kyiv repel Russia's invasion, according to two Sources briefed on the matter.

18:21 Lavrov briefs BRICS on Russian military campaign in Ukraine Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov briefed his counterparts from the BRICS countries on Russia's military campaign in Ukraine today, Thursday, during a ministerial meeting of the group comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. "Lavrov reported in detail on the main aspects of the development of the situation in Ukraine within the framework of the special military operation," reads the Foreign Ministry statement sent today, Thursday.

18:13 ' Europe, Europe', the analysis of the continent convulsed by the Ukrainian war "What are we talking about when we talk about Europe? Again that question with as many answers as there are interlocutors. If only it were as easy as drawing an equal sign in mathematics. Answers, moreover, fleeting, because they soon cease to be valid. Europe as a cursed puzzle, as a well-intentioned projection, abyss and paradise in the same space, solution and problem, model and counter-example", Marta Rebón reviews in La Vanguardia the complicated dynamics that have transformed Europe and how the old continent is responding to the war in Ukraine initiated by a Russia increasingly distant from the West.

18:03 G7 finance ministers want to help Ukraine financially The finance ministers of the G7 countries, the world's most industrialized, want to help Ukraine financially to ensure its ability to pay in the wake of the direct consequences of the Ukrainian war. Germany's Finance Minister, the liberal Christian Lindner, said today, Thursday, that his country will help Ukraine with 1 billion euros after deliberating with his G7 counterparts at the Petersberg Hotel in Königswinter, outside Bonn.

The call came six days after a telephone conversation between the two countries' defense ministers, the first since Russia launched what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine.

17:45 Erdogan declares Sweden "a nest of terrorists" and rules out allowing it to join NATO Recall that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Thursday that "Sweden is a nest of terrorists" and that "there is no place for terrorists in a security organization," referring to the Nordic country's request to join NATO. Erdogan has been forceful in a message to Stockholm, which he accuses of giving asylum to militants of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), at war with the Turkish government and also to the fugitives of Fethullah Gülen's brotherhood.

17:36 At least 12 killed in Russian shelling of Severodonetsk At least 12 people were killed and 40 others wounded today Thursday in Russian shelling of the eastern Ukrainian city of Severodonetsk, almost surrounded by Moscow forces, the regional governor said this afternoon. The Russians "started shelling the regional center in the morning randomly with heavy weapons. The shelling is continuing", Serguiï Gaïdaï, regional governor, indicated via the social network Telegram.

17:28 Russia demands Slovenia to withdraw four diplomats from embassy Russia on Thursday demanded Slovenia to withdraw four members of its diplomatic staff from the embassy in Moscow. It also demands that they leave the country within ten days, the Russian Foreign Ministry has reported. Russian diplomacy handed over to the chargé d'affaires of the Slovenian legation "a notification with a demand to reduce the number of diplomatic staff by four persons within ten days," an official statement issued today reads.

17:19 U.S. poised to release $40 billion for Ukraine The U.S. Congress is preparing today to release a $40 billion package for Ukraine, a sign of Joe Biden's promised support for Kyiv. "The Ukraine aid package is more than just charity," Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell defended today. "American security and strategic interests will be determined by the outcome of this conflict," he insisted a few hours before a vote in the upper house of Congress, which should approve this funding, if there is no (unlikely) surprise.

17:10 Life sentence demanded for Russian soldier on trial for war crimes Ukraine's prosecutor's office on Thursday demanded life imprisonment, the maximum sentence, against the first Russian soldier on trial for war crimes in Kyiv. The serviceman is accused of killing a civilian in late February. Speaking on the second day of the trial, the prosecutor asked the court to pronounce "a sentence of life imprisonment" for Vadim Chichimarine, 21, according to an AFP journalist present in the courtroom. To know more: The first Russian soldier tried in Ukraine apologizes to his widow.

Biden says Finland and Sweden meet all requirements to join NATO U.S. President Joe Biden today insisted on his "resounding support" for Finland and Sweden's applications to join NATO, defending that they "meet all the requirements to join" the Alliance. In addition, Biden announced that today he will begin the process for the U.S. Congress to ratify the applications of these Nordic countries to join the Atlantic Alliance. He said this at a press conference at the White House together with his Finnish counterpart, Sauli Niinistö, and the Swedish Prime Minister, Magdalena Andersson.

16:53 Johnson and Zelenski study routes for Ukrainian grain outlets British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski discussed possible new routes for Ukrainian grain exports on Thursday. The aim is to combat the boom in food prices caused by falling supply. Faced with the blockade of Black Sea ports following the invasion by Russian troops, the two leaders "explored options for opening critical sea and land supply routes for Ukrainian grain stocks," Downing Street said in a statement today.

16:44 First Russian soldier on trial for war crimes "begs forgiveness" The Russian soldier at the center of the first war crimes trial staged in Ukraine "begged forgiveness" Thursday from the widow of the Ukrainian civilian he killed, in a moving exchange in a Kiev courtroom.
