title: Russia sanctioned? The global economic dimension of the conflict in Ukraine
text:
Last February 24, Russia launched a "special military operation" in Ukraine, escalating a conflict that quickly unleashed the intervention of the "West", under the leadership and coordination of NATO. On the same day, the Ukrainian government called for economic sanctions that would come only a few days later.Instrumented by the United States and Europe, they were applied with many hesitations and tensions, due to the fear that they would produce a "boomerang effect" on the countries of the old continent, mainly in the supply of raw materials from Russia.

Five days after the start of the large-scale armed conflict, on March 1, the USTreasury Department announced a ban on all transactions with the Russian Central Bank, while the European Union officially announced a list of Russian banks to be excluded from the SWIFT financial communications system. VTB Capital Bank PJSC, Bank Rossiya, Bank Otkritie, Novikombank, Promsvyazbank PJSC, Sovcombank PJSC and the Russian Development Bank - VEB.RF appeared on the list. This last entity had been named by the Western powers as the "nuclear option" of the financial sanctions (El Cronista, 01/03/2022).

At the same time, the freezing of the Russian Central Bank's assets abroad was established. As a consequence, the Russian currency plummeted nearly 30% against the US dollar. In this scenario, the French Minister of Economy, Bruno Le Maire, stated: "We are waging a total economic and financial war against Russia, Putin and his government, and let us be clear, the Russian people will also pay the consequences". The Ukrainian president, Volodomir Zelensky, celebrated the decision by stating that the financial sanctions carried out meant the "disconnection from global financial civilization" (Financial Times, 04/03/2022).

While the Russian Federation received sanctions of all kinds, the Republic of Ukraine placed new bonds on the markets to finance the war and received immediate assistance of US$ 1.4 billion from the IMF. In other words, the economic and financial assistance to the Caucasus country were the first maneuvers of the "West" to sustain the conflict and project it over time. The first assistance was economic, the second of mercenaries ("volunteers") and, finally, arms. Three staggered contributions in a conventional war in which Germany and the United States, key players in the leadership of NATO, do not wish, for various reasons, to enter directly, that is to say, with "their own troops".

The financial war is not only decreed by governments.The economic "sanctions" did not come only from the hand of the States. Dozens of global companies from all sectors of the economy, mainly of U.S. and European origin, officially ceased their activities in Russia. Among them, the technological giants Google, Apple, Meta, Disney, as well as some of the main global energy companies, such as Shell, or automobile manufacturers such as Toyota, Ford and General Motors, among many others.

In the financial sphere, Visa, Mastercard and American Express announced the suspension of their business in Russia. Their objective was to prevent the normal functioning of the payment systems, both in the internal and external economy. The Financial Times defined this situation as "a full-scale financial war of unprecedented nature and scope" (FT, 04/03/2022). This was a major blow on the Russian payments market. In 2020, 74% of credit card transactions in Russia were made through Visa and Mastercard.

Of course, Russia did not sit idly by. In response to the various sanctions, Moscow decreed a plan to protect its economy that included, among other things, a ban on foreign currency transfers abroad in an amount exceeding $10,000, the suspension of the activities of the Moscow stock exchange and the obligation for Russian exporters to convert 80% of their revenues earned in foreign currencies into rubles as of January 1, 2022. Days later, the Russian Central Bank banned the sale of foreign currency to its citizens and, faced with the blocking of credit cards, began working with other banks to issue cards under its own branded network, Mir, which as of March 22 already had 75 million debit cards throughout Russia. In addition, UnionPay, a Chinese company, partnered with 30 local Russian banks and issued more than 4 million cards as of March 6 (La República de Colombia, 22/03/2022).

The giants of the global financial network also joined the pressures. More than 26 foreign asset management firms operating in Russia froze funds with significant exposure to that country. Notable sanctions included JP Morgan, BlackRock, Amundi Asset Management, Ubs Investment Bank, Bnp Paribas, Abrdn PLC, Schroders and Pictet Asset Management, among others. (FT, 04/03/2022)

Ukraine has become a stage on the global chessboard, where the big players are playing, and where the battle for who will impose the rules of the game in trade, finance and technological development in these times is also being debated.

Russia in the face of sanctionsDespite the catastrophic results that were announced, the reality continues to indicate that Russia can still resist the pressures, demonstrating its capacity to anticipate and respond. It can be assumed that the Russian government foresaw the possibility of financial sanctions in its decision to move forward with the operation deployed over Ukraine, a territory long targeted by NATO forces and their allies.

There are two noteworthy facts regarding the sanctions. Firstly, the disconnection from the SWIFT system is not total, since it continues to allow the payment of hydrocarbons (gas and oil), the key supplies that Europe still needs, despite having announced a gradual "disconnection", which allows Russia to continue to receive income from its main export resources.

On the other hand, the sanctions are not new. The financial exclusion falls on "some banks", which had already been sanctioned, mainly during the Crimean conflict. Already in 2019, faced with threats of disconnection from SWIFT, the Central Bank of Russia reported the development of an alternative platform, the SPFS, and joining the China International Payment System (CIPS). Although both systems are not sufficiently developed to face SWIFT, it is what has allowed Russia to sustain the flow of its domestic transactions and to China, its great economic, political and strategic ally, thus avoiding the collapse of its domestic economy.

In addition, the Russian Federation was able to meet its outstanding foreign debt payments, initially in rubles, which earned it a "debt default" rating from rating agencies such as Standard & Poors. Eventually, it also managed to make its scheduled payments in dollars.

On April 18, President Vladimir Putin went so far as to affirm that "the strategy of the economic blitzkrieg (of the West) has failed", and reported that the balance of payments in the first quarter stood at a "historical maximum" of US$ 58,200. The situation is stabilizing", added the president (Ámbito, 22/04/2022).

In the same sense, this week Bloomberg reported that the ruble is the best performing currency in the world so far in 2022, with a growth of 11% against the US dollar, which places it at higher levels than those recorded prior to the war.

A few days ago, the Russian Ministry of Finance came out to deny a report by Bloomberg Agency that stated that the Russian Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would fall by 12% during 2022, according to the Ministry. At the end of April, the estimates of the Central Bank of Russia were published, which foresees a contraction of between 8% and 10% this year, due to the fact that "the external environment of the Russian economy remains challenging and significantly limits economic activity", but added that it will return to "rapid growth in 2023, thanks to a structural economic transformation". At the same time, the monetary entity cut the benchmark interest rate from 17% to 14% as "risks to prices and financial stability ceased to increase", giving a sign of strength to its economy (Deutsche Welle, 04/29/2022).

For its part, the IMF's World Economic Outlook report announced that global production will slow down this year to 3.6%, as opposed to an initial forecast in January of 4.4%, i.e. 1.2% more. Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, IMF chief economist, said that "the world economic outlook has been seriously affected, largely due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine" (La Nación, 19/04/2022). It would seem, then, that the economic war against Russia has had enormous effects. However, most of them end up hitting other territories, due to their growing impact on international trade and the worsening of the energy and food crisis. Argentina is no exception.

War as a manifestation of a structural crisisOn March 24, Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, stated that "the Russian invasion of Ukraine has put an end to the globalization we have experienced over the past three decades. Businesses and governments will also look more broadly at their dependencies on other nations," and warned that "the potential impact of the Ukraine war will be seen in the acceleration of digital currencies" (Financial Times, 3/24/2022).

The battery of "Western" sanctions on Russia also set off alarm bells in Beijing. China met on April 22 with major banks to try to protect their assets from U.S. and European sanctions. "President Xi Jinping's administration has maintained staunch support for Vladimir Putin throughout the crisis, but Chinese banks and companies remain wary of doing any business with Russian entities that could trigger U.S. sanctions," said the Financial Times. The British media added that this meeting "included officials from China's central bank and finance ministry, as well as executives from dozens of local and international lenders, such as HSBC" (Financial Times, 1/05/2022).

The structural crisis that the economic system is going through has a long way to go, and the war conflict can only be considered as "the continuation of the pandemic, by other means". The acceleration of organic transformations, which are giving birth to a new phase in the world economic system, are unfolding a deeper war, for the imposition and conformation of a new world order that is advancing, worryingly, towards a strategic-military moment.

The full digitalization of the economy, the relocation of production centers, the reconfiguration of supply chains, the imposition of an energy transition that reduces dependence on resources geographically located in other nations, are some of the transformations in full swing. In this scenario, disputes are intensifying and, as Machiavelli's old premise says, the end seems to justify all means.

title: Tough economic war between the West and Russia enters a new phase
text:
While Russia continues its military offensive in Ukraine, another war, of a financial nature, is developing between Russia and the West.

This Monday, European Union energy ministers are meeting to discuss what to do with Russia: European gas companies are debating whether to give in to Vladimir Putin or face an eventual supply cut-off, as happened last week with Poland and Bulgaria.

In March, Putin decreed that "hostile countries" - among them all those of the European Union - pay for their gas imports in rubles, instead of euros or dollars, the currencies used for most contracts. The measure is a sort of revenge against Western sanctions, since the mechanism involves the Russian central bank, punished by the United States and Europe. It also allows Putin to raise the price of the ruble by creating more demand for the national currency.

Russia-Ukraine War, LIVE, Day 68: Kiev sank with drones two Russian ships in the Black Sea

Russia-Ukraine War: Putin threatens blitzkrieg attacks on countries that intervene in the invasion.

But more importantly, it is a political test for the unity of the European Union as, in the short term some countries are more dependent on Russian gas than others and there is no united front on the issue.

Russia proposes that companies open two accounts at Gazprombank (excluded from the financial sanctions), one in foreign currency and one in rubles: companies should deposit their payments in the original currency and the bank would be responsible for converting it into rubles, via the Russian central bank. The payment is only considered done when the conversion into rubles is completed.

Poland and Bulgaria refused to comply with the decree. Both account for about 8% of the European Union's Russian gas imports, and the countries do not believe that the supply cut will have a major impact on the population. Poland, for example, has gas reserves at 76% and with the northern summer approaching, consumption is expected to drop. In fact, both countries were planning not to renew their contracts with Gazprom when they expire at the end of the year.

But not all European countries depend on Russian gas to the same extent: between 40% and 50% of Italy's and Germany's gas imports, respectively, come from Russia. Germany, the European Union's largest economy, has refused to make the payment in rubles but says it can pay Gazprom in euros without violating economic sanctions imposed by the bloc.

Italy's Eni said it had not yet opened a ruble account - although it is preparing to do so, according to Bloomberg - and said it will continue to make payments in euros, according to the contract, and observing all international sanctions.

On the other side, the European Commission, the European Union's executive body, warned companies that giving in to Russian conditionalities could imply a "violation of EU sanctions and therefore a high risk for companies".

War in Ukraine: Biden called for $33 billion in aid for Kiev, while Russia warns about testing his patience

The next few days will be decisive as companies will have to start making April payments.

Meanwhile, Russia avoided defaulting on its sovereign debt, but at a cost. The Russian Finance Ministry said it made payments of u$s 564.8 million and u$s 84.4 million for two bonds maturing in 2022 and 2042.

A senior U.S. official confirmed that the payments had been made and said the source of the funds was unclear.

As Russia Threatens World War III, U.S. and Europe Send More Weapons to Ukraine

Four days after Russia launched the invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. froze Russian reserves in that country (about u$s 630 billion) and banned U.S. entities from doing business with the Russian central bank. Then, the Biden Administration went a step further and revoked a special exception for Russia to use US banks to pay its Western creditors, leaving the country closer to default.

Concern grew in early April, when JPMorgan Chase refused to process the payment of two bonds for US$649.2 million, after consultation with the U.S. Treasury, sources familiar with the transaction said.

Following the blockade, Russia said it paid its creditors the amount owed, but in rubles, because sanctions prevented it from meeting its obligations. However, both bonds were denominated in dollars and both rating agencies and the Credit Derivatives Determination Committee (CDDC) said that payment in rubles could be considered a default.

Russia finally made the payments through the UK branch of Citibank, just before the grace period expired next Wednesday. But although it avoided what could have been a historic default - the last time it defaulted was in 1918 - Russia had to wire the money to London from its domestic reserves, which was precisely what the Western sanctions sought: to force the Kremlin and drain its resources to finance the invasion.

title: Russia.War Russia Ukraine day 65: Minute by minute what's happening live
text:
The war between Russia and Ukraine has reached its 65th day, since its beginning on February 24, when the Russian president sent military troops to carry out a "special military operation" to liberate the Donbas region.

That he himself declared as independent territories Lugansk and Donetsk, part of this region.

On the 65th day of this war, just over two months, during the visit of António Guterres, the Secretary General of the United Nations (UN), Russia shelled Kiev on Thursday, April 28.

You can also readInternationalWorld War III: China calls for dialogue between Russia and Ukraine to avoid itInternationalRussia applies sanctions to 29 Americans, including Mark Zuckerberg and Kamala HarrisInternationalFor sinking of Russian Ship Moskova in the Black Sea, Russia launches attack on KievOnhis visit on Thursday, António Guterres lamented the "failure" of the Security Council to avoid the conflict

.Also in other international support for Ukraine, U.S. President Joe Biden asked Congress for $33 billion in additional aid for Ukraine, of which more than $20 billion will go to military assistance.

According to Joe Biden, this aid is not to attack Russia, but to assist Ukraine in defending itself against Russian aggression.

Similarly, Joe Biden, on Thursday criticized Russia for making "idle" claims about the possible use of nuclear weapons in the Ukrainian conflict, and said that such assertions showed "desperation" on the part of the country administered by Vladimir Putin.

Despite UN attempts to end this war and foreign intervention in support of Ukraine, attacks continue between the two nations.

It is recorded that after withdrawing from the north and the vicinity of Kiev, the Russian offensive concentrated in the south and east of the country.

In addition, during the visit of António Guterres it is reported that at least one person was killed in the Russian attack on Kiev, reported Friday the mayor of the city, Vitali Klitschko, on Telegram.

U.S.lower house approves Joe Biden to give more weapons to Ukraine with a law dating back to World War IITheU.S.lower house approved last Thursday a legislative measure that allows the country's president, Joe Biden, to use a law dating back to World War II to lend more weapons to Ukraine

.With 417 votes in favor and only 10 against, the measure was supported by both Democrats and Republicans, as was previously the case in the Senate, and allows Joe Biden to deliver weapons more quickly and with less bureaucracy to Kiev.

It is a type of legislation first used in 1941 during World War II - before the United States entered directly into that conflict - by then President Franklin D. Roosevelt to provide armaments to the United Kingdom Armed Forces in their fight against Germany.

That same Thursday, just hours before the House of Representatives voted in favor of the legislation, Joe Biden formally asked Congress for $33 billion in additional aid for Ukraine, of which more than $20 billion will be military assistance to defend against Russia, in the face of the possibility of a long war.

In a speech from the White House, Joe Biden explained that it is "crucial" that Congress give the green light to this aid, because giving in to Russian aggression would be much more costly.

"Either we back the Ukrainian people to defend their country or we stand by as the Russians continue their atrocities and aggression against Ukraine. "

Joe Biden recalled that the assistance the United States has sent so far has made a difference on the battlefield and helped Ukraine "win the battle of Kiev," referring to the success of Ukrainian forces in repelling Russian advances toward the capital

.Joe Biden's request for assistance includes, in addition to sending arms and ammunition to Ukraine, 8.5 billion in direct economic assistance and 3 billion in humanitarian aid.

Ukrainian and Russian presidents invited to G20 summit: IndonesiaJokoWidodo, the president of Indonesia, informed on Friday that he invited his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymir Zelenski to the G20 summit in November in Indonesia, in which Vladimir Putin confirmed his participation

. "I invited President Zelenski to participate in the G20

summit″Despite Western pressure to exclude Russia, both nations were invited

.Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski noted in a tweet on Wednesday that he had been invited to the summit following a telephone conversation with his Indonesian peer.

Joko Widodo also spoke with the Russian leader on Thursday. According to the Indonesian president, at that time, President Vladimir Putin thanked Indonesia for the invitation to the G20 summit and said he would participate.

The G20 summit is scheduled to take place in Bali in November.

Two British humanitarian volunteers "captured" by Russian forces in Ukraine: NGOTwoBritish volunteers were "captured" by Russian soldiers in Ukraine, a non-profit organization called Presidium Network and the family of one of the imprisoned aid workers reported Friday

.Paul Urey and Dylan Healy were "captured" by Russian soldiers on Monday at a checkpoint south of the town of Zaporiyia in southwestern Ukraine, Presidium Network said.

The volunteers were operating independently to try to help Ukrainians flee and were arrested while assisting a woman and her two children in Zaporiyia.

The organization said it offered to help Urey and Healy after receiving reports of their work on the ground, but clarified that the volunteers were not affiliated with its network in Ukraine.

Presidium Ntework reported that Urey is a seasoned humanitarian worker who spent eight years in Afghanistan and reported that Healy, born in 2000, worked in the kitchen at a hotel chain in the UK.

The NGO confirmed that it is working with the British Foreign Office.

Russian economy to contract by 8-10% this year due to sanctionsTheRussian economy will contract by 8-10% this year due to Western sanctions imposed on Russia for its military campaign in Ukraine, marking the worst drop in Russian GDP since 1994, when the country's GDP contracted by 12.7%

.Despite this possible decline, the Russian Central Bank cut its main interest rate this Friday, April 29, from 17% to 14%, as it estimated that "risks to prices and financial stability ceased to increase".

The Russian Central Bank, which had dramatically raised its rate to 20% following the first Western sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine in late February, had already cut the interest rate a first time to 17% on April 8.

The local currency, the ruble, had also fallen to record lows against the dollar and the euro, but has recovered.

Also the Central Bank said that current growth rates of consumer prices have slowed significantly after peaking in the first half of MarchAccording to

the bank, this is due to the "strengthening of the ruble and the cooling of consumer activity."

The Russian central bank recorded year-on-year inflation of 16.5% in March, a level it has not seen since 2015.

The bank forecasts that this year inflation could reach 23%, before slowing in 2023

.

title: Ukraine - Russia war, live: breaking news on the invasion
text:
???? Keys of the day:

- Russia begins cutting off gas to Europe by suspending shipments to Bulgaria and Poland.

- Fighting continues with heavy shelling in Kherson and nearby Izium area

- The UN assures to be "preparing" the evacuation of Mariupol

- Shelling continues in the city of Kharkiv and the blockade and shelling of the Azovstal plant near the port of Mariupol

- Guterres arrived in Kyiv on peace mission to meet with Zelenski after seeing Putin

21:00 Ukraine goes a step further and launches several attacks inside Russian territory, two small towns in Donbass will decide the fate of the Russian offensive.

20:46 Ukraine calls shelling on Kyiv a "barbaric act" Ukraine has called the Russian shelling on Kyiv a "heinous act of barbarism", amid the visit of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres to the Ukrainian capital. "With this heinous act of barbarism, Russia once again demonstrates its attitude towards Ukraine, Europe and the world," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba wrote on Twitter.

20:35 Biden launches $33 billion package for "continued aid" to Ukraine in arms and money The U.S. president has proposed to Congress to approve a $33 billion package to arm Ukraine "without interruption" and help its citizens and government weather the Russian invasion. La Vanguardia's Washington correspondent, Fernando García, details Biden's proposal and its possible political consequences.

20:22 ENLARGEMENT | Two missiles hit Kyiv during Guterres' visit Two projectiles fired by Russia have hit Kyiv during the visit of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, as reported by the capital's own mayor, Vitali Klitchko. "Tonight, the enemy fired on Kyiv. There have been two hits in the Shevchenkivski district. All emergency services are on the spot. Information about possible casualties is being clarified," the ex-boxer wrote on his Telegram channel. For his part, President Volodimir Zelenski's advisor Mikhail Podoliak remarked that the shelling took place during Guterres' visit: "The day before he was sitting at a long table in the Kremlin and today there are explosions over his head. A postcard from Moscow?" he wrote on his Twitter account.

20:08 Shelling continues in Kyiv Despite the apparent withdrawal of Russian troops, two explosions have rocked a central district of the city of Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko has claimed. The attack comes on the same day that UN Secretary General António Guterres visited the Ukrainian capital.

19:53 Zelenski confident of "successful outcome" in attempt to unblock Azovstal Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski has assured that he is confident of a "successful outcome" in the attempt to unblock the besieged Azovstal metallurgical plant in the port city of Mariupol, where some 1,000 civilians and 2,000 Ukrainian soldiers are sheltering. "I believe that a successful outcome is possible in the unblocking" of Azovstal in which Ukraine is working together with the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross, Zelenski said at a press conference after meeting with UN Secretary General António Guterres.

19:40 Guterres says UN is doing "everything possible" to evacuate Mariupol UN Secretary General António Guterres has assured that the UN is doing "everything possible" to evacuate civilians from the Azovstal metallurgical plant in the Ukrainian city of Mariupol, where about 1,000 people still remain refugees together with about 2,000 Ukrainian soldiers. "We are doing everything possible to make it a reality. My first and only priority is the people who are suffering and have to be rescued," said the UN Secretary General at a press conference after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski.

19:29 Russia calls the US initiative to include the country on the list of sponsors of terrorism "idiotic" Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has called the US government's initiative to include the country on the list of sponsors of terrorism "idiotic". In her own words, it is a measure "of an idiotic nature" which will bring, moreover, its "consequences" and against which Russia will take measures, TASS news agency noted. "All the measures they take, even if they are idiotic, will be analyzed and monitored. They will be followed up and, of course, will not go unanswered, this must be understood," she has said. Zakharova has warned that the international community has not yet addressed the legal issues of U.S. actions in countries such as Syria, Libya or Irakh, so she has assured that if Washington continues to take measures against Moscow because the alleged crimes committed against Ukrainians could have repercussions in the United States.

19:14 Bulgaria will repair damaged Ukrainian military equipment Bulgaria has announced that it will take over the repair of Ukrainian military equipment damaged in combat in the war against Russia. This was made public by Bulgarian Prime Minister Kiril Petkov after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky in Kyiv. "Specialized companies of works in the military sphere will repair heavy Ukrainian military equipment. I will submit to the Cabinet of Ministers such a request and I think it will be approved by the Parliament next week as military technical assistance to Ukraine," Petkov said. In addition to repairing an unspecified amount of military equipment, the Balkan country will offer Ukraine the Black Sea port of Varna for export of agricultural products. During his visit, the Bulgarian prime minister thanked Zelensky for the leadership shown by Zelensky during the Russian invasion. "Ukraine will win this war and all democracies are behind you, there is no doubt that this is the only way out," Petkov has declared to the Ukrainian president. The announcement comes hours after Russia cut off gas supplies to Bulgaria for non-payment of amounts in rubles.

19:00 UN confirms the death of some 2,830 civilians in Ukraine The UN Office for Human Rights has already counted 2,829 civilians killed in Ukraine as a result of Russia's military offensive. Within this figure, 205 children stand out, although it assumes that the real figure would be "considerably higher". The UN has also recorded 3,180 wounded, including 303 minors, according to a count which places most of the victims in territories controlled by forces loyal to the Ukrainian government. Moreover, the High Commissioner for Human Rights has assured that it still lacks more information on some areas where there is still "intense" fighting and includes in this group the area of Mariupol.

18:46 Peace talks stall for almost a month It has been almost a month since the last face-to-face meeting between Russian and Ukrainian negotiators. Although talks between experts from both countries continued telematically after the meeting in Istanbul last March 29, the sides still have not brought their positions closer and today Moscow assured that it has not yet received Ukraine's response on its latest proposals to reach a possible peace agreement. "This morning, at the time of preparing the press conference, the Russian side had not received a reply," said Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. Zakharova was referring to Russian counter-proposals sent to Kyiv after studying its version of a possible agreement between the parties. Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky has repeatedly insisted on the need for a direct meeting with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, because contacts through mediators and third countries will not produce the "desired result".

18:34 Ukrainian justice says it has identified "more than 8,000 cases" of alleged war crimes Ukrainian investigators say they have identified "more than 8,000 cases" of alleged war crimes since the beginning of the Russian invasion, Ukrainian Prosecutor General Iryna Venediktova has said. "We have more than 8,000 cases," she said in an interview with German media outlet Deutsche Welle. "We are actually talking about 8,600 cases that only concern war crimes and more than 4,000 cases that are related to war crimes," Venediktova said. These alleged war crimes include "killings of civilians, shelling of civilian infrastructure, torture" and "sexual crimes" reported in the "occupied territory of Ukraine", according to the judge.

18:24 Russia continues to advance into the Donbass Russian troops continue their advance into the Donbass from Kharkiv, a region considered key to being able to outflank Ukrainian positions in northern Donetsk, while consolidating their control over the south of the country, bordering the annexed Crimean peninsula. According to the Ukrainian General Staff, the Russian army has spent the last hours concentrating troops and weapons around Izium, while intensifying attacks to definitively control that area. In addition, Moscow has reportedly moved airborne units and up to 500 military equipment to Izium, which is located 70 kilometers from Kramatorsk, a Ukrainian military stronghold in the Donbass.

18:12 War in Ukraine fuels right-wing extremists in the Netherlands Dutch intelligence services have warned that Russia's war in Ukraine is fueling "the narrative of right-wing and anti-government extremists" in the Netherlands. Director of the General Intelligence and Security Service, Erik Akerboom, has said that the war in Ukraine is being seen "becoming part of the narrative of right-wing extremists and anti-government extremists," which is also fueling polarization in the Netherlands. Russian President Vladimir Putin's narrative about the war he launched in Ukraine at the end of February "fits" with the ideas already held by some radical groups and "that inspires to be against the government, in this against the institutions," he said.

18:00 OSCE announces the closure of its special mission in Ukraine The OSCE Chairman-in-Office, the Pole, Zbigniew Rau, has announced the end of the Special Monitoring Mission in eastern Ukraine, which had been in operation since 2014. The decision follows the lack of consensus at the OSCE Permanent Council on March 31, 2022 to extend the mission's mandate. All decisions of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which has 57 partner states from Europe, Central Asia and North America, must be made with full consensus among its members. "It is not an easy decision to make. We have explored all possible options through political dialogue with the participating states to achieve the renewal of the SMM's mandate, but Russia's position left us no choice but to take steps to close the mission," Rau said. In a statement, the Pole assured that the SMM has played a "crucial role" in providing objective information on the ground, facilitating the ceasefire and working to alleviate the effects of the conflict on the civilian population."

17:44 Biden proposes $33 billion more in aid to Ukraine U.S. President Joe Biden has asked the U.S. Congress for $33 billion in additional aid to Ukraine, of which more than $20 billion will go to militarily support Kyiv's fight against the Russian invasion. "As long as the assaults and atrocities continue, we will continue to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian aggression," Biden said in a speech from the White House.

17:34 Gas cut-off to Poland and Bulgaria complicate Western sanctions Russian gas company Gazprom's decision to cut off supplies to Poland and Bulgaria for not paying for deliveries in rubles has tangled up the complex framework of EU sanctions, which are intended to punish Moscow economically but also leave open a way for the EU to buy hydrocarbons from Russia. "The Commission is, as a matter of principle, always in contact with the authorities of the Member States" to "ensure that gas deliveries to Europe continue," said the EU executive's chief spokesman, Eric Mamer. The supply cuts to Warsaw and Sofia are the first practical application of the decree approved at the end of March by the Kremlin, according to which European gas importers must open two accounts in the Russian bank Gazprombank before May 20, one in euros and the other in rubles, to make their purchases of the hydrocarbon. According to this mechanism designed by Vladimir Putin's regime, the purchase does not formally end until the euro deposit has been converted into rubles, but this process, which is "entirely in the hands of the Russian authorities, involves the Central Bank of Russia, whose transactions are prohibited under European sanctions.

17:17 Sanchez expresses his support to Bulgaria in the face of Russia's "unacceptable blackmail" with the gas cut The President of the Government, Pedro Sanchez, has expressed Spain's support to the President of Bulgaria, Rumen Radev, in the face of Russia's "unacceptable blackmail" against his country, whose gas supply was cut off yesterday. Sánchez met with Radev at the Moncloa Palace. As indicated by the President of the Government on his Twitter, he took the opportunity to convey to the Bulgarian leader "Spain's support in the face of the unacceptable Russian blackmail of suspending gas supplies". In Sánchez's opinion, "the effects of Putin's attack on Ukraine redouble the importance of the already excellent Spanish-Bulgarian relations".

17:02 Kyiv still not safe Kyiv authorities have reported that they still cannot guarantee the safety of the residents waiting to return, even after Russian forces withdrew from the area. There are more than 200 buildings in the city damaged by shelling, with reconstruction potentially costing around $100 million. "We don't know how long the war will last and how much it will cost in the coming weeks, maybe months, maybe years," former boxer and Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko has maintained. Since Russian forces withdrew from northern Ukraine, many residents have begun to return to Kyiv, even as the city continues to be the target of sporadic missile attacks. The capital remains barricaded, some bridges remain impassable, and the metro runs only until 8 p.m., so its stations can serve as air-raid shelters during regular attack alerts.

16:47 Why Transnistria may be relevant in the Russia-Ukraine war. Ukraine has recently accused Moscow of trying to drag the border region of Transnistria, a self-proclaimed breakaway republic of Moldova, into the war against Kyiv. La Vanguardia's journalist explains why this region may be key in the Ukrainian war.

16:35 Transnistria could prove key in Ukraine war Recent infrastructure explosions in the pro-Russian region of Transnistria, officially still part of Moldova, have triggered rumors that the Kremlin could launch a new offensive here. The appeal was made by the commander of the 36th Marine Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces (FAU), Serhiy Volynsky, one of about half a thousand Ukrainian servicemen who remain encircled in the facilities of the Azovstal plant. "We have been fighting a complete encirclement for 62 days, now we are at the Azovstal plant, performing tasks together with units of the Azov regiment and other units that have been encircled due to hostilities in Mariupol," Volynsky said in a video message posted on his Facebook page and reported by Interfax-Ukraine.

08:52 Putin defends Russia's right to recognize Donbass as the West recognized Kosovo, Gonzalo Aragonés reports from Moscow While UN Secretary General António Guterres explained his concern about the humanitarian situation in Ukraine and in the city of Mariupol, Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday preferred to take the beginning of his conversation to Kosovo to compare this case with that of the pro-Russian entities in eastern Donbass in eastern Ukraine. After meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Guterres was received by Putin in the Kremlin. The meeting lasted an hour and only the first parts were made public, through images on the Russiya 24 TV channel.

08:45 Borrell: "Europe's dependence on Russian gas has gone too far" European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Josep Borrell said Wednesday that the bloc must reduce dependence on Russian gas and oil, after the Kremlin cut off supplies to Poland and Bulgaria over their refusal to pay in rubles. "Our dependence on Russian gas and oil has undoubtedly gone too far (...) This latest decision by Russia will only accelerate Europe's conversion to green energies that do not create dependencies and do not harm the climate," said Borrell, who is on an official visit to Chile. Poland and Bulgaria are the first countries to which Russia, which represents for both of them their main gas supplier, is cutting gas supplies, although it is maintaining them for the rest of Europe. So far, it is Moscow's harshest reaction to the measures imposed by the West to the freezing of the reserves of the Central Bank of Russia and the disconnection of several Russian banks from the SWIFT international interbank system.

08:37 Russia-Ukraine War | The Russian invasion of Ukraine began on February 24 and has reduced towns and cities to rubble and forced more than 5 million people to flee abroad. Western countries have responded with sanctions and weapons for Ukraine to fight a war that has raised fears of a wider conflict in the West, unthinkable for decades. Russia calls its intervention a "special operation" to disarm Ukraine and protect it from fascists. Ukraine and the West say it is a false pretext for an unprovoked war of aggression by President Vladimir Putin.

08:30 Putin warns West of withering retaliation as sanctions punish Russia Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that he will retaliate witheringly if other countries interfere in Ukraine, as European leaders accused Russia of "blackmail" over its gas supply cuts. Russia has called on the United States to stop sending arms to Ukraine, claiming large Western shipments of weaponry were exacerbating the conflict.In a speech to parliamentarians in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Putin said the West wanted to cut Russia into different pieces and accused it of pushing Ukraine into conflict with Russia. "We have all the tools for this, things that no one else can boast of having now. And it's not about boasting, we will use them if necessary. And I want everyone to know that."

08:22 US House passes bill urging sale of seized Russian yachts The US House of Representatives on Wednesday overwhelmingly passed a bill, urging US President Joe Biden to sell assets of Russian oligarchs affected by sanctions and use the funds to provide more military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine. The legislation is non-binding but its passage with 417 votes in favor and 8 against reflects a desire for the president to take a more aggressive stance toward Russia, as reported by The New York Times. The bill's passage comes a day after Attorney General Merrick B. Garland told the Senate that the administration would ask Congress for greater authority to seize and liquidate Russian assets.

08:15 Shockwave of Ukraine war reshapes Middle East, Jordi Joan Baños reports from Istanbul Despite the sparse use of aviation in Ukraine, to minimize civilian casualties, the devastation of Mariupol has made comparison with Aleppo inevitable. The largest Syrian city, which Russian bombers razed to the ground to subdue the insurrection, as US bombers raided Raqa. 07:52 Australia issues over 7,000 visas to displaced Ukrainians The Australian Government on Thursday revealed that over 7,000 visas have been issued to Ukrainian citizens and over 3,000 arrivals have been recorded since Russia's invasion of Ukraine began. 07:30 Ukraine puts Russian damage at $90 billion Russia has caused Ukraine infrastructure damage valued at about $90 billion (more than 85 billion euros) since the March 24 invasion, the Kiev government said Wednesday.Ukrainian Infrastructure Minister Oleksandr Kubrakov told the meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities, which was attended by President Volodymir Zelensky, that the damage to infrastructure as a result of the war launched by Russia amounted to almost $90 billion.

07:22 Robles visits today the 500 Spanish military deployed in Latvia to deter Russian threat on the border Defense Minister Margarita Robles travels this Thursday to Latvia to visit the 500 Spanish military deployed on NATO's eastern border to deter any threat from Russia. 07:00 UK calls for providing fighter jets to Ukraine The UK and other Western powers should provide weapons, tanks and fighter jets to Ukraine as part of long-term military support, British Foreign Secretary Liz Truss said Wednesday. In a speech at Mansion House, the mayor's residence in the City of London (financial center), Truss said the West "must be prepared for the long term and redouble our support" for the country so that Russian President Vladimir Putin cannot find a place to fund this "terrible war." "Heavy weapons, tanks, aircraft: deepen our inventories, increase production. We need to do all this," said the minister, who considered that "the war in Ukraine is our war, it is everyone's war, because the victory of Ukraine is a strategic imperative for all of us." 06:52 World discusses how to ensure justice for atrocities in Ukraine Countries, international organizations and human rights bodies discussed at the UN on Wednesday how to ensure accountability for the grave atrocities being committed in Ukraine, a war that will be a litmus test for international justice, they warned. Putin has added that Russia has "all the tools" to respond. "Those that no one can now boast about. And we are not going to boast. We will use them if necessary and I want everyone to know them," he has emphasized.

title: *S&PGR Affirms United Kingdom 'AA/A-1+' Ratings: Outlook Stable
text:
22 Apr 2022 16:29 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms United Kingdom 'AA/A-1+' Ratings: Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- We forecast the U.K.'s inflation will average 6.3% in 2022, the 
highest since 1991, with risks that it could turn out even higher. 
     -- Upward price pressures, aggravated by the fallout from Russia's 
military intervention against Ukraine, are driving real incomes lower. We have 
revised our GDP growth forecast down to 3.5% for 2022, from the 4.6% we 
projected in December 2021. 
     -- Inflation is also fueling a rise in the government's interest 
expenditure but public finances are strengthening overall, with net general 
government debt projected to fall to 92% of GDP by 2025 from 96% at the end of 
2021. 
     -- In our view, the U.K. benefits from strong institutional settings and 
a highly effective and credible monetary policy. The Bank of England  (BoE ) is 
in a rate-tightening cycle and we expect inflation will gradually be brought 
under control by mid-2023. 
     -- We affirmed our 'AA/A-1+'sovereign credit ratings on the U.K. The 
outlook is stable. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On April 22, 2022, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 'AA/A-1+' unsolicited long- 
and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on the U.K. 
The outlook is stable. 
 
At the same time, we affirmed our 'AA/A-1+' long- and short-term issuer credit 
ratings on the BoE  and our 'AA' issue ratings on the debt programs of Network 
Rail Infrastructure Finance PLC, The Channel Tunnel Rail Link Section 1 
Finance PLC, Affordable Housing Finance PLC, and London Continental Railways 
PLC. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects balanced risks to the U.K.'s creditworthiness over 
the next 24 months. 
 
Downside scenario 
The ratings could come under pressure if economic growth is significantly 
weaker than we anticipate, challenging fiscal consolidation. This could 
happen, for instance, if the fallout from Russia's military intervention 
against Ukraine proved more substantial for the U.K., ultimately leading to 
weaker revenue performance or pressure to increase spending to offset the 
rising cost of living. Ratings downside could also emerge if foreign financing 
for the U.K.'s large external deficit diminished, potentially weighing on the 
country's economic prospects. 
 
Upside scenario 
Ratings upside could arise if the persistent uncertainty regarding the U.K.'s 
relations with the EU subsided. Upward ratings pressure could also build if 
the government's fiscal performance and debt reduction prove stronger than we 
anticipate. 
 
RATIONALE 
Our ratings on the U.K. are supported by its high income levels; its large, 
diversified economy and financial sector; its developed product and labor 
markets; the strength and independence of its key institutions; and the 
sterling's reserve currency status. 
 
The ratings are constrained by the government's large debt stock, although the 
overall debt profile benefits from one of the longest average maturities among 
advanced economies, and the fact that almost all the debt is denominated in 
local currency. The ratings are also constrained by still lingering 
uncertainties regarding the U.K.'s relations with its key trading partner, the 
EU, given ongoing disagreements over the operation of the Northern Ireland 
Protocol. 
 
Institutional and Economic Profile: The U.K.'s "cost-of-living crisis" is 
being aggravated by the fallout from Russia's military intervention against 
Ukraine, as inflation accelerates 
     -- Russia's military intervention against Ukraine is aggravating the 
U.K.'s cost-of-living crisis as energy price rises fuel already-high inflation. 
     -- We expect this will weigh on domestic consumption and we have revised 
our headline growth forecast down to 3.5% from the 4.6% we projected in 
December 2021. 
     -- The domestic political scene will likely face several recurring 
challenges, including the implementation of the Northern Ireland Protocol and 
Scotland's continuing demands for a second independence referendum. 
 
We consider that the economic outlook for the U.K. has weakened following 
Russia's military intervention against Ukraine. Direct trade exposure to 
Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine is limited given that the three countries 
together account for around 1% of U.K. exports. Nevertheless, as a net energy 
importer, the U.K. remains exposed to the conflict's impact on oil and gas 
prices, which had already risen and recently accelerated further, fueling 
headline inflation. In March 2022, inflation measured 7% year-on-year, a 
30-year high for the U.K. In response, the BoE  embarked on a rate-rising 
cycle. It has undertaken three interest rate hikes since December 2021, with 
further tightening likely in the coming months. 
 
The current rapid pace of inflation is aggravating the U.K.'s cost-of-living 
crisis, which had already been unfolding before the recent military 
escalation. The Office for Budget Responsibility , the U.K.'s independent 
fiscal body, is projecting that real disposable incomes will fall by 2.2% this 
financial year (2022/2023)--the largest annual decline since records began. In 
our view, this will pressure domestic consumption. Additionally, the 
uncertainty around the duration and the outcome of the conflict in Ukraine is 
likely to adversely affect investments as well as export performance via 
second-round effects on the growth outlook for the EU, the U.K.'s key trading 
partner. 
 
We have revised down our growth forecast for the U.K. to 3.5% for 2022, from 
the 4.6% projection we published in December. This comparatively high headline 
growth, however, masks a substantial growth carryover effect from 2021 of 
2.6%. Effectively, we therefore project sequential growth to be 1% this year 
and believe that a recession could happen, but only if additional downside 
shocks materialize. These could include, for instance, outright cuts of 
Russian gas supplies to Europe, more acute direct supply chain challenges, or 
a significant deterioration in global financing conditions. Nevertheless, in 
our baseline scenario for now we forecast growth will remain positive. 
 
There are several factors underpinning our growth forecast. First, the U.K. 
economy entered the latest shock from a comparatively strong position. In 
January 2022, output in real terms had fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels 
and the government subsequently removed all remaining domestic- and 
foreign-travel COVID-19-related restrictions in February. Although case 
numbers have fluctuated and hospitalizations have recently risen, we do not 
expect a sizable economic drag beyond temporary staff absences in some 
sectors. We expect that high vaccination levels will reduce the likelihood of 
the government introducing social distancing restrictions again, which should 
support economic activity. Additionally, economic agents have been 
increasingly adapting to COVID-19 over the last two years, so subsequent waves 
of the virus are unlikely to disturb economic activity as much. 
 
The labor market is also strengthening. The Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme, 
also known as furlough, has successfully preserved employment. The scheme 
ended in September 2021 with unemployment averaging 4.5% in 2021, a limited 
rise from the pre-pandemic 3.8% seen in 2019. The pre-pandemic unemployment 
rate was regained in February 2022. Additional household savings were 
accumulated through the lockdowns and social-distancing restrictions. These 
savings could be deployed, at least by some households, to smooth consumption 
in the face of elevated inflation. 
 
The long-term economic impact of Brexit remains difficult to quantify, in our 
view. Since the transition period ended at the end of 2020, the U.K. has 
effectively left the single market and has been trading with the EU  under a 
new Trade and Cooperation Agreement signed in late 2020. While the new 
arrangement is purportedly tariff- and quota-free, tariffs are applicable in 
some circumstances--for example if a certain proportion of a product's added 
value originates outside the U.K. and the EU. Moreover, businesses now face 
additional costs and frictions where none existed previously, for example 
relating to documentation and certification. The trade agreement between the 
U.K. and the EU  does not cover the U.K. service sector's automatic access to 
the EU single market. 
 
U.K. trade also appears to have recently fared worse than peers. For instance, 
following a significant export contraction by 13% in real terms in 2020, the 
U.K.'s real exports contracted by a further 1.3% in 2021. This contrasts with 
the outcomes registered in Germany, France, and Italy, for example, all of 
which saw a notable rebound in exports last year. While it is difficult to 
ascertain to what degree Brexit contributed to this, particularly given the 
impact of the pandemic, it was likely among the factors underpinning this 
weaker dynamic. 
 
Since the transition period ended, the Northern Ireland Protocol has also 
remained a source of tension between the U.K. and the EU. To preserve the 1998 
Good Friday Agreement and ensure no hard border or additional checks on the 
island of Ireland, Northern Ireland remained within the EU 's single market for 
goods, under the Protocol, consequently creating a de facto customs border in 
the Irish Sea. This led to additional requirements and checks on goods being 
shipped from elsewhere in the U.K. It also raised concerns in the business 
community, as well as opposition from Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist 
Party. Northern Ireland's first minister resigned in February 2022 in protest 
against the continued implementation of the protocol. The U.K. is requesting a 
comprehensive renegotiation of the protocol and has threatened to unilaterally 
suspend parts of the agreement otherwise. This could lead the EU  to retaliate 
and impose restrictions. 
 
Despite ongoing Brexit-related uncertainties, we view the U.K.'s institutional 
arrangements as a key sovereign rating support. The U.K.'s political system is

characterized by a system of checks and balances between government bodies, 
free press, open public debate, and the effective functioning of key economic 
institutions, including the Treasury and the BoE. 
 
In May 2021, the U.K. held local elections that delivered a strong result for 
the Scottish National Party (SNP), falling just short of a majority in the 
Scottish Parliament . Subsequently, the SNP and the Scottish Greens entered a 
new power-sharing arrangement. The agreement between the two parties contains 
a commitment to hold another referendum on Scottish independence within the 
next five years, and preferably within the first half of the new Scottish 
Parliament's term. Although prime minister Boris Johnson  has said he will not 
allow such a referendum, we expect uncertainties to remain elevated and shaped 
by prevailing public opinion on the subject in Scotland. Over the last two 
years, support for independence has oscillated around 45%-55%, according to 
opinion polls. 
 
Flexibility and Performance profile: The upswing in inflation is driving a 
rise in government interest spending, but the overall fiscal picture is 
improving 
     -- We expect inflation will average 6.3% this year, the highest in 30 
years. 
     -- Elevated inflation is contributing to higher recorded government 
interest expenditure as principal is adjusted upward for retail-price-index 
(RPI) linked gilts. Nevertheless, overall fiscal performance is on an 
improving trend and we expect general government deficits to reduce to 2.5% of 
GDP by 2024. 
     -- The BoE  has hiked rates three times since December 2021 and we expect 
it will succeed in bringing inflation back to the 2% target by the second half 
of 2023. 
 
The U.K.'s fiscal performance slightly exceeded our expectations in 2021. We 
estimate the general government deficit was 8.2% of GDP last year, compared to 
the 12.9% of GDP deficit recorded in 2020. Revenue performance has been strong 
with central government tax receipts up almost 15% year-on-year across a broad 
range of categories. Income and capital gains taxes (+16.5%), corporate taxes 
(+21%), and so-called self-assessed income taxes (+35%) all performed strongly 
and notably exceeded pre-pandemic levels, following the drop in 2020. 
 
In parallel, spending remained almost flat in nominal terms in 2021 as the 
government withdrew previous pandemic-related support schemes. 
 
Stronger budgetary performance provided the U.K. government  with some 
additional headroom for ad-hoc policy measures to partially soften the impact 
of the aforementioned cost-of-living crisis. To this end, in February 2022 the 
chancellor unveiled a GBP9 billion (0.4% of GDP) package to cushion the 
consequences for households of increased energy prices, which rose in April 
after the energy sector regulator Ofgem  increased the price cap by 54%. 
Further support measures worth an additional GBP9 billion (as estimated by the 
OBR ) were subsequently introduced by the government in the Spring Statement. 
The main policy initiatives are a temporary cut in the fuel duty and an 
increase in the threshold from which national insurance contributions are to 
be paid. 
 
We forecast that the U.K. will register a further improvement in budgetary 
performance this year with the headline deficit falling to 5% of GDP. Deficits 
should keep falling toward 2.5% of GDP by 2024-2025. Nevertheless, we consider 
that fiscal performance could turn out weaker, with the government potentially 
being under pressure to do more to offset the decline in disposable incomes, 
particularly with a general election scheduled for 2024. 
 
In our view, even with continuously moderating deficits and net general 
government debt returning to a downward trend, the fiscal impact of the 
pandemic will take years to undo. We now expect that net general government 
debt will decline to 92% of GDP by 2025 from 96% last year, but still notably 
higher than the pre-pandemic 80%. Despite having the longest debt maturity 
profile of the G-7 , we note the high sensitivity of U.K. public finances to 
inflation and changes in interest rates. We project that in 2022 interest 
spending will rise to 8.0% of revenues from 6.8% in 2021 (4.8% in 2020), 
mostly as a result of elevated inflation feeding into upward adjustments of 
principal on RPI-linked gilts, which amount to around 25% of government debt 
stock. 
 
As inflation comes down closer to target, we expect the government's nominal 
accrued interest expenditure will fall again, even with recent and forthcoming 
BoE  rate hikes factored in. After these hikes, we expect the central bank will 
continue with its gradual approach of policy normalization in the medium term. 
 
One of the U.K. economy's most significant macroeconomic features is its 
current account deficit. At an annual average of close to $90 billion (3% of 
GDP) over the last five years, it is the second largest in the world in 
absolute terms, after that of the U.S. Since peaking at 5.3% of GDP in 2016, 
the U.K.'s current account deficit has been narrowing, partly on the back of a 
narrowing income deficit, reflecting lower global interest rates. Given the 
size and cross-border exposures of the U.K.'s large and profitable financial 
sector, the economy's gross external financing needs remain elevated. We 
estimate that, for 2022, short-term external debt by remaining maturity totals 
$10.5 trillion (3x the U.K.'s GDP), dwarfing nearly all other major economies 
except the U.S. 
 
Nevertheless, we do not expect the U.K. to face problems rolling over this 
elevated stock of short-term external debt. In the past, nonresidents have 
been consistently willing to fund the current account deficits and the foreign 
debt falling due. The sterling has also maintained its reserve currency 
status. According to the IMF , as of end-2021, claims in sterling constituted 
4.5% of the total global allocation of foreign-exchange reserves. 
 
The U.K. banking system fared well in the pandemic, and banks are now looking 
to put the pandemic behind them. 2021 annual results for the largest banks 
were exceptional, in our view, flattered by provision releases that will not 
be repeated. That said, despite a weakening economic outlook, 2022 should be a 
solid year for U.K. banks. Interest income is turning a corner and should grow 
in 2022 as interest rates continue to climb amid an inflationary environment. 
Also, impairment charges for the year are likely to be better than before the 
pandemic, costs are likely to grow in a controlled way, with efficiency gains 
partly mitigating rising inflation and technology investments, and the U.K.'s 
medium-term economic picture is generally stable (see "Banking Industry 
Country Risk Assessment: United Kingdom," published Dec. 9, 2021).

22 Apr 2022 16:38 ET *S&P: U.K. Upward Price Pressures, 'Aggravated by the Fallout' From Russia Invasion of Ukraine, 'Are Driving Real Incomes Lower'

22 Apr 2022 16:38 ET *S&P Revises U.K GDP Growth View to 3.5% for 2022, Compared to December 2021 Projection of 4.6%

(MORE TO FOLLOW) Dow Jones Newswires

April 22, 2022 16:38 ET (20:38 GMT)

title: UK GDP Growth Expected to Slow -- Market Talk
text:
1758 ET - S&P Global Ratings said it expects U.K. GDP growth of 3.5% this year, below its previous forecast of 4.6% made in December of last year. "Upward price pressures, aggravated by the fallout from Russia's military intervention against Ukraine, are driving real incomes lower," S&P said. The U.K. is a net energy importer, and exposed to the conflict's impact on oil and gas prices, according to S&P. Inflation in March hit a 30-year high for the U.K., coming in at 7% year-on-year, S&P said. The agency also said it affirmed its 'AA/A-1+'sovereign credit ratings on the U.K with a stable outlook. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1731 ET - S&P Global Ratings said it revised down Italy's GDP growth projection for 2022 to 3.1% from 4.4%. The downward revision is a consequence of the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, S&P said. "The Russia-Ukraine conflict poses a risk to Italy's open industrialized economy via trade, supply chains, oil and gas prices, and confidence effects," S&P said. Even as inflation hit 30-year highs in Italy, S&P said it believes "the government's ongoing delivery of key structural and fiscal reforms will boost long-term potential growth and, ultimately, benefit Italy's public finances." S&P affirmed its unsolicited 'BBB' long-term and 'A-2' short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Italy, with a positive outlook. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1654 ET - S&P Global Ratings upgraded its long-term sovereign credit rating on Greece to BB+ from BB with a stable outlook. S&P said the upgrade reflects it expectation of continuous improvement in Greece's policy effectiveness. Fallout from the war in Ukraine appears manageable, S&P said, but it also said the war is the key driver of its projection Greek GDP growth will slow to 3.4% in 2022, from 8.3% last year. Inflation was 8% in March, a 27-year high, but there is no evidence so far of upward pressure on wages, according to S&P. The agency also affirmed Greece's short-term rating at B. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1645 ET - The IPC stock index closes down 0.1% at 53191 points with conglomerate Femsa shares off 1.1%. Grupo Financiero Banorte jumps 8.2% after the group reports a 26% rise in 1Q net profit. Performing loans grew 4.2% on the year, including a 6.3% rise in consumer loans, but 2022 loan-growth guidance is cut to 5%-7% from 7%-9%. Kimberly-Clark de Mexico shares rise 2.4%. The consumer products company had record 1Q sales, up 4% on the year, while higher raw materials costs contributed to a 22% decline in Ebitda. "Margins still a ways from prepandemic levels," analysts with Barclays say in a note, although "the company did produce quarter-on-quarter improvement." The peso weakens to 20.24 against the US dollar from 20.17 yesterday as prospects of more aggressive Fed tightening fuel dollar gains. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1635 ET - Canadian stocks sink, with financials, industrials and materials posting some of the largest sector declines. The benchmark S&P/TSX Composite Index drops 2.1% to 21186.38, ending the week down 3.1%, according to FactSet . The blue-chip S&P TSX 60 Index slides 2.2% to 1281.87, ending the week down 3%. (maria.armental@wsj.com)

1626 ET - The WSJ Dollar Index is on track to gain 1.1% this week and accumulate a 2.7% increase in three weeks, which would be the largest three-week gain since March 2020. Capital Economics' Jonathan Petersen says in a research note that the equities selloff is behind the recent appreciation this time around. "The dollar is in a 'heads I win, tails you lose' situation," he says. "Either US yields rise further and widening yield gaps help the dollar, or risk appetite worsens on worries about the economic outlook and that drives dollar strength." The USD gains 2% versus the Australian dollar and 1.5% to the pound sterling. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1555 ET - The selloff on US government debt continued this week, sending the 10-year yield up 0.097 percentage point to 2.905%, its fourth consecutive weekly rise, despite falling 0.012 p.p. today. Investors are increasingly confident that the Fed will raise rates by a steep 50-basis point next month. Piper Sandler 's Roberto Perli tells WSJ the rise in yields signal that inflation expectations could get out of control and become a headache for the Fed. "History has shown that every time the Fed has to raise rates aggressively, growth suffers,' he says. "The risk of recession five to six quarters ahead is high." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1509 ET - The chorus of analysts who expect the Bank of Canada to deliver another mammoth interest rate increase grew after data on Wednesday showed Canada's annual inflation hit a fresh three-decade high, at 6.7%. Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem told reporters the following day that he was ready to be "as forceful as needed," in normalizing monetary policy. While many analysts now expect another half-percentage point increase in June, Desjardins Securities said Macklem's comments, coupled with this week's inflation report, suggest the BoC could go even further and raise rates by three-quarters of a percentage point during its next meeting. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1256 ET - Diverging interest rates will keep the Japanese yen weak and drive the USD/JPY to 140 by the end of this year, "before dropping back as the Fed takes its foot off the gas in 2023," Capital Economics' Jonas Goltermann says in a research note. Goltermann says the yen has depreciated around 10% against the dollar since early March, mainly because the BoJ "has stuck to its ultra-loose policy stance," while the Fed is aggressively tightening. Japan's terms of trade "have also worsened significantly on account of the surge in commodity prices," Goltermann says, warning that the BoJ is under pressure to change its policy, which could support the yen. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1127 ET - The People's Bank of China may welcome a potential further depreciation of the Chinese renminbi, Capital Economics economist Mark Williams says in a research note. The recent rise in USD/CNY has further to go as yield differentials move against the renminbi, consumer demand weakens in key export markets and inventory restocking in many sectors potentially runs its course, he says. The PBOC has good reason to embrace a gradual depreciation of the renminbi, Williams says. "In an environment of weaker global demand, the renminbi's current strength would increasingly hold exporters back." Capital Economics raises its year-end USD/CNY forecast to 7.00 from 6.70. USD/CNY rises 0.7% to 6.4971 after earlier hitting a near nine-month high of 6.5067.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1114 ET - The euro could rise toward $1.15 from $1.0805 currently if the European Central Bank raises interest rates by more than market expectations to tame inflation, Unicredit Research says. The ECB could raise its deposit facility rate 100 basis points above the 1.5% peak that is priced in by markets over a two-year horizon, Unicreditforex strategist Roberto Mialich says in a research note. That could prompt the forex market to favor more pronounced EUR/USD long positioning, or bets on the pair price rising, he says. "The intensity of the EUR rally would also depend on the extent to which high inflation also affects the U.S. economy, possibly forcing the Federal Reserve to deliver even more tightening than that already priced in," Mialich says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1108 ET - The rise in Mexican inflation to a new 21-year high in early April, coupled with worsening inflation expectations and hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve support another 50bp rise in the Bank of Mexico 's policy interest rate to 7% at the May 12 meeting, Goldman Sachs chief Latin America economist Alberto Ramos says in a report. Annual CPI stood at 7.72% mid-month, with core CPI up 7.16%. Ramos notes that supercore inflation -- which tracks prices most sensitive to demand conditions -- rose to 5.81% from 5.38% in the second half of March. "This is likely to keep the central bank conservative in the calibration of monetary policy despite the weak real activity backdrop," he says. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires
