title: Ukraine - Russia war, live | Latest news from Mariupol
text:
The key points of the day

- Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky claims that Russia has started "the great battle" for Donbass.

- Pedro Sanchez will travel to Kyiv in the coming days and will meet with Zelenski

-The Ukrainian army in Mariupol asks the Pope for help to evacuate civilians.

- A total of 2,072 civilians, 169 of them children, have died since February 24 due to the war in Ukraine.

- Ukraine has already filled out the form to join the European Union.

- A Russian town near the Ukrainian border has been attacked by Ukrainian forces, according to the governor of Belgorod.

- Russia gives another ultimatum to Ukrainian forces in Mariupol to surrender.

14:12 Brussels working on sanctions on Russian oil as part of its sixth package against MoscowThe

European Commission explained Tuesday that it is working on an embargo on Russian oil imports as part of the EU's sixth package of sanctions against Russia and in response to the announcement of Moscow's offensive in Donbas. 14:06 Ukraine says it has so far located 420 bodies of civilians in Bucha

Ukrainian authorities said Tuesday that they have already located a total of 420 bodies of citizens of Bucha, a locality in Kyiv region where Russian troops perpetrated a massacre of civilians before withdrawing, according to the Ukrainian government. "The police in Kyiv region continue to work. As of Saturday night, more than 420 bodies were found, only in Bucha," regional police chief Andriy Nebytov has said, his press service reports on its Facebook page. 13:59 China says it will "strengthen" its "coordination" with Russia The Chinese government has said it will "strengthen" its "strategic coordination" with Russia regardless of "the international situation", with a view to "safeguarding the common interests of both sides". Chinese Deputy Foreign Minister Le Yucheng met with Russian Ambassador to China Andrey Denisov on Monday, according to a Chinese Foreign Ministry statement released Monday, which specified that the aim was to "exchange views on Beijing-Moscow relations and the international and regional situation."

13:51 Russia affirms that the Army has started "the next phase" of the "special operation" against Ukraine Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov affirmed on Tuesday that the Russian Army has started "the next phase" of the "operation" launched on February 24 against Ukraine, before stressing that the objective is "the total liberation of the Donetsk and Luhansk republics". Lavrov further pointed out that the war "is rooted in the desire of the United States and the West to lead the world." "They want to show the world that there will be no multipolarity and created a launching pad against us on our border," he has argued, referring to Ukraine. "They sent weapons to Ukraine," he has trenched.

13:43 About 70,000 people remain trapped in Luhansk, local authorities say

The head of the Luhansk regional military administration, Serhii Haidai, claims that about 70,000 people remain trapped in the eastern Ukrainian region, where the major Russian offensive has begun, President Volodymir Zelensky confirmed on Monday. Before the conflict, which started on February 24, the region had about 350,000 inhabitants. 13:35 Morawiecki calls from Lviv to intensify aid to Ukraine Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki visited the Ukrainian city of Lviv on Tuesday, where he urged the international community to "put calculators aside" and intensify its aid to Ukraine. Morawiecki warned that the evidence of Russian "barbarism" in Ukraine is also "a call to action" for Western governments, from which Poland has been calling for stronger measures against Russia in recent weeks.

13:28 WHO brings attacks on health facilities in Ukraine to 147

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, on Tuesday condemned attacks in Ukraine on health facilities in the country. "WHO strongly condemns the increase in attacks on health facilities in Ukraine. 13:18 Poland announces it has capacity to receive and treat some 10,000 wounded Ukrainian soldiers Poland's health service has the capacity to treat at least 10,000 wounded Ukrainian soldiers, the Polish prime minister said Tuesday. His statements coincide with Russia's new offensive in eastern Ukraine. Mateusz Morawiecki told reporters during a visit to the western Ukrainian city of Lviv that Poland was already treating "several dozen" soldiers and was ready to receive more. "We are ready to receive at least 10,000 [soldiers] if necessary,"

13:09 Ukraine refugee figure now touches five million Nearly five million people have been forced to leave Ukraine since Russia launched its invasion on February 24, according to estimates by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), which come to confirm the worst forecasts put forward in the early stages of the conflict. More than 2.8 million refugees have already arrived in Poland alone, although in recent days local authorities have recorded a temporary reversal in the migratory flow, with more people returning to Ukraine than leaving, which could be due to temporary visits by Ukrainians to their country of origin.

13:00 Sanctions on Russia reopen the debate on the role of the dollar in non-Western countries, reports La Vanguardia journalist Andy Robinson. NATO ruled out the option of intervening militarily in Ukraine because of Russia's invasion, which began on February 24. Excluding the option of fighting against a nuclear power, the re-founded transatlantic alliance opted for a plan B: the so-called weaponization of the dollar.

12:49 Bulgaria is highlighting the value of its aid to Ukraine in the war with Russia. Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Teodora Genchovska has positively assessed the role her country is playing in the Ukrainian war after the meeting with her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Kuleba. "As a small country and according to our possibilities we try to help the Ukrainian people as much as possible," said the minister, who recalled the humanitarian aid, which since the beginning of the invasion amounts to 1.5 million euros, in addition to another 185,000 euros channeled through various NGOs. In addition, more than 91,000 Ukrainians have so far arrived in Bulgaria, the poorest country in the European Union (EU), according to Genchovska.

12:41 Russia does not deserve sympathy and understanding, according to Kuleba. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba said today from Bulgaria that he is "aware" of the pro-Russian sentiments of a part of the Ukrainian society, but stressed that today's Russia "destroys, murders, tortures and rapes" and therefore deserves neither sympathy nor understanding. "I am aware of Russia's role in the history of Bulgaria, as well as in the history of Ukraine," Kuleba told a press conference after meeting with his Bulgarian counterpart, Teodora Genchovska. "Historically Russia did some things that continue to live in the feelings of the peoples of these two countries," but today's Russia is a "different" one, he added.

12:34 Poland can take in 10,000 Ukrainian soldiers wounded by the war. The health system of Poland, a country bordering Ukraine and the main destination of people who decide to leave the former Soviet republic because of the war unleashed by Russia, has the capacity to care for at least 10,000 wounded Ukrainian soldiers, Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki said on Tuesday. The Polish leader assured reporters during a visit to the western Ukrainian city of Lviv that Poland is already treating "several dozen" soldiers and is ready to take in more. "We are ready to take in at least 10,000, if necessary [...] We are doing everything possible to take in and treat all wounded soldiers from Ukraine," he detailed.

12:27 Russia rules out using nuclear weapons in the war with Ukraine. Moscow has assured on Tuesday that it will only use conventional weapons in the conflict that has been going on in Ukraine since February 24. This was confirmed by the Russian Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, in response to a question about the possible use of nuclear weapons in the war in an interview granted to India Today. This is one of the strongest comments made by the head of Russian diplomacy on this issue. However, it should be kept in mind that Lavrov is not the ultimate military decision-maker.

12:20 Killing with God's forgiveness, chronicle of the special envoy of La Vanguardia in Kyiv, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs. Kyiv and Moscow. In both cities, capitals of Ukraine and Russia respectively, the faith is strained and the commandments are distorted in the midst of war. On the one hand, Father Lorenzo Zhivchik acknowledged in St. Michael's Cathedral, seat of the Ukrainian Patriarchate, that "killing is not a sin when we kill to defend the homeland, to protect ourselves from evil". In parallel, Kirill I, the Patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church, thinks the same from the dark side of faith. In his case he looks favorably on Putin's war and has not condemned the death of civilians in the conflict.

12:13 Russian troops will take control of the Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol, according to a Chechen leader. Ramzan Kadyrov, leader of the Russian region of Chechnya and ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has assured that Russian troops will take control of the Azovstal plant in the port of Mariupol on Tuesday. It should be recalled that a group of Ukrainian defenders is holding out at this facility. Russia has given an ultimatum to these fighters, also foreigners, to surrender and hand over their weapons before noon, guaranteeing them that they will be allowed to stay alive. "Today, with the help of the Almighty, we will take Azovstal completely," Kadyrov has said in an audio message on his Telegram channel.

12:05 Russia accuses Western countries of wanting to prolong the war in Ukraine. The United States and other Western countries are doing everything possible to prolong the "special military operation" in Ukraine, according to the Kremlin. This was assured on Tuesday by Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu in statements quoted by the Russian news agency TASS. "The growing volume of foreign arms supplies clearly demonstrates their intentions to provoke the Kiev regime to fight to the end in Ukraine," Shoigu said, according to the same source.

11:56 Access to the Human Rights Watch (HRW) portal in Russia restricted. Russia's communications regulator has restricted access to the website of the New York-based human rights group Human Rights Watch (HRW), state news agency TASS has detailed. The move is related to HRW's publication of what Roskomnadzor, the watchdog, considered false information about the behavior of the Russian military in Ukraine, TASS has reported.

11:49 Lavrov confirms that Russia has started the next phase of the military campaign in Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov confirmed on Tuesday that they have already started the next phase of the country's military campaign on Ukrainian territory, which began last February 24. This campaign is focused on the "complete liberation" of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. "The operation in eastern Ukraine is aimed, as already announced, at the complete liberation of the Donetsk and Luhansk republics. This operation will continue, the next phase of this special operation is beginning," he has detailed in statements to the India Today channel and broadcast by the Foreign Ministry.

11:42 Sanchez will travel to Kyiv to meet with Zelenski and reopen the Spanish embassy, reports the journalist of the Politics section of La Vanguardia, Juan Carlos Merino. The Moncloa has confirmed to La Vanguardia that the President of the Government will travel to Kyiv "very soon" to attend the reopening of the Spanish embassy in the Ukrainian capital and to meet with President Volodymir Zelenski, among other meetings that are planned. No exact date of the trip has been detailed. "No details can be given for security reasons," government sources justify.

11:34 Russia will denounce the freezing of its international reserves due to the war in Ukraine. Western countries froze Russia's international reserves in response to the invasion of Ukraine, launched last February 24. Moscow has expressed its opinion on this issue, which considers this measure to be unprecedented and will therefore denounce it in court. This has been assured by the governor of the Central Bank of Russia (BCR), Elvira Nabiullina. "This is an unprecedented freezing of gold and foreign exchange reserves, we will prepare lawsuits, we are preparing to file them. Because it is unprecedented that, on a global scale, the gold and foreign currency reserves of such a large country are frozen," she has maintained at a meeting in the Duma. Nabiullina has pointed out that, due to this measure, the Russian monetary entity has had to introduce currency controls. "If we had gold and foreign exchange reserves, there would be no need for such draconian measures for capital movement," she has insisted.

11:26 Russian gas flow to Europe via Ukraine falls. Russian gas deliveries to Europe via Ukraine have dropped Tuesday morning, in line with customer requests, while flows to Germany via Nord Stream 1 have remained stable and increased eastward to Poland from Germany via the Yamal pipeline between Russia and the European Union. Daily nominations of Russian gas deliveries to Slovakia via Ukraine have fallen on Tuesday, according to data from Slovak operator TSO Eustream. Nominations through the Velke Kapusany border point stood at around 398,774 megawatt hours (MWh) per day on Tuesday, down from 420,099 MWh per day on Monday, the data showed.

11:14 ???? Sanchez will travel to Ukraine and meet with Zelenski. The President of the Government, Pedro Sánchez, will travel to Kyiv in the coming days and will meet with his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodímir Zelenski, and the Prime Minister of this country. The meeting between the two leaders will take place at a time when Spain is considering, like other European countries, reopening its embassy in the Ukrainian capital, which was closed following the escalation of violence in the war and after evacuating the Spanish residents in that country who requested them. The decision to reopen the Spanish embassy in the capital of the former Soviet republic corresponds to the "commitment" of the Government with the Ukrainian people.

11:10 Russia starts the battle for Donbass in eastern Ukraine. Russian forces are attempting Tuesday to break through Ukrainian defenses along almost the entire front line in the east of the former Soviet republic, beginning what Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky has dubbed the "battle for the Donbass." "A very large part of the entire Russian army is now concentrated in this offensive," the Ukrainian leader said in a video released early this morning. "No matter how many Russian troops they send there, we will fight. We will defend ourselves," he added. On the other hand, the chief of staff of the Ukrainian president, Andriy Yermak, has assured citizens that his forces will be able to contain the offensive in "the second phase of the war". "Believe in our army, it is very strong," he said.

11:00 Sanctions on Russia reopen the debate on the role of the dollar in non-Western countries, reports La Vanguardia journalist Andy Robinson. NATO ruled out the option of intervening militarily in Ukraine because of Russia's invasion, which began on February 24. Excluding the option of fighting a nuclear power, the re-founded transatlantic alliance opted for a plan B: the so-called weaponization -transformation into a weapon- of the dollar.

10:52 Stellantis suspends production in Russia as a result of the war in Ukraine. Automaker Stellantis on Tuesday announced the suspension of production at its Russian plant due to logistical difficulties and sanctions imposed on Moscow. The company has a van manufacturing plant in Kaluga, some 201 kilometers southeast of Moscow, in co-ownership with Japanese automaker Mitsubishi. This plant already halted production earlier this month as a result of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. "Given the rapid daily increase in cross-sanctions and logistical difficulties, Stellantis has suspended its manufacturing operations in Kaluga to ensure full compliance with all cross-sanctions and to protect its employees," Stellantis said in a statement. The world's fourth-largest automaker, which produces and sells the Peugeot, Citroen, Opel, Jeep and Fiat brands in Russia, has only 1% of the country's car market. 10:44 Putin decorates the soldiers Ukraine accuses of the Bucha massacres, reports La Vanguardia's correspondent in Moscow, Gonzalo Aragonés. The massacre in Bucha, a town near Kyiv where a large number of civilian corpses were found with signs of having been executed, is again in the news. This past Monday the President of Russia, Vladimir Putin, has decorated the unit of the Russian army that Ukraine points out as the perpetrator of the massacre. In a decree signed on Monday, the head of the Kremlin awarded the honorary name of "Guards" to the 64th Motorized Infantry Brigade. "For their enormous heroism and bravery, the endurance and courage shown by the brigade's personnel in protecting the Fatherland and the interests of the State in armed conflicts, I decide: to award the 64th Motorized Infantry Brigade with the honorary title of 'Guards'", the text details.

10:37 Russia gives another ultimatum to Ukrainian forces in Mariupol to surrender. Moscow has given another ultimatum to Ukrainian forces still holding out in the port city of Mariupol, heavily besieged since the first days of the war in Ukraine. These troops are holding out mainly at the Azovstal steelworks in the town's port. Russia is giving them until noon to lay down their arms in exchange for saving their lives. "Taking into account the catastrophic situation that has developed at the Azovstal metallurgical plant, as well as being guided by purely humane principles, the Russian Armed Forces once again offer militants of nationalist battalions and foreign mercenaries to stop hostilities and lay down their arms as of 12:00 (09.00 GMT)," the Russian Defense Ministry said. "All those who lay down their arms are guaranteed the preservation of life," said the head of the Russian Federation's National Defense Control Center, Colonel General Mikhail Mizintsev.

10:27 Ukrainian forces are holding out in Mariupol, one of Russia's targets in the war in Ukraine. The port city of Mariupol, besieged by the Russian army since the first days of the invasion, has not yet fallen under full control of Moscow despite heavy shelling. This has been assured by the deputy mayor of the town, Petro Andriushchenko, through his Telegram account. "The occupation troops not only drop bombs on the Azovstal plant (which is still defended by Ukrainian soldiers), but chaotically shell the city's residential quarters, where they only recently allowed civilians to return," the municipal aide noted.

10:19 Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities come under fire again for the third day in a row . The Ukrainian capital and its metropolitan area continue to be targeted by Russia in the Ukrainian war. Likewise, Kharkiv, Dnipro and Mikolaiv, near Odessa, have also been targeted by Russian missiles in the last hours, reports La Vanguardia's special envoy in the former Soviet republic, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs. In these cities the Ukrainian defenses manage to keep the invading forces at bay, but the cost for the civilian population is higher every day, as many have been without water and electricity for weeks and with hardly any food.

10:12 Major cities suffer more Russian attacks in the last hours of war in Ukraine. In the last hours, several Ukrainian cities have been victims of attacks and shelling by Russian troops. One of them is Kreminna, in the Luhansk region, where four people have been killed and another injured when Russian soldiers opened fire on their vehicle. These people were trying to leave the village. The advance in Kreminna brings the Russians closer to the city of Sloviansk, which is considered a key target in Putin's offensive and which was seized by pro-Russian fighters in 2014, reports La Vanguardia's special envoy in the country, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs. On the other hand, Russian troops have already seized Izium, which is located on a road north of Sloviansk, and are ready to advance into the city from the north and east.

10:04 Greece seizes a Russian oil tanker on the island of Evia over the war in Ukraine. Greece has seized a Russian oil tanker off the island of Evia as part of sanctions imposed on Moscow by the international community due to the war in Ukraine. This has been confirmed by an official of the Greek Ministry of Maritime Transport. The Russian-flagged Pegas, with 19 Russian crew members on board, has been seized near the coastal town of Karystos in Evia. "It has been seized as part of EU sanctions," this same public worker has said. A coast guard official has said the ship had been seized, but not its oil cargo.

09:53 Denmark will temporarily increase natural gas production because of the war in Ukraine. Denmark's government has assured Tuesday that it will temporarily increase natural gas production from its North Sea fields, but planned to phase out natural gas in the long term to become independent of Russian supplies. "We will increase natural gas production in the North Sea for a limited period of time," Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday. "We are convinced that it is better to produce gas in the North Sea than to buy it from (Russian President) Vladimir Putin," Frederiksen has said.

09:43 Pro-Russian forces try to take control of Azovstal. Moscow-backed separatist forces are trying to seize control of the Azovstal metallurgical plant in the port city of Mariupol, RIA news agency details quoting separatist spokesman Eduard Basurin. The aim of the pro-Russians in this locality is to "liberate" the facility as quickly as possible, RIA quoted another separatist, Denis Pushilin, as saying.

09:33 Russia on Tuesday denounced an attack in a village in the Belgorod region. Russian authorities have denounced in recent hours the attack on a small village in the Belgorod region, near the country's border with Ukraine, and caused one wounded. According to the governor of the region, Vyacheslav Gladkov, the attack has been carried out from the Ukrainian territory. "A local woman was wounded," the head of state said via Telegram, where he added that the incident also caused damage. The governor added that he will personally go to the site to assess the damage.

09:23 New Zealand imposes sanctions against 18 Russian banks and financial institutions. The New Zealand Executive announced Tuesday the imposition of new sanctions against 18 Russian banks and financial institutions as part of the response to the invasion of Ukraine ordered by Moscow and specifically by its president, Vladimir Putin. "These large institutions represent approximately 80% of Russia's total banking assets," New Zealand's Foreign Minister Nanaia Mahuta detailed through a statement. The measures affect in total three Russian government financial institutions, as well as 15 banks, including those linked to the oligarchs, military and those responsible for the annexation of Crimea, the note has added. Among them are the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the Black Sea Development and Reconstruction Bank, the Moscow Credit Bank, Gazprombank, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, the Russian Agricultural Bank, Sberbank and the Industrial Savings Bank.

09:10 No agreement on opening new humanitarian corridors today in Ukraine. Ukraine has failed to reach an agreement with Russia on opening new humanitarian corridors this Tuesday to evacuate civilian population from some of the localities most besieged by Russian troops' attacks, Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Iryna Vereshchuk has confirmed. "Today, April 19, unfortunately there are no humanitarian corridors," the Ukrainian leader wrote via Facebook, from where she also assured that intensive shelling has continued in the Donbass region in eastern Ukraine. Efforts to create a safe passage for civilians to leave the besieged southern city of Mariupol have repeatedly failed, with each side blaming the other. Russia has denied targeting civilians.

09:00 UK does not want to exchange Medvedchuk for two British fighters. Britain will not seek to help Russia, a senior minister has disclosed when asked about the possibility of exchanging pro-Russian politician detained by Ukrainian authorities Viktor Medvedchuk for two British fighters who were captured in Ukraine by Russian forces. The Britons appeared Monday on Russian state television and asked to be exchanged for Medvedchuk, a Ukrainian ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin who is being held by Ukrainian authorities.

08:50 France assures that it is working on an embargo on Russian oil at the European level. French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire assured on Tuesday that an embargo on Russian oil is being worked on at the European Union level and added that French President Emmanuel Macron, looks favorably on such a measure. "I hope that in the coming weeks we will convince our European partners to stop importing Russian oil," Le Maire said in statements to the radio station Europe 1.

08:41 More Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. Ukraine suffered this past Monday one of the worst air strikes since the war started last February 24. The main cities of the country, such as Kharkiv and Lviv, in geographically opposite places, were targeted by Russian shells. As reported by the special envoy of La Vanguardia in Kyiv, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs, a rain of missiles left dozens of civilian victims. Seven people died in the town of Lviv, in the west and a few kilometers from the border with the EU, and another two in Kharkiv, close to the border with Russia. The shelling began at dawn and continued throughout the day.

08:30 Street battles in Kreminna, according to a Ukrainian military official. A Ukrainian military official has assured in the last hours that street battles have started and that evacuation from the town of Kreminna is impossible. That is one of only two places where Ukrainians said the Russians have managed to break through Monday along a front that stretches for hundreds of miles. Luhansk regional military administrator Serhiy Haidai said the city was attacked with heavy artillery overnight, setting fire to seven residential buildings, and that the Olympus sports complex was also hit. Also, according to Haidai, the Russians have taken control of the city after "razing everything to the ground," so his men have withdrawn to regroup and continue fighting. "It just doesn't make sense to stand in one place, die for everyone, without causing significant damage to the enemy," he has detailed.

08:19 U.S. warns that Russia is sending reinforcements in the Donbass. The Pentagon has warned in the last hours that Russia is sending reinforcements of material and soldiers to the Donbass region to launch a major offensive to take control of this area of eastern Ukraine. The Defense Department spokesman, John Kirby, has assured in a press conference that there is an influx of artillery equipment, helicopter support and elements to facilitate Russian command and control operations in the Donbass. "We believe they have reinforced the number of their battalion tactical groups in eastern and southern" Ukraine, Kirby said.

08:12 Russia decorates the military unit that Ukraine holds responsible for the Bucha massacre. Russian President Vladimir Putin has condemned the military unit that Kyiv blames for the massacre in Bucha, a town near the capital where a large number of civilian victims were found with signs of having been executed. Putin has justified this decoration for "heroism and courage of the masses", but without mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine. The decree signed by Putin has awarded the 64th Motorized Infantry Brigade with the honorary title of Guards, which was identified by the Ukrainian authorities as the perpetrator of alleged war crimes.

08:00 Russia destroys weapons storage near Lviv. Russian troops continue to attack key points in western Ukraine, despite their intentions to concentrate on the Donbass area in the east of the former Soviet republic. In recent hours, the Russian military has claimed to have destroyed a facility in the Lviv region that contained weapons shipped to Ukraine from the United States and other countries, according to Interfax. Pentagon spokesman John Kirby assured a few hours ago in statements to the media that he could not confirm such an attack.

07:52 Spain plans to reopen its embassy in Kyiv soon. The war between Russia and Ukraine continues at a delicate moment, when the Ukrainian authorities consider that Moscow has started the definitive offensive on Donbass to take control of the area. However, several European countries are considering reopening their embassies in Kyiv, including Spain. This was stated by the President of the Government, Pedro Sanchez, in declarations to Antena 3. It should be noted that the European Union reopened its mission in the Ukrainian capital just over a week ago after Russian troops withdrew from the region, although the capital has been attacked again in recent days.

07:44 U. S. wants to send back diplomats in Ukraine. Washington has raised its desire to send back US diplomats in Ukraine as soon as possible, although it has not yet set a specific date. This was detailed by US State Department spokesman Ned Price. "When the security situation permits, and not a second later, I can assure you that we will have a restored diplomatic presence on the ground in Ukraine," Price said.

07:32 EU plans solidarity fund for Ukraine reconstruction. The EU bloc is looking for ways to pay for the reconstruction of Ukraine after the war with Russia. The EU-27 plan to set up a solidarity trust fund to finance Ukraine's reconstruction, as member states were told they should pay the lion's share of the costs. The issues of post-war reconstruction and possible reparations are expected to focus talks in the coming weeks, as senior officials from Brussels and Washington plan to discuss ways to financially support Kyiv and ensure that the huge amount of money is not wasted.

07:20 Killing with God's forgiveness, chronicled by La Vanguardia's special envoy in Kyiv, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs. Kyiv and Moscow. In both cities, capitals of Ukraine and Russia respectively, the faith is strained and the commandments are distorted in the middle of a war. On the one hand, Father Lorenzo Zhivchik acknowledged in St. Michael's Cathedral, seat of the Ukrainian Patriarchate, that "killing is not a sin when we kill to defend the homeland, to protect ourselves from evil". In parallel, Kirill I, the Patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church, thinks the same from the dark side of faith. In his case he looks favorably on Putin's war and has not condemned the killing of civilians in the conflict.

07:11 The U.S. Treasury plans to meet with Ukraine's Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen contemplates holding a meeting with Ukrainian Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal during this week's major meetings of world economic leaders in Washington, but she will try to avoid most contact with theRussian officials who will attend telematically. Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and how world powers should handle spillover effects on economies, including food insecurity, will take center stage at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank spring meetings, which run through Friday and will be both face-to-face and virtual. Yellen is expected to use this week's meetings to work with allies on efforts to increase economic pressure on Russia and mitigate spillovers, call for the implementation of a global minimum tax agreement and address food security issues.

07:00 Kyiv tries to protect its monuments from the ravages of Russian invasion. Ukraine's cultural heritage is being damaged because of attacks by Russian troops. Even the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell, has assured that the Russian troops are doing it "on purpose". Faced with this situation, and in order to protect their monuments from Russian shelling and fire, the Ukrainian authorities have chosen to cover them with sandbags.

06:52 EU accuses Russia of purposefully destroying Ukraine's cultural heritage. The European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell, has recently warned that Russia is "purposefully" destroying cultural heritage in Ukraine during its invasion. "Objects of cultural heritage are destroyed on purpose in Russia's war against Ukraine," the leader of European diplomacy has pointed out through his official Twitter profile, in a message in which he has also stressed that it is "an important part of European heritage." For all these reasons, he assured that the EU "supports artists, cultural professionals and cultural organizations affected by the war".

06:45 Russian offensive in the Donbass, chronicle of the special envoy of La Vanguardia in Kyiv, Xavier Mas de Xaxàs. The Ukrainian president, Volodímir Zelenski, informed last night that Russia "has begun the great battle for the Donbass", announcing a new turn in the evolution of the war in the heart of the former Soviet republic. Zelensky said so in a video message broadcast on the Ukrinform news channel, in which he warned that the Ukrainian soldiers "will fight" and "will not give up" any territory in this great offensive of the Russian army to control the entire east of the country.

06:37 Ukraine attacks a Russian locality near the border. Ukrainian forces have attacked the Russian locality of Golovchino, close to the border between the two countries, resulting in one person wounded. This was reported by the governor of the Russian province of Belgorod, Vyacheslav Gladkov, via Telegram. At first it was not clear whether this attack was carried out with artillery, mortars, missiles or whether it was an air strike. If this information is confirmed, it would be a new Ukrainian attack on Russian soil, after the one by helicopters against a fuel depot in Belgorod.

06:28 Ukrainian army in Mariupol asks the Pope for help to evacuate civilians. The port city of Mariupol continues to represent Ukrainian resistance to the Russian invasion. However, the situation is becoming increasingly complex and more and more voices are calling for new humanitarian corridors to evacuate civilians. In the last hours, Ukrainian troops have even asked the Pope for help to evacuate civilians. The commander of the 36th Ukrainian Marine Brigade, Sergiy Volyna, has written a letter to the Pontiff asking him to intervene "to save the exhausted civilian population of the city", as detailed by the Ukrainian ambassador to the Holy See, Andrii Yurash, on his social networks.

06:18 Zelensky claims that Russia has started "the great battle" for Donbass. Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky reported last night that Russia has already started "the great battle for Donbass," referring to the major offensive to control eastern Ukraine. "We can confirm that Russian troops have started that battle," the Ukrainian leader assured in a video message broadcast by Ukrinform. Zelensky then added that Ukrainian soldiers "will battle" and "will not give up" any of the country's territory. "No matter how many Russian troops are deployed: we will fight," he stressed.

06:10 A total of 2,072 civilians killed, 169 of them children, in war in Ukraine. The UN has confirmed in the last hours the death of 2,072 civilians, including 169 of them children, since the beginning of the war in Ukraine. The civilian victims who have been injured number 2,818, according to the data that the UN agency has been able to corroborate. However, according to data published Monday by the Ukrainian Prosecutor General's office on its Telegram account, the number of children killed in Ukraine since the Russians invaded the country has reached 205.

06:00 Ukraine urges Russia to open a humanitarian corridor from Mariupol. Ukrainian authorities have urged Russia to open a safe humanitarian corridor with Mariupol, where an estimated 100,000 civilians remain, in addition to Ukrainian troops holding out in the besieged port city. "The situation in Mariupol has worsened. I call on the military-political leaders of the Russian Federation to open a humanitarian corridor from Mariupol to Berdyansk," Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Iryna Vereshchuk has called on.

05:52 White House insists "no plans" for Biden's trip to Ukraine. U.S. President Joe Biden has no upcoming trip to Ukraine on his agenda to travel to Ukraine, the White House has insisted in recent hours. This follows a request by Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky for the Democratic leader to travel to the former Soviet republic to see first-hand the damage of the Russian invasion. "There are no plans for President Biden to travel to Ukraine," White House spokeswoman Jen Psaki insisted at a press conference.

05:45 Russia-Ukraine war | Latest news on the conflict and Putin, live. Good morning and welcome to the minute-by-minute coverage of everything related to the Russia-Ukraine war. Kyiv has already filled in the form to be recognized as an applicant country to join the European Union, according to the Ukrinform portal, which cites sources close to the country's president, Volodymir Zelensky. This followed the steps and deadlines set by the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, who recalls the recent visit of the German politician to the Ukrainian capital.

title: The game is afoot: central banks ramp up inflation fight
text:
LONDON (Reuters) - Central banks are racing to get on top of surging inflation, with New Zealand and Canada delivering aggressive half-point rate hikes this week and the ECB on Thursday sticking with plans to dial back stimulus this year.

But policymakers must also, while watching inflation, guard against the fallout from the war in Ukraine. The hit to consumer confidence from higher energy prices and disrupted supply chains might well darken the economic outlook, constraining monetary tightening.

Here is a look at where policymakers stand on the path out of the pandemic-era stimulus, ranked in terms of hawkishness.

Graphic: The rate hiking cycle is off - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/akvezjbkwpr/rates1404.PNG

1) NORWAY

The Norges Bank hiked rates by 25 basis points to 0.75% on March 24 and announced plans to hike at a faster pace than previously planned.

Including the March move, the bank now plans eight hikes to bring rates to 2.50% by end-2023, three more than projected in March, and two more than anticipated in March by a Reuters poll.

2) NEW ZEALAND

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand on Wednesday reinforced its position as one of the world's most hawkish central banks.

It raised the cash rate by 50 bps to 1.5%, the biggest rise in two decades and the fourth hike in the current cycle, and maintained its forecast for rates to peak around 3.35% by end-2023.

Graphic: RBNZ gets aggressive - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/byvrjbgrjve/RBNZ.PNG

3) CANADA

Having kicked off its rate-rise cycle in March, the Bank of Canada raised key rates on Wednesday by 50 bps to 1%, its biggest single move in more than two decades.

From next week, the BoC will also let maturing bonds roll off its balance sheet. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem reckons rates are still far below neutral levels, estimated between 2%-3%. Markets expect rates will hit 2.5% by year-end.

Graphic: Canada most certainly in the hawkish camp - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/znpneqwrqvl/CANADA.PNG

4) BRITAIN

With inflation at a 30-year high, the Bank of England is under pressure to tighten policy further after three hikes since December.

Markets are all but certain it will raise its benchmark by 25 bps to 1% on May 5, and then to 2%-2.25% by end-2022.

However, with soaring energy prices threatening growth, the BoE has softened its language on the need for further tightening.

Graphic: UK inflation hits 30-year high of 7% - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/dwvkrqxakpm/UKINFLATION.PNG

5) UNITED STATES

The Federal Reserve raised rates by a quarter point in March to a 0.25%-0.5% range and has flagged a half-point move on May 4. It is also discussing trimming its asset portfolio.

Inflation, which hit a 40-year high at 8.5%, may be starting to peak, but is expected to remain above the Fed's 2% target at least through 2023.

Graphic: Central Bank balance sheets set to shrink - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/gdvzyjxqopw/CABNKS1.PNG

6) AUSTRALIA

Markets' campaign to get the Reserve Bank of Australia to pivot hawkish succeeded on April 5, when it finally opened the door for its 0.1% cash rate to rise this year.

Data later this month is expected to show annual inflation at 3.2%, while a survey published on April 12 showed robust business conditions with the jobless rate possibly dropping below 4% this year for the first time since the 1970s.

Futures price a 25 bps hike in June and imply a cumulative 200 bps of tightening by year-end.

7) EURO ZONE

The European Central Bank is among the most cautious of major central banks. On Thursday, it stuck to plans to slowly unwind extraordinary stimulus, weighing worries over record-high inflation against the risk that the war in Ukraine could drive the euro zone economy into recession.

Economists still expect the ECB to hike rates later this year and markets price around 60 bps of tightening by year-end.

Graphic: Euro zone inflation at record highs - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/zjpqkdreapx/EZinflation.PNG

8) SWEDEN

Sweden's 6.1% inflation, the highest since 1991, may leave the dovish Riksbank no choice but turn into a hawk.

The bank will have to rethink its policy approach at its next meeting on April 28, deputy governor Martin Floden said last week. Governor Stefan Ingves, whose vote in February was the decider in keeping balance sheet plans unchanged this year, has made similar comments recently.

Current Riksbank guidance still sees a 2024 hike; markets see rates rising from zero to 1% by November..

9) SWITZERLAND

The Swiss National Bank remains in the dovish camp but with 2022 inflation projected at an above-target 2.1%, it is paying closer attention to prices.

Flight to safety sparked by the Ukraine conflict has forced the SNB to step up currency intervention, boostin Swiss sight deposits by 8 billion Swiss francs ($8.58 billion) in the past three weeks.

Graphic: SNB deposits - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/gkplgqnxkvb/SNB%20deposits.JPG

10)JAPAN

The Bank of Japan remains the holdout dove.

Governor Haruhiko Kuroda has warned the recent inflation spike, driven by import costs, could hurt the economy, stressing the BOJ's resolve to keep monetary policy ultra-loose.

With policy tightening a long way off, traders have ramped up bets on a weaker yen, driving it to two-decade lows against the dollar and eliciting a rare warning from its finance minister.

Graphic: BOJ balance sheet - https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/jnpwekmwmpw/BOJ%20balance%20sheet.JPG("https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/mkt/jnpwekmwmpw/BOJ%20balance%20sheet.JPG")

($1 = 0.9329 Swiss francs)

(Reporting by Sujata Rao, Saikat Chatterjee, Yoruk Bahceli and Dhara Ranasinghe; Editing by Tomasz Janowski)

title: REFILE-TEXT-Czech  central bank  March 31 board meeting minutes
text:
(Corrects dateline to April 8 from April 7)

PRAGUE, April 8 (Reuters) - Following is the full text of the minutes from the Czech central bank (CNB) governing board's March 31 monetary policy meeting, released on Friday:

Present at the meeting: Governor Jiri Rusnok, vice-governors Marek Mora and Tomas Nidetzky, board members Vojtech Benda, Oldrich Dedek, Tomas Holub and Ales Michl.

The meeting opened with a presentation of the second situation report, underpinned by an assessment of the currently available information, which related largely to the economic impacts of the war in Ukraine. The war had significantly changed the outlooks for the foreign and domestic variables included in the winter forecast. Consistent with the winter forecast had been a substantial rise in market interest rates, followed by a gradual decline from the second half of this year onwards.

The Board assessed the risks and uncertainties of the winter forecast as being markedly inflationary, especially in the short run. These risks also required significantly tighter monetary policy, and probably for longer. A majority of the board members continued to regard the strong domestic demand, bolstered by a long-overheated labour market, as a significant source of domestic price growth. Jiri Rusnok said that the underlying inflationary factors had been forming for a long time and the second-round effects in the price vertical were clear. Monetary policy had to respond actively to these domestic inflation pressures, which were not diminishing. Marek Mora, Tomas Nidetzky, Vojtech Benda and Tomas Holub agreed. However, the cost pressures from the external environment were also growing significantly. These included in particular a sharp rise in prices of energy and commodities.

The board members emphasised that we were in a situation of unprecedented growth in uncertainty, which, from a monetary policymaker’s perspective, was even greater than it had been at the outbreak of the Covid pandemic. Tomas Holub and Marek Mora said that if the Russian invasion of Ukraine had hit the Czech economy in the steady state, it would have been a typical inflationary shock, one whose first-round price impacts could have been disregarded. The appropriate response would then have been to focus solely on its second-round effects. However, the economy had been hit by the shock in a situation of high, broad-based inflation where there was a need to maintain the CNB’s monetary policy credibility.

Oldrich Dedek and Ales Michl said jointly that the outbreak of the war in Ukraine constituted a structural shift that was making the policy of raising interest rates sharply even more problematic. In their view, the predominantly cost-push nature of the present inflation, now exacerbated by the war, would continue to make it impossible to subdue inflation with the use of interest rates. At the same time, raising interest rates would exacerbate the decline in economic output. According to Ales Michl, two anti-inflationary measures were now needed: a gradual reduction in the government budget deficit and the prevention of indexation of wages to inflation. The board members agreed that it was not possible to declare the inflation pressures to be purely cost-push in nature and to abandon monetary policy.

There was a consensus that the economic consequences of the war and the economic sanctions against Russia would be stagflationary. The key question according to Marek Mora was to what extent would the economic slowdown have an autonomous anti-inflationary effect, or what would be the resulting combination of anti-inflationary demand and inflationary supply factors. He noted that the dramatic decline in GDP seen during the coronavirus pandemic had not had an anti-inflationary impact. Vojtech Benda said that the expected additional fiscal expenditure of the Czech government connected with the influx of refugees could be inflationary. According to Tomas Holub, the tightness in the domestic labour market could be partially reduced by the effect of additional labour force in the form of war refugees, albeit selectively in only some sectors. Tomas Nidetzky pointed out that the first signs of a deterioration in consumer and investment sentiment were already appearing, and the monetary policy question was whether, given the length of the transmission mechanism, it still made sense to respond with another sizeable rate hike.

A large part of the debate was devoted to the anchoring of inflation expectations. According to Vojtech Benda, this anchoring could be weakened if the central bank failed to send out strong enough signals that monetary policymakers intended to fight inflation and fulfil their mandate. Tomas Holub said that some unanchoring of inflation expectations was already apparent in firms’ pricing. Instead of dampening the impacts of the cost shocks in the usual way, manufacturing and retail chains were currently amplifying them by preventively increasing their profit margins. According to Tomas Nidetzky, the maintenance of inflation expectations could also be put at risk if the koruna started to weaken without fundamental cause. In such case, it would be appropriate to curb excessive exchange rate volatility. Conversely, Oldrich Dedek felt that the sizeable decline in real wages and the harsh impacts of the energy crisis on firms and households would prevent a wage-price spiral from forming.

Several of the board members commented on the effectiveness of the monetary policy transmission mechanism. Oldrich Dedek and Ales Michl argued that the previous interest rate hikes had not had an impact on the inflation rate, primarily because monetary policy was unable in the short term to influence the cost shocks underlying the higher inflation. By contrast, Marek Mora and Jiri Rusnok emphasised that the sharp rise in interest rates had de facto not started until last autumn, so its effects – given the horizon of most effective transmission – would only be visible after 4–6 quarters, i.e. at the end of this year.

Part of the Board’s discussion focused on the exchange rate. It was said that the CNB’s foreign exchange market interventions against the rapid depreciation of the koruna after the outbreak of the war in Ukraine had done their job and no interventions had been needed for some time now. After a discussion, the Board therefore decided to resume the CNB’s activities under the programme of sales of part of the income on international reserves, which had been suspended while its foreign exchange market interventions had been going on. The Board also debated the potential use of the exchange rate in an effort to subdue inflation. Jiri Rusnok said that in this situation, we should not dismiss thoughts of using the exchange rate channel, because the interest rate channel would not suppress inflation sufficiently quickly on its own. Vojtech Benda agreed. Conversely, the other board members said they did not feel the need to use the exchange rate as an additional monetary policy instrument alongside the standard one (interest rates).

In view of the aforementioned factors, a majority of the Board felt it was necessary to respond to the further marked increase in inflation pressures in the Czech economy. At the same time, the direct impacts of the war in Ukraine on consumer prices could be partially disregarded for the time being. However, monetary policy would react to the indirect price effects of these pressures, ensuring that inflation returned to the 2% target in the longer run. The Board therefore also said that it was ready to continue raising interest rates so that inflation expectations did not diverge from the CNB’s 2% inflation target in the longer term. Restoring price stability soon was now the CNB’s absolute priority, because this was a necessary condition for long-term prosperity of the Czech economy.

At the close of the meeting the Board decided to increase the two-week repo rate by 50 basis points to 5%. At the same time, it increased the discount rate by the same amount to 4% and the Lombard rate to 6%. Five members voted in favour of this decision: Jiri Rusnok, Marek Mora, Tomas Nidetzky, Vojtech Benda and Tomas Holub. Two members, Oldrich Dedek and Ales Michl, voted for leaving interest rates unchanged.

(Reporting by Jason Hovet)
