title: Ukraine - Russia war, live today | Latest news on the bombings
text:
The key points of the day

- The UN humanitarian chief will go to Moscow to push for a truce in Ukraine.

- Russia has declared its readiness to continue negotiations with Ukraine.

- More than 4,200 civilians evacuated through humanitarian corridors on Saturday in Ukraine.

15:11 Seven buses set to take some 500 civilians out of Mariupol this Sunday Seven buses will attempt to leave the besieged Ukrainian city of Mariupol this coming Sunday with some 500 civilians inside as the Red Cross tries again to enter the city with humanitarian aid after the failure of its first raid on Friday. The buses are part of a civilian initiative announced on Telegram and, if successful, will move residents to Zaporiyia, while some 100,000 people still await their turn in the siege-ravaged city.

15:02 Ukraine demands "devastating new sanctions" against Russia after denouncing Bucha "massacre" Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dimitro Kuleba on Sunday accused Russian forces of orchestrating a "massacre" in Bucha and called on the G7 to issue a series of "devastating new sanctions" against Moscow, with immediate effect, and estimated "hundreds" dead as Russian troops passed through the recently liberated areas near Kiev. "The massacre of Bucha has been deliberate. The aim of the Russians is to eliminate as many Ukrainians as they can. We have to stop them and kick them out," he said via his Twitter account.

14:52 Russia will only export food to friendly countries in rubles or in their currencies Russia will only export food and crops to "friendly countries" in rubles or in their national currencies, RIA news agency has reported Sunday, citing Dmitry Medvedev, deputy secretary of Russia's Security Council.

14:43 UN brings to 1,325 civilians killed in war The United Nations Office for Human Rights has reported that at least 1,325 civilians have died since the start of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Among these dead, 120 are children, as indicated by the UN, which has clarified that these are the verified victims but that the real figure may be much higher. As for civilians wounded in the conflict, the UN has confirmed 2,017, including 168 children. The actual number of casualties "could be considerably much higher" as there is only partial information from some of the areas of major hostilities, including localities besieged by Russian troops such as Mariupol, Volnovaja, Izium or Irpin.

14:34 Ukraine says Bucha "massacre" was deliberate and calls for sanctions Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has accused Russia of carrying out a "massacre" in the town of Bucha outside Kiev and called on the G7 to impose new sanctions on Moscow. "We are still gathering and searching for bodies, but the number has already exceeded a hundred. Dead bodies are in the streets. They killed civilians while staying there and when leaving these villages and towns," the minister has posted on his Twitter account.

14:25 Explosions heard in Russian town of Belgorod near Ukraine border Two explosions were heard in the Russian town of Belgorod near the Ukrainian border on Sunday, two witnesses told Reuters, days after Russian authorities accused Ukrainian forces of attacking a fuel depot there. The cause of the explosions was not immediately clear. One witness said the explosions were so powerful that they shook the windows of his house in Belgorod.

14:16 Russia fires missiles near Odessa as evacuation of Mariupol is reattempted Ukraine claims Sunday that missiles are falling near the port of Odessa in southern Ukraine. Russia claimed this morning that it had destroyed an oil refinery used by the Ukrainian army, while attempts to evacuate civilians from the devastated city of Mariupol were expected to continue. For its part, the Odessa city council has said that "critical infrastructure facilities" have been hit by missiles, although for the moment, no casualties have been reported.

14:07 Twelve Spaniards have joined the Foreign Legion fighting the Russians in Ukraine At least a dozen Spanish citizens are already in Ukraine, enrolled (or with the intention of enrolling) in the International Legion for Territorial Defense created by the Government of Volodymir Zelenski against the Russian invasion, according to the figures handled by the Spanish security forces. Four are Catalans, eight from the rest of Spain. Their names and lives are known and they are and will be under the radar the day they return, because of the military baggage they will have acquired in the war. If they return.

13:58 Theater as a shelter during the war A Ukrainian theater company born in a World War II bomb shelter, keeps alive the art of drama in Kyiv, as an antidote against dehumanization in the midst of war aggression by Russian troops. And when the anti-aircraft sirens sound, they welcome the whole neighborhood into their lair. The legend of the theater tells that this armored basement of a building in the Shevchenko district was used by the Gestapo for interrogations, but for the last eight years it has been the headquarters of the Ukrainian company ProEnglish Theater, the only one that performs plays in English.

13:49 Ukraine calls for ICC mission after at least 280 bodies found Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has called for an International Criminal Court (ICC) mission to be sent to the Kiev district of Bucha after several civilian bodies were found. Kuleba has asked the ICC and other international organizations to go to Bucha and the other areas north of the capital that have been under Russian control until Friday to collect evidence of possible war crimes.

13:40 European Council President calls for more sanctions against Russia after "atrocities" uncovered near Kyiv European Council President Charles Michel on Sunday accused Russia of committing "atrocities" in the Kyiv region and called for more sanctions against Moscow. "Shocked by disturbing images of atrocities committed by the Russian army in the liberated Kyiv region," Michel wrote on Twitter, with the keywords #BuchaMassacre."

13:31 Ukraine assures that Russian troops have shelled OdessaTheUkrainian authorities have assured this Sunday that several missiles launched by Russian troops have hit the city of Odessa and damaged a refinery, without it being known yet if any casualties have been recorded.This was announced by the city council of the city on its Telegram channel, where they have asked citizens not to open the windows of their homes and not to interfere with the work of the relevant services.

13:22 Ukrainians in the rear, the report of the special envoy of La Vanguardia to Chop, Maria-Paz Lopez. The rearguard is a place where the war is far away but it is breathed everywhere. In Chop, a town of 8,800 inhabitants on the border with Hungary and an important railway junction from where refugee trains leave for Hungary and Slovakia, the convoys are no longer so full of passengers. As the fighting stalls, women and men over the age of 60 - the only adults allowed to leave the country - who fled from their bombed-out towns to these safer regions in the west are now choosing not to leave Ukraine.

13:13 Donetsk separatists accuse Ukraine of the deaths of 72 civilians since the start of the Russian invasion Authorities in the Moscow-friendly self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic have accused Ukrainian forces of the deaths of 72 civilians since the start of the Russian invasion of the country on February 24. "During the 46 days of the escalation, 72 civilians were killed," according to a message posted by the Joint Center for Control and Coordination on its Telegram channel and picked up by TASS news agency.

13:00 Russia says it is too early for more talks with Ukraine Russia's chief negotiator in talks with Ukraine says it is too early to talk about a meeting between the presidents of the two countries. Vladimir Medinsky, who led the Russian delegation at Tuesday's talks in Istanbul, Turkey, said "there is still a lot of work to be done" to finalize a draft agreement before Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Zelensky can meet.

12:55 Ukrainian Army announces it has taken full control of the border with Belarus The Ukrainian Army announced today that its troops have taken full control of the border with Belarus, as well as the area around the Chernobyl power plant. "Today, April 3, units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine took control of the Pripyat district and the area of the State Border of Ukraine with the Republic of Belarus," they announced in a statement posted on their official Facebook account.

12:46 EU pledges new sanctions after accusing Russia of committing "atrocities" in the Ukrainian town of Bucha European Council President Charles Michel has pledged new European Union sanctions after accusing the Russian Army of committing "atrocities" in the recently liberated Ukrainian town of Bucha. "Appalled by the shocking images of atrocities committed by the Russian Army in the liberated region of Kiev," Michel has made known in a message on Twitter, accompanied by the hashtag "Massacre in Bucha."

12:37 Seven buses set to take some 500 civilians out of Mariupol this Sunday Seven buses will try to leave the besieged Ukrainian city of Mariupol this coming Sunday with some 500 civilians inside as the Red Cross tries again to enter the city with humanitarian aid after the failure of its first raid on Friday. The buses are part of a civilian initiative announced on Telegram and, if successful, will move residents to Zaporiyia, while some 100,000 people still await their turn in the siege-ravaged city.

12:28 Poland opens the door to hosting US nuclear weapons on its territory Polish Deputy Prime Minister Jaros?aw Kaczy?ski said Sunday that Poland would be willing to host US nuclear warheads, as well as advocating reinforcing the country's troops on NATO's eastern flank. "Basically, it would make sense to expand the nuclear presence on the eastern flank," said the president of the Law and Justice Party (PiS) in an interview with the Sunday edition of the German daily Die Welt, although he clarified that the initiative would have to come from Washington. Kaczy?ski has proposed increasing the US troop presence in Europe from 100,000 to 150,000, of which half should be permanently stationed in the Eastern European countries on the borders with Russia.

12:19 Russian lawmakers will propose measures to punish the implementation of sanctions in Russia "My colleagues from the State Duma and I have finished the work and on Monday we will introduce amendments to the Criminal Code for the implementation of restrictive measures (sanctions) imposed by foreign states on the territory of the Russian Federation," senior Russian lawmaker Andrei Klishas wrote on his Telegram channel. "We expect prompt consideration of the amendments by the State Duma." Although, Klishas has not specified how Russia would identify or punish those who implemented the sanctions. Russian lawmakers passed amendments to the code in early March that make the dissemination of "false" information a crime punishable by fines or imprisonment. They imposed fines also for those carrying out public calls for sanctions against Russia.

12:08 Russia increases pressure in the Donbas and gives Kyiv a respite This Saturday Russian troops continued to advance in the Donbas, eastern Ukraine, a place where the Ukrainian Army is withstanding the onslaught of Russian artillery and aviation, whose goal is to conquer the entire territory of the Donetsk and Lugansk regions, while Kyiv manages to breathe with some tranquility after more than a month of siege. "Russian forces are massing in Donbas, towards Kharkov, and are preparing for even more powerful attacks," Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelensky said in a video message broadcast online. Since early yesterday, pro-Russian militias from Donetsk partially seized the locality of Novobakhtumovka, located north of the regional capital, after clashing with units of the 25th airborne brigade of the Ukrainian Army, the Russian Defense Ministry reported in its morning briefing. The spokesman of the Russian military entity, Igor Konashenkov, pointed out that the militias would have caused up to 40 casualties to the Ukrainian troops, besides destroying a tank platoon, two motorized infantry platoons, and a mortar battery.

11:57 Colombia shows its support to Zelenski before the "vile attack" on Ukraine The President of Colombia, Ivan Duque, had a telephone conversation with his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodimir Zelenski, to whom he expressed his country's support before Russia's "vile and disproportionate attack" on Ukraine, and highlighted the humanitarian aid provided to the Ukrainian people. The call, which lasted about 20 minutes, took place during Duque's visit to La Uribe, in the department of Meta (center), from where he said it was "a moving call". Duque said at an event that Zelenski "has shown the world his courage" and is "an example in the defense of the sovereignty of his people", while insisting on the "condemnation" of Russia's attacks. Ukraine "has been the victim of a vile and disproportionate attack, of a systematic violation of international humanitarian law and of atrocious acts such as the bombing of maternity hospitals and the destruction of its infrastructure", lamented the Colombian president.

11:47 Ukraine alleges Russian troops killed photojournalist Maxim Levin The Ukrainian Prosecutor's Office on Saturday accused Russian forces of having shot dead Ukrainian photojournalist Maxim 'Max' Levin, missing since the middle of last month near the capital, Kyiv. The journalist's body was found in the village of Guta Mezhyhirska, Vishgorod municipality. "According to preliminary information, Maxim Levin was unarmed and was killed by servicemen of the Russian Armed Forces with two shots from small arms," according to the statement picked up by the Ukrainian news portal Vgolos. The Prosecutor's Office has opened a criminal case against Russia for violating the laws on armed conflict.

11:40 Russia reorganizes its troops La Vanguardia's special envoy in Kyiv, Joaquin Luna explains how the latest developments of the Russian invasion in Ukraine are being experienced, with siren songs about a possible withdrawal sounding loudly. "Russian troops are not withdrawing, they are repositioning. Russia has repeatedly lied about its intentions," summarized yesterday the secretary general of the Atlantic Alliance, Jens Stoltenberg, to express the mistrust, shared by Kyiv, about a supposed military de-escalation in the Kyiv and Chernobyl areas.

11:31 Russia fires missiles near Odessa as evacuation of Mariupol is reattempted Ukraine claims Sunday that missiles are falling near the port of Odessa in southern Ukraine. Russia claimed this morning that it had destroyed an oil refinery used by the Ukrainian army, while attempts to evacuate civilians from the devastated city of Mariupol were expected to continue. For its part, the Odessa city council has said that "critical infrastructure facilities" have been hit by missiles, although for the moment, no casualties have been reported. Russia's Defense Ministry has detailed that its military's strikes have destroyed an oil refinery and three fuel storage facilities near Odessa. It has further explained that the facilities have been used to supply Ukrainian troops near the town of Mykolaiv.

11:23 Orbán appeals to Hungarians to vote with Ukraine war as background Hungary's ultranationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has appealed Sunday to vote in legislative elections, in which he is seeking a fourth term, claiming they are crucial as the choice is between "war or peace." Orbán presents himself as the guarantor ofthe country's stability and accuses the opposition, which appears to have a chance of winning for the first time since 2010, of wanting to involve Hungary in the war by showing solidarity with Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski, whose country is being invaded by Russia. "It is the war of two big countries and it is a dangerous thing. We should not get involved. Our political rivals do not consider the seriousness of the situation and want to take steps with which they would involve the country in the war. That would be tragic for Hungary," Orbán said after voting at a polling station in a residential area of Budapest.

11:14 Ukraine claims to have expelled all Russian forces from Kyiv "Irpin, Bucha, Gostomel and the entire Kiev region have been liberated from the invader". This was confirmed on Saturday by Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Maliar announcing that there are no more Russian forces in the administrative region surrounding the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. In the last few hours, Ukrainian troops have seized some thirty towns in the region, according to presidential spokesman Oleksii Arestovich, who warned however that "tough battles lie ahead" in the south and east of the country, according to Ukrainian public television. "Let us have no illusions. There is still heavy fighting in the south, for Mariupol, for the east of Ukraine," the spokesman explained. These Ukrainian advances would fit in with Moscow's declaration that it would desist from its offensive in the Kyiv and Chernobyl region to concentrate on the east of the country. Thus, Ukrainian sources quoted by the DPA news agency speak of Russian shelling of factories and industrial zones in Mariupol, Kharkov and Chernobyl.

11:05 Ukrainian ambassador to Germany accuses President Steinmeier of maintaining a "web of contacts" with Russia Ukraine's ambassador to Germany, Andri Melnik, on Sunday once again accused Berlin of having exhibited a timid response to the Russian invasion of his country after pointing to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier for maintaining a "web of contacts" in Russia that has made a more forceful reaction impossible. "For Steinmeier, relations with Russia were and remain fundamental, even sacred, no matter what," Melnik told 'Der Tagesspiegel' in an interview. "He seems to share the idea" of Russian President Vladimir Putin "that Ukrainians are not really a people," he added. Melnik also said that the Russian invasion "does not play an important role" for the German president in his consideration of his relations with Moscow, and that the backing of practically the entire German Council of Ministers is conspicuous by its absence, with one notable exception. The ambassador has spoken about the co-chairman of the Greens and German vice-chancellor assuring that: "Only Robert Habeck answers my messages".

10:57 Greece to start humanitarian aid in Odessa this Sunday Greek Foreign Minister Nikos Dendias will land in Odessa today, Sunday, at the head of a humanitarian aid mission in the southern Ukrainian port city, the Foreign Ministry has confirmed. The humanitarian aid will be delivered to the city's municipal authorities. The minister also plans to establish a continuous Greek aid distribution mechanism and reopen the Greek consulate in the city, the Foreign Ministry said in a statement. At least 10 Greek people have been killed and several injured since Russia began targeting Mariupol. According to the Greek government, more than 150 Greek citizens, boat crew and ethnic Greeks have been evacuated from the region.

10:46 Johnson congratulates Zelensky on the retreat of Russian forces in several areas of Ukraine British Prime Minister Boris Johnson has congratulated Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelensky on the retreat of Russian forces in several areas of Ukraine, the official Downing Street residence reported Sunday. The prime minister's official office has detailed that this Saturday in a telephone conversation, Johnson acknowledged the immense suffering of civilians and "enormous challenges" still in Ukraine. The head of the British government also updated Zelenski on a recent donor conference convened by the UK with the participation of 35 countries, while pledging continued defensive support. In their conversation, both leaders agreed on the importance of increasing sanctions to maintain economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin as long as Russian troops remain on Ukrainian territory.

10:38 A film director and documentary filmmaker has died in Mariupol, according to Lithuanian media Lithuanian film director and documentary filmmaker Mantas Kvedarivicius died Saturday while trying to leave the Ukrainian city of Mariupol Lithuanian media reported Sunday. Kvedarivicius was in Ukraine in order to "capture the brutal reality of war," according to the Lithuanian news portal Delfi and died after his car was hit by a rocket. The 45-year-old director's death was announced by his Russian-Lithuanian colleague Vitalijus Manskis, who wrote on his Facebook account that Kvedarivicius died "with the camera in his hands". The Lithuanian was known precisely for "Mariupolis" (2016), a documentary that focused on the experiences of the inhabitants of the port city to reflect the conflict in eastern Ukraine.

10:31 Kyiv denounces that the towns left by the Russians are full of mines, reports La Vanguardia's special envoy in Kyiv, Joaquin Luna. Ukraine claims to have recovered 30 towns in the region of the capital and Chernobyl, thanks to the "rapid withdrawal" of the invaders, as certified by the British Ministry of Defense, a reliable source. The bad news is that all these villages are mined, another demonstration that the Ottawa Treaty of 1997 was a toast to the sun in view of the fact that Russia, China and the USA have still not signed it. And in Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, the picture was bleak, with at least twenty corpses in the unpopulated streets, some with their hands tied and in civilian clothes.

10:22 Eurogroup resumes on Monday its economic analysis on the impact of the war in Ukraine The Ministers of Economy and Finance of the Eurozone (Eurogroup) will resume on Monday their deliberations on the impact of the war in Ukraine, knowing that it will lead to lower than expected economic growth and higher inflation due to energy prices and supply problems. The Nineteen face a new meeting, which will be attended by the Vice President for Economic Affairs, Nadia Calviño, with the assumption that Russian inflation will lead to an expansion of European economies "significantly lower" and a few days after knowing the inflation data for March, which in the eurozone soared to 7.5%. "The eurozone is likely to be very resilient this year, but growth will be significantly lower than anticipated and the war is causing a long-standing rise in inflation," summed up a senior European official ahead of the Eurogroup meeting.

10:13 Russian forces maintain blockade in the Black Sea The latest intelligence from the British Ministry of Defense indicates that Russian naval forces are maintaining a blockade of the Ukrainian coast in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, preventing resupply from Ukraine by sea. Russia still retains the capability to attempt an amphibious landing, but such an operation is likely to have its risks due to the time Ukrainian forces have had to prepare, Sunday's report explains. In addition, the report states that mines that may be in the Black Sea pose a risk to maritime activity, although the origin of those mines is still unclear, their presence is almost certain due to Russian naval activity in the area and demonstrates how the Russian invasion of Ukraine affects civilian interests.

10:02 Putin and Zelenski to meet soon, Ukrainian chief negotiator says The head of the Ukrainian negotiating group, David Arahamiya, has reported that negotiations between Ukraine and Russia are sufficiently advanced that a face-to-face meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodimir Zelenski, may take place soon. "The Russian team confirmed our thesis that the draft agreement is sufficiently developed to hold direct consultations between the two leaders, the presidents of Ukraine and Russia," Arahamiya wrote on his official Telegram channel. According to Arahamiya, Putin himself said on Friday in a telephone conversation with Turkish President Tayip Erdogan that "he is ready for such a meeting to be organized in the near future." "Neither the date nor the place is closed yet, but it is very likely that it will take place in Istanbul or Ankara, both in Turkey," the parliamentary spokesman of Zelenski's "People's Servant" party has pointed out. Arahamiya explained that in the talks held so far, Russia accepts, in the absence of putting it in writing, "almost all" of Ukraine's positions on its territorial integrity and sovereignty, except for its claims to Crimea, annexed by Moscow in 2014.

09:49 Russia claims that Ukraine is making slow progress in fulfilling the agreements The head of the Russian negotiating group, Vladimir Medinsky, has criticized the "optimism" of his Ukrainian counterpart, David Arakhamia. He has stated that the Ukrainian authorities are making very slow progress in the fulfillment of the political agreements reached at the Russia-Ukraine negotiations held in Istanbul. "Regarding the preparations for drafting the agreement for a summit between Putin and Zelensky, I unfortunately do not share Arakhamia's optimism. We still have a lot of work ahead of us," he told Russia's Interfax news agency on Sunday. According to Medinsky, Ukraine's military and diplomatic services "are marching with a big delay even in fulfilling the agreements already reached at the political level." "Arakhamia said that Russia accepts the Ukrainian position with the exception of Crimea," the Ukrainian peninsula illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014. He also recalled that "previously agreed issues, specifically the neutral, non-aligned and non-nuclear status of Ukraine, the ban on foreign bases, on the presence of foreign troops or any kind of missile systems," among other points, "were precisely the demands put forward by Russia since 2014." "We see that the Ukrainian side now has a more realistic approach to this," he noted, although he stressed that "Russia's position on Crimea and the Donbas is unchanged."

09:40 Theater as a shelter during the war A Ukrainian theater company, born in a World War II bomb shelter, keeps alive the art of drama in Kyiv, as an antidote against dehumanization in the midst of the war aggression of Russian troops. And when the anti-aircraft sirens sound, they welcome the whole neighborhood into their lair. The legend of the theater tells that this armored basement of a building in the Shevchenko district was used by the Gestapo for interrogations, but for the last eight years it has been the headquarters of the Ukrainian company ProEnglish Theater, the only one that performs plays in English. Now, the space has regained its original function and has permanently sheltered, since the first day of the invasion, some twenty members of the company, who also decided to take refuge in art to calm the anxiety and uncertainty of an armed offensive against the capital.

09:31 Twelve Spaniards have joined the Foreign Legion fighting the Russians in Ukraine At least a dozen Spanish citizens are already in Ukraine, enrolled (or with the intention of enrolling) in the International Legion for Territorial Defense created by the Government of Volodymir Zelenski against the Russian invasion, according to the figures handled by the Spanish security forces. Four are Catalans, eight from the rest of Spain. Their names and lives are known and they are and will be under the radar the day they return, because of the military baggage they will have acquired in the war. If they return. For now, 50 Georgians, between 60 and 70 French, 40 Dutch, about 600 Canadians (Canada has a huge community of Ukrainian origin), about 150 British, at least a hundred Americans and about thirty Croatians have traveled to the wheat fields, according to estimates published so far.

09:23 Ukrainians in the rear, the report of the special envoy of La Vanguardia to Chop, Maria-Paz Lopez. The rearguard is a place where war is far away but it is breathed everywhere. In Chop, a town of 8,800 inhabitants on the border with Hungary and an important railway junction from where refugee trains leave for Hungary and Slovakia, the convoys are no longer so full of passengers. As the fighting stalls, women and men over the age of 60 - the only adults allowed to leave the country - who fled from their bombed-out towns to these safer regions in the west are now choosing not to leave Ukraine.

09:13 Lithuania abandons Russian gas imports Lithuania's Energy Ministry announced Saturday that the country has been operating without Russian gas imports since the beginning of the month with the intention of achieving "full energy independence" from Russia in response to "Russian energy blackmail" and the invasion of Ukraine. Data from Lithuanian gas transmission system operator Amber Grid has confirmed this. It shows that on April 2 the import of Russian gas for Lithuania's needs through the Lithuanian-Belarusian interconnection has been equal to zero megawatts (MWh), the Ministry has reported in a statement. "We are the first EU country among Gazprom's supplier countries to become independent from Russian gas supply, and this is the result of a coherent process of several years' energy policies and timely infrastructure decisions," Lithuanian Energy Minister Dainius Kreivys has assured.

09:04 Zelenski will speak before the Congress of Deputies this Tuesday The President of Ukraine, Volodymir Zelenski, will intervene by videoconference in the Congress of Deputies this Tuesday before the President of the Government, Pedro Sánchez; the President of the Lower House, Meritxell Batet, and deputies and senators, in a week where another conflict, that of Western Sahara, will once again be the focus of parliamentary debates. Zelenski's act will last about half an hour and will be similar to the interventions he has had before other parliaments. This intervention comes at a time when Turkey has reiterated its offer to organize a meeting between the presidents of Russia and Ukraine to promote peace negotiations. Both the President of the Congress and the Chief Executive will address a few words to the Ukrainian leader in a session in which senators are also participating, so the plenary session of control of the Government in the Upper House will begin around 17:15 hours.

08:55 Ukraine claims no casualties in attack on Odessa refinery This morning's missile attack on a refinery in the southern Ukrainian city of Odessa has so far caused no casualties, Ukrainian Army Southern Operational Command Colonel Vladislav Nazarov said. In a video broadcast by the official Telegram channel of the Odessa City Council, Nazarov has detailed that the attack has been against a "critical infrastructure" of the city. Several missiles hit the refinery in the Ukrainian city of Odessa at around 6 a.m. local time (04.00 GMT), whose fuel tanks are on fire. The colonel explained that firefighters are on the scene trying to control the flares caused by the missiles, which are coming from several fuel tanks where, from time to time, explosions occur when their contents catch fire.

08:46 HRW accuses Russia of committing war crimes in different Ukrainian regions Human Rights Watch (HRW) said Sunday that it has documented several cases showing that Russian military forces have committed war crimes in the occupied areas of Kharkov, Chernobyl and Kyiv regions. These include one case of repeated rape; two cases of summary execution, one of six men, the other of one man; and other cases of unlawful violence and threats against civilians between February 27 and March 14, 2022. On the other hand, soldiers were also allegedly involved in looting civilian goods, including food, clothing and firewood. "The cases we documented amount to deliberate and unspeakable cruelty and violence against Ukrainian civilians," said Human Rights Watch Europe and Central Asia director Hugh Williamson, who believes that all war crimes should be investigated.

08:37 Polish Prime Minister regrets that sanctions against Russia are not working Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki has publicly regretted that economic sanctions against Russia are not working. Morawiecki has demanded a tightening of the measures to curb the strengthening of the Russian currency, theruble. The Polish politician has called for immediate seizure of property and assets of both the Russian government and its oligarchs. "There's the new money. That's what I've been saying for weeks: hundreds of billions of dollars in European banks, in the central bank, in the accounts of the oligarchs. Freezing for the sake of freezing is not going to do anything. The seizure of these properties is necessary to contribute to the reconstruction of Ukraine," he told journalists.

08:29 Russia plans to resort to barter to avoid sanctions in its trade with Morocco Russia and Morocco can minimize the impact of Western sanctions against Moscow on their trade exchanges by resorting to barter or using currencies other than the dollar and the euro, Russian Ambassador to Rabat Valeryan Shuvaev has explained. "It is possible to discuss barter operations as well as to seek solutions for mutual settlements using currencies other than the dollar and the euro, or national currencies," Shuvaev said.

08:22 UN humanitarian chief to Moscow to push for truce in Ukraine UN humanitarian chief Martin Griffiths of Britain will travel to Moscow on Sunday to try to push for a truce in Ukraine, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Friday. Griffiths plans to visit Kyiv later to discuss with the Ukrainian authorities the initiative for a humanitarian cease-fire that Guterres himself raised for the first time this week.

08:13 Ukraine accuses Russia of leaving mines "all over the territory" Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski warned his people Saturday that retreating Russian forces are creating "a complete mess" outside the capital as they leave mines "all over the territory," including around houses and corpses. Zelensky, on the other hand, has criticized Europe for "reacting in silence" to the humanitarian catastrophe in the southern Ukrainian city of Mariupol caused by Russian shelling and siege. According to the Ukrainian president, an estimated 160,000 citizens have been living for more than a month without basic services in Mariupol, a port on the Sea of Azov which has become the main target of Russian troops in Ukraine because of its strategic position between the Crimean peninsula and the Dombass.

08:05 Russia denounces that the Ukrainian Army carries out shelling in the Chernobyl region The head of the Russian National Defense Control Center, Colonel Mikhail Mizintsev, denounced on Saturday that the Ukrainian Army carries out shelling in the locality of Navoaya Basan, in the Chernobyl region. Mizintsev warned that the Ukrainian Armed Forces shelled the settlement for more than two hours, causing during the operations "numerous casualties among local residents". The Russian official also warned that mines are being ordered from Kyiv to be laid in the discharge locks of a hydroelectric power plant in the town of Aleksandrovskaya in the Nikolaev region.

07:57 UN brings to 1,325 civilians killed in war The UN Office for Human Rights has reported that at least 1,325 civilians have died since the beginning of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Among these dead, 120 are children, as indicated by the UN, which has clarified that these are the verified victims but that the real figure may be much higher. As for civilians wounded in the conflict, the UN has confirmed 2,017, including 168 children. The actual number of casualties "could be considerably much higher" as there is only partial information from some of the areas of major hostilities, including localities besieged by Russian troops such as Mariupol, Volnovaja, Izium or Irpin.

07:47 Russia attacks with missiles a refinery in Odessa Several missiles have hit this morning a refinery in the Ukrainian city of Odessa, whose fuel tanks are on fire, without knowing yet if there have been any casualties in the attack. According to Efe news agency, the missiles hit this infrastructure located in the north of the city, next to its port, where an oil pipeline from Russia arrives. The City Council of the city has informed through Twitter of the attack: "Odessa was attacked from the air", that "some missiles were shot down by the air defense" and that "fires have been reported in some areas". The explosions (at least six of varying intensity) have been felt kilometers from the site and from the refinery complex three columns of black smoke can be seen from all over the city.

07:36 Ukraine claims to have recaptured 30 villages around Kyiv The Ukrainian government said Saturday that the country's military forces have recaptured more than thirty villages in the region surrounding the capital, Kiev. Presidential spokesman Oleksii Arestovich has reported these advances and that "tough battles lie ahead" in the south and east of the country, according to Ukrainian public television. "Let us have no illusions. There is still heavy fighting in the south, for Mariupol, for the east of Ukraine," the spokesman explained. Besides, Arestovich stressed that Ukrainian troops are being able to hold the front line in the east of the country. Ukrainian forces have taken control of such localities as Bucha or Brovari and also Russian forces have withdrawn from the Antonov airport in Gostomel, where they have been entrenched for several weeks, reported the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.

07:28 More than 200 arrested in Russia during protests against the war in Ukraine More than 200 people have been arrested in Russia for protest actions against the offensive in Ukraine, announced the NGO OVD-Info, which specializes in monitoring arrests in the country. "More than 178 people were arrested in 15 Russian cities," the organization said in a statement. In Moscow, a sit-in against Russian military intervention in Ukraine was planned in the morning in Zariadié Park near the Kremlin. Shortly afterwards, police began arresting people sitting on park benches in the middle of a snowstorm.

07:19 Ukraine blames Russia for manhandling and murdering civilians in Bucha One of Ukraine's presidential aides, Mykhailo Podolyak, on Saturday accused Russia of manhandling and murdering civilians found lifeless by Ukrainian troops after recapturing the town of Bucha, northwest of Kyiv. "The bodies of people with their hands tied, who have been shot dead by Russian soldiers, lay on the streets. These people were not in the army. They had no weapons. They posed no threat. How many more cases are happening right now in the occupied territories," Podolyak has questioned on his Twitter account. Podolyak has shared an image where several bodies are shown on the ground, one of them can be seen with his hands tied behind his back. The presidential aide has argued that Russia "is waging a war to destroy the Ukrainian people", and has used the message on social networks to ask Western allies for more weapons for the protection of Ukrainian citizens.

07:08 Russia assures readiness to evacuate foreigners from the city of Mariupol The head of the Russian National Defense Control Center, Colonel General Mikhail Mizintsev, has assured on Sunday that Russia is ready to assist in the evacuation of foreign citizens who are in the besieged city of Mariupol, southeastern Ukraine, according to the Russian agency TASS. "In accordance with the request of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russia will provide assistance in the evacuation of foreign citizens held hostage by nationalists in Mariupol," Mizintsev explained. The colonel-general has maintained that Russia is carrying out "purposeful and coordinated work" to evacuate civilians and foreigners from dangerous regions of Ukraine. "To this end, we are in constant interaction with the United Nations, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the International Committee of the Red Cross and other international organizations," he stressed. He also added that the Russian Armed Forces would open a humanitarian corridor from Mariupol to the city of Berdiansk, 80 kilometers to the west, for evacuation of foreign citizens.

07:00 Pope warns of the risk of "an extended cold war" Pope Francis has warned in Malta of "the childish and destructive aggressiveness that threatens us" in reference to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the risk of it becoming "an extended cold war that can suffocate the lives of entire peoples and generations." The Pontiff lamented that from Eastern Europe, "where the light once shone, the darkness of war has arrived", before adding: "We thought that the invasions of other countries, the brutal fighting in the streets and the atomic threats were dark memories of a distant past".

06:53 More than 4,200 civilians evacuated through humanitarian corridors on Saturday in Ukraine A total of 4,217 civilians have been evacuated on Saturday through the humanitarian corridors set up, including 1,263 from the city of Mariupol, which has been besieged by Russian forces for weeks. The Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister, Irina Vereshchuk, reported these figures and explained that the evacuees from Mariupol, also from Berdiansk, have already arrived in the city of Zaporiya, many of them using their own vehicles.

06:45 About 300 people buried "in mass graves" in the Ukrainian town of Bucha, according to the mayor Anatoly Fedorouk, mayor of the Ukrainian town of Bucha, northeast of Kiev, has assured that they have found the corpses of about 300 people in a mass grave. The town was retaken by Ukrainian troops. Earlier, a journalist from the AFP news agency confirmed that there were at least 20 bodies scattered on a street in the locality. One of the corpses had its hands tied, the reporter said. They were wearing civilian clothes.

06:38 Russia declares readiness to continue negotiations with Ukraine Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Saturday expressed Russia's readiness to continue negotiations with Ukraine and reproached Kyiv for vetoing Belarus as the host of these contacts. "We would love to continue negotiations in Belarus, but the Ukrainians do not want to. We have to recognize that the most important thing is to look for a place where we can meet with Ukrainian negotiators and, most importantly, that they continue either in Istanbul or elsewhere," Peskov said in an interview with Belarusian Belarus-24 television. Peskov said that "Ukraine is a very difficult country for us." "In the current situation it is a country that is hostile," he has noted. "It is also not a friendly country for Belarus," he has stated in reference to Kiev's support for the 2020-2021 mobilizations of the Belarusian opposition.

06:30 Russia - Ukraine war | Latest news from the conflict and negotiations, live | Good morning and welcome to the minute-by-minute coverage of everything related to the Russia - Ukraine war and its consequences on an international scale. Ukraine has assured that it has expelled Russian forces from the entire Kyiv region. In the last few hours Ukrainian troops have seized about thirty towns in the region, according to presidential spokesman Oleksii Arestovich, who warned however that "tough battles lie ahead" in the south and east of the country, as reported by Ukrainian public television.

08:37 Polish Prime Minister regrets that sanctions against Russia are not working Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki has publicly regretted that economic sanctions against Russia are not working. Morawiecki has demanded a tightening of measures to curb the strengthening of the Russian currency, the ruble. The Polish politician has called for the immediate seizure of property and assets of both the Russian government and its oligarchs. "There's the new money. That's what I've been saying for weeks: hundreds of billions of dollars in European banks, in the central bank, in the accounts of the oligarchs. Freezing for the sake of freezing is not going to do anything. The seizure of these properties is necessary to contribute to the reconstruction of Ukraine," he told journalists.

08:29 Russia plans to resort to barter to avoid sanctions in its trade with Morocco Russia and Morocco can minimize the impact of Western sanctions against Moscow on their trade exchanges by resorting to barter or using currencies other than the dollar and the euro, Russian Ambassador to Rabat Valeryan Shuvaev has explained. "It is possible to discuss barter operations as well as to seek solutions for mutual settlements using currencies other than the dollar and the euro, or national currencies," Shuvaev said.

08:22 UN humanitarian chief to Moscow to push for truce in Ukraine UN humanitarian chief Martin Griffiths of Britain will travel to Moscow on Sunday to try to push for a truce in Ukraine, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Friday. Griffiths plans to visit Kyiv later to discuss with the Ukrainian authorities the initiative for a humanitarian cease-fire that Guterres himself raised for the first time this week.

08:13 Ukraine accuses Russia of leaving mines "all over the territory" Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski warned his people Saturday that retreating Russian forces are creating "a complete mess" outside the capital as they leave mines "all over the territory," including around houses and corpses. Zelensky, on the other hand, has criticized Europe for "reacting in silence" to the humanitarian catastrophe in the southern Ukrainian city of Mariupol caused by Russian shelling and siege. According to the Ukrainian president, an estimated 160,000 citizens have been living for more than a month without basic services in Mariupol, a port on the Sea of Azov which has become the main target of Russian troops in Ukraine because of its strategic position between the Crimean peninsula and the Dombass.

08:05 Russia denounces that the Ukrainian Army carries out shelling in the Chernobyl region The head of the Russian National Defense Control Center, Colonel Mikhail Mizintsev, denounced on Saturday that the Ukrainian Army carries out shelling in the locality of Navoaya Basan, in the Chernobyl region. Mizintsev warned that the Ukrainian Armed Forces shelled the settlement for more than two hours, causing during the operations "numerous casualties among local residents". The Russian official also warned that mines are being ordered from Kyiv to be laid in the discharge locks of a hydroelectric power plant in the town of Aleksandrovskaya in the Nikolaev region.

07:57 UN brings to 1,325 civilians killed in war The UN Office for Human Rights has reported that at least 1,325 civilians have died since the beginning of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Among these dead, 120 are children, as indicated by the UN, which has clarified that these are the verified victims but that the real figure may be much higher. As for civilians wounded in the conflict, the UN has confirmed 2,017, including 168 children. The actual number of casualties "could be considerably much higher" as there is only partial information from some of the areas of major hostilities, including localities besieged by Russian troops such as Mariupol, Volnovaja, Izium or Irpin.

07:47 A refinery in Odessa has been attacked with missiles Several missiles have hit this morning a refinery in the Ukrainian city of Odessa, whose fuel tanks are on fire, it is not yet known if there have been any casualties in the attack. According to Efe news agency, the missiles hit this infrastructure located in the north of the city, next to its port, where an oil pipeline from Russia arrives. The City Council of the city has informed through Twitter of the attack: "Odessa was attacked from the air", that "some missiles were shot down by the air defense" and that "fires have been reported in some areas". The explosions (at least six of varying intensity) have been felt kilometers from the site and from the refinery complex three columns of black smoke can be seen from all over the city.

07:36 Ukraine claims to have recaptured 30 villages around Kyiv The Ukrainian government said Saturday that the country's military forces have recaptured more than thirty villages in the region surrounding the capital, Kiev. Presidential spokesman Oleksii Arestovich has reported these advances and that "tough battles lie ahead" in the south and east of the country, according to Ukrainian public television. "Let us have no illusions. There is still heavy fighting in the south, for Mariupol, for the east of Ukraine," the spokesman explained. Besides, Arestovich stressed that Ukrainian troops are being able to hold the front line in the east of the country. Ukrainian forces have taken control of such localities as Bucha or Brovari and also Russian forces have withdrawn from the Antonov airport in Gostomel, where they have been entrenched for several weeks, reported the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.

07:28 More than 200 arrested in Russia during protests against the war in Ukraine More than 200 people have been arrested in Russia for protest actions against the offensive in Ukraine, announced the NGO OVD-Info, which specializes in monitoring arrests in the country. "More than 178 people were arrested in 15 Russian cities," the organization said in a statement. In Moscow, a sit-in against Russian military intervention in Ukraine was planned in the morning in Zariadié Park near the Kremlin. Shortly afterwards, police began arresting people sitting on park benches in the middle of a snowstorm.

07:19 Ukraine blames Russia for manhandling and murdering civilians in Bucha One of the advisers to the Ukrainian Presidency, Mykhailo Podolyak, on Saturday accused Russia of manhandling and murdering civilians found lifeless by Ukrainian troops after recapturing the town of Bucha, northwest of Kyiv. "Bodies of people with their hands tied, who have been shot dead by Russian soldiers, lay in the streets. These people were not in the army. They had no weapons. They posed no threat. How many more cases are happening right now in the occupied territories," Podolyak has questioned on his Twitter account. Podolyak has shared an image where several bodies are shown on the ground, one of them can be seen with his hands tied behind his back. The presidential aide has argued that Russia "is waging a war to destroy the Ukrainian people", and has used the message on social networks to ask Western allies for more weapons for the protection of Ukrainian citizens.

07:08 Russia assures readiness to evacuate foreigners from the city of Mariupol The head of the Russian National Defense Control Center, Colonel General Mikhail Mizintsev, has assured on Sunday that Russia is ready to assist in the evacuation of foreign citizens who are in the besieged city of Mariupol, southeastern Ukraine, according to the Russian agency TASS. "In accordance with the request of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russia will provide assistance in the evacuation of foreign citizens held hostage by nationalists in Mariupol," Mizintsev explained. The colonel-general has maintained that Russia is carrying out "purposeful and coordinated work" to evacuate civilians and foreigners from dangerous regions of Ukraine. "To this end, we are in constant interaction with the United Nations, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the International Committee of the Red Cross and other international organizations," he stressed. He also added that the Russian Armed Forces would open a humanitarian corridor from Mariupol to the city of Berdiansk, 80 kilometers to the west, for evacuation of foreign citizens.

07:00 Pope warns of risk of "an extended cold war" Pope Francis has warned in Malta of "the childish and destructive aggressiveness that threatens us" in reference to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the risk of it becoming "an extended cold war that can suffocate the lives of entire peoples and generations." The Pontiff lamented that from Eastern Europe, "where the light once shone, the darkness of war has arrived", before adding: "We thought that the invasions of other countries, the brutal fighting in the streets and the atomic threats were dark memories of a distant past".

06:53 More than 4,200 civilians evacuated through humanitarian corridors on Saturday in Ukraine A total of 4,217 civilians have been evacuated on Saturday through the humanitarian corridors set up, including 1,263 from the city of Mariupol, which has been besieged by Russian forces for weeks. The Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister, Irina Vereshchuk, reported these figures and explained that the evacuees from Mariupol, also from Berdiansk, have already arrived in the city of Zaporiya, many of them using their own vehicles.

06:45 About 300 people buried "in mass graves" in the Ukrainian town of Bucha, according to the mayor Anatoly Fedorouk, mayor of the Ukrainian town of Bucha, northeast of Kiev, has assured that they have found the corpses of about 300 people in a mass grave. The town was retaken by Ukrainian troops. Earlier, a journalist from the AFP news agency confirmed that there were at least 20 bodies scattered on a street in the locality. One of the corpses had its hands tied, the reporter said. They were wearing civilian clothes.

06:38 Russia declares readiness to continue negotiations with Ukraine Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Saturday expressed Russia's readiness to continue negotiations with Ukraine and reproached Kyiv for vetoing Belarus as the host of these contacts. "We would love to continue negotiations in Belarus, but the Ukrainians do not want to. We have to recognize that the most important thing is to look for a place where we can meet with Ukrainian negotiators and, most importantly, that they continue either in Istanbul or elsewhere," Peskov said in an interview with Belarusian Belarus-24 television. Peskov said that "Ukraine is a very difficult country for us." "In the current situation it is a country that is hostile," he has noted. "It is also not a friendly country for Belarus," he has stated in reference to Kiev's support for the 2020-2021 mobilizations of the Belarusian opposition.

06:30 Russia - Ukraine war | Latest news from the conflict and negotiations, live | Good morning and welcome to the minute-by-minute coverage of everything related to the Russia - Ukraine war and its consequences on an international scale. Ukraine has assured that it has expelled Russian forces from the entire Kyiv region. Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Maliar announced on Saturday that there are no longer Russian forces in the administrative region surrounding the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. "Irpin, Bucha, Gostomel and the entire Kyiv region have been liberated from the invader," Maliar posted on her Facebook page. In the last few hours Ukrainian troops have seized about thirty towns in the region, according to presidential spokesman Oleksii Arestovich, who warned however that "tough battles lie ahead" in the south and east of the country, as reported by Ukrainian public television.

title: *S&PGR Cuts Turkey LC Rtg To 'B+', Affrms 'B+' FC Rtg; Otlk Neg
text:
1 Apr 2022 16:12 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Cuts Turkey LC Rtg To 'B+', Affrms 'B+' FC Rtg; Otlk Neg


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- The fallout of the Russia-Ukraine military conflict, including rising 
food and energy prices, will further weaken Turkey's already tenuous balance 
of payments and exacerbate inflation. The latter is on course to average 55% 
in 2022, the highest level of all the sovereigns we rate. 
     -- While we expect Turkey's net general government debt to amount to 34% 
of GDP by the end of 2022, preserving some fiscal space, the government's 
foreign and domestic borrowing costs have increased, and the key fiscal risk 
remains the underlying health of Turkey's recently recapitalized state banks. 
     -- The government's balance sheet and the broader economy have become 
increasingly dollarized, with over 50% of resident deposits now denominated in 
foreign currency. 
     -- We lowered our unsolicited long-term local currency (LC) rating on 
Turkey to 'B+' from 'BB -' and affirmed our unsolicited long-term foreign 
currency (FC) rating at 'B+'. The outlook remains negative. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On April 1, 2022, S&P Global Ratings lowered its unsolicited long-term local 
currency sovereign credit rating on Turkey to 'B+' from 'BB -'. At the same 
time, we affirmed the unsolicited long-term foreign currency rating at 'B+' 
and the unsolicited foreign and local currency short-term ratings at 'B'. The 
outlook remains negative. 
 
We also lowered Turkey's transfer and convertibility assessment to 'B+' from 
'BB -' and the unsolicited national scale ratings to 'trAA-/trA-1+' from 
'trAA+/trA-1+'. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The negative outlook reflects what we view to be rising balance-of-payments 
and financial stability risks over the next 12 months amid the economic 
fallout from Russia's military intervention in Ukraine, global monetary 
tightening, and possible policy missteps in the run-up to Turkey's 
parliamentary and presidential elections in mid-2023. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower the ratings if the adverse economic spillover from either the 
Russia-Ukraine conflict or global monetary tightening became more significant 
for Turkey, weakening its already vulnerable balance of payments and 
complicating the task of controlling inflation. We could also lower the 
ratings if policy missteps, for example, ahead of the elections next year, 
further undermined exchange-rate stability and worsened the inflation outlook. 
This would heighten the risk of banking system distress and thereby imply 
potential contingent liabilities for the government. Weakened asset quality 
following several rounds of large-scale credit stimulus in recent years could 
also weigh on the banking system in such a scenario, particularly state-owned 
banks that have seen their balance sheets expand more rapidly in recent years. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could revise the outlook to stable if we observed sustained and enhanced 
predictability of public policy and effectiveness of monetary policy while 
Turkey's balance-of-payments position strengthened, particularly the central 
bank's net foreign-exchange (FX) reserves. 
 
RATIONALE 
The lowering of the local currency rating reflects what we now view as similar 
credit risks characterizing Turkey's foreign- and local-currency debt. A 
differentiation between foreign and local currency ratings is a comparatively 
rare phenomenon, with only 12 sovereigns benefiting from uplift for the local 
currency rating among all 137 sovereigns we rate. In our view, the conditions 
for such uplift are no longer present in Turkey's case. 
 
We typically differentiate between the local and foreign currency ratings for 
sovereigns that can set interest rates and manage their local currency 
independently, that is, without reference to its external value. In our view, 
this is not the case in Turkey at present, as the multiple tools that it 
deployed previously effectively aimed at influencing the exchange rate, 
including foreign-currency interventions and the introduction of the 
FX-protected deposit scheme late last year. We also note that Turkey's 
interest expenditure on local-currency government debt constitutes about 70% 
of total interest expenditure. We consider that, in a downside case, this 
could reduce the government's flexibility to accord a higher priority to 
servicing its local-currency obligations, thus eroding the credit-risk 
distinction between the two types of debt. 
 
In parallel, Turkey's economy has been persistently dollarizing in recent 
years. Resident deposits in foreign currency amounted to 55% of the total at 
the end of 2021, up from 39% at end-2017. If precious-metal deposits are 
included, this rises to about 60%. Meanwhile, the currency composition of 
government debt has also been shifting in favor of foreign currency, with 
foreign-currency debt at 66% at the end of 2021, up from under 40% at 
end-2017. 
 
Our affirmation of the foreign currency rating primarily reflects our view 
that Turkey has some fiscal headroom in case of need. At 36% of GDP at 
end-2021, net general government debt looks favorable vis-a-vis other emerging 
markets such as Brazil or South Africa. We expect Turkey's net general 
government debt to stabilize at close to 32% of GDP over the medium term. 
Balance-of-payments risks, however, remain elevated, and public debt could 
increase further in the event of a more significant depreciation of the 
Turkish lira, or if the government provided more extensive support to the 
banking sector in a downside scenario. We consider that the global economic 
effects of Russia's military intervention in Ukraine in February 2022, as well 
as the tightening monetary policy of central banks in developed markets, 
present additional balance-of-payments risks. 
 
Overall, our ratings on Turkey remain supported by the country's diversified 
economy and resilient and adaptive private sector, which, in the past, has 
weathered external shocks, currency volatility, and frequent changes in 
economic policy. Contained net general government debt, which we forecast will 
amount to 34% of GDP by the end of 2022, also supports the ratings. 
 
The ratings on Turkey are constrained by its vulnerable balance-of-payments 
position and the limited effectiveness of its monetary policy. The ratings are 
also restricted by what we view as weak institutional arrangements. We see 
limited checks and balances between government bodies, with power concentrated 
in the hands of the executive branch, which renders policy responses difficult 
to predict. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Turkey's growth prospects have weakened in 
the aftermath of Russia's military intervention in Ukraine 
     -- We project economic growth in Turkey of 2.4% in 2022, less than our 
3.7% forecast at the end of 2021. 
     -- Turkey's institutional arrangements are weak, with limited checks and 
balances in place. 
     -- We think that economic policy uncertainty will remain elevated in the 
run-up to the 2023 general election, with possible additional stimulus 
measures at the expense of longer-term economic stability. 
In our view, Russia's intervention in Ukraine in February 2022 presents 
downside risks to global growth and we now expect weaker economic performance 
for European emerging markets, including Turkey. Last year, Turkey's growth 
outcome exceeded our previous forecasts, reaching 11%. Around half of this 
growth is attributable to a carryover effect due to a lower base stemming from 
the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the quick recovery in the latter part 
of 2020. However, quarterly growth was still very strong, with consumption and 
exports performing particularly well. In contrast, we expect a sharp slowdown 
to follow in 2022. 
 
Turkey remains exposed to the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine conflict across 
several dimensions. Specifically: 
     -- Turkey's important tourism sector, which generates earnings in foreign 
currency, has in the past depended significantly on arrivals from Russia and 
to a lesser degree Ukraine. In 2021, arrivals from Russia constituted 19% of 
all foreign visitors to Turkey (16% pre-pandemic in 2019), while Ukraine had a 
share of 8% (3% in 2019). There is likely to be a significant reduction in 
these tourism flows in 2022 due to the direct impact of the military conflict 
in the case of Ukraine, and the large economic impact of sanctions, as well as 
disruption to transport and payment systems in Russia. In the case of tourists 
from Russia, this could be partially mitigated by the fact that Turkey is 
currently one of few destinations with direct flights from Russia still in 
place, as well as visa-free travel. Stronger European tourism thanks to an 
improved pandemic situation and a competitive lira could also provide support, 
but we consider the overall risks to be on the downside. 
     -- Russia and Ukraine's share of Turkish goods exports is more modest, at 
a combined 4% in 2020. However, given the scale of recessions (we expect a 
real GDP contraction of 8.5% in Russia and 22% in Ukraine this year), 
logistical challenges, and supply chain disruptions, this could still 
materially dampen Turkish exports, particularly taking into account 
second-round effects on European economies. 
     -- Turkey remains an energy importer and therefore significantly higher 
global prices for oil and gas will complicate the task of bringing inflation 
under control, with a likely adverse effect on domestic demand dynamics. 
Inflation rose to 54% year on year in February 2022, the highest level in 20 
years. 
Consequently, we now forecast real growth of 2.4% in 2022, compared with our 
previous forecast of 3.7%. We expect a significant slowdown in exports and 
consumption growth, while we project that real investment will contract by 
3.5% owing to high uncertainty and dwindling global growth momentum. 
 
The future direction of government policy also remains highly uncertain. The 
political pressure on the central bank continues after it made a series of

interest rate reductions in the latter half of 2021 against a background of 
soaring inflation. We also think that policy missteps could occur in the 
run-up to the 2023 general elections. Recent opinion polls suggest declining 
popular support for the ruling Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve 
Kalkinma Partisi; AKP), with the pandemic, high inflation in food prices, and 
a hit to real incomes likely to be contributing factors. In that context, 
additional policy-stimulus measures--for example, to boost the availability or 
reduce the price of credit--cannot be ruled out in 2022, even though Turkey 
still faces lingering imbalances from previous such measures, including lower 
useable FX reserves and higher inflation. 
 
We consider that Turkey's broader institutional arrangements remain weak and 
continue to constrain the sovereign credit ratings. In the June 2018 
presidential and parliamentary elections, the president and the AKP-led 
alliance secured a victory that marked the final chapter in Turkey's 
transition to an executive presidential system. We see limited checks and 
balances between government bodies. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Economic imbalances persist, with high 
inflation and weak balance of payments 
     -- We forecast that Turkey's inflation will average 55% in 2022, the 
highest level of all the sovereigns we rate. 
     -- Net general government debt should remain about 32% of GDP through 
2025, still leaving some fiscal policy space. 
     -- Turkey's balance-of-payments position is weak, while its monetary 
policy flexibility is limited, underpinning the risk of a disorderly external 
adjustment. 
In our view, over the past year, Turkey's economic policy has become 
increasingly unpredictable and less conventional, presenting economic and 
balance-of-payments risks. Over the second half of 2021, and under political 
pressure, the central bank persistently lowered the policy rate (one-week repo 
rate) to 14% from 19%, even with inflation hitting multi-year highs and 
reaching 54% in February 2022, the highest rate of all the sovereigns we rate. 
In turn, this contributed to a significant disorderly depreciation of the 
exchange rate toward the end of 2021, similar in magnitude to that during the 
August 2018 currency crisis in Turkey. 
 
Although the authorities managed to arrest the slide in the lira through sales 
of FX reserves and the introduction of the so-called FX-protected deposit 
scheme, we consider that Turkey's balance-of-payments position remains 
fundamentally weak and is a key constraint for the sovereign ratings. The 
country has consistently run a current account deficit in the past, except in 
2019, when imports contracted following the impact of the currency crisis in 
2018. Following a reduction in the current account deficit to 1.8% of GDP in 
2021 from almost 5.0% of GDP in 2020, the current account appears to be 
deteriorating again. In January 2022, the current account deficit totaled $7 
billion, which in nominal U.S. dollar terms is almost half the entire deficit 
for 2021. 
 
We consider that Turkey's longstanding structural external vulnerabilities are 
aggravated by what we view as an end to a period of ultra-loose monetary 
policy by developed-market central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve . 
Additionally, the likely loss of tourist inflows from Russia and Ukraine and 
higher oil and gas prices following the onset of conflict in Ukraine could 
weaken Turkey's balance of payments as the country remains a net energy 
importer. 
 
In parallel, the amount of external debt maturing over the next 12 months 
remains significant as of January 2022, at $174 billion, or 25% of GDP, around 
half of which pertains to the banking sector. At the same time, the central 
bank's FX reserves are weak. As of mid-March 2022, they amounted to $109 
billion (16% of GDP). However, excluding the institution's foreign-currency 
obligations to domestic residents, useable reserves--which represent the 
central bank's effective capacity to intervene--remained much lower, at $22 
billion (3% of GDP) at the end of 2021. 
 
We forecast that Turkey's current account deficit will widen to 3.6% of GDP in 
2022 as oil prices are significantly higher, while tourism inflows will suffer 
from the impact of Russia's intervention against Ukraine, and goods exports 
might take a hit if there is a more pronounced slowdown of the global economy. 
There are downside risks to our forecasts, but the key reason for not 
projecting an even higher current account deficit is that we expect the 
availability of and appetite for external funding for a more sizable shortfall 
to be more limited in the future, including because of global monetary 
tightening. Given the central bank's limited capacity to intervene, we expect 
the lira to correct itself further in such a scenario, in turn putting a lid 
on import growth, rather than the current account deficit continuing to expand 
unchecked. 
 
Positively, available data so far suggest that confidence in Turkey's 
externally leveraged banking sector endures, with households choosing to keep 
their savings in the banks rather than withdraw them. Additionally, Turkish 
banks managed to roll over their sizable foreign debt coming due during 
previous episodes of financial market stress. 
 
Nevertheless, financial stability risks are elevated, in our view. These 
could, in turn, present a contingent liability risk to the government if the 
government had to rescue a bank in a downside case, either because of a loss 
of confidence among domestic depositors, or if foreign creditors' appetite for 
rolling over Turkish banks' foreign debt were to reduce. The government has 
already contributed capital to public banks several times, with the latest 
capitalization worth 0.5% of GDP taking place in March 2022. We think that in 
a hypothetical scenario of a loss in banking sector confidence, the government 
may be called upon to contribute significantly higher amounts of equity and 
loans to the banks. 
 
Banks' asset quality could also face further pressure, since about 38% of 
loans were denominated in foreign currency as of December 2021, effectively 
making this debt more expensive to service as the lira depreciates. Risks to 
loan-book quality are particularly pertinent for public banks, in our view, 
since they have been heavily involved in episodes of rapid credit expansion at 
low rates in the past, raising questions about the borrowers' subsequent 
ability to repay these lines of credit. The other risk to Turkey's banks stems 
from rising global interest rates and a worsening of market conditions for the 
refinancing of external debt. We estimate the financial sector's short-term 
external debt by remaining maturity at about $83 billion or 12% of GDP as of 
end-January 2022. 
 
The rapid depreciation of the lira also contributes directly to a rise in net 
general government debt. At the moment, about 66% of government debt is 
denominated in foreign currency, a marked shift from under 40% before 2018. An 
additional source of vulnerability for the government's balance sheet stems 
from the FX-protected lira deposits under a scheme that the authorities 
introduced at the end of 2021 as a measure to stabilize the currency. Under 
this scheme, the government has committed to compensate deposit holders for 
the difference between the rate of exchange-rate depreciation and the interest 
earned on the Turkish lira deposits. Essentially, on top of its own FX risk 
stemming from the debt denominated in foreign currency, the government has now 
assumed contingent liability risks to compensate private-sector depositors. We 
expect the government to account for the compensation directly in the budget. 
The total amount of such deposits currently stands at about $38 billion (5.5% 
of GDP), with around half of that amount being sponsored by the Treasury (that 
is, the Treasury is liable for compensation payments on that half) and the 
rest by the central bank. 
 
That said, we consider that Turkey still has some fiscal headroom. At 34% of 
GDP, net general government debt looks favorable vis-a-vis some other emerging 
markets such as Brazil or South Africa. In our base case, we forecast that the 
general government deficit will widen to 4.2% of GDP in 2022 from an estimated 
3.1% in 2021, driven by additional expenditure to offset the impact of higher 
energy and food prices, as well as potential additional spending ahead of the 
elections in 2023. 
 
Positively, Turkey maintains a liquidity buffer that could help cover upcoming 
debt maturities. We estimate that liquidity buffer at about 6% of GDP at the 
end of 2021. The authorities also aim to reduce the foreign-currency portion 
of domestic borrowing, while the average maturity of new domestic borrowing 
has increased from 37 months in 2020 to 55 months in 2021. 
 
In our view, inflation will accelerate in the coming months, and we have 
revised our annual average inflation forecast for 2022 up to 55%. In monthly 
year-on-year terms, reported consumer price inflation could peak at over 60% 
in the coming months. Producer price inflation is even higher, reaching 105% 
year on year in February 2022.
