title: Vladimir Putin, the head of the new Russian autocracy
text:
When the admirable Carlos Fayt said that "facts are not disputed", he seemed to be talking to the ideal world. A world where there is no Donald Trump who ignores the origin of Climate Change and Alberto Fernández who forgets his condition of President of the Republic.

But reality no longer admits ironic or philosophical reflection. The facts have shown that a large part of the West was unable to predict the invasion of Ukraine or to understand COVID-19.

Qualified observers such as John Sawers, a former member of the specialized intelligence service in that country (MI6) and former British ambassador to the UN, who confirmed at Oxford University a different prognosis about Vladimir Putin's delusions and ambitions, dared to take a closer look at what we are seeing.

The planet has always defined the Russian President as a man educated in espionage, subjected to the shake-up of the confessional structure of Soviet communism and someone who could embrace the scripts of the nationalist ultra-right. None of his traits defined him as a leader of democratic sobriety, so why so many doubts and hesitations?

With such a profile, valid discussion required accepting that the West, and moderate Asia, were dealing with the reflexes of a dangerous autocrat.

Vladimir acquired a profile similar to that often attributed to Yuri Andropov, the former head of the KGB, who in the last stage of his life served as General Secretary of the Communist Party. Andropov gained influence for his contributions to the violent extraterritorial repression exercised by the former USSR in the 1954 Hungarian uprising, a recipe that the Kremlin used again in Czechoslovakia and Afghanistan.

This also explains why, when Putin began to make his first steps after the fall of the USSR, he had in mind the appropriate recipe for "disciplining" the populations of Chechnya and Crimea.

In view of this curriculum, Vladimir is irritated by the fact that Western rulers never gave serious answers to his continuous demands for geopolitical balance.

If they had gone deeper into these questions, experts in political science and military strategy would have detected that Putin is obsessed by the desire to build a quasi-imperial vision of a backyard.

They would also have seen that the delirium is more serious than it seems, since the Russian government raised the nuclear alert level without saying a word and its Chancellor raised the language of war bluster without saying a word.

According to Robert Litwak, a highly respected analyst at the Wilson Center, Moscow has what it takes. It has the largest nuclear arsenal in the world, which exceeds 6,000 usable pieces, to which it adds the inventory of tactical weapons based on the same technology.

The crux of the situation is that, like the Tsarist regime and the former Soviet leaders, the current occupants of the Kremlin believe it is normal to "discipline" governments or opposition movements in the so-called satellite countries of the former USSR.

In the particular case of Ukraine, Moscow's intervention was explained by the alleged fragility implied by the disappearance of the buffer zones, which is a unilateral entelechy conceived in equivalent terms by the respective strategists of the United States, Russia and, with a different view, the Chinese government.

Moscow considered it insulting that the current President, Volodymyr Zelensky, announced his desire to make his country a member of NATO and the European Union, processes that the West had been treating with tongs.

The prognosis for the ongoing responses is guarded. Although the economic sanctions of the main OECD governments will seriously hurt the Russian people and many of its trading partners, the relevant question is whether such a move will serve to twist the arm of a leader intoxicated with messianism.

Not for nothing did the Russian Central Bank go to the trouble of amassing some $640 billion in international reserves to mitigate the effects of the anticipated international retaliation to its absurd invasion. This indicates that Putin's government assumed that an extensive bank run could be fixed with patches or corralitos, which was a major mistake.

The Kremlin did not calculate that half of the foreign currency holdings could be frozen by the foreign banks that decided to participate in the retaliatory measures for the invasion.

Moscow's economic partners are not going to have an easy time either. The nations of the European Union are, at least for now, dangerously addicted to Russian gas and oil (see my last column).

In view of this new scenario, Brussels will have to reformulate the origin of the most sensitive supplies with alternative sources of energy, something that is already underway through the use of strategic reserves, a very ephemeral resource that can also undermine the fight against Climate Change outlined in the Green Pact.

Eight years ago Henry Kissinger caught the Ukrainian case on the fly, which is why he elaborated a project that was meant to negotiate, peacefully and preemptively, a rational status for that country's nascent democracy ("Henry Kissinger: To resolve Ukraine crisis, you need to start at the end," Washington Post of 5/3/2014).

His ideas encompassed the notion of preserving that nation's millennia-old ties with Russia; gradual economic-social integration into the European Union (EU) (an issue on which Ukraine has just taken an unexpected first step in the midst of the invasion); and a modern link with the rest of the Western world. The package should be conceived as a bridge, not a tug of war, between the former "Cold War" blocs.

The approach also called for getting the Kremlin, Brussels and Washington to agree to Ukraine being governed harmoniously, and without external pressure, by its different ethnic, political and religious groups (Catholic and Orthodox), to ensure a peaceful link between East and West.

But the proposal went unheeded. Western governments are only now realizing the size of the challenge and the vulnerability of their policies.

Jorge Riaboi is a diplomat and journalist.

title: Russia acknowledges that it has €270 billion frozen due to sanctions, almost half of its reserves
text:
The financial blockade to which the West is subjecting Russia for invading Ukraine is having a more than remarkable scope. Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov acknowledged Sunday that the United States, the European Union and the other countries that have taken a stand against Russia have managed to block about $300 billion of the Russian Central Bank's gold and foreign currency reserves with the sanctions, almost half of Russia's reserves. "This is about half of these reserves we had.

 We have a total amount of reserves of about $640 billion and of them about $300 billion are now in a situation where we cannot use them," Siluanov assured, in an interview with Russian public television, as reported by Russian agencies.After the beginning of the invasion, Western countries rejected a direct military intervention in Ukraine and opted to supply armaments to Ukraine to defend against Russian aggression and impose harsh economic sanctions on Russia to strangle its finances and thus stifle its war effort. In what is the toughest package of punishments to date, the EU and the US have frozen the assets of the oligarchs on European soil; disconnected seven Russian and three Ukrainian entities from the Swift payment system and dealt a severe blow to Russia's foreign currency reserves, which are essential to prop up the ruble. This latest setback has led to the free fall of the Russian currency, higher interest rates and capital controls. In addition, the EU has also placed cryptocurrency transactions involving Russian citizens under surveillance to prevent them from using this resource to circumvent sations.In his statements, the minister has accused the West of putting pressure on China to limit Russia's access to its yuan reserves. Siluanov recalled that part of the Russian Federation's gold and foreign currency reserves are denominated in the Chinese currency, which has prompted this pressure on Beijing. "We also see pressure exerted by Western countries on China to limit mutual trade with China. Of course, there is pressure to limit access to those reserves that we have in yuan," according to Siluanov. However, the Russian finance chief said he believes that his country's partnership with China "will still allow us to maintain the cooperation we have achieved and not only maintain it, but also increase it in the conditions when Western markets are closed," he stressed.The finance chief also assured that Russia will not refuse its debt obligations and will pay in rubles as long as Western countries continue to keep gold and foreign exchange reserves frozen, and stressed that the country has enough resources to ensure the production of necessary goods.

title: Russia's economy, from BRIC to collapse: crisis, corporate flight and the concrete chance of becoming an unprecedented global pariah
text:
The invasion of Ukraine is the last link in a chain of missteps, miscalculations and negative twists and turns in the international situation that have diverted Russia from its attempt to recover the role of economic power it used to play in the past. The damage suffered by its economy due to the costs of the war, the political isolation in which it was placed and the sanctions it is the target of will not only be short term: it will take decades to recover.

Infobae consulted national and international specialists regarding the effect of the war conflict and the future that can be sketched for Russia in the economic and geopolitical planes that are configured from now on.

A truncated renaissance

At the beginning of the 21st century, and after the fall of the Berlin Wall, Russia had begun the slow path towards recovering its place in the world and positioned itself as one of the major emerging markets, forming together with Brazil, India, China and then South Africa, a bloc called BRICS called to dominate the global economy due to its large population, territorial extension, natural resources and very high Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth. But the years went by and that promise was not fulfilled: the countries that make up the bloc today navigate very different waters and in recent years certain economic differences began to emerge that were so marked that the ratings agency S&P came to pronounce the "death" of the group.

Subsequently, the global economic crisis of 2008 after the real estate and credit bubble that had been inflating in the United States, followed by the sanctions imposed by that country and by the European Union in 2014, pushed Russia into recession and Putin's government relaunched its austerity policy.

Since then, the European country's economy began to suffer a series of ups and downs such as the fall in oil prices, the Coronavirus pandemic that hit the entire planet and, more recently, the invasion of Ukraine on February 24 this year.

This last action resulted in a counter-offensive by the West through strong economic sanctions that decimated the Russian economy with consequences that are still difficult to measure. The war adventure may be the coup de grâce for the former power's attempt to return to being a leading player on the international scene.

The costs to come

Luis Palma Cané, economist and expert in international finance, told this newspaper that Putin's "move" will have extremely negative consequences for Russia. In this sense, he warned: "With each passing day, Russia will be worse off. If this goes on for example for six months, the GDP may fall 20 or 25% without any doubt".

"The longer the war is delayed the more Russia will fall in economic terms. 65% of Russia's tax revenues come from energy exports and now they have a choked and isolated economy. The ruble is wrecked, the stock market is wrecked and they are technically in default. Any bonds maturing today they can't pay," he stressed.

"With every day that goes by, Russia is going to get worse. If this goes on for six months, for example, the GDP may fall 20 or 25% without any doubt" (Palma Cané).

In outlining the diagnosis of Russia, Palme Cané considered that today the European country has a stifled economy and financially isolated from the world. "It can neither import nor export. The outlook is chaotic. There is going to be more inflation, more poverty and a fall in the level of activity. In this way, it is going to cease to be the power factor it represents at the moment", he analyzed.

Economic analyst Marcelo Elizondo emphasized the effects of the economic restrictions on Russia and estimated a thorny outlook for the country led by Putin for the future. For the specialist, due to its size and relevance in international trade, the country cannot afford to isolate itself for a prolonged period of time since it needs its buyers to finance itself and its suppliers to keep its economy going.

"Russia is an intermediate-sized economy, not one of the most powerful. Its GDP is $1.7 trillion. It is the 12th largest economy in the world. It is not a powerhouse. So it's more vulnerable economically than politically. That makes quite a bit of sense why the West has reacted on the economic side and not the military side," he told Infobae.

"Its exports are about $400 billion a year, so affecting them is a hard blow. While their imports are about $350 billion and they are also hit. This makes it difficult for companies to access inputs or capital goods to produce", he pointed out.

Likewise, Elizondo evaluated that the exodus of foreign companies in Russia as a result of the invasion of Ukraine may weaken the productive framework of the country in a much deeper way than the initial blow to the activity, due to the loss of key pieces of the gears that move different sectors and whose efficiency, knowledge and innovation capacity cannot be replaced overnight.

"The default, the non-functioning of the financial system, the 40% devaluation and the difficulty of access to foreign currency obstruct, both internally and in Russia's relationship with the rest of the world, the functioning of its economy. This may lead first to a fall in GDP, then to a fall in employment and subsequently to a weakening of the functioning of the domestic value chains, which will slowly abort economic normality", he said.

An unprecedented pariah

Bombs are exploding in different parts of the Ukrainian territory and although the final offensive to put an end to the resistance is not yet on the near horizon, analysts are already wondering what Russia's position will be once the conflict is over.

"Never before have there been sanctions of such depth against one of the big five of the Security Council, made up of Russia, China, the United Kingdom, France and the United States" (Jaramillo).

Mauricio Jaramillo, a specialist in international relations and professor at the Universidad del Rosario, Colombia, told Infobae that there are two scenarios for the future of the Russian economy following the aggression against Ukraine.

"One is that they effectively become a kind of pariah, but it is difficult to foresee because never before have there been sanctions of such a depth against one of the big five of the Security Council, made up of Russia, China, the United Kingdom, France and the United States. There had been very tough sanctions on Iraq, Cuba, Venezuela, Syria and Burma, which had become pariahs. But we had never been in a situation where there was such a consensus to isolate one of the big players. That is one option, that it becomes a pariah and that these alternative systems of social, financial and monetary networks, on which Russia is betting with the support of China, fail", he said.

"The other scenario is that we return to a war by blocs, a 'cold war' in which they confront each other in third party territories, such as Syria," he added.

For Jaramillo, the Russian situation benefits states that can put stocks of goods that are in short supply on the market. "One could immediately think of Venezuela, the United States and Iran as some of the nations that can benefit from the Russian weakening. But I don't think that from a logistical point of view it would be easy to replace it as a supplier of energy and grains because this dependence between Russia and Europe has been going on for more than 30 years. You cannot change a chain of exchanges in the course of a few months," he said.

Lasting wounds

In turn, Gabriela Siller Pagaza, director of Economic Analysis at Banco Base de México told Infobae that although the war is not over yet, "there is still a wound on Russia because it invaded a country and somehow its assets will continue to be affected for a period of time".

"It is not going to be easy for companies to return to that country after Putin said he was going to nationalize the assets that left Russia. On the other hand, the ruble is not going to recover that fast," he considered.

"There remains a wound on Russia because it invaded a country and somehow its assets are going to remain affected for a period of time."(Siller Pagaza)

In line with the rest of the colleagues, Siller Pagaza assured that Russia is going to suffer the consequences of the invasion of Ukraine. "GDP is going to contract and there will also be an impact on its foreign trade numbers. It is very possible that Russia will experience a recession and then a long period of economic stagnation. There will be a wound left. I think there will be some kind of treaty or rules to prevent something like this from happening again," he told this newspaper.

Meanwhile, Brenda Estefan, a Mexican international analyst, told Infobae that what could affect Russia the most are the sanctions coming from the European Union, given that in the case of the United States the impact is more limited.

"The Russian economy is very concentrated in hydrocarbons. As Europe has a huge dependence, it has them tied up. In that context, the sanctions imposed are going to limit the export of technology to Russia and that is something they do need. Technological elements are important to continue with the extraction of their oil fields. In the medium term they will need technology and they will not be able to import it", he pointed out.

According to Estefan, Russia's relationship with China may moderate the impact on its economy, although he considered that this will not be enough. "Russia will have to have a relationship with other countries. We have to see what happens with Brazil, Argentina, Turkey, Israel, among others. These countries may continue to trade with Russia," he said.

He added: "Yes, it will become a country far away from most of the global markets. And also distant in terms of air connectivity. The Russian economy is going to become detached from the rest of the world. They are going to tighten their belts in a brutal way, as well as their incomes and sources of employment. That will happen as punishment for the invasion of Ukraine."

Russia and an economy without a floor

Russian President Vladimir Putin won the presidential elections in March 2000 and, following his victory, began to turn around his country's economic policy after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Gross Domestic Product began to grow, the ruble stabilized, inflation was brought under control and investment began to grow slowly.

Well into the 21st century, the European country made large debt repayments on IMF loans and managed to increase its international reserves. These were years in which Russia began to regain its place as an economic power and positioned itself as one of the major emerging markets, one of the booming BRICS.

"The Russian economy is going to take off from the rest of the world. They are going to tighten their belts in a brutal way and also their incomes and sources of employment" (Estefan).

However, the global economic crisis of 2008 after the bursting of the real estate and credit bubble that had been inflating in the United States, followed by the sanctions imposed by the United States and the European Union in 2014, pushed Russia into recession. Since then, the Russian economy began to suffer a series of ups and downs also as a consequence of falling oil prices.

For Pablo Kornblum, economist and doctor in international relations, Russia's role in the last time was to sustain a boost with the accumulation model of the beginning of this century based on an empowerment of hydrocarbon production and the revival of the war economy.

"Russia will be a pariah for many years to come in the NATO world, with clear short-term adverse economic and financial effects. What will not happen is an implosion as with the fall of the Soviet Union, which was due to expansion into the military technological area to the detriment of other areas of the economy where domestic needs were disregarded," the expert told this media outlet.

"Russia will be a pariah for many years for the NATO world, with clear short-term adverse economic and financial effects" (Kornblum).

Meanwhile, Gustavo Perego, director of the consulting firm Abeceb, said that what Russia will achieve with this process is to suffer a hard blow to its currency in the international financial market. In that sense, he considered that Russia "will find it very difficult to operate in international trade because many countries will also deny the use of their ports as a secondary port to trade with Russia".

"There they have a problem because the whole scheme of international credit and financing to be able to negotiate letters of credit with Western banks will be complicated. Chinese banks are going to be the main players and that is already a complication from the beginning," he said.

The trigger for the collapse of the Russian economy

On February 24 of this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin took the plunge and concretized the invasion of Ukraine through his "special military operation". The West refused to intervene with troops or its air forces, but the sanctions response was much harsher than could have been initially calculated,

The main measures range from the decision by Western countries to exclude Russia from the SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) system, the highly secure network that facilitates payments between 11,000 financial institutions in 200 countries, allowing billions of dollars in transactions around the world, to the decision by the United States to ban Russian oil and gas imports.

There were also new restrictions on the debt and equity of major Russian companies and entities. And additional total blocking sanctions on Russian elites and their families.

Some of the consequences so far were the fall of more than 50% of the Moscow stock exchange, the plunge of the ruble, which reached its historic low against the dollar after recovering more than 60% since the day before the beginning of the invasion of Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the economic sanctions unleashed by the United States, the European Union and other countries in response to the invasion of Ukraine have the financial system on the verge of collapse, international reserves frozen and Russian savers standing in long lines to recover their money. So much so that Russia's central bank had to resort to a measure like the one in force in Argentina since 2019 to try to limit foreign currency purchases: a 30% commission was imposed on foreign currency purchases in an attempt to support the Russian ruble.

In this context, inflation in Russia is expected to accelerate to 20% and its economy could contract by up to 8% this year, according to an independent survey of analysts requested by the country's central bank.

Likewise, following the economic sanctions applied by the West, the IMF joined a growing group that warned about the risk of the country presided by Vladimir Putin defaulting on its debt obligations after its invasion of Ukraine, according to Bloomberg news agency.

A Russian debt default is "no longer an unlikely event," IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told reporters on Thursday. "It's not that Russia doesn't have money, it can't use this money," she stressed.

Indeed, Fitch Ratings said this week that a bond default by Russia is "imminent" as a result of measures introduced since the war broke out.

However, the downfall of the Russian economy does not end there: since invading Ukraine, hundreds of companies have announced the abandonment of their operations in Russia. Some of the firms that stopped operating are: Nike, Apple, Microsoft, BP, Shell, Equinor, Exxon Mobil, PWC, General Motors, Ford, Volkswagen, Toyota, Samsung, Microsoft, Apple, HP, Intel, Inditex, Netflix, EA, Airbnb, Google, Ikea, Oracle, Dell, Boeing, Airbus, Spotify, Walt Disney, Paramount, WarnerMedia, Universal and TikTok, among others from a long list of more than 300 companies.

These are transnational companies, with production chains that transcend borders and are unlikely to be replaced by new government-sponsored corporations hoping to fill the vacuum they leave behind.

Putin may have had in mind to restore Russia's old imperial glory when he ordered his troops to cross the border. But from the moment the first soldier set foot in Ukraine he set his country in the opposite direction. Closer and closer to being left out of the world.

Due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the BCRA relaxed the import restrictions for oil companies that it had implemented a week ago.

Agreement with the IMF: in the first two months of 2022, the Government has already doubled its spending on energy subsidies.

Stigliz once again supported his disciple Guzmán for the agreement with the IMF, but warned that "Argentina will inevitably experience shocks".

title: *S&PGR Keeps Ukraine 'B-/B' Ratings On CreditWatch Negative
text:
11 Mar 2022 16:07 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Keeps Ukraine 'B-/B' Ratings On CreditWatch Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Russia's military intervention in Ukraine continues to pose 
significant risks to the country's economic growth, financial stability, 
external position, and public finances. 
     -- We expect the government's debt service and borrowing needs will be 
fully covered by international financial support over at least the next 12 
months; its ability to receive such support and make debt service payments, 
including to nonresidents, remains uninterrupted for now. 
     -- Our 'B-/B' long- and short-term foreign and local currency ratings 
remain on CreditWatch with negative implications. 
     -- The CreditWatch status indicates that we could lower the ratings if 
the military conflict were to significantly weaken Ukraine's economy, its 
external liquidity, its financial system, or the government's administrative 
capacity. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On March 11, 2022, S&P Global Ratings said its 'B-/B' long- and short-term 
foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Ukraine remain on 
CreditWatch with negative implications. 
 
Our 'uaBBB-' national scale rating on Ukraine also remains on CreditWatch 
negative. 
 
CREDITWATCH 
The CreditWatch negative reflects multiple risks to Ukraine's economy, 
external balances, public finances, and financial and political stability 
stemming from Russia's military operations. 
 
We expect to resolve the CreditWatch placement within 90 days. We could lower 
the ratings should we expect military actions to prevent the authorities from 
servicing commercial debt. The rating might also come under pressure should 
the conflict lead to a drain on Ukraine's external liquidity or a rise in 
fiscal contingent liabilities from its commercial banking system. 
 
RATIONALE 
The ratings on Ukraine are constrained by Russia's military operations within 
the country, which bring about significant downside risks for the economy and 
financial sector. We see the potential for governance disruptions, putting 
commercial debt servicing at risk. The ratings are also constrained by 
Ukraine's low GDP per capita income and developing institutions. 
 
Despite the conflict, Ukraine is continuing to honor its domestic and foreign 
debt service obligations and has pledged to continue doing so. On March 1, the 
Ministry of Finance made a scheduled coupon payment of roughly $290 million on 
one of its eurobonds. At the same time, strong committed international 
financial support to Ukraine and still relatively high foreign exchange (FX) 
reserves support the sovereign ratings. 
 
Ukraine's GDP proved relatively resilient to the COVID-19 pandemic during both 
2020 and 2021. However, the ongoing armed conflict with Russia has upended the 
gradually improving economic outlook. Ukraine now faces disruption to key 
economic sectors, significant loss of life, and broad damage to essential 
infrastructure. 
 
The ultimate economic fallout caused by the current events is difficult to 
quantify, but a double-digit contraction in output for 2022 appears almost 
inevitable. Economic consequences from the conflict have already started to 
take hold via the suspension of commercial shipping from ports. This will 
weigh on Ukraine's export capacity and its ability to benefit from the 
currently favorable global prices for the country's key exports goods, 
including metals and wheat. 
 
Output contraction, as well as military and emergency spending needs, will add 
significant pressures, increasing government financing requirements in 2022 
severalfold compared with those expected before the conflict. 
 
At the same time, even these elevated borrowing needs will likely be covered 
by different types of international financial support. The National Bank of 
Ukraine  (NBU ) estimates the overall international financial and humanitarian 
support committed to date at about $15 billion (some 8.6% of 2021 GDP). This 
includes international loans, grants, and guarantees, namely: 
     -- A $1 billion guarantee from the U.S. government ; 
     -- A EUR1.2 billion emergency macrofinancial assistance program from the 
EU; 
     -- A loan for budgetary purposes of up to $500 million from the Canadian 
government , in addition to a $120 million loan announced on Jan. 21, 2022; 
     -- A $500 million guarantee from the U.K. government  to support Ukraine 
and mitigate the economic effects of the Russian military actions; 
     -- EUR300 million in financial aid from Germany; 
     -- $100 million in emergency loans from Japan; 
     -- $350 million disbursement from the World Bank  to support short- and 
long-term financing needs. 
 
The above come on top of Ukraine's $5 billion Stand-By Arrangement with the 
IMF , of which, $2.2 billion remains undisbursed. The IMF  program was agreed in 
June 2020 and extended until end-June 2022. Ukraine has requested emergency 
financing of $1.4 billion under the IMF 's Rapid Financing Instrument. In 
addition, the National Bank of Poland  has offered NBU  a currency swap 
equivalent to $950 million. The recent statements by the international 
community and international financial institutions suggest that the size of 
donor support could be further increased. We assume it will at least cover 
Ukraine's financing requirements in 2022. 
 
Nevertheless, as the conflict continues, Ukraine's technical ability to use 
international financial support and meet its ongoing debt service obligations 
could erode. 
 
The NBU  has adopted several measures to mitigate exchange rate and financial 
market volatility as well as the resulting risks to macroeconomic stability 
stemming from the ongoing military conflict. These measures include the 
suspension of Ukraine's FX market (except for FX sales by customers), cash 
withdrawal limits, unlimited unsecured refinancing loans to banks, a 
moratorium on cross-border financial transactions (excluding those related to 
debt service), and a fixed hryvnia exchange rate. As of March 2, the NBU  had 
official reserve assets of $27.5 billion. As per international convention, 
these are kept outside the country, mostly in G-7 counties. 
 
Ahead of the military conflict, we estimated nonperforming loans in the 
Ukrainian banking system would decline to about 25% by year-end 2022 from 30% 
at end-2021. However, given the substantial fallout of current events on the 
private sector, the outlook for asset quality has deteriorated substantially, 
while confidence could also weigh on banks' liquidity positions. The potential 
recapitalization needs of Ukraine's state-owned banks will likely put 
additional pressure on the government's budget. 
 
S&P Global Ratings acknowledges a high degree of uncertainty about the extent, 
outcome, and consequences of the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine. 
Irrespective of the duration of military hostilities, sanctions and related 
political risks are likely to remain in place for some time. Potential effects 
could include dislocated commodities markets--notably for oil and gas--supply 
chain disruptions, inflationary pressures, weaker growth, and capital market 
volatility. As the situation evolves, we will update our assumptions and 
estimates accordingly. See our macroeconomic and credit updates here: 
nflict". Note that the timing of publication for rating decisions on European 
issuers is subject to European regulatory requirements. 
 
KEY STATISTICS

After the primary analyst gave opening remarks and explained the

title: Negotiations fail; Ukraine and Russia accuse each other for hospital attack
text:
Vladimir Putin 's government described the attack on the hospital in Mariupol as a "staged provocation" to stir up anti-Russian sentiment, leaving in the background the new failure in the negotiations between foreign ministers to define humanitarian corridors and cease-fire.

In response, President Volodymyr Zelensky asserted that this "genocidal" escalation shows the world that Ukraine is dealing with a terrorist state, as the accusations against it always turn out to be a foretaste of what they are planning.

And the Russian Defense Ministry cast doubt on the bombing by disassociating itself from it. It explained that this was a plan to stir up anti-Russian sentiment, a fact for which three civilian deaths are reported, among them a girl, and at national level the figure amounts to 71 minors dead and 100 wounded, innocent victims.

Arguing that he has evidence, which he did not show, the spokesman of this Ministry, Igor Konashenkov, explained that this was internal and staged, since explosives were placed very close to the area, contradicting the Ukrainian version of the fall of projectiles which left a huge crater several meters deep. And he ratified that the targets of the "demilitarization operation" are the war infrastructure and not civilian areas.

This position was supported by the Russian embassy in Great Britain, which denounced on Twitter the use of influencers as victims, a publication that the social network deleted for being Russian propaganda.

Buildings, government offices and homes evidence the devastation wrought by enemy troops in the region.Photo:APSeparately, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov asserted that the building was not a hospital but an extremist base. After talking with his counterpart Dimitro Kuleba in Turkey, he said that the devastated site was occupied by a radical Ukrainian battalion, so that there were no longer any patients, denying agency photos of evacuated pregnant women with visible wounds.

He reiterated that these versions only favor the interests of the West, which supports Ukraine, and reproached the handling of the conflict in the media; an issue that the Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova , described as "information terrorism", since Ukrainian allies restrict the broadcasting of Russian channels and media.

Lavrov added that in yesterday's talks a cease-fire was not raised, as he reiterated that this discussion is not the same as in Belarus, so he said he was surprised that his counterpart criticized that there was no progress, when this issue was not even on the agenda.

Meanwhile, Zelenski disqualified Russia's position that it does not attack and sells itself as a promoter of peace; he affirmed that its allies are watching what the Russian troops are doing in their territory, where they prevent the evacuation of citizens and the arrival of humanitarian aid to besieged areas such as Mariupol and Volnovaja, while in one of the most affected areas, Kharkov and Donbas, the volley of projectiles persists. In this regard, he said that they are already preparing the reconstruction of the country in view of the siege for which, he insisted, those responsible will pay.

His Chancellor, Kuleba, backed him up by rejecting any indication of a possible use of biological weapons, questioning "the maniacal obsession with which several Russian officials fantasize", in view of the insistence that there are biological or chemical weapons in the invaded country.

Despite the clash of versions, both nations pointed out that there will be new safe corridors. Ukraine detailed that those interested will be able to leave Sumi and Mariupol through seven routes to Poltava, Zaporiyia, Volnovaja and up to Kiev; while the Kremlin said it will open specific spaces for refugees on a daily basis.

Buildings, government offices and homes are evidence of the devastation wrought by enemy troops in the region.Photo:APSHowever, it was said that this plan is unilateral and will only lead to their territory. Some media even indicated that in order to facilitate the exits they will request lists of possible evacuees and the units used for that purpose. And it even boasted that it has already helped 187,000 people to leave Ukraine, although as of yesterday's cut-off the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) only counts 82,000 internments in Russia.

Aday after this war crime, France, Canada and Germany joined the condemnations for the "atrocity" denounced by Zelenski

.French President and mediator, Emmanuel Macron , called the launching of explosives clearly intended to kill civilians "unworthy acts of war", which goes against demands to end the war. And although he expressed his support for Ukraine, he commented that it is not the time for its accession to the European Union (EU). Separately, the German Chancellor, Olaf Scholz , once again reiterated his call for a ceasefire.

Meanwhile, the Prime Minister of Canada, Justin Trudeau , warned that Putin is making serious mistakes that will lead him to lose this war and he will also pay for each of the events provoked in the nation where multiple devastated areas are reported.

One of these is Mariupol, where the International Red Cross sees an "increasingly serious and desperate" humanitarian situation, as food and all the necessary supplies are already scarce, and the mayor Vadim Boichenko accused that shells are falling almost every half hour.

In the same vein, the Ukrainian Minister of Defense, Oleksi Reznikov, stated that in 15 days the enemy troops have killed more civilians than soldiers, without revealing the total number of casualties.

The fact: Facebook and Twitter platforms have announced that they will allow the dissemination of messages calling for violence against Russia, only if they are attached to the context of the war.Putin mocks sanctions and says "we will overcome it"

15 days after the impact of the war and sanctions, the President of Russia, Vladimir Putin , stated that the current difficulties are only a stumbling block that will be overcome, therefore, he called on the citizens to remain calm, since "there is no event that we cannot solve".During a meeting with his cabinet, he asserted that "in the end, everything will lead to an increase of our independence, self-sufficiency and sovereignty", minimizing the blow from the West with multiple restrictions and hostilities from governments, which continue to accumulate.

He maintained that, contrary to what some countries think, they will even benefit by strengthening them in the midst of the rejection of the military operation in Ukraine, which he insisted there was no alternative and he was forced to act due to the repeated violations of that government against its own citizens in Donbas, an area he recognized as a republic in direct affront against Volodimir Zelenski.

This contrasts with those who exert pressure against him, since countries he called "hostile" are already suffering from the rise of products with "high prices, unprecedented inflation and reaching historic highs", for which they now blame them, and their territory, he says, will resist what he called "de facto economic warfare".

He ratified that the Kremlin will not compromise its sovereignty over economic gains, which he insisted will be short term, because in a crisis it is normal that "the demand for certain goods increases, but we have no doubt that we will solve these problems".

Although he admitted that the effects are already being felt in the country, Putin explained that in the past they have already overcome similar restrictions such as freezing assets and curbing trade exchanges, so this will not be an exception.

The Kremlin leader added that he was already expecting these sanctions, as he said that, even if they had not made military incursions, some countries were already taking coercive measures against them, so they would have applied them anyway.

However, he emphasized that these are hostile and illegitimate acts, and minimized any attempt of the powers to weaken its economy, since it will manage to overcome this phase, of which he did not give a deadline or advance a possible end to the attacks on Ukraine, supported by its oil production, since he considered that its former partners will resent the blow more by running out of energy, as well as other materials such as railroad cars, turbines and more, a fact for which, he said, they are already asking their population to "tighten their belts".

He also explained that Russia will fulfill its energy obligations, since despite the break reported by the United States and Great Britain, it still supplies Europe and other places, guaranteeing gas transportation in Ukraine.

It should be noted that the Kremlin has already announced restrictions on its own territory, in order to prevent capital outflows. In this regard, the Minister of Finance, Anton Siluanov , recalled that these measures will reduce the impact to stabilize the financial climate and the nation will continue to pay its foreign debt, but no longer in dollars but in rubles.

Meanwhile, his Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov , pointed out that these sanctions, which he described as "political aggression", only make them see that they will no longer depend on Western governments or companies. He stated

that contrary to the blow they believe they will cause to the nation, they are giving it the opportunity to no longer depend on someone else, since returning to negotiate means giving the power to another government to violate or try to destroy its economy

.In declarations to the Russian media, he dismissed the claims that they will use energy supplies -oil and gas- as a weapon to condition governments, since, he insisted, they are not like the US.

Inview ofthe exit of many global companies, the Russian government threatened to take control of their assets, while the list of those that are suspending their participation in the region by joining the "economic war" is growing

.The Eurasian region said that it is contemplating changes to the law to take control of the companies that are temporarily leaving its territory or plan to suspend operations; therefore, President Vladimir Putin referred "there are enough legal and market instruments for this", anticipating a freezing of assets in case they try to return by the time the military intervention in Ukraine concludes.

After the withdrawal of transnationals such as Coca Cola , Pepsi, McDonald's , Starbucks , Sony and Apple , among others, the Ministry of Economy stated that they have the capacity to take control of foreign property, but the list continues to grow, since even companies that do not operate directly in their territory, but do participate in the supply chain, have announced a breakup, such as Burger King .

In view of the President's plans, the Prime Minister, Mikhail Mishustin , announced that they would modify the law for an external administration and thus transfer or nationalize such resources to sectors that will work, since they affirm that their population is not against the war, although protests persist in rejection of the conflict for which the neighboring nation invaded. Among the alternatives is a bankruptcy process or the nationalization of foreign organizations, and he pointed out that "foreign companies must understand that returning to the (Russian) market will be difficult".

Despite this plan, Putin said that they remain open to work with all partners who wish to do so by guaranteeing protection to investors who will remain in the region.

However, it was not specified whether such actions would be the government's response to the possibility of defaulting on its debt payments or some other existing loans.

Less growth due to Russia-Ukraine conflictDue tothe war conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the International Monetary Fund (IMF ) expects to cut its expectations for world economic growth, said Kristalina Georgieva, director of the world organization, assuring that Moscow's default is no longer an improbable event

.Georgieva pointed out that there is a "tragic impact of the war against Ukraine", so she assured that a significant contraction is in store for Russia. "We see the likely impact on our outlook for the global economy... Next month (during the spring boreal meetings) we will have a downward revision of our global growth projections," she added.

Russia's default puts pressure on that country's expansion and therefore on that of other nations, as he explained that it is not that Vladimir Putin 's country does not have money to meet its obligations; but rather, it cannot use the money it has.

"The unprecedented sanctions against the nation will make it difficult for the country to convert its IMF reserve assets, known as special drawing rights, into currency," he stressed.

In addition to the economic sanctions Russia is facing due to the conflict, there is another one from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), which on Thursday suspended the Russian central bank .

According to agencies, the entity suspended the access of the banking establishment of the Russian Federation to "all BIS services" to the country, under the premise that this international organization is not "and will not be a way to avoid sanctions".

Its head of the Monetary and Economic Department, Claudio Borio , warned at the time that the war in Ukraine would complicate the task of the central banks, which were already in the process of modifying their monetary policy, preparing for an interest rate hike to face the increase in inflation.

Around 300,000 companiesin the United States and Europe, not counting Latin America, have been affected by the war between Russia and Ukraine, said Bertha Martinez Cisneros, coordinator of the International Logistics degree program at CETYS University Mexicali Campus

.She said that based on a study by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) , Ukraine has become a major supplier of essential metals and raw materials for global value chains, mainly in the production of semiconductors, automobiles and even medicines.

These industries have been severely affected by the interruption of commercial activities in this country, he said during the forum on "Semiconductor crisis, the future of the automotive and transportation industry", organized by CETYS.

Martínez Cisneros explained that, to give an idea of the complexity of global supply chains, there are 2,100 U.S. companies and 1,200 European companies that have at least one direct supplier in Russia. In addition, more than 450 companies in the United States and 200 in Europe have first-tier suppliers in Ukraine.

"The numbers increase as we move from direct suppliers to indirect relationships (tier two or three). More than 15,100 companies in the United States and eight thousand 200 European companies have tier two suppliers based in these two countries and tier three we would be considering 190 thousand companies in the United States and 109 thousand companies in Europe; in total around 300 thousand companies would be affected in the United States and Europe, not counting Latin America", he added.

With information from Berenice Luna and Alina Archundia

title: UPDATE 1-Hawkish Glapinski says Polish MPC resolute in inflation fight
text:
(Adds details)               

By Anna Koper               

WARSAW, March 9 (Reuters) - Poland's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) is determined to fight a surge in inflation that will be fuelled by the war in Ukraine, the central bank governor said on Wednesday, striking a hawkish tone a day after the bank raised rates more than expected.               

Central European currencies have taken a beating as a result of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and this has combined with a surge in oil and gas prices to boost inflation that was already amongst the highest in Europe, piling pressure on central banks.               

"(The Monetary Policy Council) is determined to bring inflation to the target as soon as possible, and we will be consistent and tenacious in this," governor Adam Glapinski told a news conference.               

"I stand in front of you as a hawk... a hawk at the head of the hawks who form the Monetary Policy Council at the moment."               

Glapinski said the war in Ukraine could add two percentage points to Polish CPI, which is already running at its highest level in more than two decades, hitting 9.3% in January.               

The National Bank of Poland (NBP) raised its main interest rate by 75 basis points to 3.5% on Tuesday. The hike was above analysts' estimates, but lower than some market participants had hoped for.               

"We are still in the rate-hike cycle... and we will remain in it. It is hard to say for how long," Glapinski said, adding he would now say the peak of rates would be higher than the 4.0-4.5% he has previously talked about.               

Glapinski also said the MPC was determined to strengthen the zloty, whose recent depreciation he labelled unjustified.               

After having softened more than 7% versus the euro between the start of Russia's invasion on Feb. 24 and Monday's close, the zloty, in common with regional peers, has rebounded strongly over the past two days.               

It gained around 1% during the course of Glapinski's news conference and was trading at 4.757 to the euro at 1607 GMT, a gain of 3.7% on the day.               

The NBP has intervened in the foreign exchange market three times since the Ukraine war started to shore up the zloty, and Glapinski said it was ready to continue doing so.

title: Countries "hostile" to Russia will collect their debts with devalued rubles
text:
MOSCOW

The Russian government yesterday established a list of "hostile" countries, to which individuals and companies will be able to repay their debts in rubles, a currency that since the beginning of the invasion in Ukraine depreciated by more than 60 percent.

The Kremlin's measure, established through a presidential decree over the weekend, responds to the economic sanctions it received from the West in recent weeks due to the invasion of Ukraine.

The list includes, among others, countries of the European Union (EU), Australia, USA, Canada, Switzerland and Japan.

As of this measure, Russian companies will be able to pay creditors in these countries in rubles, even if the securities are denominated in other currencies.

For this purpose, the debtor will be able to ask a Russian bank to create a special ruble account in the name of the foreign creditor and send him a payment in Russian currency for the amount due, at the exchange rate of the day in question, as indicated by the Central Bank of that country.

This measure shall apply to payments in excess of 10 million rubles per month.

SPECIAL PERMISSION TO OTHER COUNTRIES

On the other hand, countries that are not part of the lists will still be able to receive payments in foreign currencies through a special permit.

This is one of Russia's first responses to sanctions imposed by numerous foreign countries following its military intervention in Ukraine.

At the same time, Russia is trying to show that it can still meet its financial obligations, in a context of uncertainty in which it is believed that it may default.

To counter the fall of the ruble, Vladimir Putin's government established various measures, including prohibiting its residents from transferring foreign currency abroad; charging a 30 percent commission to exchange rubles into dollars, euros or pounds; and obliging exporters to convert 80 percent of their revenues earned in foreign currencies into rubles.

The currency controls cast a pall of doubt over whether or not Russia can pay its foreign creditors.

Although last Wednesday Russia paid $98 million of a sovereign debt coupon (OFZ) in rubles, foreign holders did not receive the money due to restrictions on foreign payments, generating a debate on whether or not it has already defaulted.

On March 16 there will be another round of maturities for 117 million dollars that do not allow payment in another currency.

If Russia decides to pay in rubles, the country could eventually default and trigger credit default swaps (CDS), the insurance for creditors in case of default, whose values rebounded yesterday to a figure that indicates that the country has an 80 percent chance of defaulting.

Over the weekend, Moody's downgraded for the second time in less than seven days its long-term local and foreign currency debt rating from B3 to Ca, only one notch above the default rating.

The rating agency explained that the downgrade was triggered by the expectation that capital controls introduced by Russia's Central Bank will restrict cross-border payments, including on government bond debt service.

"The downgrade to 'Ca' is driven by serious concerns about Russia's willingness and ability to service its debt obligations," Moody's justified, for which the risk of a default occurring "has increased significantly."

The provision comes on top of a similar downgrade by the Fitch agency last week, and the reclassification of the MSCI Russia index from "Emerging Market" to "Isolated Market".

CLOSED STOCK MARKET

In this context, the Russian stock exchange has been closed since February 25, the day after the start of the Russian offensive in Ukraine. Since that date, the Russian currency lost almost half of its value. (AFP and AP)

The "hostile" list includes countries of the European Union, the USA, Australia and Canada, among others.

title: Ruble plunges more than 20% in week because of sanctions on Russia
text:
The ruble ended the week down more than 20% against the dollar and euro in Moscow trading on Friday (4), with the Russian economy under pressure from sanctions aimed at isolating Russia in response to its invasion of Ukraine.

The ruble ended the week at 115 per dollar in Moscow, down from 83 per dollar last Friday, though it appreciated 1% on Friday over Thursday. Against the euro it closed just below 119 per euro, down from 93 per euro at the end of last week. The currency hit record lows against the U.S. currency on Thursday and the euro on Friday.

Russia's currency has plummeted more than 20 percent this week - Dado Ruvic/Reuters "Russian assets are being destroyed in value," said Cristian Maggio, head of portfolio strategy at TD Securities

. Russia's five-year CDS -- a measure of the cost of protection against a debt default -- stood at 1,565 basis points, up from Thursday's 1,412 basis points, but still some distance from Monday's record 1,973 basis points, data from IHS Markit showed.

Trading on the Moscow Stock Exchange remained virtually closed on Friday, the fifth day of restrictions imposed by the Russian central bank.

In spot market trading outside Russia, the ruble was down 10.4 percent at 121.033 per dollar in mid-afternoon New York after hitting a record low of 122.033 per dollar. Buying and selling offers were between 120 and 128 per dollar, which traders characterized as a sign of evaporating liquidity.

For the week, the ruble was down 30.7%, deepening the 2022 low to 36.2%.

G7 threatens Russia with new sanctions The group of seven most industrialized countries in the world (G7) threatened on Friday (4) to impose new "severe sanctions" against Russia for its military intervention in Ukraine and proposed to counter Russian "disinformation" campaigns about the war.

The G7 countries "will continue to impose severe sanctions in response to Russian aggression," the foreign ministers of the group formed by the United States, Canada, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Japan said in a statement.

The G7 also indicated that it will act to curb the "Russian disinformation campaign," which "puts more lives at risk."

The statement urged Russia to end its attacks "in the vicinity of Ukrainian nuclear power plants," following Russian bombings that on Friday caused a fire at the Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest, with no consequences on radioactivity levels.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Sanctions response to Russia's invasion offers clues for China
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

By Tony Munroe

BEIJING, March 3 (Reuters) - Under President Xi Jinping, China has pushed for self-reliance in key areas of technology and the payments needed to settle trade to minimise its vulnerability to economic pressure over flashpoints, from trade policy to Taiwan.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the tough global response, including curtailment of access to the SWIFT payments system and a freezing of Russian assets, provide a case study for China on the economic and financial vulnerabilities analysts expect it will continue to address.

The unexpectedly heavy sanctions, led by the West, have exposed vulnerabilities for Russia, including dependence on the U.S. dollar, that China would want to mitigate before becoming the target of any such measures.

While the China-U.S. trade war during the Trump administration forced China to seek greater self-sufficiency, the sanctions on Russia are a louder wake-up call, said Abraham Zhang, chairman of Shenzhen-based China Europe Capital.

"Just as China needs food security, China also needs oil reserves, and a complete industrial system, so that if China is one day cut off from external supplies as Russia is now, China can still be self-sufficient, maintain internal circulation, and survive," Zhang said.

China has in recent years ramped-up efforts to develop home-grown technologies, from semiconductors to advanced materials to aircraft, to ease reliance on imports. Huawei Technologies, crippled by sanctions preventing its access to high-end chips, is a cautionary example.

"China needs to accelerate the development of key technologies. Otherwise, it would be too late once you're suffocated by sanctions, if Russia offers any lessons," he said.

To be sure, China has a much bigger and more diversified economy than Russia's, although it depends on imported energy and food, and relies heavily on global commerce as the world's largest trading economy.

Also, Ukraine is not Taiwan, which Beijing has vowed to bring under its control, by force if necessary.

The political and geostrategic circumstances are vastly different, including the likely response to a Chinese attack on the democratically controlled island, which among other factors is a linchpin in the global technology supply chain.

Where the United States has ruled out intervening militarily in Ukraine, its policy of "strategic ambiguity" towards Taiwan and its strengthening defence ties with the island, including stepped up arms sales and the development of the AUKUS grouping with Australia and Britain, convey a warning.

China, which has declined to condemn Russia's attack or call it an invasion, has blamed the Ukraine conflict on NATO expansion.

Taiwan has reported no unusual Chinese military movements since the Ukraine war began and U.S. President Joe Biden this week dispatched a team of former senior officials to visit the island in a show of support.

CURRENCIES, PAYMENTS

China has in recent years sought to internationalise its currency by settling more trade with the yuan, including with Russia. The yuan accounted for 13.1% of the Russian central bank's foreign currency reserves last June, compared with just 0.1% in June 2017

China's central bank is developing a digital currency, which would have the benefit of further encouraging yuan settlement for trade, but the project, while ahead of efforts elsewhere, is still in its early days.

China has an alternative system to bypass SWIFT, the Cross Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which saw a 75% increase in processing volume last year, although 80% of CIPS transactions still involve SWIFT.

Bert Hofman, director of the East Asian Institute at the Lee Kuan Yew School of the National University Singapore, said China has been concerned about dollar dominance of international payments since the global financial crisis.

"The sanctions may therefore lead China to accelerate the development of alternative options, including the China-led CIPS system, and the further internationalisation of the (yuan)."

WORRY ABOUT ISOLATION

While the unity and strength of the diplomatic response to the invasion, which many experts believe Russia underestimated, may be instructive to China, the unexpectedly sluggish early performance of Russia's forces in Ukraine is less applicable, with the United States not engaged there militarily.

U.S. intervention would be China's biggest worry in the event that it attacked Taiwan, said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Washington-based Stimson Center.

"The international isolation of Russia, and the broad coalition ... make China worry about the potential international isolation of China in a similar event on Taiwan," she said.

Still, she said, China would take comfort that countries that have joined in sanctions against Russia remain in the minority, and the fact that China has yet to face secondary sanctions for its Russia ties.

Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said Beijing was unlikely to be happy with the way things are going in Ukraine but the ultimate effectiveness of the international response would determine its outlook.

If Russia was not brought to its knees, "China will be relatively relaxed about what the West could do when China is finally ready to take Taiwan," he said.

"If the responses should prove effective against Russia, Xi will be a lot more cautious about when and how he will try to bring Taiwan into the fold," he said. (Reporting by Tony Munroe; Editing by Robert Birsel)
