text:
This Wednesday marks seven days since Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a military invasion of Ukraine, which has claimed the lives of dozens of citizens. There are also reports of injuries, thousands of people displaced by the war and destruction.

The military offensive continues as the Ukrainian government waits for the European Union to accept the country as a member of the organization.

This is a minute-by-minute account of the seventh day of the Russian military invasion of Ukrainian territory.

3:45 p.m. Russian missile breaks heating distribution pipeline in Kiev. "A major heating pipeline in Kiev was damaged as a result of the missile attack in the area of the central railway station. A part of the city could be deprived of heating tonight," Ukrainian Interior Minister's adviser Anton Gerashenko wrote on Telegram. The missile was intercepted by anti-aircraft defenses with a loud explosion and, falling, hit the pipeline.

3:20 p.m. Moscow admits death of Russian soldiers. The Moscow Defense Ministry admitted the death of 498 Russian soldiers in the war against Ukraine. Among the Ukrainians there are 2,870 dead and about 3,700 wounded.

Russia's largest bank announces its exit from the market due to sanctions and 9 other economic news around the world on Wednesday

02:40 p.m. Spain will send grenade launchers, ammunition and machine guns to Ukraine. Spain will send next Friday two planes with a first shipment of offensive military material to Ukraine, including 1,370 grenade launchers against tanks, 700,000 cartridges for rifles and machine guns, as well as light machine guns.

In a television interview, the Minister of Defense, Margarita Robles, has detailed that this first shipment will arrive in Poland, at a point very close to the Ukrainian border, in two planes.

Macron: Europe must spend more to become an independent power. The French president assured in a televised speech that Europe must spend more to be "an independent and sovereign power", because its "freedom is not guaranteed". Macron called for a definitive push for renewable energies and the construction of new nuclear reactors on the continent.

Next week's European Union summit in Versailles should begin to take decisions on these issues, he advanced. Macron assured that the invasion of Ukraine signals "a change of era", in which "democracy is not considered as an unquestionable regime", so Europe must take "historic decisions" in its defense.

02:10 p.m. Zelenski's chief of staff calls for more sanctions "from a bunker". Andriy Yermak, Ukrainian chief of staff, signs an op-ed in The New York Times today written "from a bunker," in which he calls on the West for more economic sanctions and warns of Russia's imperialist intentions. "As I write, President Zelenski is at my side. Please help us show Putin the mistake he has made," the caption reads.

Yermak, who applauds civilians who have turned to arms and warns about Russian attacks on residential areas, reminds that there is a 64-kilometer military caravan heading to Kiev, so he also calls for anti-tank and anti-aircraft equipment, as well as ammunition.

01:50 p.m. The United States "will support diplomatic efforts" by Kiev to reach a cease-fire and the withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukraine, Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Wednesday.

"If there are diplomatic steps that we can take that the Ukrainian government believes would be helpful, we are prepared to take them, even as we continue to support Ukraine's ability to defend itself," he told a news conference in Washington.

01:30 p.m. Blinken will visit Poland, the Baltic countries and Moldova in support of Ukraine. U.S. chief diplomat Antony Blinken will travel in the coming days to Belgium, Poland, the Baltic countries and Moldova to reaffirm Washington's support for Ukraine in the wake of the Russian invasion, the State Department announced Wednesday.

The trip, March 3-8, "continues extensive consultations and coordination with our NATO allies and European partners on the continuation of the Russian Federation's premeditated, unprovoked and unjustified war against Ukraine," State Department spokesman Ned Price said in a statement.

01:00 p.m. The U.S. announced sanctions on 22 entities related to the Russian Defense sector and restrictions on technology exports that could support Russia's ability to refine oil.

In addition, the U.S. Commerce Department extended to Belarus the export controls it has imposed for Russia in order to "significantly degrade" Minsk's ability to support Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

U.S. accuses Russia at the UN of mobilizing banned weapons. "It appears that Russia is preparing to increase the brutality of its campaign against Ukraine," U.S. Ambassador to the UNLinda Thomas-Greenfield told the General Assembly. "We have seen videos of Russian forces moving exceptionally lethal weaponry into Ukraine that has no place on the battlefield. That includes cluster and vacuum bombs and munitions, which are banned by the Geneva Convention," she asserted.

1:00 p.m. Russian fighter jets violated Swedish airspace. The Swedish Army reported that four Russian fighter jets violated Swedish airspace in the Baltic.

12:30 p.m. European Commission suspends scientific cooperation with Russia. In a statement, the European Commissioner for Innovation, Research, Culture and Education, Bulgarian Mariya Gabriel, indicated that she has instructed her collaborators "not to undertake any more cooperation projects" with Russia following that country's attack on neighboring Ukraine. Ongoing initiatives were suspended and outstanding payments were frozen. Gabriel also called for "maximum flexibility" with Ukrainian students in Erasmus+ programs" so that they can cancel or postpone scheduled activities.

Ukraine puts Russian casualties at more than 7,000. Since the beginning of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, more than 7,000 Russian soldiers have been killed, while hundreds have been taken prisoner, including senior officers, Oleksiy Arestovich, military adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Wednesday. The first figure offered by the Russian Defense Ministry a short time earlier fell short of half a thousand dead.

12:00 p.m. Russia does not plan to use nuclear weapons under any circumstances. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stated that her country under no circumstances intends to press "the nuclear red button", following Russian President Vladimir Putin's recent order to put Russia's nuclear forces into "special service regime".

"We start from the point that this apocalyptic script will not be carried out under any pretext and under any conditions," he said in an interview to the Colombian channel W Radio, stressing that Moscow has made its position clear on the matter. "Apparently they confuse us with the United States, but Russia has never spoken" of using nuclear weapons.

11:50 a.m. The European Union adopted new economic sanctions against Belarus for its role in the Russian-initiated invasion against Ukraine. In an official note, the EU Council reported that it adopted restrictions "on trade in goods used in the production or manufacture of tobacco products, mineral fuels and bituminous substances." Earlier, sanctions had been announced against 22 high-ranking military officials.

11:30 a.m. UN General Assembly condemns Russian invasion of Ukraine. The UN General Assembly passed a resolution condemning the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with the support of 141 of the 193 UN member states. The text "deplores" the Russian aggression against Ukraine and "demands" that Moscow put an end to it and immediately and unconditionally withdraw its troops from the neighboring country.

The resolution, which is not binding, received only five votes against (Russia, Belarus, Syria, North Korea and Eritrea) and 35 abstentions, including Nicaragua and El Salvador.

11:00 a.m. A Ukrainian delegation is heading to Belarus for a second round of negotiations with Russia, which invaded Ukraine last week, the government in Kiev said Wednesday.

"The Ukrainian delegation is heading to the venue of the negotiations," the Ukrainian presidency said.

Russia said the venue of the meeting is near the Belarusian-Polish border and that the agenda includes discussions on a cessation of hostilities.

10:57 a.m. Russia says it lost 498 soldiers in Ukraine, in first balance since the invasion. In the first casualty balance sheet published by the Russian Defense Ministry, it admitted losing almost five hundred soldiers and more than a thousand wounded. "Unfortunately (...) we had losses. 498 Russian servicemen were killed (...) 1,597 of our comrades were wounded" during the Russian military operations launched on February 24, declared the army spokesman, Igor Konashenkov, in images broadcast by the Russian public television. Casualties among "Ukrainian military and nationalists" amounted to "2,870 dead and about 3,700 wounded," he said.

Germany uses its oil reserve to contain prices. "It is our contribution to the international concert. In times like these it is important to act with unity," declared Economy Minister Green Robert Habeck, according to the ministry.

The German contribution corresponds to the 5.4% that its oil consumption represents in relation to the total of the International Energy Agency, whose member countries agreed yesterday to release 60 million barrels, or 435,000 tons of crude. That is 3% of Germany's strategic reserve.

10:55 a.m. The World Health Organization reiterated the "urgent need" to establish a safe corridor to facilitate the arrival of medical supplies. The director general of this organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, pointed out in a virtual press conference that the first shipment with sanitary material, transported from Dubai, will arrive tomorrow in Poland.

"There is some access to material, but given the evolution of the conflict, we fear a worsening of the situation," said WHO-Ukraine director Jarno Habicht, who focused concerns on the lack of oxygen and medicines and problems in carrying out the polio vaccination campaign.

German supermarkets exclude Russian products. From vodka to toothpaste, several supermarket chains in Germany have decided to exclude products imported from Russia, as a sign of solidarity with Ukraine.

10:50 a.m. France vetoes cultural events and artists linked to the Russian government. The French Minister of Culture announced on Twitter that her country has decided to suspend the holding of any new cultural events linked to official Russian institutions or Russian artists who are in favor of Russian intervention in Ukraine.

"We stand in solidarity with hard-hit Ukrainian artists, cultural professionals and journalists. We do not forget Russian dissidents. Together, they keep democracy and culture alive every day, a ferment of peace and dialogue between peoples," he said. And he added that "this geopolitical crisis is accompanied by a war of information and propaganda".

Borrell offers cyber and anti-disinformation help to Moldova. "Disinformation has become a war in itself and is an active component of what is happening in Ukraine," EU High Representative for Foreign Policy Josep Borrell said after meeting with Moldovan President Maia Sandu.

"We stand ready to support Moldova in its efforts to guarantee the right to information for its citizens," said Borrell, who also offered cybersecurity support and welcomed the effort to receive refugees.

10:42 a.m. President Joe Biden assured that a ban on Russian oil imports into the United States is not "off the table" in retaliation for the invasion of Ukraine.

"Nothing is off the table," he told reporters when asked if oil could be the next target of unprecedented U.S. and Western sanctions against Moscow.

10:40 a.m. Ukraine's ambassador to the United Nations, Sergiy Kyslytsya, denounced that the Russian invasion is causing a "genocide" in his country before the rostrum of the UN General Assembly that is to vote on a resolution condemning such an attack.

"It is already clear that Russia's goal is not just occupation. It is genocide," the ambassador said.

10:20 a.m. The U.S. Justice Department tasked a dozen prosecutors with prosecuting "corrupt Russian oligarchs" and anyone who violates Washington's sanctions against Moscow following the invasion of Ukraine.

"We will spare no effort to investigate, arrest and prosecute all those whose criminal acts enable the Russian government to continue this unjust war," U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland said in a statement.

10:00 a.m. The World Health Organization (WHO) World Health Organization (WHO) expressed "concern" over reports of attacks on hospitals and health sites during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

"We are very concerned because of reports of attacks on health facilities," WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus said at an online press conference.

09:55 a.m. A draft resolution condemning the Russian invasion of Ukraine is being voted on Wednesday.

Much of the international community accuses Vladimir Putin's Russia of violating Article 2 of the UN Charter, which urges its members not to resort to threats or force to settle disputes.

09:50 a.m. Biden does not rule out sanctions against Russian oil imports.

Pope donates medical supplies to be sent to Ukraine. Pope Francis has donated medical material to be sent in the coming days to Ukraine to help a population that is suffering from Russia's invasion, informed the head of the Vatican limosneria, Polish Cardinal Konrad Krajewski. Through the limosneria, the organism in charge of carrying out charitable works on behalf of the Pope, Francis sent medical material to the Basilica of St. Sophia in Rome, a reference point for the Ukrainian community and from where for days now truckloads of food and subsistence items have been leaving for Ukraine. The papal almoner today personally took it upon himself to bring to the basilica "the Pope's help and closeness, taking up an appeal launched in recent days by the Ukrainian community in Italy asking for medical supplies," the Vatican explained.

09:00 a.m. Hundreds of citizens and employees of the Zaporozhie nuclear power plant, in the east of the country, prevented Wednesday with barricades and tankers the advance of a column of the Russian Army. "We explained to them (the Russian military) our position, that the Zaporozhie Nuclear Power Plant and the city are under secure protection. The residents will not let them take a single step in the city," the city's mayor Dmitry Orlov said, according to UNIAN agency.

Vodka and other Russian products are out of several German supermarkets. From vodka to toothpaste, several supermarket chains in Germany have decided to exclude products imported from Russia as a sign of solidarity with Ukraine.

Until now, the 'discounter' Aldi Nord only offered a single item from Russia: vodka in 0.70-liter bottle.

08:40 a.m. Belgium announced Wednesday the shipment of humanitarian aid supplies, such as tents, blankets and cold-adapted sanitary equipment, to Ukraine in solidarity with the Kiev authorities and the population suffering from Russia's military invasion. The shipment is to be channeled through the B-FAST emergency aid mechanism, an inter-ministerial intervention mechanism for disasters abroad, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. Belgium is thus responding "to the request for assistance sent by Ukraine through the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism (EUCPM) following Russia's military invasion of Ukraine," the ministry said.

Bank of Russia is keeping the stock market closed for the third day for the third consecutive day on fears of a plunge in major stocks due to heavy economic sanctions imposed by the West over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

"The Bank of Russia decided not to resume trading on March 2, 2022 on the Moscow Stock Exchange in the securities market section (...)" with some exceptions, it said in a statement. The exceptions concern direct orders with settlements in rubles, derivatives - except for derivatives market instruments in the currency pairs section - precious metals and some contracts for futures in closing positions, among others.

08:20 a.m. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) ruled out Wednesday that Ukraine is developing nuclear weapons, as Russia alleges to justify, among other issues,its invasion of the neighboring country.

"For us this issue is very clear. We have no information that would call into question Ukraine's (nuclear) non-proliferation credentials," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told a press conference in Vienna. "We have no information about any detour of any kind of material, any undeclared material or activities aimed at the development of nuclear weapons" in Ukraine, the IAEA official said.

08:10 a.m. Ukrainian delegation for the Beijing Paralympic Games (March 4-13) has arrived safely in China despite the conflict in Ukraine, the International Paralympic Committee (IPC) International Paralympic Committee (IPC) announced Wednesday.

"I am happy to say that just a few hours ago, the Ukrainian team consisting of 20 athletes and 9 guides has arrived safely in Beijing" said at a press conference Andrew Parsons, president of the international organization.

Ukraine reports more than 2,000 civilians killed. More than 2,000 Ukrainian civilians have died since the beginning of the invasion launched by Russia on February 24, denounced Wednesday the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS, for its acronym in Ukrainian). "During the seven days of the war Russia has destroyed hundreds of transport infrastructure, housing, hospitals and kindergartens. In this time more than 2,000 Ukrainians have died, not counting our defenders," the DSNS noted on its Facebook page.

08:00 a.m. The Spanish Prime Minister, Socialist Pedro Sanchez, announced Wednesday that his country will follow the lead of other nations and deliver "offensive military material" to "the Ukrainian resistance."

"As I see that there are (political) groups that question the commitment of the government of Spain" to Ukraine, "I also want to announce to them that Spain will deliver to the Ukrainian resistance offensive military material," Sanchez declared in the Congress of Deputies.

Boris Johnson accuses Russia of "war crime". British Prime Minister Boris Johnson on Wednesday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a war criminal and urged UN member countries to condemn the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Johnson made the remarks in the House of Commons in London, where the Ukrainian ambassador was present and received a standing ovation from MPs.

07:56 a.m. Ukraine invites mothers of captured Russian soldiers to fetch them.

The Ukrainian military on Wednesday invited mothers of captured Russian soldiers to fetch them to Ukraine, on the seventh day of the invasion launched by Moscow during which it claims to have taken dozens of prisoners.

"It was decided to hand over the captured Russian soldiers to their mothers if they come to fetch them to Ukraine, to Kiev," the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said in a statement.

Refugees. The number of Ukrainian refugees in neighboring countries rose by 200,000 people in 24 hours, according to the latest UN figures released Wednesday, bringing the total number to 874,000 since the start of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine borders seven countries, Russia to the north and east, Belarus in the north, Poland and Slovakia to the west and Romania, Hungary and Moldova in the southwest.

07:40 a.m. The "consequences" of the war in Ukraine for the U.S. economy are "very uncertain," Jerome Powell, chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve (central bank, Fed), said in a speech prepared for his appearance before the House of Representatives on Wednesday.

With prices rising at a pace not seen in four decades and oil above $100 a barrel, the Fed chief repeated that they are willing to raise interest rates to curb inflation. But "the economy is evolving in unexpected ways," he said, and "we will have to be nimble to respond." The Fed is due to decide how much to raise interest rates at its March 14-15 meeting.

War in Ukraine triggers oil, gas, aluminum and nickel prices. Oil prices continued to soar Wednesday, natural gas and aluminum hit record highs and nickel hit a decade high, driven by the war in Ukraine, which fuels fears of energy and commodity supply disruption.

U.S. WTI crude rose to $111.50 a barrel, its highest price since 2013, while Brent North Sea crude hit $113.02 a barrel, a high since 2014.

title: UPDATE 2-Hungary  central bank  ready to act 'at any moment' to shore up markets
text:
* Forint reined in from record lows by cenbank intervention

* Still down sharply since start of Russian invasion of Ukraine

* Cenbank must continue tightening cycle -deputy governor

* Inflation developments harming growth prospects -deputy governor (Adds comments from deputy governor, updates market reaction)

By Gergely Szakacs

BUDAPEST, March 1 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) is ready to intervene "at any moment" with all tools at its disposal to ensure the stability of local financial markets, it said in a reply to Reuters questions on Tuesday, reining in the forint from record lows.

The NBH raised its base rate by 50 basis points to 3.4% last week, as expected, after consumer prices grew at their fastest rate in almost 15 years in January and mounting Ukraine-Russia tensions fuelled market uncertainty.

The NBH said it was closely monitoring the situation, adding that current market moves were not justified by economic fundamentals after the forint fell as much as 2% on the day to record lows versus the euro.

"It is the NBH's clear intention to prevent the heightened risks stemming from geopolitical circumstances from threatening Hungary's price and financial stability," it said.

"Financial market moves are not justified by fundamentals, however, they add to upside risks for inflation."

Deputy Governor Barnabas Virag told private broadcaster Info Radio in an interview that the NBH must continue its monetary tightening cycle in a predictable way, but also stand ready to act in a flexible manner, if needed.

"The situation will be more difficult throughout the year because of the war," Virag said. "We must prepare for an increase in inflation risks and a deterioration of the economic growth outlook."

Virag said given the high degree of uncertainty over the outcome of the military conflict, it was not possible to give predictable economic forecasts, adding that the road back to the bank's 3% inflation target will be a long one.

Earlier on Tuesday, economists at Raiffeisen Bank sharply raised their inflation forecasts for Hungary to 9% this year and 7% for 2023, with the average rate for two years projected at the highest for the entire Central European region.

"The National Bank of Hungary is closely monitoring the situation and stands ready to intervene at any moment," it said. "If necessary, the NBH will use all tools at its disposal to ensure the stability of local financial markets."

The war over the eastern border in neighbouring Ukraine, home to a large ethnic Hungarian community, has hammered Hungarian financial markets.

The forint has fallen some 4% versus the euro since Russia invaded Ukraine last week, sinking to record lows at 379 per euro on Tuesday. The currency pared some of its losses after the central bank remarks, but was still down more than 1% on the day, extending its losses for the year.

Shares in central Europe's largest independent lender, OTP Bank, plunged 21.5% on Tuesday, hitting their lowest level since November 2020. The bank's shares have lost about a third of their value since Russia invaded Ukraine last week.

The NBH's next regular policy meeting is due on March 22. It will hold a non-rate setting meeting next Tuesday, while the weekly tender of its one-week deposit facility, which it uses to tackle short-term market volatility, is due on Thursday. (Reporting by Gergely Szakacs and Anita Komuves in Budapest Editing by Alex Richardson and Matthew Lewis)

title: Russia-Ukraine conflict: A first negotiation amidst the bombs
text:
From Paris

Triple billiards around the Russian occupation of Ukraine. The Russian army intensified its offensive in several points of Ukraine at the same time that Russia and Ukraine held the first negotiations in Belarus and that the French President, Emmanuel Macron, met again by telephone with Vladimir Putin to agree on the conditions that could put an end to the conflict. Both the direct negotiation and the talks between Macron and Putin do not contain, so far, elements to lower skepticism. Moscow increased its military actions in the second city of the country, Kharkov, with the prospect of dialogue between the Russian and Ukrainian delegations. Former Russian Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky is leading the negotiations and has said that they are seeking to reach an agreement that "takes into account the interests of both sides". Ukrainian Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov, leading the Ukrainian delegation, stressed that the condition was an immediate "cease-fire" and the departure of Russian troops from his country. The talks will continue on Tuesday, March 1.

Almost all the cards seem to be in Putin's hands, despite the unprecedented package of sanctions adopted in the last hours by the European Union and the group of the most industrialized countries, the G7. The measures have already caused the ruble to plummet by 20% and the Russian Central Bank has doubled its interest rate (9.5 to 20%). FIFA joined this cannonade of sanctions when, on Monday, it excluded Russia from the World Cup in Qatar (2022). Despite this encirclement, the head of the Russian state has a double military advantage: the first is that he is about to take control of the city of Berdiansk and this places Russian forces very close to seizing Mariupol. This is the port town on the Sea of Azov. If Moscow manages to control Mariupol it would have within its reach the famous corridor that connects with Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014, and the Donbas, which is Russia's priority target. That is the meaning of the telephone conversation between Macron and Putin. The Russian presidency issued a statement with the new fold of conditions it presented to Macron in which the "recognition of Russian sovereignty in Crimea," not recognized by the West, figures. Putin also demanded "demilitarization and denazification of the Ukrainian state" as well as a "neutral status" prior to any solution. Paris, in its turn, advanced that Putin had been asked not to bomb civilians, not to destroy civilian infrastructure and not to violate roads.

According to the Elysée Palace, the Russian president "confirmed his willingness to commit himself" to these points. Paris also insisted on "the need for a cease-fire" and the importance of maintaining an open channel of dialogue. The French president proposed "to remain in contact in the coming days. We will exchange again". Putin has been adding many powerful pieces on this war chessboard with a very effective anticipation. Not least of all, last Sunday, a referendum was held in Belarus in complete secrecy, opening the door to a modification of the Constitution to put an end to the "neutrality" of Belarus and to the prohibition of the installation of nuclear weapons on its territory. The consultation was approved by 65% of the population.

Europe is both proud of its unprecedented decisions and at the same time blocked from going any further. It cannot call on the Atlantic Alliance (NATO) and, as it lacks a common defense, cannot intervene as a whole. The division of responsibilities between NATO and the EU limits a military response, all the more so since the EU's vocation is not to return to the times of war that the continent has already known. The "activation" of the nuclear response announced on Monday by Putin also raises fears of an abyssal conflict.

NATO and the UN NATO took part in several missions that were not its own responsibility and left in its wake a trail of deaths and shipwrecks: in Kosovo (1999), in Afghanistan (2003) and, more recently, in the international coalition that put an end to the Libyan regime of President Muammar Gaddafi (2011). In Afghanistan it lost the war alongside the United States and in Libya, in 2011, it decapitated a country and unleashed the greatest humanitarian crisis of the century. This intervention (Unified Protector (OUP), requested by the United Nations, led to the flight of millions of people across the Mediterranean Sea to Europe. Previously, in Kosovo, starting in 1999, another mission was undertaken at the request of the UN, the result of which can be summed up in the phrase left by that conflict: "collateral damage". Each time it was the Security Council that requested its intervention. It did not do so this time for three reasons: Russia is a nuclear power: neither Europe nor NATO wants a direct confrontation with Russia: to intervene, among other conditions, NATO requires a request from the UN Security Council. In this month of February, the Council was chaired by Russia and, therefore, Moscow was not going to request an intervention against itself.

Ukraine asks to join the EU The EU and NATO divide tasks; the EU is in charge of managing crises outside the Union and NATO is in charge of defending the territories of the 30 countries of the Atlantic Alliance. Ukraine is neither a member of the EU nor of NATO. The Ukrainian president, Volodymir Zelenski, reiterated on Monday, February 28, his request for the European Union to accept his country as a member by means of "a special procedure". We will have to wait. In fact, the EU hit Russia for what it is, an economic giant, and got stuck in its geopolitical and military smallness. Yet, this conflict did upset the course: for the first time in its recent history, the EU came out of its mold when it agreed to deliver arms to Ukraine through an "assistance" fund in the amount of 450 million euros. The conflict in Ukraine pushed Europe into another world. 77 years after World War II (1939-1945) Europeans set aside their creed of peace on which the Europe we know was built. The turnaround is gigantic, even if the help may seem modest. The countries of Eastern Europe played a decisive role in this shift. Occupied first by the Nazis and then by the Soviets, Eastern Europe sees the specter of a new occupation rising again. Even countries like Sweden broke the doctrine of not supplying arms to a country at war. The last time it had done so was in 1939, when Finland was attacked by the Soviet Union. This Monday, February 28, the EU expanded its range of action. It agreed to coordinate the purchase of arms requested by Ukraine and to enable its satellites to provide "intelligence" support to Kiev.

Gas The EU is also constrained by the energy emergency. The Brussels Commission and the Member States blocked the assets of the Russian Central Bank, removed certain Russian banks from the SWIFT international banking exchange system and even proposed to ban Russian channels such as Russia Today and Sputnik from broadcasting in EU countries (a measure, moreover, very difficult to implement). However, the one thing that would have set Russia back was left untouched: gas. It is all the more decisive because not even in the most tense moments of the Cold War did Russia stop supplying gas to Europe and Europe stopped buying it. Russian gas exports are as key for Russia as they are for the West. Europe is Moscow's first customer, for whom gas exports account for 60% of the foreign currency it earns. In turn, Europe is Russia's first gas customer with an overall dependence of 40%. The percentage reaches 65% in Germany and 75% in countries such as Austria and the crown of nations that were once satellites of the USSR: the Baltic countries, Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The German Chancellor, Olaf Scholz, decided to halt the process by which the Russian Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which passes under the Baltic Sea and goes directly to Germany and from there to Europe, was to be put into operation. However, this pipe-line, whose construction ended in 2021 and which was always opposed by the United States, was not yet in operation. In contrast, the other pipeline, Nord Stream 1, has been supplying gas since 2012 and no one, neither in Germany nor elsewhere, has mentioned suspending supplies. There are, in addition, three other Russian-European gas pipelines in activity: Yamal, Brotherhood and Soyouz. Neither Algeria, Turkey, Azerbaijan nor the United States are in a position to replace all the gas coming from Russia.

The future comes with another immense problem. The management of refugees and displaced persons. For the EU it is a head-scratcher. The magnitude of what is expected has no recent examples: four million refugees, 7 million displaced persons and 18 million people affected by war. Those are the projections emerging from last Sunday's meeting between EU Interior Ministers. "The war will be long," said Macron. And like all wars, impossible to foresee. A major catastrophe lurks in Europe. However, there was time and diplomatic means to avoid it.

title: Wall Street has a second negative month due to Ukraine invasion
text:
New York, Feb 28 After a January marked by the Federal Reserve's shift towards a more aggressive monetary policy, Wall Street closed this Monday its second negative month on the stock market due to the anticipation and geopolitical effect of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Risk aversion led to significant cuts in the US stock market: the Dow Jones Industrials index fell by 3.5 %, the S&P 500 by 3.1 % and the Nasdaq index by 3.43 %. In Europe, the results were generally worse, as Frankfurt fell by 6.53 %, Paris by 4.86 %, Milan by 5.21 %, Madrid by 1.55 % and London by 0.08 %. The New York stock market seemed to bounce back at the beginning of the month, but the spirits were dampened by the escalation of tensions in Eastern Europe which led on February 24 to the order for military intervention in Ukraine by the Russian President, Vladimir Putin.

 Some analysts noted that the market then followed a "sell the rumor, buy the news" strategy that led to a surprising turnaround in the stock market, bouncing from the worst losses of the year to the best session on record since late 2020. However, the past few days have been dominated by volatility as the U.S. and its Western allies imposed tough economic sanctions on Moscow, with the latest day's focus on negotiations that have failed to bring a truce. The news of the war in Ukraine has added new worries on Wall Street due to the consequent increase in the price of raw materials and fuels, precisely when inflation is rising globally and in the US at a rate not seen in almost 40 years. Most sectors fell in February, especially communications (almost 5 %), non-essential goods (3 %) and industrial goods (-2.7 %), but following the economic punishment of Russia by the West, the financial sector also suffered, by almost 4 %. On the other hand, the energy sector has appreciated by almost 9 % in parallel with the rise in the price of crude oil, with notable gains for oil companies such as Devon Energy (17 %) and Occidental Petroleum (16 %), and more meager gains for the giants Exxon Mobil (3 %) and Chevron (9 %). In the oil market, which was already very tight due to the growing global demand before the outbreak of the conflict in Eastern Europe, the fear of a reduction in the supply of Russian fuels has raised the barrel of Brent to 100.99 dollars and that of Texas to 95.72 dollars. Also noteworthy was the rise in the stock market, coinciding with the shipment of arms from NATO countries to Ukraine, of the specialized defense manufacturers Lockheed Martin (up 11 % cumulatively), Raytheon (13 %) and Northrop Grumman (18 %). In their flight to assets considered safe, investors have flocked to government bonds and slowed the rise in Treasury yields associated with the imminent interest rate hikes anticipated by the Federal Reserve. The 10-year yields are at 1.83%. Precious metals have also soared and the ounce of gold is above 1,900 dollars, while palladium, of which Russia and Ukraine are important suppliers and which is used to manufacture semiconductors, is touching 2,500 dollars. Cryptocurrencies came out of their slump today after several days of decline and the bitcoin jumped 10%, approaching $42,000, followed by other currencies such as ethereum (7%) after Washington froze the assets of the Russian central bank in the US.

title: Ruble records record drop after new Western sanctions
text:
The Russian ruble posted record declines against the dollar on Monday (28) after Western nations announced a set of tough sanctions over the weekend to punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, including restrictions on the country's currency reserves.

The ruble even fell to 119.50 per dollar in Asian trading, a record low of 30 percent from last Friday's close (25). It subsequently recovered to around 110 per dollar.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military command to put its nuclear-armed forces on high alert on Sunday (27) in response to Western reprisals for its war against Ukraine - the biggest attack on a European state since World War II.

Illustration shows Russian ruble currency in front of chart on downward trajectory - Dado Ruvic - 24.Feb.2022/Reuters Russia's central bank (CBR) announced a series of measures on Sunday to support domestic markets as it struggles to manage the fallout from sanctions that will block some of the country's banks from the Swift international payments system

title: Russian rouble tumbles to record low
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble tumbled to a record low against the dollar on Monday, after Western nations announced a harsh set of sanctions over the weekend to punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, including sanctions on the country's currency reserves.

The dollar/rouble rate was up 41.50% at a record 119.00 per dollar, in Asian trading. So far this month, the dollar is up 53.77% versus rouble.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military command to put nuclear-armed forces on high alert on Sunday, in response to Western reprisals for his war on Ukraine - the biggest assault on a European state since World War Two.

Russia's central bank announced a slew of measures on Sunday to support domestic markets, as it scrambled to manage the fallout of the sanctions that will block some banks from the SWIFT international payments system.

The central bank said it would resume buying gold on the domestic market, launch a repurchase auction with no limits and ease restrictions on banks' open foreign currency positions.

The currency had found some support last week from the first Russian central bankcurrency interventions since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

Analysts at Rabobank said the sanctions on currency reserves removed what little support the rouble had.

"Even the gold is not liquid if nobody can use FX in exchange for it. There will be a complete collapse in the rouble today..." they wrote.

Ray Attrill, head of FX strategy at National Australia Bank, said in a note on Sunday, "a collapse in the rouble appears inevitable on Monday morning", and there was an increased risk of a Russian debt default as a result of the weekend developments.

"For the rouble whilst you might see it should sell off somewhat, I really doubt you are going to see people put on fresh bets to sell the rouble at these levels – so you might well see it weakening, but I don’t think you will see people transacting all that heavily," said Peter Kinsella, London-based global head of FX strategy at UBP.

"There is a general lack of liquidity, and where you do see liquidity it is one sided, skewed to rouble sellers. It will be tricky, I can see rouble weakening quite severely – but just because it is weakening doesn’t mean it will be transacting heavily." (Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan Additional reporting by Karin Strohecker in London Editing by Shri Navaratnam)

title: What was the economic cost of Argentina's neutrality in the main war conflicts in Europe and what damages can be repeated?
text:
The great war conflicts that had their epicenter in Europe in the 20th Century left a deep imprint on the course of the Argentine economy. Will that impact be repeated with the war between Russia and Ukraine, which marked a more interventionist orientation in the local economic policy, or will the change of global context towards a more globalized world -although hit by the Covid-19 pandemic- prevent thinking of a return to the unfinished paradigm of Aldo Ferrer's "Vivir con lo Nuestro" (Living with what is ours)?

Will there be a new false step in the "neutrality" that the country usually adopts in international conflicts, when the Government -which this year presides over the United Nations Human Rights Council- now needs the support of a group of key countries in the International Monetary Fund (IMF) board of directors to avoid an unmanageable crisis?

During World War I, as a product of its enormous and diverse number of immigrants from various European countries, the government of Hipólito Yrigoyen remained neutral but did not reduce its affinity with Great Britain, the country's main trading partner. However, for a country that was already suffering the full effects of the changes in trade and financial flows, that decade was devastating. The European war was perceived as a conflict between empires in the face of which Argentina felt no need to get involved, historian Alejandro Gómez told Infobae.

"The upheavals that World War I generated in Argentina began before the war itself; already in 1913 the complicated situation in the Balkans affected the entire world capital market. The increase in the London bank rate prevented the country from financing its balance of payments deficit; the moment could not have been more inopportune, due to the bad harvests of 1913 and 1914″, highlighted Pablo Gerchunoff and Lucas Llach in the book "El Ciclo de la Ilusión y el Desencanto" (The Cycle of Illusion and Disenchantment). The four years of the conflict were very negative: GDP fell 10.4% in 1914, rose 0.5% in 1915, fell 2.9% in 1916 and another 8.1% in 1917. The monetary anemia, which triggered the crisis, took a long time to be cured.

In this sense, economist Darío Judzik said that "although at international level, the Great Depression was the most severe macroeconomic blow of the 20th century, however, in Argentina the impact of the First World War was much more important. Economic historians who reconstructed the GDP per capita series find a dramatic fall between 1913 and 1917, around the First World War, while between 1929 and the first years of the 1930s there was a relevant but smaller fall".

Although at the international level, the Great Depression was the most severe macroeconomic blow of the 20th century, in Argentina, however, the impact of the First World War was much more important (Judzik).

One of the reasons for this difference is that in 1913 a process of strong growth in countries such as Argentina, based on international trade and foreign investment (mainly British), began to slow down. The world was culminating the first great globalization, which took place between the mid-nineteenth century and the First World War, with improvements in transportation and communications, a period in which huge foreign investments were arriving to Argentina, which was a very promising project. This began to slow down in 1913, shortly before the Great War.

After those anemic figures of 1914-1918, the country began to recover steadily, although with less convincing figures than before the war. "None of the countries that most resembled Argentina registered such high rates, whether one considers overall growth or per capita value; during the 1920s, Argentina grew more than the United States, Canada and Australia. By 1929, the country's total output had surpassed that of Australia, and was on its way to catching up with Canada.

This translated into greater social relaxation and fewer strikes," said Gerchunoff and Llach. On the other hand, for Arturo O'Connell, Argentina then suffered the "problems of an open economy". This problem was based on the fact that, as a producer of raw materials in a temperate zone, Argentina was a natural competitor of the central countries and, therefore, was more exposed than other nations to variations in trade and capital flows; in particular, the Argentine fiscal system depended excessively on taxes linked to foreign trade, an error that would be corrected in the 1930s.

On the other hand, for Carlos Díaz Alejandro, the growth prior to 1930 was caused precisely by the open character of the local economy. "Growth prior to 1930 was generated by exports, not because these and the associated capital inflows supplied a growing global demand (in the Keynesian sense), but because -and this is more important- because exports and capital inflows originated a more efficient allocation of resources than that which could have resulted from autarkic policies. In particular, the domestic cost of capital goods in an autarkic regime (in 1880, for example), was reduced to a level through market exports produced with the generous use of an input -land- whose economic value in an autarkic regime would be quite small".

In any case, as mentioned, the recovery was slow: it was not until 1923 that the GDP per capita of 1913 was reached. The rebound was reflected in an expansive fiscal policy, so typical of the various Argentine economic cycles: public spending rose from 8.5% to 13% of GDP between 1920 and 1929, when the deficit of the public accounts already amounted to 4% of GDP.

Gerchunoff and Llach pointed out that Argentina's propensity to consume a lot and save little during times of bonanzas and optimism was also noticeable in the State. The practice of spending in excess of tax revenues had not been infrequent in the past. It had been a typical feature of Argentine finances to alternate between deficit cycles with growing debt and cycles of moderation in which obligations were cancelled.

Unlike many countries in the region or in other continents, there were no countercyclical measures to provide a "cushion" in lean times. Although in relative terms fiscal management during the Alvear administration was more predictable and orderly than under Yrigoyen, there was no tendency to save. "The total public debt increased 50%. For a country in expansion, this was not an unsustainable increase, but it was worrisome that the tendency to deficit was accentuated over the years. In 1927 the fiscal deficit was the highest ever recorded. It would be difficult to doubt the solvency of the Argentine State as long as the wind of the international economy was blowing in its favor and a certain control over the deficit was maintained. This was the case between 1924 and 1928, a period in which the Argentine State could comfortably finance itself abroad by taking American loans of close to USD 290 million", detailed Llach and Gerchunoff.

The problem, of course, arose when the international economic climate changed after the 1929 crisis: in two years, the public debt increased 35% and the tendency to fiscal imbalance, which had been hidden in the placid climate of Alvear's times, suddenly became a visible and pressing problem, the historians pointed out.

When the international economic climate changed after the 1929 crisis, in two years, the public debt increased 35% and the tendency to fiscal imbalance suddenly became a visible and pressing problem.

The economic growth of the decade was accompanied by higher indebtedness and lower savings. Debt payments were higher than the trade surplus, so more foreign exchange inflows were required annually, O'Connell stressed, to avoid serious problems in the balance of payments and the domestic economy.

Although Great Britain was the country's main trading partner, the United States in the 1920s became the main supplier of capital: in 1927, American capital installed in the country was 25 times greater than in 1909, basically directed more towards the industrial sector, infrastructure and transport, where British investments still predominated. However, despite the traditional revisionist reading of those years, these investments did not mean a greater foreignization of capital, since, as a percentage of the total, it fell from 41 to 34 between 1909 and 1927.

The country participated actively in international trade: in 1929 the value of Argentine products exchanged with the rest of the world was 3% of the total, despite having a population that represented 0.6% of the global population. Argentine exports had also grown more than the average: 57 against 15 between 1913 and 1929.

The impact of World War II

World War II consolidated the pattern of import substitution and increased state regulation that had begun in the interwar period in Argentina under conservative governments.

Historian Alejandro Gómez commented to Infobae that "every time there is a war, governments spend more and then neither that spending nor the controls disappear. Besides, in the 1930s the idea of the welfare state prevailed, because the idea of the minimum state was attacked by communism on the left and by Nazism and fascism on the right".

Every time there is a war, governments spend more and then neither that spending nor the controls disappear (Gómez).

In this sense, economist Miguel Kiguel told this media that "between 1946 and 1949 the State used a strong monetary and fiscal expansion and increased the control of its economy".

"On the external front, the Peronist administration expected that the recomposition of international trade would be slow and even interrupted by a third world war between the victorious powers. Therefore, it bet its chips on industry and the domestic market. The State guided the path of development with deliberate industrial policies, such as the nationalization of international trade and the protection of domestic industry through import restrictions. Domestic industry, especially light industry, grew to the point that it almost entirely supplied the domestic market", said Kiguel in his book "Argentina's Economic Crises".

According to Kiguel, "on the international front, the world did not support Argentina's plans: the Marshall Plan allowed the main European economies to recover quickly, but Argentina did not receive this help because of its poorly disguised sympathy for the Axis during almost the entire war".

On the international front, the world did not support Argentina's plans: the Marshall Plan allowed the main European economies to recover quickly, but Argentina did not receive this aid because of its poorly concealed sympathy for the Axis (Kiguel).

In this regard, Roberto Cortés Conde said in "La Economía política de la Argentina en el siglo XX" that "Perón did not have very precise ideas about the economy, but he shared those ideas that were common, after the crisis of 1930, in the post-war intellectual climate: the conviction that in the market something was failing and that State intervention was an alternative, if not necessary, at least convenient". "The military had had the example of Germany, which had achieved a recovery in the 1930s, which was able to reconvert itself into a war power, and that of the planned economy of the Soviet Union, even if the regime seemed opprobrious to them."

"The autarkic and nationalist ideas were widely accepted because of the belief that in the post-war period international trade restrictions would continue. There were certain facts that were important: the autarchy that had existed de facto since the years of the Second World War and the inexistence of an international capital market," said Cortés Conde.

He also noted: "the enormous accumulation of trade surpluses, due to the restriction of imports during the war, created the impression that the accumulation of foreign currency was due to a great increase in wealth, when it was due to decapitalization".

Furthermore, "the enormous demand for food, translated into improved prices in the first two years after the war, also gave the impression of an increase in wealth and there was a pessimistic view about the possibilities of world trade to place Argentine exports", concluded Cortés Conde.

In turn, Llach and Gerchunoff observed that, with the Second War, "the economy felt the most profound change, as had happened with the two previous great international shocks, the First World War and the Great Depression".

"As the world conflict began in 1939 the post-Depression recovery was a fact. The national product, which had fallen at a rate of 2.5% between 1929 and 1933, was growing 4% per year between 1929 and 1939. But in the Argentine economy there were indelible traces of the crisis (such as the Central Bank, exchange controls and regulatory boards) and the more solid presence of a national industry favored by those same institutions", they explained.

But the greatest impact "was linked, once again, to international trade. If the protectionist wave of the 1930s already made it impossible to return to pre-crisis conditions, World War II aggravated the situation further," the historians noted.

If the protectionist wave of the 1930s already made it impossible to return to pre-crisis conditions, the Second World War aggravated the situation even more (Gerchunoff and Llach).

"The Economic Action Plan proposed by (Federico) Pinedo in 1940 failed for political reasons but also because of its pessimistic forecasts, since the economy grew 3.6% per year for a five-year period, due to the effect of industry. However, growth was lower than in other Latin American countries", Gerchunoff-Llach argue.

And they add in the book El ciclo de la ilusión y el desencanto: "The conjunction of the Third Position and the belief that the commercial difficulties of the immediate post-war period would be prolonged and could be aggravated by a new world conflict justified the government's option for economic autarky".

In this sense, they detail that "Argentina's commercial position at the end of the Second War was not comfortable, in spite of the trade surpluses that had been accumulating. In fact, the problem was the excessive surplus, since it was not the result of a great export performance but of the difficulties to obtain imports".

As a corollary, "after the Second World War, the economy began to show inflationary symptoms. From 1941 to 1945 the monetary base grew 15%, a high level compared to previous volumes. The whole world had high inflation during the war, but then it disappeared, while in Argentina it remained higher than in the most advanced countries. From the 1940s onwards, the paths of Argentine and North American inflation were definitively separated".

Part of this problem, as explained by José Luis Machinea, Sebastián Katz and Federico Grillo in "La economía de Perón", was based on the fact that consolidated public spending went from an average of 16.2% of GDP in 1945-1946 to 22.5% in 1954-1955, with a peak of 29.7% in 1948.

After the Second World War, the economy began to show inflationary symptoms.

High public expenditure, low domestic savings and a bad reading of the international situation -reflected in a pretended historical "neutrality" of the country- seem to be the driving forces of Argentine economic policy in the aforementioned international conflicts.

In this sense, historian Alejandro Gómez said that "Argentina was left out of many benefits because of its neutrality, not only during the Second World War conflict, but also afterwards with its famous Third Position. If Argentina now makes a clear statement against Russia, perhaps later on it will obtain financial relief, but if it maintains a lukewarm position it will be left aside when it has to ask for assistance from organizations such as the IMF".

With situations that can be compared between the wars of the 20th century and the current conflict: will there be time to avoid similar mistakes in the face of this new war scenario in 2022 and a local scenario of strong macroeconomic fragility?

title: Volatility grips markets: stock markets rise and oil stabilizes amid Russian troops' advance into Kiev
text:
Volatility is taking markets that seem to have gone on a roller coaster ride in the wake of the Russian attack in Ukraine. Yesterday the stock markets collapsed with the announcement of the military offensive, but towards the end of the day they recovered while oil prices fell back sharply after having surpassed the US$ 100 barrier.

This change in trend was influenced by the speech of US President Joe Biden, who, although he reaffirmed tough sanctions against Moscow by the West, gave no indication of sending troops to Ukraine, alleviating an escalation of the conflict.

This boosted Wall Street and relieved investors.

Europe's stock markets are up more than 1% at the moment, but have shown several oscillations amid the advance of Russian troops into Ukrainian territory, reaching as far as the capital, Kiev.

In this context, the Moscow Stock Exchange is up more than 22% after the collapse of more than 33% it suffered the day before, which forced it to close its operations.

Biden threatened with limitations on the importation of technology, blockades to large banks and punishments to oligarchs close to Putin. However, he was not entirely clear on the energy issue, nor did he remove Russia from the SWIFT system, which allows transfers in dollars and euros to the country.

The Russian currency, the ruble, soared 2.3% against the dollar to 83.30 units, after touching an all-time low of 89.60. The currency was supported by the Russian central bank's first monetary interventions since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine, reported CincoDías The market expects more action from the central bank, which has to address inflationary risks.

What will happen to equities in the immediate?

"We lowered our conviction on the recommendation and moved from an overweight in equities to neutral. There was a change and the current status quo, with Western countries decreeing sanctions and Russia being in Ukraine, can be maintained for a while and generate additional volatility," Cristóbal Doberti, Sura Asset Management's Regional Manager of Savings and Investment Strategies, told Pulso.

Oil prices, on the other hand, stabilized and registered practically no variations in relation to the previous day. Brent is quoted at US$ 99.12 while WTI is quoted at US$ 92.68. In any case, both benchmarks are at their highest levels since 2014.

Crude oil prices are sensitive for Chile as it imports more than 90% of what it consumes and high hydrocarbon prices have become the engine of inflation in several economies around the world. It should be recalled that in the country, gasoline and gas prices are at historic highs.

"War conflicts are difficult to forecast. Historically, when there are rumors of this type of conflicts, the worst day for the markets is the moment when it starts, but then the markets recover, it has happened with Vietnam and the annexation of Crimea by Russia, and in the months following these conflicts the markets have a positive performance. here is the inflation issue. Although here it is not exactly the same, because the issue of rates and inflation is hanging around," Francisco Errandonea, partner of Focus Capital, told Pulso.

title: EU will have to match Ukraine's massive financing needs -EU Commission
text:
PARIS, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Ukraine's financing needs after the Russian invasion will be massive and the European Union will have to come up with the money, European Commission Vice President Valdis Dombrovskis said on Friday.

Speaking after a meeting of European Union finance ministers and central bank governors, Dombrovskis said Ukraine was suffering from investor flight and its access to financial markets has been very problematic.

Also the country's currency, the hryvnia, has come under pressure and central bank reserves were being depleted in market interventions.

"So it is clear that Ukraine's financing needs will be massive, and we will need to match those financing needs," Dombrovskis said.

The EU has recently agreed on 1.2 billion euros in macro-financial assistance emergency programme for Kyiv, of which the first half will be disbursed soon, but Dombrovskis said it was clear EU support would have to go far beyond this.

He said before Russia started amassing troops on the Ukrainian border, the estimated financing gap for Ukraine for this year was around 2.5 billion euros. This rose to 5 billion after the build-up of troops as investors fled expecting war.

"Now, the financing needs are off-the chart," Dombrovskis said. "We cannot really estimate them, but we need to be ready to support Ukraine in every way we can." (Reporting by Jan Strupczewski and Leigh Thomas)

title: UPDATE 1-Russia to tap rainy-day fund as sanctions hit borrowing abilities
text:
(Adds quotes, detail)

By Darya Korsunskaya and Andrey Ostroukh

MOSCOW, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Russia will use money from its rainy-day fund this year to replace shortfalls caused by a forced reduction in state borrowing, which has grown more costly due to new Western sanctions, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said on Friday.

Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the United States, Britain and other Western nations have imposed new sanctions targeting Russian banks, sovereign debt and individuals.

Siluanov said Russia's economic and financial situation was stable in general but conceded that sanctions will change the country's borrowing plan, requiring it to tap the National Wealth Fund, which stood at $175 billion as of Feb. 1.

"Due to an increase in borrowing costs the issuing of state debt has been suspended. We are planning to reduce the amount of borrowing this year, will utilise NWF funds for it," Siluanov told a meeting with government officials.

As Russian missiles pounded Kyiv, authorities in Moscow were seeking ways to shield the economy from new penalties that sent the rouble to a record low, threatening living standards already hit by high inflation.

The finance ministry said it will offer only a new series of OFZ government bonds and stop offering existing series of debt as the U.S. government slapped restrictions on trading of Russian government debt.

The Russian central bank beefed up the banking sector with extra liquidity and started to sell foreign currency on the forex market after the rouble fell to all-time lows on the day Moscow sent its troops into Ukraine.

The central bank's forex interventions that it started this week for the first time since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine, have already born fruit, Vladimir Chistyukhin, central bank deputy governor, said at the same meeting.

"We have a serious safety margin from the financial stability point of view... The central bank is ready to support banks with liquidity," Chistyukhin said.

Siluanov said swings on the foreign exchange market were temporary and there was no immediate risk to financial stability. (Reporting by Andrey Ostroukh, Darya Korsunskaya, Elena Fabrichnaya and Alexander Marrow; Editing by David Gregorio)

title: UPDATE 3-Rouble climbs off record low, Russian stocks soar but sanctions bite
text:
* Rouble recovers from all-time lows

* Russian stocks jump after massive plunge

* Russian missiles pound Kyiv

* Investors eyeing c.bank's every move (Updates prices, adds bullets, JP Morgan)

By Andrey Ostroukh and Alexander Marrow

MOSCOW, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The rouble firmed on Friday after hitting all-time lows the previous day when Russia began invading Ukraine, while stock indexes rose sharply after their biggest one-day fall on record and the central bank stepped up support for sanctioned banks.

No Russian assets were left unscathed in heavy selling on Thursday. The fighting in Ukraine continued on Friday, with Russian missiles pounding Kyiv, families cowering in shelters and authorities telling residents to prepare Molotov cocktails to defend Ukraine's capital.

By 1600 GMT, the rouble had gained 2.6% against the dollar to 83.03 after hitting a record low of 89.60 in highly volatile trading on Thursday.

Against the euro, the rouble firmed 2% to trade at 93.27 , having hit an all-time low of 101.03 on the interbank market on Thursday.

The currency was supported by the first Russian central bankcurrency interventions since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

SANCTIONS BITE

The market was also digesting new harsh Western sanctions against Russia.

The measures stopped short of disconnecting Russia from the SWIFT global interbank payments system or targeting its oil and gas exports, and Russia has spent the past seven years building up formidable financial defences.

"However, the possibility (of disconnection from SWIFT)remains and uncertainty hurts the market more than the worst sanctions – focus will be on developments in Ukraine, the potential for negotiations, and any further sanctions," BCS Brokerage said in a note.

But analysts said Russia's economy is unlikely to withstand the onslaught of coordinated sanctions from the West in the long run.

Clients of some Russian banks under Western sanctions will no longer be able to use their cards abroad or with mobile payment systems from Apple and Google, the central bank said, as it stepped up support for banks.

Russian stock indexes pared heavy losses after Thursday's record one-day fall.

The dollar-denominated RTS index soared 26.1% to 936.9 points. The rouble-based MOEX Russian index gained 20% to 2,470.5 points, heading away from its weakest level since early 2016 of 1,681.55 that it hit on Thursday.

JP Morgan said it was interested to see what would happen to dividend payments, with the top five listed companies in Russia forecast to dish out $18 billion in dividends.

"Will a sanctioned Russian financial system be happy to pay away that much money to largely foreign shareholders when they are excluded from the financial system?"

VTB Bank on Friday said it may still pay dividends for 2021, Russian news agencies reported, but would analyse all possibilities between now and April.

INFLATION

The market expects more action from the central bank, which has to address inflationary risks. The weakening in the rouble after the invasion of Ukraine is expected to dent living standards in Russia and to stoke inflation that is already close to 9%.

The central bank may now carry out an unplanned interest rate hike as it did in late 2014, when it raised the key rate to 17% from 10.5% late at night as the rouble plummeted, analysts say.

"We think a prompt out-of-schedule 400bp or bigger hike by the CBR is likely with the key rate exceeding 13%," Morgan Stanley said in a note.

Alor Brokerage said the central bank could hike the rate by 2-3 percentage points in the near future, aiming at keeping the rouble near 80 to the dollar and 90 to the euro.

The central bank, which targets inflation at 4%, is next due to consider raising rates at its board meeting on March 18.

(Reporting by Andrey Ostroukh and Alexander Marrow; additional reporting by Elena Fabrichnaya in Moscow and Marc Jones in London; Editing by Kim Coghill, Gareth Jones and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

title: Stocks, Commodities Gyrate After Moscow Begins Attack -- WSJ
text:
Major indexes recover after invasion sends stocks lower and oil above $100 a barrel 


By Hardika Singh, Anna Hirtenstein and Caitlin Ostroff 

U.S. stocks fluctuated wildly Thursday, starting the day with a sharp drop and then recovering as investors piled into growth and technology stocks in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Stocks fell in the aftermath of the attacks on cities across Ukraine, while oil, gold and government notes rose. Investor optimism grew, however, after President Biden in an afternoon address announced new sanctions on Russian elites, state-owned enterprises and banks. The European Union later announced its own sanctions.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's "aggression in Ukraine will end up costing Russia dearly, economically and strategically," said Mr. Biden.

The S&P 500 closed up 63.20 points, or 1.5%, to 4288.70. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite finished ahead 436.10 points, or 3.3%, to 13473.59. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 92.07 points, or 0.3%, to 33223.83.

The Russian ruble weakened to a record low, declining 4.5% against the dollar, while the MOEX benchmark for Russian stocks tumbled by about a third. The Russian central bank said it would intervene in the foreign-exchange market and banned short selling. Ukraine's foreign-exchange market suspended operations, according to its central bank. The country's stock exchange also said it was postponing activity.

Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, topped $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014, with the front-month contract settling up $2.24 per barrel, or 2.3%, to $99.08. Prices for its U.S. equivalent, West Texas Intermediate, also rose.

The invasion has heightened the pressure on a global economy already reeling from snarled supply chains and some of the highest inflation in years, with Europe likely to bear the brunt of the economic impact. Some investors, betting that the Federal Reserve won't act as aggressively to curb inflation at a time of heightened tensions, reopened their pandemic-era playbooks, piling into riskier assets in the second half of the trading session.

A pullback in the yield of the benchmark 10-year Treasury note Thursday added wind to the sails of growth companies. Yields settled at 1.969%, from 1.976% on Wednesday. Bond yields fall as prices rise.

"That makes people more comfortable buying growth stocks," said Gary Black, manager of the Future Fund Active exchange-traded fund. Mr. Black owns Alphabet and Palo Alto Networks, among other growth stocks.

Dramatic moves marked Thursday's trading. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 3%, then closed up more than 3%, for the first time since November 2008, according to Dow Jones Market Data. The S&P 500 finished higher after falling at least 2.5% for only the 16th time in the past 15 years. The Cboe Volatility Index rose to the highest level in over 15 months.

The S&P 500's information-technology and consumer-discretionary sectors were the biggest gainers, adding 3.5% and 2.5%, respectively. Netflix added $22.57, or 6.1%, to $390.03; Twitter gained 2.22, or 6.8%, to $34.98. Alphabet advanced $102.06, or 4%, to $2,653.82.

The Defiance Next Gen SPAC Derived exchange-traded fund, which tracks special-purpose acquisition companies, advanced $0.54, or 3.2%, to $17.40. Meme stocks also rose: AMC Entertainment jumped $1.95, or 12%, to $17.68, while GameStop climbed $9.71, or 8.5%, to $124.58.

Natural-gas futures in Europe surged 50%. Benchmark prices for aluminum and nickel, two metals of which Russia is a major producer, rose to their highest levels in about a decade. Wheat and corn futures advanced to multiyear highs. Russia and Ukraine are major grain producers.

"We haven't had any serious military conflict in Europe for a very long time, so there's no playbook for this," said Gregory Perdon, chief investment officer at Arbuthnot Latham. "A lot has changed since last night."

Gold, which like U.S. Treasury bonds typically rallies in times of stress, rose in price. The front month gold futures contract rose $15.90 per troy ounce, or 0.8%, to $1,925.10.

The dollar strengthened, with the WSJ Dollar Index gaining 0.8%. Currencies considered to be havens, such as the Japanese yen, also appreciated, while bitcoin recovered losses, trading up 2.2% to $38,395.65 from its 5 p.m. ET level on Wednesday.

The Russian attack came as volatility in markets was already heightened because of looming changes in Fed monetary policy.

Investors are building up cash buffers because of the market stress, said Florian Ielpo, head of macro at Lombard Odier Investment Managers. The company's multiasset funds currently hold the most cash since the market crash in March 2020.

Markets are expecting a standard 0.25 percentage point increase at the Fed's meeting next month, rather than a more aggressive 0.5 percentage point increase. As of Thursday, market pricing showed the probability of a bigger rate increase fell to 13% from 34% the day before, according to CME Group data.

"We might move past the geopolitical impact, but the market is still going to be concerned about the Fed's intentions to move rates higher," said Lindsey Bell, Ally's chief markets and money strategist.

In economic data, weekly U.S. jobless claims came in at 232,000, a decline from the previous week and in line with analysts' expectations in the midst of a tight labor market.

Global markets fell. The pan-continental Stoxx Europe 600 dropped about 3.3%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index decreased over 3%. Japan's Nikkei Stock Average closed at its lowest level since November 2020.

-- Megumi Fujikawa, Will Horner and Quentin Webb contributed to this article.

Write to Hardika Singh at hardika.singh@wsj.com, Anna Hirtenstein at anna.hirtenstein@wsj.com and Caitlin Ostroff at caitlin.ostroff@wsj.com

This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (February 25, 2022).
