Taxation in Ukraine - production taxes

Since Poltava Petroleum Company's ('PPC's') inception in 1994 the Company has operated in a regime where conflicting laws have existed, including in relation to effective taxes on oil and gas production.

In order to avoid any confusion over the level of taxes due, in 1994, PPC entered into a licence agreement with the Ukrainian State Committee on Geology and the Utilisation of Mineral Resources ('the Licence Agreement') which set out expressly in the Licence Agreement that PPC would pay royalties on production at a rate of only 5.5% of sales value for the duration of the Licence Agreement.

Pursuant to the Licence Agreement, PPC was granted an exploration licence and four 20-year production licences, each in respect of a particular field. In 2004, PPC's production licences were renewed and extended until 2024, Subsoil Use Agreements were signed and attached to the licences and operations continued as before.

The Company and PPC have continued to invest in Ukraine on the basis that PPC would pay a royalty on sales at a rate of 5.5%.

In December 1994, a new fee on the production of oil and gas (known as a 'Rental Payment' or 'Rental Fee') was introduced through Ukrainian regulations. On 30 December 1995, JKX, together with its Ukrainian subsidiaries (including PPC), was issued with a Joint Decision of the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance and the State Committee for the Oil and Gas ('the Exemption Letter'), which established a zero rent payment rate for oil and natural gas produced in Ukraine by PPC for the duration of the Licence Agreement for Exploration and Exploitation of the Fields. Based on the Exemption Letter PPC did not expect to pay any Rental Fees.

Rental Fees paid since 2011

In 2011, new laws were enacted which established new mechanisms for the determination of the Rental Fee. Notwithstanding the Exemption Letter, in January 2011 PPC began to pay the Rental Fee in order to avoid further issues with the Ukrainian authorities but without prejudice to its right to challenge the validity of the demands.

Since 2011, the Rental Fees paid by PPC have amounted to more than $180 million. These charges have been recorded in cost of sales in each of the accounting periods to which they relate.

International arbitration proceedings

In 2015, the Company and its wholly-owned Ukrainian and Dutch subsidiaries commenced arbitration proceedings against Ukraine under the Energy Charter Treaty, the bilateral investment treaties between Ukraine and the United Kingdom and the Netherlands, respectively. In these proceedings, the Company sought repayment of more than $180 million in Rental Fees that PPC paid on production of oil and gas in Ukraine since 2011, in addition to damages to the business.

During 2015 Rental Fees in Ukraine were increased to 55% and capital control restrictions were introduced. On 14 January 2015, an Emergency Arbitrator issued an Award ordering Ukraine not to collect Rental Fees from PPC in excess of 28% on gas produced by PPC, pending the outcome of the application to a full tribunal for the Interim Award. On 23 July 2015 an international arbitration tribunal issued an Interim Award requiring the Government of Ukraine to limit the collection of Rental Fees on gas produced by PPC to a rate of 28%.

The Interim Award was to remain in effect until final judgement is rendered on the main arbitration case, which was heard in early July 2016. A decision from the tribunal was awarded on 6 February 2017.

The tribunal ruled that Ukraine was found not to have violated its treaty obligations in respect of the levying of Rental Fees but awarded the Company damages of $11.8 million plus interest, and costs of $0.3 million in relation to subsidiary claims.


JKX Oil & Gas PLC Half-year Report -15-

In March 2017 the Company received a notice by Ukraine's Ministry of Justice to the High Court of the United Kingdom naming JKX as a defendant in an application seeking to set aside the arbitration award for damages against Ukraine and in favour of JKX. The High Court will consider the appeal in October 2017.

Rental Fee demands

The Group currently has two claims (2016: two) for additional Rental Fees being contested through the Ukrainian court process. These arise from disputes over the amount of Rental Fees paid by PPC for certain periods since 2010 (2016: 2010), which in total amount to approximately $37.2 million (31 December 2016: $33.9 million) (including interest and penalties), as detailed below. All amounts are being claimed in Ukrainian Hryvnia ('UAH') and are stated below at their US$-equivalent amounts using the period end rate of $1:UAH26.1 (2016: $1:UAH 27.2).

-- August - December 2010: approximately $11.3 million (31 December 2016: $10.6 million) (including $6.8m (31 December 2016: $6.1) million of interest and penalties). On 11 March 2014 PPC won the case in the Poltava Court. The tax office appealed and the Kharkiv Appellate Administrative Court reversed the earlier decision. PPC then lost an appeal in the High Administrative Court of Ukraine and the Supreme Court rejected PPC's application for the appeal. PPC has discovered that there were in fact certain procedures that were not followed regarding the tax notifications that formed the basis of the original claims against PPC. Certain documentation was found to be missing from the files of the tax authorities. In April 2017 the Poltava Circuit Administrative Court found in favour of PPC and cancelled the tax notification decisions on the grounds that due process had not been followed. On 1 June 2017 the Kharkiv Appellate Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the Poltava Circuit Administrative Court. The tax authorities filed a cassation complaint and the case is currently being transferred from the Kharkiv Appellate Administrative Court to the High Administrative Court of Ukraine (the HACU). If the HACU rejects the claim of the tax authorities, it would render the basis for the 2010 claims invalid.

As part of these proceedings, property, plant and equipment that cost UAH158m (31 December 2016: UAH158m (approximately $6.1million (31 December 2016: $5.8 million) at the period end rate of $1:UAH26.1 (31 December 2016: $1: UAH27.2) was required to be pledged as security against the non-settlement of the 2010 Rental Fee claim that may arise in the event that the Ukrainian authorities are successful. The net book value of the property, plant and equipment is $22.0 million based on the historical exchange rates at the dates of acquisition which were between $1:UAH5 and $1:UAH8.

-- January - December 2015: approximately $25.9 million (31 December 2016: $23.3 million) (including $11.4 million (31 December 2016: $10.8 million) of interest and penalties). Following the commencement of international arbitration proceedings at the beginning of 2015 (see above), from July 2015 PPC reverted to paying a 28% Rental Fee for gas production (instead of the revised official rate of 55%) as a result of the awards granted under the arbitration. PPC also declared part of its Rental Fee payments at 55% for the first 6 months of 2015 as overpayments and consequently stopped paying the Rental Fee for gas in order to align the total payments made in 2015 with the 28% rate awarded made under the arbitration proceedings. The Ukrainian tax authorities have issued PPC with claims for the difference between 28% and 55%. PPC is in the process of court hearings in respect of the claim, although the Company considers such claims to be in direct violation of the Interim Award received from the arbitration tribunal, noted above. In addition, in April 2016, the tax authorities issued PPC with a separate demand for $0.1 million of penalties and interest on unpaid Rental Fees for the period of August-October 2015. PPC also filed lawsuits against the tax authorities to cancel the application of such additional penalties and interest.

Following the tribunal's dismissal of the Company's claim for overpayment of Rental Fees, an exceptional charge of $24.3 million was charged to the Consolidated income statement in 2016 relating to the January - December 2015 claim. Following recognition of further interest and penalties during 6 months of 2017, which are presented as an exceptional charge, the provision recorded at 30 June 2017 is $25.9million.

No adjustment has been made to recognise any possible future benefit to the Company that may result from the tribunal award in the Company's favour for damages of $11.8 million plus interest, and costs of $0.3 million.

In the prior year there was a claim of approximately $6 million (including $3 million of interest and penalties) relating to the period January - March 2007. In 2016 the Supreme Court of Ukraine ruled in favour of the Company in respect of this claim and a second parallel case related to this claim was won by PPC with the High Administrative Court of Ukraine.

title: UDPATE 1-Ukraine cbank sells dlrs for 6th straight day
text:
(adds new comment, background)   

KIEV, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sold dollars at 5.06 hryvnias for the sixth straight trading day on Tuesday despite few imbalances on the foreign exchange market, dealers said.   

"We have been stuck over the past couple of days at about the level offered by the central bank," said one dealer. "The bank is selling dollars without any problem. There is no urgency as the market is pretty calm."   

The central bank has been defending the hryvnia within a tight band of 5.00-5.06 to the dollar since August 2005.   

Most transactions over the past two days stood at about 5.0635/5.065. But last week the hryvnia sank to a 16-month low as investors scrambled for dollars to shore up losses from global market volatility.   

"The market is calmer, but the situation remains unsteady," said another dealer. "It is possible that if the central bank fails to come onto the market we could again see things go to 5.07."   

The central bank bought dollars practically throughout 2007, with the exception of December, to keep the hryvnia within the narrow band.   

Over the year, with dollar supply outstripping demand, the bank purchased the equivalent of $7.9 billion on the interbank market, mostly in euros.   

Given a growing foreign currency deficit, dealers believe that demand by importers for foreign currency will exceed supply by exporters.   

This, however, could be offset by an inflow of funds from privatisation of large enterprises, like fixed-line telephone operator  Ukrtelekom or the Odessa Pre-Port chemical plant.   

"The inflow of direct foreign investment is estimated at $7 billion to $10 billion and this could cover the trade deficit and boost currency supply," said one dealer.   

"But this is likely to happen closer to the summer and be a factor in strengthening the hryvnia." (Reporting by Natalia Zinets, writing by Ron Popeski)

KIEV, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The Ukrainian central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, selling dollars at 5.06 hryvnias to support the currency which sank to a 16-month low, dealers said.   

They said the hryvnia had weakened to 5.075, as foreign investors, hit by global market volatility, sought to retreat from Ukrainian currency and stocks to gain dollars.   

Stocks around the world fell for the second day running, dragging down with them emerging markets as well as oil and commodity prices, over fears that the United States will descend into recession.   

"Almost everyone is buying (dollars) including foreigners and they could be making an exit from these kind of securities, as has been seen around the world," the dealer said.   

Dealers said large banks hit by the U.S. crisis would be wanting to amass dollars in markets they consider peripheral to shore up any losses.   

Ukraine's fledgling stock exchange market has fallen by several percentage points in the past three working days.   

"If foreigners are buying dollars, then for sure they are selling stocks for hryvnias, buying dollars and coming out of our stock market," the dealer said.   

Another dealer said several large foreign banks muscled into the market to buy dollars in connection with natural gas and other energy trades.   

The central bank has defended the hryvnia within a band of 5.00-5.06 to the dollar since August 2005. This is the first time it had intervened this year. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets; writing by Sabina Zawadzki; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

KIEV, Dec 27 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on the interbank market, selling dollars at 5.06 hryvnias when the Ukrainian currency was pushed down to the lower depth of its permitted range, traders said on Thursday.   

"There was continued high demand for the U.S. currency on the interbank market and the central bank stepped in to sell dollars," said one dealer, saying trades had been conducted at 5.06/5.064.   

A top central bank official said, meanwhile, that foreign reserves had dipped slightly to $32.2 billion from a record high of $32.768 billion at the end of last month.   

First Deputy chairman Anatoly Shapovalov gave no reason for the slight decline.   

"We allowed no sharp fluctuations in the hryvnia," he told reporters. "These were generally no more than one percent. The rate was generally favourable for exporters and the current figure of $32.2 billion is optimal."   

Dealers linked the dip to recent central bank interventions. The bank, which has maintained a narrow band for the hryvnia of 5.00 to 5.06 since August 2005, has sold dollars on about 10 occasions in December.   

Dealers say increased demand for dollars has been prompted by the need to conclude import contracts, particularly purchases of energy, and an end-of-year outflow of portfolio investment.   

Reserves have risen by nearly $10 billion since the beginning of the year thanks to excess supply of foreign currency. Over the first 11 months of the year, the central bank bought $7.774 billion in excess currency.   

Shapovalov said he expected excess supply to remain on the market next year and would continue to consider chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh's proposal in October of expanding the hryvnia's narrow corridor. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets; Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov also told Reuters the bank would make no moves until the end of the year to its policy of defending a narrow corridor of 5.00-5.06 hryvnias to the dollar, within a wider range of 4.95-5.25.   

"There will be no change to the currency policy until the end of the year," Shapovalov said.   

"(Afterwards) we need to calculate how this new price will impact the demand for the dollar. By our calculations, demand for the currency will increase by about $2.7 billion."   

Ukraine signed an agreement with Russia's gas export monopoly  Gazprom on Wednesday to pay $179.50 per 1,000 cubic metres next year against $130 now.   

"It looks as though the (bank's) figure is simply based on the amount of gas imported this year and multiplied by the change in the average price between 2007-2008, without taking into account any possible effects from increased energy-use efficiency,"  UniCredit economist Simon Quijano-Evans said.   

Speculation had been mounting in recent months that the central bank would make good on its long-stated objective of moving towards greater currency flexibility.   

The hryvnia had been straining at the 5.00 ceiling for much of the year, contained only by central bank intervention throughout May to September.   

But demand for the dollar has since increased as business, especially energy firms, paid year-end bills. The bank let the hryvnia slip through the 5.06 floor late on Friday.   

On Wednesday, it sold dollars for the first time since April to bring it back into the band.   

Deputy Chairman Olexander Savchenko told a daily newspaper on Wednesday that the bank was getting ready to increase currency flexibility the moment there was some political stability in the country.   

Politicians have yet to form a government two months after a parliamentary election, the third vote in as many years, produced a shaky coalition of two parties linked to the 2004 pro-Western "Orange Revolution".   

Savchenko also dismissed the notion of moving away from a dollar corridor into other currencies or a basket.   

"The first thing that discourages us from moving to a currency basket is that 80 percent of our external trade is tied to the dollar, including turnover from both the European Union and Russia," he said.

KIEV, May 22 (Reuters) - The head of Ukraine's central bank has put himself at variance with one of his deputies by saying the hryvnia currency should be kept stable to guard against any sharp move on the currency market prompting a rise in inflation.  

Volodymyr Stelmakh's comments, published in the weekly Zerkalo Nedeli, opened fresh debate on the policy to be applied in overseeing the hryvnia on Ukraine's markets.  

One of his deputies told the EBRD weekend meeting in London that Ukraine intended to allow more exchange rate flexibility.  

But the bank's policy of keeping the currency within strict limits was confirmed again on Monday as the central bank intervened, buying dollars at 5.0 hryvnias.  

"I believe that our currency must be stable," the weekly quoted Stelmakh as saying at a round table discussion.  

"And a rate that remains stable, such as exists now ... is a normal, objective thing."  

The hyrvnia has remained at a level of 5.05 to the dollar for the past year, with the central bank routinely intervening on the currency market since last August -- buying excess dollar supply at 5.0 hryvnias and selling when required at 5.06.  

On Monday the central bank bought dollars as per its normal practice at 5.0. Dealers said the intervention, the first since last Wednesday, did not reflect a marked new trend on the market and was aimed at adhering to central bank policies.  

"Today was an ordinary trading day. There simply were greater volumes of dollars than there were buyers and the central bank took action by buying," said one dealer.  

Throughout 2005 the central bank bought $10.4 billion in interventions.  

But it sold $2.1 billion in the first four months of 2006 to offset political instability triggered by a March parliamentary election and talks still to be concluded on forming a stable coalition government.  

EXPORT MARKETS, GAS PRICES  

Worsening export markets and a sharp increase in the price of Russian gas also contributed to higher demand for dollars.  

Stelmakh told the gathering that a hryvnia depreciation could trigger higher inflation.  

"Given the external challenges -- headed by energy prices, particularly gas -- our actions must be such not only to control inflation but to restrain it," he was quoted as saying.  

In London, bank deputy governor Oleksander Savchenko said once a coalition government was formed the bank would gradually move towards targeting inflation.  

"We treat the exchange rate as a managed float, but we'll do considerable exchange rate flexibility after the formation of the new government," he said.

Zerkalo Nedeli quoted Valery Geyets, head of the bank's council as saying Stelmakh's position enjoyed general support.  

"If we start adding instability on the currency markets to all our current difficulties, we will end up with inflation," he told the discussion.  

The outgoing government initially said it would contain inflation within 10 percent for 2006, but has revised the figure upward to 11.4 percent to take account of the nearly twofold increase in gas prices agreed with Russia in the New Year.

title: UPDATE:EBRD:Growth To Slow In Eastern Europe As FDI Falls
text:
(This updates a story that ran at 1135 GMT with additional forecasts from the Institute of International Finance)

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Economic growth in the countries of eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union will slow over the next five years as inflows of foreign investment level off, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development said Sunday.

In its twice-yearly Transition Report, the development bank said the economies of the 27 countries in which it invests will grow on average 5.3% this year, marking a slowdown from the 5.6% rate of growth recorded in 2005 and the 6.7% rate of growth recorded in 2004.

But for the five years from 2007, the EBRD said annual growth will average 4.5% as inflows of foreign investment, which in recent years have been high by historic standards, tail off. Foreign direct investment totaled $55.6 billion in 2005, more than double the $25.6 billion recorded in 2000. The EBRD expects FDI to fall to $44.7 billion in 2006.

"In the region as a whole we think foreign direct investment will level off and the signs we are seeing right now of a cooling of interest in emerging markets will contribute to that," said Erik Berglof, the EBRD's chief economist.

The EBRD warned that growth may slow even further if there were to be a crisis of confidence in emerging markets.

"Any loss of confidence in emerging markets would have an impact in the region and could cause a significant drop in growth and FDI (foreign direct investment)," the EBRD said.

While emerging markets around the globe have benefitted in recent years from strong inflows of foreign investment, rising interest rates in the U.S., the euro zone and the prospect of higher rates in Japan have in recent weeks led to an outflow of funds from some.

However, in a separate report also published Sunday, the Institute for International Finance - a Washington, D.C. based group that counts many of the world's largest banks among its membership - forecast that foreign investment in the region's equity markets would rise over the next two years, to $14.7 billion this year and $9 billion in 2007 from $4 billion in 2005.

The IIF expects investment in the region's equity markets to rise despite a loss of momentum in the process of economic reform.

"Reform momentum has diminished across the region as a result of recent or forthcoming elections and the rising appeal of populist parties opposed to market-oriented reforms and foreign investment," the IIF said.

Inflows of FDI have been particularly important as a driver of growth in the eight central European countries that joined the European Union in 2004. FDI surged to $22.7 billion in that year from $8.2 billion in 2003, and rose again to $28 billion last year.

Berglof said one of the challenges faced by the eight new members is to generate growth in those sectors of the economy that aren't controlled by foreign investors.

"A lot of the growth comes from foreign-controlled enterprises," he said. "The big challenge is to get the rest of the economy to catch up."

The EBRD said the large budget deficits being run by a number of governments in the E.U.8 could make them vulnerable to a reversal of investment flows.

"Many countries...face continuing difficulties in balancing public spending with government revenues," the EBRD said. "This reflects the relatively high level of social expenditures, substantial enterprise subsidies, and large infrastructure investments. The larger...countries especially need to tighten their fiscal policies."

The Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland have all said they want to join the euro zone by the end of the decade or shortly thereafter. But some are running budget deficits that exceed the 3% of gross domestic product limit set as one of the euro-zone's entry criteria.

In the short term, the EBRD expects their budget deficits to widen, taking them further away from adopting the euro. In 2006, it expects Hungary's budget deficit to widen to 6.2% of GDP from 6.1%, while it expects the Czech Republic's budget deficit to widen to 3.9% of GDP from 3.2%, Poland's to widen to 3.2% from 2.9% and Slovakia's to widen to 3.5% from 3.0%.

"With voters turning away from advocates of genuine fiscal reform, governments have shied away from many of the measures needed to scale back social spending and solidify fiscal adjustment," the IIF said. "Slovakia alone has enacted reforms bold enough to bring within reach a medium-term deficit path complying with the Maastricht fiscal criteria."

Despite the continued high price of oil and gas, the EBRD expects the Russian economy to slow this year, growing 5.5% as against 6.4% in 2005 and 7.1% in 2004.

"There has been a marked slowdown in the natural resources sector due to capacity constraints and ineffective government policies," the EBRD said.

The development bank expects other natural-resource rich parts of the former Soviet Union to post some of the highest economic growth rates in the world this year. Azerbaijan topped the world growth league in 2005 with an expansion in its GDP of 26.4%, and the EBRD expects 2006 to be only a little weaker, with GDP growing 25.0%.

But it also forecasts that Kazakhstan's economy will grow 8.5%, marking a slowdown from 9.4% in 2005, and that Turkmenistan's economy will grow 10.6%, a pickup from 9.6% in 2005.

As a whole, however, the EBRD expects growth in the former Soviet Union excluding the Baltic States to slow significantly to 5.7% in 2006 from 6.6% in 2005 and 8.0% in 2004.

"The rate of growth...is declining sharply and is likely to fall further in 2006, reflecting the limited investment to date in productive capacity," the EBRD said.

By contrast, the EBRD expects growth in southeastern Europe to pick up this year to an average rate of 4.8% from 4.5% in 2005.

It said the region is benefiting from improved trade and investment links with the E.U., led by Romania, where growth is forecast to pick up to 5% from 4% last year.

However, the EBRD said the region faces a number of risks, largely of a political nature.

"In the western Balkans, significant political risks persist due to several unresolved issues - the future of Kosovo, the possible break up of...Serbia and Montenegro," the development bank said.

Despite the cooling of investor appetite for emerging markets securities in recent weeks, the IIF said it doesn't expect to see widespread depreciations of local currencies in the region, the main exception being Ukraine, where the central bank has been intervening heavily in support of the hryvnia.

"In Ukraine...a sizable hryvnia correction looks likely later this year due to a growing current account shortfall and heavy outflows of resident capital," the IIF said.

-Paul Hannon, Dow Jones Newswires; 44 20 7842 9491; paul.hannon@dowjones.com [ 21-05-06 1300GMT ]

title: Ukraine  c.bank to cut  currency intervention
text:
LONDON, May 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank will start targeting inflation rather than the exchange rate from next year and will gradually start reducing currency market interventions, the bank's deputy head Oleksandr Savchenko said on Sunday.  

"We are going to make the exchange rate more flexible which means we are going to leave the forex markets and appear on that market only when something extraordinary happens," Savchenko told reporters on the sidelines of a meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London.

He said inflation targets would be met despite a rise in gas prices after a price hike by Russia, and inflation should come in at no more than 10 percent this year.

The central bank has already spent over $1.8 billion from its reserves since the start of the year, trying to defend the hryvnia from political volatility linked to a March parliamentary election and talks on a new coalition government.  

The central bank sold dollars on Tuesday at 5.06 hryvnias, the level it has been defending since August 2005.  

"The central bank is selling dollars but they have set limits. Why have they set limits? Probably, they have their own helicopter view from above," a dealer said.  

"A fast drop in reserves might be a cause for concern. Besides, sources to replenish them are not clearly seen."

"Two or three more days of continued uncertainty and the hryvnia would slip below 5.07 to the dollar. Nobody can see sources to change the situation. Everything depends on politics," a dealer said.  

"The budget contains plans for privatisation revenues. It means hard currency inflow. But privatisation will have to wait for a new government."  

Ukrainian politicians have been locked in talks over the government coalition for more than three weeks already, but with little sign of progress. Parliament is expected to gather for its first session in May and has about 2 months to form a coalition and name the government.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Up after Fed report; rouble eases
text:
* Emerging stocks bounce 0.4 percent after Fed

* Rouble pulls back; authorities signal measures to curb FX

* Rand rises on gold price; inflation back in target band

By Sujata Rao

LONDON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks rose 0.4 percent on Wednesday due to the Federal Reserve's positive assessment of the U.S. economy while the rouble eased after a rate cut and on signs Russia will step up efforts to curb speculative inflows.

World stocks were higher after the U.S. central bank in the minutes of its latest meeting expressed confidence in the durability of the economic recovery and raised 2010 growth forecasts. Also higher gold and oil prices along with a weaker dollar were giving a boost to emerging markets.

The MSCI emerging index rose half a percent <.MSCIEF>.

"The market has chosen to interpret the Fed minutes to say that any exit strategy is a long way off. They talked of zero interest rates fuelling risk taking but they seem unwilling to do anything about it ... that's been taken as a signal that the risk rally can continue a while longer," said TD Securities chief emerging markets strategist Beat Siegenthaler.

Siegenthaler said talk by emerging central banks about steps to cap currency strength is weighing on investors' minds and could keep a lid on emerging market gains until year-end.

"But unless banks take drastic action which most of them will not ... the rally should continue until year-end but maybe at a slower pace," he added.

Russia is the latest country where talk of capital controls has surfaced, following measures across South America and Asia.

The rouble eased 0.3 percent to a five-day low versus its euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> after a half point rate cut and comments from a central banker and the finance minister.

Tuesday's rate cut took rates to a record low 9 percent and took cumulative easing this year to 400 basis points.

Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin said local stock markets had become overheated due to speculative overseas flows but said only soft measures would be needed to combat this. The central bank has already pledged some measures to cap the rising rouble, including changing reserve requirements. [ID: nGEE5AO0Q8].

"These are significant comments...net-net we now have a firmer message from the Russian authorities that they are less likely to tolerate rouble appreciation, which will likely cap rouble strength over the next few months," said Tim Ash, head of emerging Europe research at RBS.

"Assuming oil prices remain elevated we should expect further rate cuts plus heavy FX intervention," he added.

UKRAINE, SOUTH AFRICA

The picture was also brighter for Ukraine where the acting finance minister reassured investors the country would pay the December coupons on its Eurobonds and that debt restructuring efforts by the state railway carried no danger of cross default.

Ash said an affirmation of Ukraine's rating by Moody's had helped, as had news that Russia had relaxed gas import demands on Kiev and waived fines on this year's supply [ID: nGEE5AN2Q7].

"A few things seem to be coming together for Ukraine," he said. "Much of the bad news is already priced in."

Five-year credit default swaps for Ukraine reflected this, upfront fees falling to 29.5 percent from 30.5 in the previous session while in Romania, mired in political stalemate, CDS fell to 288.9 basis points from 292.7, CMA DataVision said.

The gainer of the day was South Africa which saw stocks up almost one percent <.JTOPI> and the rand <ZAR=> at a one-week high against the dollar, thanks partly to record gold prices.

Latest data showed consumer inflation back within the central bank's 3-6 percent target band for the first time in 2-1/2 years [ID: nGEE5AO0RY]. The economy has also finally returned to growth after three quarters of contraction.

In central Europe, all eyes were on Poland where the central bank is expected to keep rates steady at 3.50 percent.

In bond news, Dubai sold $5 billion in bonds to two UAE banks [ID: nGEE5AO0WS] as part of a $20 billion borrowing plan.

JP Morgan's EMBI Plus index <11EMJ> saw yield spreads versus U.S. Treasuries fall 4 bps to 306 bps. (Additional reporting by Carolyn Cohn; editing by Chris Pizzey) ((sujata.rao@thomsonreuters.com; +44 207 542 6176; Reuters Messaging: sujata.rao.reuters.com@reuters.net))

KIEV, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank will stop intervening on the interbank market at a fixed rate, but will carry out auctions at which it is willing to sell $1 billion in September, Chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh said on Monday.

The hryvnia currency has lost almost 15 percent in the past two months, while the central bank last intervened last Tuesday, refraining from intervening last Thursday and Monday, as it normally would have.

"As of tomorrow, we will move to a new system of participation on the currency market -- auctions. This means that we will sell to whoever bids the highest," Stelmakh told journalists.

He said the bank would spend about $1 billion on supporting the hryvnia, which is the average amount it has spent every month since January.

Since the start of the year, the central bank has intervened on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays and carried out foreign currency auctions on Wednesdays and Fridays.

"We will carry auctions as often as our previous interventions," Stelmakh said, but without confirmation how many days a week and what if anything would take place the current currency auctions on Wednesdays and Fridays.

Stelmakh also said the government's 2010 budget was calculated at a hryvnia rate of 8.5-8.6/$, though he declined to give his own forecast for the hryvnia next year.

The finance ministry had said before it would prepare the budget based on the hryvnia's current rate because the central bank had not given its forecast for the hryvnia next year.

"It has already been announced that next year's budget is calculated at a rate of 8.5-8.6 hryvnias a dollar," Stelmakh said.

title: Ukrainians queue for dlrs as cbank  intervenes
text:
KIEV, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank injected over $250 million this week into the cash foreign exchange market through intervention but long queues formed at banks on Friday as ordinary people clamoured for the dollar.

The hryvnia currency has lost over 10 percent of its value to the dollar in the past two months, trading at about 8.5/$ this week from 7.7/$ at the start of July as the state and banks have to pay more foreign debt than before and imports rise.

The hryvnia's fall has been far slower than the plunge of about 30 percent last December alone when the currency hit a historic low of 9.5-10/$. But this time, even the central bank has acknowledged that Ukrainians were "panicked" by the rate.

The bank, which has been intervening or conducting foreign currency auctions practically every day since the start of the year, limited its sales of the dollar this week to banks needing to supply their foreign cash exchange booths.

"This had to be done to clam people down. When we saw the panicked mood, we sold $92 million the day before yesterday (Tuesday) and $170 million today (Thursday)," First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov told a talk show late on Thursday.

However, not all banks managed to buy the dollars from the central bank and that meant those who were successful sold dollars on Friday at 8.1/$ and those who were not, at 8.5/$.

One of the conditions of the central bank's interventions has been that the cash sale rate should be no more than 2 percent above the intervention rate.

Long queues formed throughout the day outside banks with the cheaper rate.

Shapovalov said the central bank had spent $8 billion on intervention since the start of the year, including $1.12 billion in July alone when the hryvnia started slipping.

That is worth a quarter of the bank's reserves as they stood at the beginning of this month. But Shapovalov said the volumes do not break any conditions set by the International Monetary Fund with which Kiev has a $16.4 billion loan programme.

"We have a programme with the IMF, which has been signed by all the leaders in the government... Intervention is being carried within the limits (set by the IMF)," Shapovalov said.

The IMF has already disbursed $10.6 billion of the total since November, including $3.3 billion last month. But that last tranche went directly to the government to plug a hole in its budget and pay external debts. "This has reduced our possibility to intervene by $3.3 billion," Shapovalov said. KIEV, July 1 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said it was ready to sell dollars at 7.65 hryvnias on the interbank market on Wednesday to meet growing demand for the U.S. currency.

The bank took its action as Ukrainian officials proceeded with talks with the International Monetary Fund to secure the release of a third tranche of a $16.4 billion loan programme.

Dealers said pressure was building up on the hryvnia from several sources -- including seasonal factors, currency speculation and a fresh bout of political uncertainty in the run-up to a presidential election next January.

The hryvnia has slipped in the past week in trading on the interbank market to 7.77/7.787 to the dollar from 7.6.

In its latest intervention on Tuesday, the bank sold dollars at 7.64 and was ready to buy them at 7.61. On Wednesday, it was offering the same purchase rate as the previous day.

The central bank normally does not intervene on the market on Wednesdays but conducts selected currency auctions for a limited number of individuals.

Wednesday's intervention also removed restrictions for purchasing dollars -- previously limited to buyers for payment for imports contracts and foreign debt within strict deadlines.

In addition to Wednesday's intervention, the bank was auctioning dollars at 7.6405 compared to 7.63 -- the rate that has prevailed over the past month.

The central bank has been engaged in nearly daily action -- selective interventions and currency auctions -- since last year to prop the hryvnia -- which lost about 60 percent of its value at one point, falling to 9.0 to the dollar.

IMPORTS, SPECULATION

Dealers said much of the demand for dollars was linked to import contracts. But speculation also played a role.

"The hryvnia's current weakness is seasonal in nature linked to demand for currency at the end of the quarter," said Oleksander Pecherytsin of ING bank.

But Oleksander Okhrimenko of Ukrgazbank said speculators were trying more and more to frighten the market through a hyperdevaluation of the hryvnia.

"Such forecasts have a single aim -- to jolt the market, instal panic and allow speculators who got stuck with dollars at 8-9 to shed expensive currency on the market."

Central bank chief Volodymyr Stelmakh told Reuters last week that the interbank market was subject to a "fragile balance" supported by the bank's interventions but subject to disruption at the start of the presidential campaign.

Ukraine has been gripped by political turmoil since pro-Western politicians took power in the 2004 "Orange Revolution". Most upheavals have focused on policy rows pitting President Viktor Yushchenko against his estranged ally, Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko.

Central bank intervention dipped to $215.7 million in May from $946.3 million in April -- monthly intervention in the first three months of the year exceeded $1 billion.

And bank officials had suggested for a time that an improvement in the foreign trade balance in June would lead to further declines in intervention levels.

But dealers said uncertainty surrounding the election was already prompting outward capital flows to offshore zones.

Dealers also say the hryvnia's level could be affected by the actions of state energy company Naftogaz which must settle its monthly bills for imported Russian gas in dollars.

The company paid more than $600 million in May and must settle its next bill -- at least $250 million, by July 7 -- and a further $1 billion a month later. (Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Andy Bruce)

KIEV, June 3 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Wednesday it would sell dollars at 7.63 hryvnias in its Thursday intervention, compared to 7.65 on Tuesday but leaving its "buy" rate unchanged at 7.61.

The central bank did not intervene on the interbank market on Wednesday, but sold dollars at auction at 7.63 hryvnias. The hryvnia traded on the interbank market at 7.58 to 7.65.

After months of propping the hryvnia by selling dollars through intervention and auctions, the bank has in recent weeks begun operating on both the sell and buy side.

The daily action in support of the hryvnia enabled the Ukrainian currency to claw back some ground after losing 60 percent of its value from October to late February.

The central bank last week said reserves had risen for the first time since November, jumping by around $3.3 billion due to the second tranche of an IMF loan and currency purchases by the central bank -- totalling $133 million last month. title: RPT-INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1- Ukraine intervention  boosts  FX  reserves
text:
(Repeats story first published on Monday)

 (Recasts, adds recent comments from Prime Minister)

 By Natalya Zinets

 KIEV, May 25 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank last week bought more foreign currency than it sold for the first time in eight months, boosting the country's reserves by $130 million, the bank's top adviser said on Monday.

 "The central bank is boosting reserves not only through borrowing, not only through the International Monetary Fund, but now through its own interventions on the interbank market," Valery Lytvytsky said in an interview.

 "Last week, we bought $133 million and sold $2.6 million."

 Foreign currency has been in chronic short supply on the interbank market since last October, sending the hryvnia currency into a prolonged tailspin. It lost 60 percent of its value by the end of January, though it has since made up some lost ground.

 Although Ukraine received the initial $4.5 billion tranche of an IMF credit programme last November, reserves fell to $24.5 billion as of April 30 compared to a historic high $38.1 billion as of August 31, 2008.

 Last week, Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko said the hyrvnia will continue to strengthen thanks to the IMF loan tranche.

 Over the last three months, however, sharp reductions in imports and sustained currency intervention have not only halted the fall but clawed back some of the currency's value.

 The hryvnia fell at one point last December to 9.0, but rebounded to 8.0 in April. It now stands at about 7.6-7.7.

 "The strengthening of the exchange rate we now see is not based so much on fundamental issues as it is linked to a correction of an excessive devaluation," Lytvytsky said.

 "For now, this is a psychological and political effect. From the end of February, when political pressure began to ease on the central bank and with the bank intervening every day, people stopped taking money out of banks and buying foreign currency."

 Last month, the sale of foreign currency from central bank reserves fell to $946.3 million from $1.077 billion the previous month and $1.73 billion in February.

 Last October, the central bank sold a record $4.115 billion -- and sales over the fourth quarter hit $10.285 billion.

 "But fundamental changes are beginning to take hold which could bolster the currency further," he said.

 Ukraine's monthly current account deficit, he said, was nearly in balance in April and capital account figures showed little change compared to the previous month.

 According to official figures, the current account deficit fell in April to $70 million from $434 million a month earlier. The capital account was all but unchanged at $986 million against $970 million in March.

 "The inflow of direct investment and an end to the outflow of individual deposits from banks are two elements which can help balance the capital account," Lytvytsky said.

 "If this continues, last week's central bank purchases on the interbank market will become a solid trend."

 Lytvytsky said it was vital for the central bank to keep buying excess currency supply on the market not only to build up reserves and also to prevent rapid strengthening of the hryvnia.

 "I do not recommend any move towards an excessive strenthening of the hryvnia as long as there is an absence of fundamental factors bolstering the currency," he said.

 "If inflation exceeds 15 percent (April year/year), if there is a sizable hidden budget deficit, a 20 percent decline in the economy, what sort of major strengthening can there be? For now, it is a correction."  (Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Andy Bruce/Ruth Pitchford)

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine  C.Bank cuts  forex intervention  in April
text:
(adds details, comment)

KIEV, May 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Friday its spending on intervention in the interbank market to support the hryvnia currency fell to $946.3 million in April from $1.077 billion in March.

Although the bank continues to intervene nearly every day, the amount devoted to intervention has been declining steadily since the beginning of the year as the hryvnia steadies after losing about 60 percent of its value since last September.

A total of $1.729 billion was spent on intervention in February and $1.611 billion in January.

The dip in intervention appears directly linked to a decline in imports after the hryvnia's value began to slide last year.

"There is no demand for foreign currency. Importers have significantly decreased volumes of currency purchases," said one dealer from a major Ukrainian bank.

Central bank data showed demand for foreign currency still outstripped supply on the retail market, though the difference was reduced -- with purchases by consumers in April standing at $1.293 billion and sales at $1.128 billion.

In March, purchases stood at $1.476 billion and sales at $909 million.

The calmer atmosphere on the interbank market has been reflected in a series of central bank moves.

On Thursday, the bank announced the first change in its intervention rate since Feb. 20, offering to sell dollars on the market at 7.75 hryvnias.

It had been offering to sell dollars at 7.9 hryvnias and buy them at 7.7 for over two months. The buy rate remains the same.

The central bank also said it was altering the hryvnia's official rate for the first time since December 28 -- this would now stand at 7.71 to the dollar instead of 7.7.

In accordance with the terms of an International Monetary Fund credit, the bank said it would close the gap between its official rate and the rate on the interbank market to 2 percent.

The IMF agreed to lend Ukraine $16.4 billion last year to help offset the effects of the world financial crisis, but the flow of credits was halted amid policy differences.

After a visit to Kiev by an IMF mission, the Fund's Board of Directors is expected to endorse the release of the second tranche of $2.8 billion. (Reporting by Yuri Kulikov, writing by Ron Popeski, editing by Victoria Main)

KIEV, May 7 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank has changed its intervention rate for the first time since Feb. 20, offering to sell dollars on the interbank market on Thursday at 7.75 hryvnias, according to its data. The bank had been offering to sell dollars at 7.9 hryvnias and buy them at 7.7 hryvnias for over two months. The buy rate remains the same.

The central bank also said it was altering the hryvnia's official rate for the first time since December 28. It would now stand at 7.71 to the dollar instead of 7.7.

The bank announced on Thursday that it would close the gap between its official rate and the rate on the interbank market to 2 percent.

This had been a condition for securing a $16.4 billion credit agreed with the International Monetary Fund late last year.

Dealers said the change in the rate -- however slight, had been expected after the statement and taking into account the relative stability in the past two weeks on the interbank market with the hryvnia strengthening slightly.

"Trading today ended with the dollar falling -- there were even rates of 7.93/$. There has been a trend in the past few days of the dollar being offered and the hryvnia strengthening," said one dealer.

The central bank spent $1.077 billion on intervention in March, lower than $1.73 billion in February. It spent far less on intervention in the first quarter of this year -- $4.418 billion, than in the last quarter of 2008 -- $10.284 billion.

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine  C.Bank cuts spending on  intervention
text:
(adds intervention rates for Tuesday, para 6)

KIEV, April 6 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Monday its spending of reserves to prop up the hryvnia currency against its sharp falls of recent months, had declined 38 percent in March compared to the previous month.

A central bank statement said it had spent $1.077 billion in March against $1.73 billion in February on intervention and sale of dollars at auctions.

Spending in the first quarter of 2009 was $4.418 billion, 57 percent down from $10.284 billion in the last quarter of 2008.

The hryvnia has lost 60 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since last September in Ukraine, but clawed back 1.7 percent in March. Central bank intervention has sought to help borrowers meet foreign debt requirements in difficult conditions of obtaining credits and an outflow of funds from the country.

"The central bank's intervention has reduced the shortage of foreign currency on the domestic market," the bank said, noting how the hryvnia gained ground on the interbank market last month.

The central bank later said it would offer to sell dollars at 7.9 hryvnias on Tuesday and buy at 7.70, rates that have in place for more than month.

The dollar traded on Monday on the interbank market at 8.12/8.25.

The central bank generally intervenes three or four times a week, selling dollars at advantageous rates to buyers needing to repay debts, and has also begun organising auctions for dollars and other currencies once or twice a week.

It says the introduction of auctions has cut demand for foreign currency significantly.

The bank said the hryvnia's average rate to the dollar, calculated on the basis of all transactions on the interbank market, rose in March to 7.9743 from 8.108 in February.

Dealers say demand for foreign currency has fallen because imports have declined in conditions of economic crisis, regular central bank intervention and the prospect of restored credits from the International Monetary Fund.

An IMF mission is due to return to Kiev this week to discuss resuming credits under a $16.4 billion loan -- suspended in a disagreement over reforms.

Dealers also say restrictions on who may purchase dollars and regulations aimed to change the structure of banks' open currency positions have also propped the hryvnia. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets, writing by Ron Popeski, editing by Victoria Main)

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine central bank  auctions dollars, euros
text:
(adds intervention rates for Monday, para 6)

KIEV, March 20 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Friday it intended to sell dollars at 7.8 hryvnias and euros at 10.66 at its weekly auction of hard currency funds.

The central bank has sought to strengthen its hold over the currency since December after the hryvnia tumbled in the final months of 2008 on rising bank problems, a collapsing steel sector and growing worries over Ukraine's solvency.

Since the start of the year the central bank has tried to keep the rate at around 7.7 per dollar, well below the 2008 peak around 4.5 per euro.

At its last auction, it sold $68.6 million at a rate of 7.8 hryvnias and 1.01 million euros at 9.97 hryvnias -- its first such auction of the European currency.

Participation is limited to banks presenting a calendar of payments in March for individuals or small businesses. The central bank said banks had set aside 368.8 million hryvnias for the purchase of currency.

The central bank later announced it would intervene on the interbank market on Monday, buying dollars at 7.7 and selling at 7.9 -- rates which have varied little over the past month.

The central bank intervenes from Monday to Thursday in support of the hryvnia, offering to sell dollars at what amounts to discounted rates. It holds auctions on Fridays, also at rates more favourable to buyers than on the interbank market.

Exchange offices were offering to sell dollars on Friday at about 8.5 and euros at 11.7.

Banks have been reluctant to post hryvnia rates in view of warnings from the central bank that they would face punitive measures if the figures differed significantly from an "average" rate calculated from the previous day's transactions. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets, writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Marius Zaharia/Ruth Pitchford)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks lower, zloty weakens further
text:
* Emerging equities broadly weaker led by Asia

* Regional currencies are mixed, zloty lower

* Latvian lat remains above intervention level

* Ukraine assets little hit by ratings downgrade

By Martina Fuchs

LONDON, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Emerging equities were broadly lower on Thursday, led down by Asian stocks and underperforming global markets, with Poland raising the spectre of intervention as the zloty currency weakened again after Wednesday's rate cut.

Benchmark emerging equities <.MSCIEF> fell 0.27 percent by 1145 GMT, after a 1 percent rise the previous day, but remain down 11.11 percent on the year -- still above multi-year lows set late last year.

In contrast, the benchmark global equity markets index <.MIWD00000PUS> was up 0.15 percent supported by fresh steps from the British government to shore up its banking sector.

Much of the emerging fall was down to Asian stocks, with Chinese equities <.SSEC> down 3.87 percent. Israeli stocks <.TA25> lost 0.32 percent, but some of the other exchanges in the region were up.

Hungarian equities <.BUX> were amongst the largest gainers, up 0.76 percent but still down 18.62 percent on the year, while Czech stocks <.PX> were up 0.55 percent.

"We've had a slight rebound in the last couple of days, but now we are back and worries have not gone away," said Danske Bank chief emerging markets analyst Lars Christensen. "There is a little weakness in the currencies but it's relatively neutral."

Benchmark emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> were five basis points narrower at 648 over US Treasuries, implying a slight rise in appetite for emerging debt compared to US government paper.

Two of the region's worst performing currencies -- Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> and Russia's rouble <RUS=MCX=> -- were slightly stronger, up 0.51 and 0.17 percent respectively but both remain down around 13 percent this year.

POLISH INTERVENTION?

The Czech crown <EURCZK=> was up 0.49 percent, but the Polish zloty <EURPLN=> lost 0.1 percent to deepen its recent losses, but remained above all time lows set earlier this month.

Poland's central bank cut interest rates by 25 basis points on Wednesday, saying a sharp slowdown in the economy justified the cut. Poland has now cut rates by 200 basis points in recent months to 4.0 percent, although Wednesday's cut was not as sharp as previous ones.

Polish central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek said on Thursday that the bank might intervene in the currency markets to support the zloty. [ID:nWAR007969]

The Latvian lat <EURLVL=> was slightly weaker within its trading band but remained short of Wednesday's intraday lows, when it fell sharply to the level where the central bank intervenes to support it.

A government collapse, ratings downgrade and accelerating economic crisis have increased pressure on the currency, but it could get short-term support in the coming days as Latvia receives the first part of a 7.5 billion euro International Monetary Fund and the European Union-led package.

The cost of protecting Ukranian sovereign debt in the credit default swaps market fell 124.5 basis points to 4162.5, meaning it would cost $4.16 million a year to cover $10 million of five-year debt -- amongst the highest in emerging markets.

Standard & Poor's slashed Ukraine to a CCC+ "junk" rating on worries about destabilised banks, falling industrial output and political disunity that puts at risk a $16.4 billion International Monetary Fund loan programme. [ID:nLP372975]

"The two-notch ratings downgrade appears premature in terms of timing and too aggressive in terms of magnitude," said Sergei Voloboev, emerging markets analyst at Credit Suisse. "There was no significant market reaction. It seems that the market has not paid too much attention to the arguments that the rating agency made yesterday. But of course, Ukraine continues to trade extremely wide." (editing by Peter Apps ad Toby Chopra)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Shares down as emerging Europe  FX  weaken
text:
* Emerging shares fall to 11-week lows on global selloff

* South African markets hit by GDP data

* Emerging Europe FX selling pressure resumes

* Ukraine hryvnia continues slide on IMF aid suspension

By Sebastian Tong and Martina Fuchs

LONDON, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Emerging shares sank nearly 2 percent on Tuesday amid a global selloff sparked off by renewed fears over the financial system while central European currencies weakened a day after joint verbal intervention from the region's central bankers offered brief respite.

Ukraine's hryvnia currency continued its slide as an IMF aid programme remained suspended, while South African markets came under pressure after figures showed its economy shrinking for the first time in a decade in the fourth quarter of 2008.

Investors are growing nervous that the various bailout packages unveiled by governments around the world may not be enough to stabilise the global banking sector as Washington mulled a possible increase in its stake in Citigroup and insurer AIG looks to more state funds.

A wave of global selling knocked world stocks <.MIWD00000PUS> to their lowest since April 2003, sending Wall Street to 12-year lows on Monday. However, emerging equity losses were more modest with the benchmark index <.MSCIEF> down to its lowest level since Dec. 5.

By 1145 GMT, the key emerging share index was down 1.66 percent to 501.67 while emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> widened 3 basis points to trade at 674 bps above U.S. Treasuries.

"Emerging Europe is suffering more than many Asian or Latin American countries. The region is getting hit by the global trade shock and directly by the credit crunch, as the banks don't want to lend. Markets seem to be wanting to price this in as quickly as possible," said Charlie Robertson, chief Europe, Middle East and Asia economist at ING.

Among the day's biggest equity losers were Romania <.BETI> and Poland <.WIG20>, which saw their bourses fall over 2 percent.

South African shares suffered the largest falls with the key index <.JTOPI> down nearly 3 percent following data showing a bigger-than-expected contraction in South Africa's economy in the fourth quarter. [ID:nLO6887]

The country's rand, already down 6 percent versus the dollar <ZAR=> since the start of the year, also eased 0.25 percent amid growing expectations of an early interest rate hike.

"BLUFFING" ATTEMPT

Selling pressure on emerging European currencies resumed a day after they bounced back on a coordinated push among the region's central bankers to talk up their currencies. [ID:nLI344803]

The unprecedented move saw the Czech and Polish central bankers join their Hungarian and Romanian counterparts to say that recent record falls in their currencies had been overdone.

But the sharp gains seen on Monday had mostly faded by Tuesday morning with few investors convinced that policymakers could back their words with actual intervention.

"We rather believe that it was a good attempt of bluffing as the central banks in central and eastern Europe most likely want to spare their reserves as much as possible due to coming outflows...While the currencies may have suffered "more than deserved" the key issue remains - very weak fundamentals and a struggling bank sector," said SEB in a client note.

Poland's zloty was down 0.77 percent against the euro <EURPLN=> while Romania's leu slipped 0.30 percent versus the common currency. <EURRON=>

Meanwhile, ratings agencies Fitch and Moody's issued fresh warnings on Latvia, Lithuania and Ukraine, warning of growing banking system and currency risks from deteriorating macroeconomic conditions. [ID:nLO466428] [ID:nHKG366757] [nLO688554] [nLA378825]

Ukraine's hryvnia, which fell nearly 7 percent on Monday, was quoted 3.7 percent weaker against the dollar. <UAH=>

Volumes remain thin with little dollars seen on offer in the market after the central bank said it would not sell dollars to banks in its daily interventions if the local currency traded at rates higher than its average rate.

Investors say the unit will remain pressured as long as Ukraine's deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is stalled.

The IMF agreed to lend Ukraine $16.4 billion in a two-year plan of tranches and reforms promised by Kiev. But after pencilling in a three percent budget deficit this year -- contrary to IMF conditions -- the fund suspended the loan programme.

(Reporting by Sebastian Tong and Martina Fuchs; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: UPDATE 1-Ukraine cbank: IMF says initial conditions for loan met
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

KIEV, Jan 28 (Reuters) - A senior Ukrainian central bank official said on Wednesday the IMF had confirmed that initial conditions set for a $16.4 billion loan had been met.

An International Monetary Fund mission is in Kiev to assess progress on fiscal and monetary conditions it has set before disbursing the next tranche of the loan. Ukraine received $4.5 billion in November.

"The IMF has confirmed that all obligations which we undertook at the initial stages were fulfilled," the central bank's First Deputy Chairman, Anatoly Shapovalov, told a news conference.

The IMF required that foreign currency reserves be no lower than $26.7 billion by the end of last year and the monetary base to be no higher than 190 billion dollars.

It also required the difference between the official rate, set by the central bank, and the market rate to be no more than 2 percent.

That has not been the case for some of January when the official rate was 7.7/$, but the hryvnia traded above 8.6/$. But Shapovalov said he hoped the IMF would accept the central bank's explanations that it was working to bring the rates closer.

"The hryvnia depreciated 1.5-2 percent since the start of January. But we did not move the official rate in order not to create panic if only because after such a depreciation (in 2008) there is clearly no economic basis for it," he said.

He said the huge depreciation in the last four months of 2008, from 4.676 hryvnias per dollar to historic lows touching upon 10/$, had helped the trade deficit in January.

He said exporters earned $2.339 billion, while payments for imports were at $2.008 billion. But pressure on the hryvnia remained from foreign currency debt repayment and the central bank intended to continue with intervention for now.

He said Ukraine owed $1.6 billion in foreign debt in January and had paid up $1.536 billion.

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW- Ukraine  c.bank to continue with  intervention
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

KIEV, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank is determined to press ahead with currency intervention despite a $1.6 billion drop in reserves since the beginning of the year, a senior central bank official said on Wednesday.

The hryvnia <UAH=> fell sharply at the end of last year reflecting market worries about the health of Ukraine's economy, losing half of its value to the dollar in December despite persistent central bank intervention.

Central Bank adviser Valery Lytvytsky said currency reserves had already fallen to $29.9 billion from $31.5 billion at the end of 2008.

"Last year, we lost reserves for the second time in the past 10 years. And this is continuing. Today reserves are already at $29.9 billion," Lytvytsky told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Although its plunge has jolted confidence in the banking system, with some officials warning of failure to repay debt, the hryvnia has inched up to around $7.85 against the dollar as panic on the market eased.

The International Monetary Fund approved a $16.4 billion loan package for Ukraine in November to help the country withstand the financial crisis and Kiev has also come to terms with Moscow in a damaging gas dispute.

Lytvytsky said that under its agreement with the IMF, the central bank was allowed to spend $4.5 billion out of its reserves to prop up the currency before the end of March.

"(So far this year) we have spent about $875 million on intervention, which is less than we first assumed because the market did a lot on its own. We can spend about $4.5 billion to the end of the quarter," he said.

Lytvytsky said the bank would intervene to ensure the interbank exchange rate moved in line with the official central bank rate, currently at 7.7 to the dollar and reviewed daily.

"Today the gap (between the two) is 1.9 percent," he said, adding it should be no more than two percent.

Lytvytsky said that with global prices for its key metals exports falling and prices for Russian gas imports growing, it would be hard to see the hryvnia strengthen significantly any time soon.

"I think we should be able to keep the hryvnia at at least 8 against the dollar over the next few days, possibly weeks," he said. (Writing by Maria Golovnina; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: Ukraine's hryvnia set for further slide as gas row drags
text:
LONDON, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Ukraine's embattled hryvnia <UAH=> currency steadied on Tuesday, but analysts back it to slide further as new year trading gets underway against the backdrop of a gas row with Russia, now entering its third week.

Growing strains on the central bank's ability to prop up the exchange rate are also likely to weigh on the currency, which has halved in value against the dollar in the last three months.

On Monday, the unit plummeted 12 percent to 8.79 against the dollar, its biggest intra-day fall in more than a decade. It held at around similar levels on Tuesday.

"There's a very serious risk that Ukraine, if it's not already, will turn into an Iceland-kind of meltdown. There is no reason to buy the Ukrainian hryvnia today or any time soon," Lars Christensen, head emerging markets at Danske Bank.

"The situation is extremely serious so the currency is considered to be in a freefall."

Analysts say the gas contract dispute between Kiev and Moscow is spurring dollar-buying in Ukraine with growing concern over higher gas prices and the economic impact of the two-week Russian gas embargo on Ukrainian industry [ID:nLD708539]

At 1300 GMT, the Reuters conversational dealing system put the hryvnia flat at 8.79 while the local-bank quote for the currency <UAH=UA> showed a wider bid/ask level at 7.700/8.210.

"Today the rates on the market were 8.75-8.90 hryvnias per dollar and deals were done at around 8.80," said a Kiev trader.

INTERVENTION LIMITS

Ukraine's central bank sold dollars at a currency auction on Tuesday at 7.86 hrvnias [ID:nLD330196], a stronger level than its offer of 8.62 hryvnias per dollar on Monday.

Liquidity in the foreign exchange market has thinned amid trading restrictions introduced by authorities last year but Ukrainian currency forwards <GFIU> now put the unit at 10.06 to the dollar in a month, 12.5 in six months and 14.25 in a year.

Analysts polled by Reuters at the end of December saw the hryvnia at 7.97 per dollar by the end of 2009 but some say they are already reconsidering forecasts given continuing volatility after it fell to record lows around 10 to the dollar last month.

There is still some doubt over the impact of an expected recession and the likelihood of higher gas prices on a struggling Ukrainian economy.

Moscow wants Kiev to pay 2-1/2 times more for its gas while Kiev is demanding higher fees for the transit of Russia gas to Europe through Ukraine.

"A lot depends on what the two countries eventually agree. We're unsure whether higher gas prices will be offset by higher transit fees," said Jon Harrison, emerging markets currency strategist at Dresdner Kleinwort. He sees the hryvnia sagging to 9.7 against the greenback in six months.

The gas dispute compounds a deepening domestic political crisis in Ukraine, which turned to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in November for a $16.5 billion loan.

But the IMF bailout is likely to curb Ukraine's ability to shore up its currency by drawing on its fast-depleting reserves, which stand at around $31 billion, some $0.3 billion higher than the IMF requirement set quarterly. [ID:nL6498806]

"The IMF is not there to finance capital flight. Its loan was meant to cover the shortfall arising from Ukraine's balance of payments," said Citi economist Ali Al-Eyd. "Under the IMF loan agreement, Ukraine has to move towards a flexible exchange rate but they have been slow to meet the conditions."

A further hryvnia slump could trigger widespread foreign debt default among Ukrainian companies, which according to IMF data, face $38.2 billion in external debt obligations this year.

(Additional reporting by Kylie MacLellan in London and Sabina Zawadzki in Kiev; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: POLL-Analysts cut Ukraine's '08-'09 GDP, hryvnia fcasts
text:
KIEV, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Analysts cut their forecasts for Ukraine's economic growth to 2.4 percent this year and to a contraction of 3.1 percent in 2009, citing global slowdown and domestic debt defaults as the biggest risks, according to a Reuters poll published on Monday.

The 10 analysts polled by Reuters also cut their forecast for the rate of the hryvnia currency to a median of 7.90/$ by the end of this year and to 7.97/$ by the end of 2009, after the currency hit record lows earlier this month, having lost half of its value to the dollar in the past four months.

"Much will depend, unfortunately, on external factors -- demand for metals, the readiness of foreign investors to invest in financial projects linked to Euro-2012 (soccer tournament)," said Veronika Movchan, of the Institute for Economic Research and Political Consulting.

"The key risks are renewed global growth coming no earlier than 2010, a large amount of default in the real economy, the fall of several large banks due to the defaults and financing the budget deficit."

Ukraine's economy has experienced a sharp downturn in the past two months -- falling 14.4 percent in November year-on-year after industrial output fell 30 percent. A recession next year would put an end to eight years of robust growth averaging 7 percent annually.

The hryvnia began slipping to the dollar in September as foreign investors began pulling their funds out and continued its slide, weighed down by a fast widening current account deficit and a sharp fall in exports.

The central bank has spent billions trying to prop up the currency and Ukraine has received $4.5 billion of a $16.4 billion loan, although IMF-set reserves targets mean Ukraine cannot spend it merely on intervention.

Analysts saw the hryvnia rate stronger than its lowest point two weeks ago, when it touched 10/$, by the end of this year and next. But a divergence in their forecasts -- 7.5-9/$ this year and 6-10/$ for next year underscored political and financial uncertainty underlining the economy in the coming year. Oleksander Valchyshyn of Invest Capital Ukraine said risks to the currency included "mistakes in government and parliament's decision-making on budgetary and trade policies.

"Spending budget funds wastefully, apart from on investment, together with trade protectionism, could accelerate inflation and create new devaluation pressures on the real currency rate."

Analysts were also split on next year's current account deficit and trade gap. Some thought imports could sink next year as Ukraine goes through a deep recession.

But Kiev has yet to negotiate a price for Russian gas imports next year. Russia has raised these prices steeply since 2005 and they have been the key factor behind both deficits.

title: Trade in Ukraine hrvynia drying up amid crisis
text:
LONDON, Dec 19 (Reuters) - Trade in Ukraine's troubled hvrynia looked to be drying up on Friday with banks reporting no demand after the currency slumped in value and the central bank tightened capital controls amid a deepening economic crisis.

After hitting historic lows in consecutive sessions, the hryvnia recovered on Friday, supported by central bank auctions of dollars, a spike in the overnight refinancing rates and stability in the neighbouring Russian rouble.

The Reuters conversational dealing system quote for the currency in local trade <UAH=> showed the hryvnia up 10.6 percent at 8.05 to the dollar but demand was almost non-existent.

At 1500 GMT, the system had not recorded any new prices since 1216 GMT -- although traders said occasional deals were being done.

The unit has lost roughly half its value to the dollar since June, much of it in the last few days when it fell to a record low beyond 9.5.

Liquidity in general across central and eastern European currencies has fallen sharply, with investors seeing the region as particularly exposed to the global financial crisis.

But after the collapse of Iceland, Ukraine is seen as the most likely next casualty despite an International Monetary Fund bailout.

Analysts say the plight of Ukraine -- suffering slumping steel prices, local banking problems and now a threatened cutting of Russian gas supply in the New Year -- is not as severe as Iceland, which had banking debts several times the size of its gross domestic product.

But the demise in trade in its currency does bear some resemblance to the fate suffered by the Icelandic crown in September, when it likewise became practically impossible to exchange in international markets.

"It is not as bad as Iceland but it is close," said Lars Christensen, head of emerging markets research at Danske Bank in Copenhagen.

"No one wants to take any risks on the currency. But overall the situation with liquidity across Central and Eastern Europe is very, very bad."

Ukraine had been intervening to hold its currency higher but after haemorrhaging reserves and getting a $16.5 billion IMF deal, it has let the unit slide.

"The IMF plan called for a greater flexibility in the exchange rate and in a sense they are going back to that," said emerging markets currency strategist Elizabeth Gruie at BNP Paribas.

International banks cannot trade the hrvynia except in the local market through local subsidiaries, and trade in the international non-deliverable forward (NDF) market -- in which they can trade -- looked to have dried up as well.

There were no forward trades from international banks showing on the Reuters system <UAHNDFOR=> on Friday.

"For the last three days, everyone has been looking for the right hand side (the sell side)," said a trader at a bank in London, adding that the occasional trade was going through but only driven by the needs of clients generally keen to ditch their positions.

(Additional reporting by Sebastian Tong and Carolyn Cohn; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: UPDATE: Hryvnia Hits New Low, Raises Credit Default Fears
text:
(Adds details, context, economist comments.) 
 
   By Lidia Kelly 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--In what is becoming a daily occurrence, the Ukrainian hryvnia tumbled to a historic low Wednesday, raising fears of consumer credit default.

The currency weakened to UAH9.45 against the dollar as investors and the general public alike continued to desert the hryvnia in favor of the dollar.

The slump came only two days after breaking through UAH8.0 and dragging the hryvnia's purchasing power to barely half of what it was in the late summer.

The National Bank of Ukraine seems to have stepped back from interventions after buying some of the currency Tuesday, traders said.

Meanwhile, an economic aide to President Viktor Yushchenko, said the hryvnia's current distressed level threatens consumer default.

"We can estimate that 60% of credits won't be paid back," Ukrainian news agencies cited the aide, Roman Zhukovsky, as saying.

The bank has been backed in its depreciation policy by a part of the $16.5 billion stabilization loan from the International Monetary Fund.

Last week, the head of the IMF's mission to Ukraine said the country has successfully absorbed a traumatic currency devaluation.

Timothy Ash, head of Central and Eastern European research at Royal Bank of Scotland Group PLC, estimated that the National Bank still has some spare cash from the IMF loan to support the currency, but warned that serious anti-crisis measures and reforms must be enforced.

"Having an IMF program isn't sufficient to ensuring an economy's passage through the current global crisis," Ash said in a research note.

New central bank data showed the country's external debt increased by $7.4 billion in the third quarter to $105.4 billion, or 60% of gross domestic product, with short-term liabilities estimated at $30 billion.

The news, compounded by a widening current account deficit, further political wrangling about anti-crisis policy and uncertainty over the new coalition between the parties of Yushchenko and Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, only adds to the hryvnia's woes, economists said.

"In Ukraine, the evidence is still that policymakers don't quite understand the seriousness of the challenges they face," Ash said.
