title: FACTBOX-Ukraine's politics and finances
text:
KIEV, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko on Wednesday pronounced Ukraine's political crisis over and vowed to strengthen her government team to tackle the impact of the world financial crisis on the country.

Following are key facts about Ukraine's politics and finances and why the ex-Soviet state is especially vulnerable to heightened risk aversion among international investors.

POLITICS

* Ukraine has been plagued by political turbulence since "Orange Revolution" protests in 2004 brought to power President Viktor Yushchenko and a team committed to moving closer to the West and joining NATO and the European Union.

Rows pitting Yushchenko against his former ally Yulia Tymoshenko, who has twice served as his prime minister, undermined the "orange" camp and brought down governments.

A coalition between parties backed by the two leaders was reinstated on Tuesday, resolving for now the latest deadlock and avoiding a snap parliamentary poll.

* Upheaval -- and trouble forming a stable ruling coalition -- reflect Ukraine's longstanding division into the nationalist west and centre, which looks to the EU and United States, and the Russian-speaking east and south, friendlier towards Moscow.

* Relations with Russia, bumpy throughout the post-Soviet period, have sunk to unprecedented lows over Yushchenko's denunciation of Moscow's military intervention in Georgia. Ukraine depends heavily on Moscow for energy supplies.

CURRENCY POLICY

* The hryvnia currency continued to sink to a fresh historic low of 7.6-7.66/$ on Wednesday. It has lost over 60 percent of its value since September, weakened by global risk aversion, a lack of confidence in the currency and a drop in exports which bring dollars into the market.

* In mid-2008, the hryvnia had strengthened as far as 4.5/$, after the central bank abandoned a policy of keeping it in a corridor of 5.00-5.06 per dollar, within a 4.95-5.25 band.

* The central bank has scrapped a trading band and repeatedly devalued its official rate despite spending $7.7 billion on propping up the currency between September-November.

FINANCES

* Ukraine has received a $4.5 billion tranche from an IMF loan which it secured at the beginning of November. The loan came on condition of fiscal prudence, recapitalisation of banks and a more liberal exchange rate mechanism.

* Analysts say the funds should be used as a bridge loan for Ukraine's government, which has been unable to issue Eurobonds this year, and to recapitalise banks. They worry, however, that the funds will be spent on just supporting the hryvnia.

* Foreign exchange reserves as of the end of November rose to $32.7 billion against $31.9 billion at the end of October, helped by the IMF tranche.

* The current account deficit was running at $10.5 billion, or 6.5 percent of GDP, in the first 10 months of this year. Analysts see the full-year deficit at between $10-14 billion but diverge on next year's forecast, citing between $3-$20 billion due to uncertainties over gas prices and the hryvnia's rate.

* Prices and demand for steel exports have dropped, while Russia's Gazprom has suggested next year's price for gas imports could soar to $400 per 1,000 cubic metres from $179.50 now.

CURRENCY RISKS

* The central bank risks whittling away its reserves, and encouraging imports and further widening the trade gap, if it supports the hryvnia. Letting it float freely would introduce uncertainty and speculation, removing an important anchor for domestic and foreign businesses in the export-driven economy. * Many people hold debt in foreign currency and are having increasing difficulties paying it off as the hryvnia weakens.

* Consumers are extremely sensitive to currency movements -- they lost savings when the Soviet Union collapsed and again through hyperinflation and a currency crisis in the 1990s that more than halved the hryvnia's value to about 4/$ and beyond.

* Ukraine was forced to restructure its debts in 2000 and made the final payments just last year. Credit default swaps -- a tradeable instrument that measures risks of debt default -- have consistently been some of the highest for emerging markets.

FOREIGN DEBT

* Ukraine's foreign debt totalled just over $100 billion as of July 1, of which about $15 billion was government debt.

* A central bank official has said companies and banks must pay off $5 billion in debts by the end of this year and another $30 billion next year.

* Analysts estimate Ukraine's 2009 external financing requirement to be $55-66 billion, of which $32-40 billion is in the private sector. Foreign banks own 40-42 percent of total banking assets and 25 percent of short-term banking debt is owed to parent banks. (Compiled by Sabina Zawadzki, editing by Mark Trevelyan)

title: UDPATE 1- Ukraine 's cbank returns to  intervention
text:
(Adds cbank official, details)

KIEV, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sold dollars on the interbank market on Friday in its weeks-long effort to support the hryvnia and said it would continue with intervention and auctions to find the best way to shore up the currency.

The bank has been spending billions of dollars in intervention throughout most of October and November. The currency fell to a historic low in mid-October of 7.05-7.2 per dollar.

The bank on Wednesday conducted an auction for the dollar in what had been seen as a policy shift. It failed to intervene on Thursday and the hryvnia slipped to 6.5 to the dollar from 6.2 the previous day.

The bank sold dollars at 6.17 hryvnias on Friday and the currency strengthened to 6.00-6.24.

"For now we will carry out both auctions and interventions," a central bank official said. "We need time to sharpen our auctioning method so that the process is transparent and to understand which way is the most effective."

The official said the volume of dollar sales on Friday was not high. The bank spent $4.115 billion on intervention in October, according to its own data. Dealers have said that it has spent about $3 billion so far in November.

Ukraine has agreed a loan from the International Monetary Fund, some of which may go towards propping up reserves though the fund in general prefers greater currency flexibility.

The currency fell in the past two months at first because investors sold their Ukrainian assets and bought dollars, fleeing risky emerging markets in the face of the global financial crisis.

Ukraine's exports have fallen dramatically as economies slow down, especially hurting steelmakers who account for 45 percent of exports -- which means they have far fewer dollars to trade.

A fast-expanding current account gap and an expected slowdown in foreign direct investment next year both point to a weaker currency. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets; writing by Sabina Zawadzki; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: UPDATE 2-Ukraine c.bank starts dollar sale auction
text:
(adds C.Bank selling dollars at auction at 5.98)

KIEV, Nov 19 (Reuters) - In a major policy shift, the central bank abandoned direct intervention to support Ukraine's hryvnia currency on Wednesday and sold dollars for the first time at an auction to banks offering 5.98 or more per dollar.

Dealers said all transactions occurred at 5.98, though that did not become clear until after 5 p.m. when trading closed.

The central bank had been intervening virtually every day on the interbank market since early October, but took no such action on Tuesday, allowing the hryvnia to slip to 6.0 to the dollar from 5.83 the previous day.

"They covered our bid at 5.98 though we had put our bid even higher so as to take no risks," said one dealer. "We had quite a significant volume."

The central bank gave no explanation for introducing the auctions.

"Perhaps they are hoping to reduce demand for purchases (of dollars)," said one dealer, recalling that Ukrainian authorities had promised the IMF to spend less of its reserves on intervention and pursue a flexible exchange rate policy.

The hryvnia fell further on the interbank market to 6.10-6.15 to the dollar, and not all participants were happy with the new system.

"The rate is determined under this system not by supply and demand, but through intervention and it is impossible to determine in advance whether this will happen," said one dealer. The central bank had earlier issued a directive allowing banks to buy dollars at 5.8854 hryvnias plus or minus two percent.

It said banks could buy dollars according to the rate proposed, with higher rates for the dollar first, until a fixed sum of intervention funds was exhausted. It identified no sum.

Banks need not identify the reason for buying, it said, but had to specify a rate "to within two places after the decimal point" and a volume, with a minimum purchase of $100,000.

Banks were required to submit bids by 2 p.m. (1200 GMT).

In a memorandum signed with the International Monetary Fund this month to underpin a $16.4 billion loan, Ukrainian authorities undertook to narrow differences between official, interbank, cash and intervention rates for the hryvnia.

They pledged to keep to no more than two percent the gap between the market and official rates.

The bank altered its intervention tactics after the hryvnia sank to a historic low of below 7.0 to the dollar last month by purchasing dollars on the interbank market without limit.

The hryvnia regained ground to a rate stronger than 6.0 but the interventions failed to curb excess demand for dollars resulting from foreign capital moving out of Ukraine and declining markets for Ukrainian exports. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets, writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: Ukraine  hryvnia slips with no c.Bank  intervention
text:
KIEV, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Ukraine's hryvnia slipped to 6.0 to the dollar on Tuesday from 5.83 the previous day in the absence of what in recent weeks has become routine central bank intervention to support the currency.

The central bank intervened on Monday, selling dollars on the interbank market at 5.79.

"In the absence of the central bank, trading slipped below 5.90, but I can't say there is any panic," said one dealer.

"But we could fall to 7.0 tomorrow. There were offers to buy dollars at 6.10. There were some deals this morning at 5.97 but the amounts were very small."

Traders said the central bank had given no explanation for not supporting the hryvnia as it has for nearly two months.

"People are saying it's because of the IMF, that the Fund is unhappy, that this is not a real market and that reserves are being spent -- and not on structural changes," said one dealer.

The International Monetary Fund this month agreed to give Ukraine a $16.4 billion loan to stabilise the economy and the banking system and has disbursed the first $4.5 billion tranche.

The central bank in October spent $4.115 intervening on the market to sell dollars. It had in recent weeks pledged to sell dollars without limit.

The central bank's deputy chairman, Oleskander Savchenko, told a weekly newspaper on Monday that the hryvnia would remain stable at 5.5-6.0 and strengthen in the second half of 2009. He ruled out as improbable any decline to weaker than 7.0.

But Oleskander Shlapak, top economic adviser to Ukraine's president, renewed the criticism he had directed at the central bank in October, when the hryvnia sank to 7.0. He said he was again unhappy with developments on the currency market.

"Things are not well on the market," he told a briefing. I'm talking about the level of demand (for dollars) over five or six days -- about $1 billion every day. That raises many questions."

Levels of imports and purchases of dollars by consumers did not justify that level, he said, and President Viktor Yushchenko would seek explanations at a meeting on Thursday with bankers.

"If this is psychological and speculative demand, we know how to deal with it," he said. "If we do not have a balanced rate, then measures must be taken to set down such a trend."

Dealers said the thrust of official policy was hard to gauge given the central bank chairman's pledge that the hryvnia would go no weaker than 6.0 and that there would no longer be any discrepancies between the market rate and an "official" rate.

"You have to be consistent. They said there would be a single rate. They said they would sell dollars without limit. Where is the single rate?" said one dealer.

"And the central bank is saying nothing. You cannot restore confidence with inconsistent moves. Dealers and the public will rely only on themselves. Why not buy a dollar today at 6.20, if it will cost 7.0 tomorrow?" (Additional reporting by Yuri Kulikov, writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: FACTBOX-Key facts on Ukraine's finances and politics
text:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund approved a $16.5 billion loan programme for Ukraine late on Wednesday that includes monetary and exchange rate policy shifts to ease strains from the global financial crisis.

 Following are key facts about why Ukraine is vulnerable to heightened risk aversion among international investors.

 POLITICS

 * Ukraine has been plagued by political turbulence since "Orange Revolution" protests in 2004 brought to power President Viktor Yushchenko and a team committed to moving closer to the West and joining NATO and the European Union.

 Rows pitting Yushchenko against his former ally Yulia Tymoshenko, who twice served as his prime minister, undermined the "orange" camp and brought down governments.

 Although the president dissolved parliament last month and called a December parliamentary election, he has since suspended that decree and a vote this year now seems unlikely.

 * Upheaval -- and trouble forming a stable ruling coalition -- reflect Ukraine's longstanding division into the nationalist west and centre, which looks to the EU and United States, and the Russian-speaking east and south, friendlier towards Moscow.

 * Relations with Russia, bumpy throughout the post-Soviet period, have sunk to unprecedented lows over Yushchenko's denunciation of Moscow's military intervention in Georgia. Ukraine depends heavily on Moscow for energy supplies.

CURRENCY POLICY

 * The hryvnia currency hit an all-time low of 7.2 to the dollar on Oct. 29, weakened by growing global risk aversion and regional tensions after Russia's conflict with Georgia.

 * Authorities have said they will formulate a new mechanism which would unify the market, cash and official rates.

 * In mid-2008, the hryvnia had strengthened as far as 4.5/$, after the central bank abandoned a policy of keeping it in a corridor of 5.00-5.06 per dollar within a 4.95-5.25 band.

 FINANCES

 * Foreign exchange reserves fell to $33 billion at the end of October from $37.5 billion end-September, when they covered 3.7 months of imports.

 * The current account deficit more than quadrupled in the first nine months of this year compared with the same period last year to $8.4 billion, or 5.8 percent of GDP.

 * Analysts based outside Ukraine forecast its current account deficit at $21-25 billion, or 10-12 percent of gross domestic product, by year-end; Ukraine-based analysts give lower forecasts of about 6 percent of GDP.

 * Prices for Ukraine's steel exports are dropping, while Russia's Gazprom has suggested next year's price for gas imports could soar to $400 per 1,000 cubic metres from $179.50 now.

CURRENCY RISKS

 * The central bank risks encouraging imports and further widening the trade gap if it supports the hryvnia. However, letting it float would remove an important anchor for domestic and foreign businesses in Ukraine's export-driven economy.   * Many people hold debt in foreign currency and would have to pay more to service it if the hryvnia weakened.

 * Consumers are extremely sensitive to currency movements -- they lost savings when the Soviet Union collapsed and again  through hyper inflation and a currency crisis in the 1990s that more than halved the hryvnia's value to about 4/$ and beyond.

 * Ukraine was forced to restructure its debts in 2000 and made the final payments on that restructuring just last year.

 FOREIGN DEBT

 Ukraine's foreign debt totalled just over $100 billion as of July 1, of which about $15 billion was government debt.

 * Analysts estimate Ukraine's 2009 external financing requirement to be $55-66 billion, of which $32-40 billion is in the private sector. Foreign banks own 40-42 percent of total banking assets and 25 percent of short-term banking debt is owed to parent banks.  (Compiled by Sabina Zawadzki)

title: UPDATE 4-IMF approves $16.5 bln Ukraine loan, first tranche
text:
(Adds comments by head of Ukrainian central bank council)

WASHINGTON/KIEV, Nov 6 (Reuters) - The IMF approved a $16.5 billion loan program for Ukraine to ease strains from the global financial crisis and officials expressed confidence on Thursday that the country was out of the woods.

The International Monetary Fund, in a statement issued late on Wednesday, said it would immediately disburse $4.5 billion to the government under the two-year loan agreement.

"The authorities' programme is designed to help stabilise the domestic financial system against a backdrop of global deleveraging and a domestic crisis of confidence, and to facilitate adjustment of the economy to a large terms-of-trade shock," the Fund said.

"The authorities' plan incorporates monetary and exchange rate policy shifts, banking recapitalization, and fiscal and incomes policy adjustments."

In Kiev, President Viktor Yushchenko welcomed the decision, taken after Ukraine's fractious parliament approved enabling legislation. He said it provided a "signal to the international community to boost the rating of trust in our country".

Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, the president's former ally turned rival, said the loan would "allow us to stabilise completely the financial situation in Ukraine".

The head of the central bank's policy-making council later said it was the bank's open-ended intervention that stabilised the hryvnia currency after it hit a historic low last week.

Daily intervention of up to $500 million, Petro Poroshenko said, had reduced demand for dollars and restored stability.

"Exports had earlier held foreign currency in anticipation of a higher (dollar) rate and dealers had earlier tried to make money on working the rates. But today we have a significantly reduced scope for speculative operations," he told reporters.

Poroshenko also said subsequent tranches of the IMF loan would depend on whether authorities formally requested them.

Disbursement of parts of IMF credits is generally linked to further review of conditions in the country receiving the funds.

RECESSION FORECAST

The IMF decision was issued along with forecast indicators predicting that Ukraine would sink into recession next year, with a 3 percent fall against 6 percent growth this year.

In a statement, Murilo Portugal, IMF deputy managing director, said Ukraine's economy, especially its banking system, was under severe stress, caused by a drop in global steel prices, the country's main export, and global financial turmoil.

He said Ukraine's programme would seek to restore financial and economic stability through a more flexible exchange rate regime with targeted interventions, so-called 'pre-emptive' recapitalisation of banks, and tighter monetary policy.

"The flexible exchange rate regime, backed by an appropriate monetary policy and foreign exchange intervention, will help absorb external shocks and avoid disorderly exchange market developments," Portugal said.

"The recent unification of official and market exchange rates should increase clarity about the regime."

Exchange controls recently imposed, he said, would be phased out as confidence returns to the economy.

Ukraine's central bank has been intervening since early October to bolster the hryvnia currency. It began offering buy-sell rates for currencies this week after previously only selling or buying a currency.

Portugal said as credit pressures abate, tighter monetary policy will be needed to guard against inflation.

He said the government's target of a balanced 2009 budget would be reviewed, although it could be achieved through expenditure restraint and a phased increase in energy tariffs.

Portugal said recapitalisation efforts for banks would ease liquidity pressures that could prolong an economic downturn.

"Decisive measures that have been taken to allocate public funds to recapitalise banks and to facilitate bank resolution processes will ensure that problems can be dealt with promptly," he said.

(Editing by Patrick Graham)

title: WRAPUP 1-Serbia to trim budget, Ukraine seeks IMF okay
text:
* Serbia promises to cut spending for IMF support

* Ukraine awaits approval of $16.5 billion bailout

* EBRD warns of recession in previously fast-growing ex-communist Europe

By Gordana Filipovic

BELGRADE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Serbia said on Tuesday it would cut its 2009 budget to get a safety line from the IMF and Ukraine appealed to the fund for approval of a $16.5 billion rescue plan to weather the global financial storm.

They were the latest central and eastern European states to look to the International Monetary Fund for help as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development [EBRD.UL] warned a number of countries in the region were sure to hit recession.

Analysts say that Serbia, a small but open economy heavily reliant on external borrowing and investment, is not as exposed to the global crisis as Iceland, Ukraine or Hungary, hit by market turmoil in recent weeks.

Yet Serbia's dinar was the biggest loser in an investor flight from the emerging European assets last month that has raised fears that economies in the Balkans and on the Baltic Sea could hit trouble as the crisis filters through.

"We are still in talks with the International Monetary Fund about the (2009) budget," Deputy Prime Minister Mladjan Dinkic said. "Our position is to have the precautionary programme and not to draw the money unless it is really necessary."

A top government official said later in the day the IMF was demanding that Belgrade cut its fiscal gap to 1.5 percent of GDP from 2.7 percent this year by freezing real wages and pensions.

Both spoke a day after the Finance Ministry said Serbia was negotiating a stand-by deal with the IMF, with analysts estimating the country's needs up to two billion euros in a worst case scenario if global financial turmoil triggered panic.

UKRAINE APPEALS

"As a consequence of the financial crisis, it is now clear that much of the region faces major challenges and recession in a number of countries is already certain," EBRD chief Thomas Mirow told the European Parliament on Tuesday.

Earlier on Tuesday, Ukraine's President Viktor Yushchenko told IMF Executive Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn he was "counting on support from the IMF to overcome the effects of the world financial crisis on the country's economy".

After days of domestic political bickering, the country's parliament last week backed a package of laws to stabilise the country's finances and the banking system, vital to win the IMF financial backing.

The IMF's board was due to consider the credit in a meeting in Washington later on Tuesday.

Yushchenko also called for help from the World Bank, which is considering a $500 million credit for Ukraine. The country's central bank has intervened on a daily basis for two weeks to prop up the hryvnia after it hit a record low to the dollar.

Just months ago, a new pro-western government, fast-expanding economy and a firm and stable currency had also bolstered hopes Serbia was set to catch up with its more prosperous neighbours.

Officials have repeatedly dismissed the need for the country to reach out to the IMF, but agree that its backing could be a welcome signal to investors that reforms will stay on track as the Balkan country plans to apply for EU membership next year.

Jurij Bajec, economic advisor to the Serbian prime minister, said both the IMF and the Serbian government seemed concerned the impact of the global crisis could be more serious than initially thought.

"On one hand, there is a problem to finance the budget deficit," Bajec told Reuters. "On the other hand, the IMF is concerned about Serbia's external vulnerability and ability to finance 500-600 million euros a month in external liabilities."

Serbia's commitment to belt-tightening may be challenged in parliament, where the opposition is demanding that the ruling coalition meet all pre-election pledges, including higher wages and pensions.

"Serbia has two alternatives. One is to do nothing and let the public spending and the current account deficit grow, which lead to inflation and the adjustment in the exchange rate," central bank governor Radovan Jelasic told an investor forum. "The alternative is to freeze spending." (Additional reporting by Ivana Sekularac in Belgrade and Ron Popeski in Kiev; editing by Patrick Graham)

KIEV, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank will continue to intervene in the currency markets by buying and selling unlimited amounts of dollars, First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov told Reuters on Friday.

The central bank has been intervening every day for the past two weeks to try to prop the hryvnia, which slipped on Wednesday to a historic low of 7.2 to the dollar. It has since bounced back and was quoted at 5.86-5.95 on Friday.

Shapovalov said a requirement for banks to sell dollars at the rate at which they had bought them from the central bank would remain in force for several days. It offered to sell dollars at 5.95 hryvnias on Friday and at 6.05 on Thursday.

"We intervened yesterday, selling $500 million dollars. We therefore demand that if they bought from central bank reserves, they then meet client orders at that rate and their profit is the commission," he said.

"Today, we will send a letter saying that dollars bought today at 5.95 hryvnias have to be sold at 5.95 ... This is meant to calm the market. At the very least, this will happen today, tomorrow, and then we will see."

A central bank official said the bank had sold just under $40 million on Friday -- a sharp fall from Thursday's $500 million.

MARKETS CALM

President Viktor Yushchenko's office on Thursday criticised the bank's failure to stabilise the hryvnia despite selling $5 billion in the past three weeks.

Central bank reserves were worth $37.5 billion at the end of September. Officials have since then have said the reserves stood at $33-34 billion.

Dealers said offering unlimited funds had helped calm the market and brought the interbank rate up to the intervention rate -- something the bank's intervention had failed to manage in the past two weeks.

"The central bank clearly managed to calm the market. Following the central bank were other sellers," one dealer said.

Dealers and analysts had earlier said the hryvnia slid to record lows because the central bank had not met all dollar demand, while at the same time providing large amounts of refinancing -- thus giving banks the means to buy the U.S. currency.

KIEV, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Ukraine's parliament, mired in a long-running political row over a snap election, failed again on Tuesday to consider legislation needed to secure an IMF bailout programme of credits worth $16.5 billion.

Supporters of Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who opposes the election, charged up to the chairman's rostrum to prevent what they suspected would be a move to put election finance on the agenda alongside the IMF legislation.

Chairman Arseniy Yatsenyuk acknowledged deadlock over the agenda. He scolded deputies for blocking debate -- and approval of the International Monetary Fund credit officials say is needed to stabilise Ukraine's financial and banking systems.

"Everything came down to what was supposed to be examined first -- measures to tackle the crisis or a bill on holding an early election. And that's where matters have ended," he said.

"I understand that adopting the package of measures will not save us from everything ... We cannot subdue the economic and political crisis entirely. But let's set down as a priority the economic and political baselines."

Parliament, the chairman said, would be called into session on Wednesday to approve the measures in a first reading. Parties would then submit proposals for a second and final reading.

Yatsenyuk had asked deputies to consider a compromise package to satisfy what are believed to be IMF demands for the credit. Analysts say these include a balanced 2009 budget, greater currency flexibility and banking sector reforms.

The IMF and the government announced preliminary agreement on the loan package at the weekend. The Fund has made no comment on what conditions it has set and it was unclear whether the package under consideration met the demands.

Markets remained unimpressed by the agreement. The hryvnia currency traded at 6.3-6.4 to the dollar, close to its all-time low, despite daily central bank intervention.

Ukraine was pitched into its latest bout of political upheaval by President Viktor Yushchenko's dissolution of parliament last month and call for a December election, which would be the third in as many years in the ex-Soviet state.

Both Tymoshenko and Yushchenko, allies from the pro-Western 2004 "Orange Revolution" now turned rivals, want quick adoption of the anti-crisis measures to secure IMF help.

A government statement said Tymoshenko and IMF Managing Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn had spoken by telephone, urged parliament to act promptly and called for political stability.

But Tymoshenko says an election would be "criminal" amid the world crisis. Her allies vow to disrupt debate until they get assurances no move will be made to finance the contest.

title: WRAPUP 1-Ukraine PM risks losing IMF credit: president's aide
text:
* Presidential aide criticises PM

* Hryvnia hits record low, stock dive 4 pct

* Fitch sees threat to Ukraine rating

By Ron Popeski

KIEV, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An aide to Ukraine's president accused Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko on Monday of putting a big IMF credit at risk by linking quick approval of financial legislation with the country's long-running political upheaval.

The International Monetary Fund and Ukraine agreed on Sunday on a $16.5 billion credit for the ex-Soviet state, subject to approval of financial measures by the fractious parliament, which was blockaded last week by the prime minister's allies.

Tymoshenko and her supporters last week blocked discussion of the financial package for four days in order to prevent inclusion in it of any funding for disputed early elections, called by Yushchenko for next month.

Markets were unimpressed by news of the credit. The hryvnia currency sank to a record low, prompting the central bank to abandon a corridor to control its movements.

The tiny stock market plunged a further four percent and credit default swaps, an indication of risk that Ukraine could default on debts, rose to 2,600 basis points from 300 in August.

Ratings agency Fitch said further tumbles in the currency could put Ukraine's rating under pressure, but acknowledged that the IMF accord could help restore confidence.

Parliamentary approval of financial legislation is critical to the deal. The chamber is due to consider the legislation on Tuesday after a weekend of talks to produce a compromise package to ease the effects of the world financial crisis.

But Ukraine also remains gripped by political turbulence sparked by President Viktor Yushchenko's dissolution of parliament and call for a new election.

Presidential aide Andriy Goncharuk said the prime minister was acting against the national interest by lobbying at the same time for the cancellation of the December election.

"It is a pity that the position of the prime minister's office reduces the chances for the country to receive the first tranche of the credit awaited so long by the financial system," Goncharuk said in a statement on the president's Web site.

"An election must be seen as the sole way to resolve the political crisis, not a catalyst for economic problems. The lack of a viable parliament is a much greater risk for the country than a quick campaign and formation of a stable majority."

Yushchenko, long at odds with Tymoshenko, called the election after the collapse last month of a coalition of groups led by him and the prime minister.

"CRIMINAL" ELECTION

Tymoshenko says an election would be "criminal" in the current financial crisis and her backers last week prevented any discussion in parliament of funding for the poll.

With no let up in political turmoil, the hryvnia currency slumped to a record low of 6.2 to the dollar despite the central bank's now routine intervention.

Central bank council chief Petro Poroshenko announced the elimination of a newly-widened 4.554-5.346 corridor. He said intervention had sapped 10 percent of reserves and indicated Ukraine would seek a further $3 billion in international loans.

Analysts have expressed concerned over the ability of the government, firms and banks to refinance.

The head of the IMF mission which has been in Kiev for more than a week praised authorities' resolve, while making no reference to conditions attached to the loan.

"I must say that they (the government and central bank) are being extremely proactive, they have been working on policies in parliament," Ceyla Pazarbasioglu told top officials.

Analysts believe the Fund wants a balanced budget, greater flexibility on currency markets and banking sector reforms.

Tymoshenko said she hoped the chamber would come to a consensus and approve the "anti-crisis package" without delay.

"We fully believe that tomorrow, Tuesday, a package of legislative measures to combat the crisis must be adopted in parliament," she told reporters.

Yushchenko, speaking during a visit to Turkey, also hoped parliament would act quickly on the package.

Parliament's chairman, Arseniy Yatsenyuk, last week said failure to pass the measures could imperil talks with the IMF.

On Monday, he said discussions were proceeding to narrow differences and produce a compromise document.

"There is so far no agreement on a bill and we aren't going to get one," he said.

"My experts are meeting those from different groups to put together the shortest possible document from the 40 pages proposed by the government in order to increase the likelihood of it being approved."

Oleksander Okhrymenko, senior adviser to Ukrgazbank, said the IMF deal might reduce some panic, but he remained sceptical.

"Those who follow the politics and parliament clearly believe that we will never receive the money because it is most unlikely the laws will be adopted," he said. (Additional reporting by Natalya Zinets, Sabina Zawadzki, Yuri Kulikov and by Zerin Elci in Ankara; Editing by Jon Boyle)

title: FACTBOX-Key facts on Ukraine's finances and politics
text:
Oct 20 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko expressed confidence on Monday that talks with the International Monetary Fund would prove successful and that Ukraine would secure "substantial" financial assistance. [UA-M]

Officials have suggested the IMF could lend Ukraine a sum ranging from $10-14 billion.

Following are key facts about why Ukraine is vulnerable to heightened risk aversion among international investors.

POLITICS

* Ukraine has been plagued by political turbulence since "Orange Revolution" protests in 2004 brought to power President Viktor Yushchenko and a team committed to moving closer to the West and joining NATO and the European Union.

Rows pitting Yushchenko against his former ally Yulia Tymoshenko, who twice served as his prime minister, undermined the "Orange" camp and brought down governments. The president dissolved parliament this month and called a December parliamentary election, the third in as many years.

* Upheaval -- and trouble forming a stable ruling coalition -- reflect Ukraine's longstanding division into the nationalist west and centre, which looks to the EU and United States, and the Russian-speaking east and south, friendlier towards Moscow.

* Relations with Russia, bumpy throughout the post-Soviet period, have sunk to unprecedented lows over Yushchenko's denunciation of Moscow's military intervention in Georgia. Ukraine depends heavily on Moscow for energy supplies.

CURRENCY POLICY

* The hryvnia currency hit an all-time low of 5.9/$ on Oct. 8, weakened by growing global risk aversion and regional tensions after Russia's conflict with Georgia.

* In mid-2008 the hryvnia had strengthened as far 4.5/$, after the central bank abandoned a policy of keeping it in a corridor of 5.00-5.06 per dollar within a 4.95-5.25 band.

* The central bank's council and executive board have sent mixed messages about future actions and clashed in May over revaluing the hryvnia's official rate. The board appears to take less notice of the currency band, set by the council.

FINANCES

* The central bank has said foreign exchange reserves as of the end of September at $37.5 billion covered 3.7 months of imports.

* The current account deficit was running at 7.9 percent of GDP in the first half of this year, up from 4.2 percent in 2007.

* Analysts based outside Ukraine forecast its current account deficit at $21-25 billion, or 10-12 percent of gross domestic product, by year-end; Ukraine-based analysts give lower forecasts of about 6 percent of GDP.

* Prices for Ukraine's steel exports are forecast to drop, while Russia's Gazprom has suggested next year's price for gas imports could soar to $400 per 1,000 cubic metres from $179.50 now.

CURRENCY RISKS

* The central bank risks encouraging imports and further widening the trade gap if it supports the hryvnia. However, letting it float would remove an important anchor for domestic and foreign businesses in Ukraine's export-driven economy. * Many people hold debt in foreign currency and would have to pay more to service it if the hryvnia weakened.

* Consumers are extremely sensitive to currency movements -- they lost savings when the Soviet Union collapsed and again through hyper inflation and a currency crisis in the 1990s that more than halved the hryvnia's value to about 4/$ and beyond.

* Ukraine was forced to restructure its debts in 2000 and made the final payments on that restructuring just last year.

FOREIGN DEBT

Ukraine's foreign debt totalled just over $100 billion as of July 1, of which about $15 billion was government debt.

* The central bank has said it expects banking sector debt worth $1-1.2 billion to mature in the final quarter of this year.

* Citi analysts estimate Ukraine's 2009 external financing requirement to be $55-66 billion, of which $32-40 billion is in the private sector. Foreign banks own 40-42 percent of total banking assets and 25 percent of short-term banking debt is owed to parent banks. (Compiled by Sabina Zawadzki; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: UPDATE: Ukraine Central Banker: Won't Fight Hyrvnia Trend
text:
(Adds more quotes on inflation, slowdown)

By Alexander Kolyandr

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

KIEV (Dow Jones)--Ukraine's central bank won't intervene in foreign exchange markets to "combat the trend" if the hryvnia weakens, the chairman of the National Bank of Ukraine's council said Friday.

In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires, Petro Poroshenko said the central bank would act to smooth sharp moves in the currency, and will accept moves of 10% up or down against the U.S. dollar.

Poroshenko said Ukraine has $38 billion of foreign exchange reserves, enough to cover import for 4 months.

He said that those reserves will not be used to "combat the trend of the national currency."

"We don't exclude that the National Bank will intervene when demand for currency rises sharply," he said. "We have enough reserves to flatten peaks, but are not going to fight the trend.".

The hryvnia has fallen 12 percent against the dollar since the beginning of September.

Poroshenko said the NBU will be selective if there is a need to support the country's banking system, providing liquidity if needed, but not bailing out banks that have made bad lending decisions.

"We have no aim to save all the banks," he said. "If the root of a problem of a bank is a lack of liquidity, we have no problems with refinancing it, but if the root of the problem is imprudent credit policy, a sharp rise in defaulted borrowers, it's bank's own problems and taxpayers shouldn't pay for unprofessional management of the bank."

Poroshenko said the level of deposit insurance may be increased. It now stands at 50,000 hryvnia, which Poroshenko said covers about 90% of deposits. He said it may be increased to include up to 96% of all the country's deposits.

Poroshenko said the added uncertainty that a fresh round of elections in December will bring could be the trigger for problems in the banking system.

"The election campaign may provoke a run on banks, but even in this case the National Bank has instruments to stabilize deposit situation," he said.

He also said that the government should take swift and strict measures to combat the financial crisis. He said that a balanced budget and "a pragmatic social policy" are needed for 2009 and privatization of telecommunications, power generating and petrochemical companies should be "unblocked".

He also said that the ban on selling land should be lifted, as it would attract investment in Ukraine's agriculture. Poroshenko said that Ukraine's banking system "feels better than the systems of many Western countries and Russia", as the country "has no complicated instruments, no derivatives, the currency exchange policy isn't fully liberalized and low ratings by the rating agencies prevented companies from over-borrowing".

He accepted that the country suffers from a liquidity problem, but said that the central bank "has instruments and reserves to manage liquidity and keep stability".

Poroshenko admitted that there is already a slowdown in Ukraine's construction, real estate and metal sectors. The latter provides a lion share of the country's hard currency, but the fall in metal prices "doesn't put the country's trade balance in danger, as it will be offset by the drop in prices of oil", which Ukraine imports.

Poroshenko also said that he expects inflation to reach 19% to 19.5% by the end of the year.

-By Alexander Kolyandr, Dow Jones Newswires; +44 20 7842 9410; alexander.kolyandr@dowjones.com [ 10-10-08 1555GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine  cbank offers dlrs, loans, stocks halted
text:
(Adds intervention, dealers, president adviser)

KIEV, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sold dollars on Friday at 5.0 hryvnias for the third day running to support the currency and continued to refinance banks, dealers and the bank said.

The hryvnia strengthened to 4.98-5.30, within a newly widened forecast of 4.554-5.346. It hit an all-time low on Wednesday at 5.9 hryvnias, rising only after intervention.

"The central bank sold dollars and we can say that thanks to that the hryvnia strengthened," one dealer said. Traders had said in recent days that despite the interventions, the hryvnia remained stubbornly weak.

Local media estimated that the central bank sold $475 million in Thursday's intervention, $200 million a day earlier and $343 million last Friday.

The central bank never reveals the values. Dealers were not able to assess how much the bank sold on Friday.

A senior aide to President Viktor Yushchenko suggested that the central bank had not intervened enough.

"Stability has to be supported through instruments such as high liquidity and central bank participation on the currency market, which unfortunately is not what we always see," said the deputy head of the president's secretariat, Andriy Goncharu.

"The central bank's intervention have always been positive from the point of view of balancing the market," he told a briefing.

REFINANCING

As the currency remains weak and lending grinds to a halt on global markets, analysts are concerned whether Ukrainian banks are able to refinance their debts.

Central bank data showed it spent a further 1.34 billion hryvnias (about $270 million) on Thursday to refinance banks, including a 1 billion hryvnia one-year loan at 12 percent to an unnamed bank.

This week, the bank has already lent 1.5 billion hryvnias to Nadra bank, in the process of repaying a $100 million Eurobond and a $130 million syndicated loan, and 1 billion hryvnias to an unnamed bank.

It has previously said it would loan 5 billion hryvnias to the country's sixth largest bank, Prominvest, placed in receivership this week following an ownership dispute that led to a run on the bank.

Total refinancing in the first nine days of the month amounted to 7.79 billion hryvnias ($1.6 billion) -- more than the total for September at 5.96 billion hryvnias.

Alfa Bank Ukraine, part of Russia's Alfa Group, was the latest bank to confirm it received refinancing in recent days, getting 440 million hryvnias. It successfully paid up a syndicated loan of $61 million late last month.

The credit crisis has also led many to wonder how the government will finance its projected $3.9 billion budget deficit this year. But finance ministry data showed a budget surplus of $649 million after the first nine months of the year.

As stock markets around the world fell dramatically, Ukraine's PFTS bourse was one of several to shut down completely until Monday.

The index has lost 41 percent since the start of September, when investors began pulling out of the region and 73 percent since the New Year after rising over 130 percent last year. (Writing by Sabina Zawadzki; editing by Chris Pizzey and Andy Bruce)

title: UPDATE 3- Ukraine  cbank offers dlrs after record hryvnia low
text:
(Adds intervention, central bank chief, dealers)

KIEV, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sold dollars on Wednesday at 5.0 hryvnias to lift the 12-year-old currency from an all-time low of 5.9/$, dealers said.

Central Bank Chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh was quoted as saying that the bank would sell dollars at auctions which could take place every day to ensure firms could buy key imports. He also said Ukrainian banks had no problems with liquidity.

The hryvnia began sliding at the beginning of September when the impact of the global financial crisis on emerging markets became sharper, as investors scrambled for dollars and sentiment towards the region turned sour after Russia's war with Georgia.

The central bank's deputy chairman, Oleksander Savchenko, said on Tuesday the bank would intervene to strengthen the hryvnia to 5.0/$ "very quickly". But the bank kept agitated dealers in suspense before making its offer.

"The bank sold a lot more than last time," one dealer said. "If it sold to all banks, then we'll probably hold to this level of 5.5-5.6."

The central bank last intervened on Friday, selling $342 million for the first time since February at 5.0 hryvnias.

The dealer said not all demand had been met by the central bank's sales but the consequent stable level should be a sign to exporters to sell dollars and not wait for a higher price.

"Theoretically, we should see some exporters, as long as they have something to sell," the dealer said.

Stelmakh told Interfax Ukraine news agency that the bank had bought billions of dollars in recent months and was now ready to sell them.

"We are going to carry out auctions to sell currency. But they will be based on the needs of (importers of) raw materials critical for our economy -- gas, oil, oil products and also the import of industrial equipment," Stelmakh said.

He said apart from the country's sixth largest bank, Prominvest, placed in receivership on Wednesday, [ID:nL8638256] "other banks have no problems with liquidity".

"The central bank will unquestionably support banks but on condition that the bank properly conducts its business."

CAUTIOUS DEALERS

Dealers made no connection between the hryvnia's weakness and political events in Ukraine, which is facing its third election in as many years after the collapse of the ruling coalition of parties linked to the 2004 "Orange Revolution".

President Viktor Yushchenko gave parties more time to find a solution after consultations, though politicians leaving a meeting on Wednesday said everyone appeared resigned to a snap poll.

One dealer said the central bank had sent banks a letter late on Tuesday warning them it had the authority to discipline them for irresponsible dollar rates at street exchange bureaux. (Additional reporting by Carolyn Cohn in London, writing by Sabina Zawadzki; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: UPDATE 2-Ukraine's hryvnia, stocks drop, CDS rocket
text:
(Adds cbank deputy head, analysts, more CDS, yields)

KIEV, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said it would intervene to strengthen the hryvnia to about 5.0 to the dollar after the currency sank on Tuesday to lows that weaker than those set during the 2004 "Orange Revolution".

Banking shares were hit on the PFTS exchange, which closed 8 percent down and almost 50 percent lower than Sept. 1, and the cost of insuring against a Ukrainian sovereign default rocketed as investors continued to flee emerging markets.

The hryvnia traded at 5.54-5.60 to the dollar, its lowest since February 2004. The central bank made no offer to sell dollars, according to Reuters data.

But that was about to change, Oleksander Savchenko, the deputy chairman of the central bank, said.

"We will support the hryvnia though intervention. We will intervene considerably and the hryvnia will return to its old level rather quickly," Savchenko told Fifth Channel television. He referred to 5.0 to the dollar as a favourable level.

The bank's council also widened its forecast band for the hryvnia for this year to 4.95 per dollar plus or minus 8 percent from 4.85 plus or minus 4 percent, bringing the band to 4.554-5.346.

"The central bank should keep to this band and has to start intervening tomorrow morning. The best it can do is to calm the market while they can," Unicredit analyst Dmitry Gourov said.

Savchenko's comments appeared to mark a change of heart at the central bank.

Its officials, including Savchenko, had indicated it would not intervene regularly to avoid boosting the current account gap and because the hryvnia was being battered by temporary factors.

Fitch cut Ukraine's outlook last month, warning of a higher risk of a currency crisis given the gaping current account deficit.

The bank has been building up record foreign currency reserves, but at just under $38 billion, some wonder whether that would be enough to shore up the hryvnia.

"What we do know is that the reserve coverage is below the bank's comfort zone with respect to imports. We don't know what tolerance they have," said Citi economist Ali Al-Eyd.

RECORD BROKEN

The cost of insuring against default or restructuring rose to record levels at 850-1,000 basis points, brokers said, meaning investors were quoted between $850,000 to $1 million a year for five years to insure against $10 million of debt.

CDS on Naftogaz, Ukraine's ailing state energy firm, were even higher at 1,700 basis points.

Investors typically become more cautious, demanding upfront payments in addition to annual payments, when credit default swaps reach around 1,000 bps.

Brokers started quoting Iceland's CDS on an upfront basis last week, shortly before the country went to Russia for a bail-out package for its banks.

Ukrainian yields, meanwhile, widened 133 basis points to 12.18 percent above U.S. treasury yields. The stock market closed 8.15 percent down at 319.67 points, bringing the loss since Sept. 1, when investors lost appetite for the region, to 47 percent. It suspended trading in seven companies, then in the whole index altogether for several hours.

Unicredit's unit Ukrsotsbank lost 24 percent and Raiffeisen's Bank Aval lost 23 percent. (Additional reporting by Natalya Zinets in Kiev and Carolyn Cohn in London, editing by Swaha Pattanaik)

title: Romania cbank may prop up leu near 4 per euro-analysts
text:
BUCHAREST, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Romania's central bank (BNR) could intervene this week to support the leu and shore up its inflation targets after the currency sank around 10 percent over the last month to an almost four-year low, analysts said on Monday.

With the leu bid at weaker than 3.9 per euro -- nudging a four-year low -- analysts have increasingly alluded to testing a "BNR put", in which they believe the bank will feel obliged to prop up the leu <EURRON=> at around 4.0 or 4.1 per euro.

It would be necessary, they say, to prevent a possible banking crisis. Because 55 percent of Romanian loans are in foreign currencies, firms and households could have trouble paying back loans if the leu slides more against the euro.

"The BNR has a lot to lose if EUR/RON rises substantially above the psychological level of 4.00. Therefore, the bank is likely step into the market, potentially already (this) week," said JP Morgan analyst Miroslav Plojhar.

Emerging European currencies have been pummelled as investors avoid risk and hoard cash following the downfall of major financial institutions, but none more than the leu.

On Monday morning, it shed 1.8 percent to 3.944 against the euro, following heavy losses at the end of last week.

Romania's more developed ex-communist peers -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- have seen their currencies slip 3.4 to 4.5 percent since Sept. 12 when U.S. bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, but analysts said their banks would keep to the sidelines because they were still relatively strong.

For Romania, the financial crisis has heightened concerns, voiced by rating agencies and the International Monetary Fund, that the country is more vulnerable than its peers because of a vast current account deficit, high rates of hard currency borrowing and inadequate fiscal and wage policies.

The fear is the Romanian economy could be destabilised if global cash flows and foreign investment dry up and are no longer sufficient to plug the double-digit external deficit.

"They should intervene to stop the depreciation because otherwise this will have a major impact on inflation and will throw inflationary expectations in the air," said Ionut Dumitru, head of research at Raiffeisen Bank in Bucharest.

Inflation is expected to fall to around 6 percent in December, still above the central bank's 2.8-4.8 percent target.

The bank kept its benchmark rate on hold at 10.25 percent at its last meeting in September, but analysts said another hike may be on the cards due to pledges by major parties to loosen fiscal policy ahead of a Nov. 30 parliamentary election.

Elsewhere in the region, Serbia's central bank intervened to tame dinar losses after Ukraine stepped in to buy local currency at 5 hryvnias to the dollar <UAH=> on Friday.

"We've seen interventions in Ukraine, Serbia. The next to come is Romania," said Elisabeth Gruie, currency strategist at BNP Paribas. (Editing by Victoria Main)

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine  cbank sells dlrs, cautious on  intervention
text:
(Adds cbank comments, intervention)

KIEV, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sold $342 million in dollars at 5.0 hryvnias on Friday but said it would not intervene systematically on the interbank market, the bank's top adviser said.

The hryvnia has weakened considerably in recent weeks from around 4.5 to the dollar in May and June, hitting a 3-1/2-year low of 5.11-5.12 on Wednesday. It had been trading at 5.18-5.26 per dollar when the bank offered to sell dollars earlier.

"We sold $342 million today," central bank adviser Valery Lytvytsky told Reuters. "We don't want waves, especially if those waves are psychological ... We wanted to psychologically remove nervousness from the market.

"This does not mean that we will systematically intervene on the market," he said. "We will come to the market again when a number of factors give us a reason."

He said factors included the "psychological mood" of the market, the global financial situation, needs of large companies such as state energy firm Naftogaz which needs dollars to pay for gas, foreign investor activity, liquidity and the budget.

"We wanted to give some sort of positive signal, but wanted to warn you, do not expect the old tune from us. Today, there is a new tune and this is crossing over to a flexible exchange rate," he said.

The central bank let the hryvnia fluctuate more freely in February after it abandoned a three-year policy of keeping it in a strict corridor 5.00-5.06 to the dollar.

The hryvnia steadily crept up to the dollar, but lost all of those gains as investors lost the taste for risk and scrambled for dollars at a time of higher tensions with Russia and a domestic political crisis.

Several central bank officials have indicated in the past week that the bank may not strictly keep to its view that the hryvnia should be kept to between 4.656-5.044/$.

Central Bank Council head Petro Poroshenko said he saw no reason for a significant drop in the hryvnia, on the day international ratings agency Fitch cut its outlook on Ukraine to negative, citing rising risk of a currency crisis.

On Thusrday, the central bank's deputy chairman, Oleksander Savchenko, said the bank would not prop up the currency for now because much of the weakness was temporary and any such move could deepen the current account gap by stimulating imports.

The bank on Thursday released a statement to say it would not spend its reserves when speculators were in the market, but could intervene to help with purchases of crucial imports and payments for external debt. (Writing by Sabina Zawadzki, Editing by Andy Bruce)

title: ANALYSIS-Ukraine crisis a setback for EU, NATO bids
text:
BRUSSELS, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Renewed crisis in Ukraine is a fresh setback for its EU ambitions and those who want it to join NATO, despite growing concern about Russian moves to roll back Western influence after intervening in Georgia, analysts say.

A shaky coalition between President Viktor Yushchenko and Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko collapsed on Wednesday, less than a week before an EU-Ukraine summit at which Kiev has been seeking a clear signal it can one day join the European Union.

Yushchenko wants to move his strategically important country towards the EU and NATO but bickering between him and Tymoshenko has stalled reforms in the former Soviet republic of 47 million.

"It's incredibly bad timing," said Andrew Wilson of the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank.

"The inability to keep domestic housekeeping in order is the very reason many EU states argue against Ukraine. It's not just the traditional EU divide about whether or not to offend Russia, but the genuine question about reform capacity and the short-term future of Ukraine."

EU diplomats said Tuesday's summit in the French town of Evian was expected to offer Ukraine some concessions, including talks on long-term moves to ease visa requirements.

It may also designate a broad pact governing ties as an "Association Agreement" -- wording that can imply the possibility of future membership.

However, they said divisions within the bloc meant it would fall short of any explicit statement making clear Ukraine could one day join the 27-nation European Union.

EU states including Britain, Sweden and former communist countries such as Poland want such a statement. "But it's not where the EU as a whole is right now," an EU diplomat said.

An explicit offer is opposed by the Benelux countries, and Germany and Italy are also not keen, given waning public support for further EU expansion, Kiev's poor record on EU-related reforms and a desire to avoid further straining ties with Moscow, a key supplier of energy to Europe.

The political infighting in Kiev has prevented the government adopting a unified approach to inflation, which rose to more than 30 percent in May and is still high at 26 percent, and divided the central bank as it revalued the currency.

UKRAINE VITAL FOR EU STRATEGY

Analysts say Ukraine is vital to long-term EU security and economic strategy and should be encouraged on its path towards Europe, especially in the light of Russia's attempt to counter Western influence with its intervention in Georgia.

"Regardless of the political turmoil in Ukraine, this is the right time to reach out and offer more," said Wilson. "Russia is trying to send out a clear sphere-of-influence message and we need to push back."

Russia was incensed by the promise of eventual NATO membership to Ukraine and Georgia, another former Soviet republic, and many see this as the motive behind its intervention in Georgia last month.

Regional analyst Tomas Valasek said the upheaval in Kiev was a clear setback for those who wished to see Ukraine join NATO, given the possibility of a new coalition involving Tymoshenko, who was lukewarm about alliance membership, and former Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovich, who opposed it.

But Valasek, from the Centre for European Reform think-tank, said the EU needed to clarify its message to Ukraine.

"It was important before the war in Georgia and it's become more important," he said. "It's in EU interest to have a zone of stable, democratic countries on its eastern borders and it has to be willing to run the risk of ruffling Russian feathers."

He called Ukraine the EU's most important neighbour because of it size, location and ability to influence progress in other strategically important countries.

"If it can successfully 'Europeanise', if it can become rich, prosperous and free, it will clearly demonstrate to the Central Asian republics, to Azerbaijan and to Moldova and others, that it's possible to be a former Soviet republic and a modern Western country," Valasek said.

"It will show that there is nothing inevitable about former Soviet republics always being in the Russian orbit. That's why it's important for the EU to get it right."

title: UPDATE 1- Ukraine  C.Bank  intervenes , alters official  FX  rate
text:
(adds new official rate, details)

KIEV, May 29 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank on Thursday altered the hryvnia currency's official rate, proceeding with a new policy of flexibility on the market after three years of defending a set rate.

In an announcement on its Internet site www.bank.gov.ua("http://www.bank.gov.ua"), the bank said the official rate of 4.852 hryvnias to the dollar would take effect from Friday, against the previous rate of 4.85 which had applied since the currency was revalued on May 22.

The announcement came after the central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Thursday, buying dollars at 4.84 hryvnias, compared with 4.80 at which it stepped into the market on May 23.

"The central bank is proceeding with transactions, but the dollar rose immediately after it indicated its readiness to buy," one dealer said.

"The dollar was trading yesterday and this morning at 4.715/4.73 and now it is about 4.8 and higher."

The central bank had maintained the hryvnia in a corridor of 5.0-5.06 until recent months, but revalued the currency on May 22 at 4.8 and began buying dollars at that level last week for the first time since September 2007.

The dollar had fallen on the interbank market to between 4.5 and 4.6 hryvnias in the days preceding the revaluation.

The bank's top adviser, Valery Lytvytsky, said last week the revaluation was an indication the bank now wanted to introduce a measure of flexibility on the interbank market.

COMPROMISE

Dealers believed the higher bid indicated the central bank's board was seeking a compromise with its policy-making council, which had vetoed the revaluation and called for a return to the previous official rate of 5.05.

Council head Petro Poroshenko said the board first had to agree with its members on new limits within a long-established broader corridor of 4.95-5.25 to the dollar before proceeding with a revaluation.

But the board overturned the council's veto, with central bank chief Volodymyr Stelmakh saying market realities prompted the board to go forward with the revaluation.

Ukraine's parliament summoned both Stelmakh and Poroshenko for an explanation of currency policy and urged the board and council to find a compromise.

"I believe the two sides have started to work out an agreement and find an acceptable rate," said one dealer. "I would not be surprised to see the dollar rate climb next week depending on what sort of corridor is agreed."

Poroshenko said on Monday new guidelines for a corridor would be worked out within two weeks.

Stelmakh is scheduled to hold a news conference on Friday.

Analysts said they expected the high end of the corridor to be raised beyond 4.95, while the lower end of 5.25 is seen kept intact.

An anticipated worsening of the nation's trade balance and expected new rises in the price of gas imports made any further rise in the hryvnia's value unlikely, analysts said.

"The historical trend in Ukraine is clear -- large purchases of dollars in the autumn by importers," said one dealer. "We believe demand for the dollar will be high." (Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Leika Kihara)

title: Ukraine  cbank fails to  intervene  as hryvnia jumps
text:
KIEV, March 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's hryvnia currency firmed against the dollar to its strongest since August 2005 without any intervention, far exceeding the 5.00/$ level at which the central bank normally steps in, dealers said on Friday.   

The bank has bought or sold dollars since 2005 to guard the hryvnia <UAH=> at 5.00-5.06/$, and had adopted a wider corridor of 4.95-5.25, which the hryvnia also crossed on Friday to peak at 4.915 to the dollar.   

No comment was available from the central bank on Friday. Two central bank officials said earlier this week that there was no question of revaluation at the moment, despite Ukraine's soaring inflation rate and the dollar's drop in the past two weeks to record lows against the euro.   

Both said revaluation would hit exports, exacerbating Ukraine's trade gap which boosted the current account deficit threefold last year.   

Dealers said they were left confused as to why the bank had not intervened, especially after numerous statements in recent weeks by officials that the bank is not considering revaluation or any other change in its foreign exchange policy.   

"There was an element of uncertainty on the interbank market due to the absence of reaction from the central bank," Interbusiness Consulting brokerage said.   

"This causes a panicked mood both among market participants and citizens as to the future rate of the dollar to the hryvnia, which in turn opens the door to unjustified speculation."   

The central bank is known to have left the currency alone when it slips beyond the tight band, but only when it is sure the situation would return back to normal soon.   

"Why didn't the bank intervene? What happened? It's difficult to say. The spreads were really wide, there was speculation on the market, everything," said one dealer.   

"The dollar supply was higher than the demand, but not to such an extent for the rate to rise so high."   

The hryvnia strengthened beyond its ceiling last Friday, when the bank also did not intervene, but dealers assumed the currency would drop back into its bracket.   

"Panic began to grow from the start of this week. People from the small banks began saying that managers ordered to annul currency positions, because there would be a revaluation," said another dealer. (Reporting by Natalya Zinets; Writing by Sabina Zawadzki; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

KIEV, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Ukraine's leaders on Friday appeared to have reached a consensus on the rate of the hryvnia currency in the coming months, ruling out the appreciation some officials had previously demanded.  

Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko said she saw no grounds for any significant rise in the currency.  

The central bank, which has been buying dollars for weeks at a rate of about 5.0 hryvnias to keep the currency steady, said it would intervene as dictated by the economy. It predicted only "minor" variations from a rate of 5.05 to the dollar.  

"There will be no major jump in the hryvnia on the basis of data we now have from the central bank," Tymoshenko told a news conference. "There are no grounds, economic or financial, for upward movement. I am convinced the hryvnia will be stable."  

Tymoshenko earlier this year had called for the central bank to ease its grip on the foreign exchange to allow the hryvnia to rise to fight inflation -- now running at about 14 percent.  

Dealers and some Western economists had also viewed a rise in the hryvnia's rate as inevitable in view of projected capital flows -- from exports and receipts from privatisation.  

A central bank statement marking the ninth anniversary of the hryvnia's post-Soviet introduction, said its activity on the market "will be appropriate to the economic situation and act as a correction to sharp changes in the hryvnia's rate.  

"Up to the end of the year, minor variations are expected to the current rate of around 5.05 to the dollar," it said.  

In the latest trading session, the central bank intervened at 5.0 hryvnias as it has every day this week except on Tuesday, when it bought dollars at 5.01.  

But the bank refrained from its practice, adopted last month, of advising in advance its intervention rate and volumes. The hryvnia was quoted at at 4.985-4.995 in early trading.  

The bank, which keeps tight control of Ukraine's currency market, has been committed to preventing sharp upward movements in the hryvnia after engineering a three percent rise in a single day in April.  

It has also pledged for some time to liberalise rules that bar dealers from buying and selling in a single day, but no action has been taken.  

In her comments to reporters, Tymoshenko also said the 2006 budget provided for the hryvnia to be at a level of 5.01.

title: UPDATE 3-Ukraine backs away from hryvnia rise,wants euro peg
text:
(adds new central bank intervention, dealer quote)  

KIEV, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Ukraine's Economy Ministry appeared on Tuesday to abandon a campaign for a strong rise in the value of the hryvnia which the central bank had resisted, and proposed pegging the currency to the euro from 2007.  

The Economy Ministry said it now intended to use a rate of 5.05 hryvnias to the dollar in its forecasting for next year, weaker than the central bank's intervention rate.  

The ministry also proposed the euro peg, a new development in a debate about whether the ex-Soviet state should target a basket of currencies rather than just focus on the dollar.  

Economy Minister Serhiy Teryokhin, one of the strongest advocates of a more flexible hryvnia exchange rate, has repeatedly urged the central bank to allow the currency to rise as this would help the fight against inflation.  

But the central bank has resisted the pressure in a policy aimed at protecting the interests of exporters which provide the engine of economic growth. It has intervened almost daily to prevent any rapid climb in the hryvnia since it engineered a three percent jump at a single stroke last April.  

A bank official said last week the hryvnia's rate was optimal. On Tuesday, the central bank intervened to buy dollars at 5.01 hryvnias compared with the rate of 5.0 hryvnias to the dollar used in the past seven sessions.  

"The volume of interventions is low and many orders are still not covered," a dealer said. The central bank had previously set the volume of intervention at $10 million.  

The ministry statement appeared to indicate an agreement of sorts between the two sides. It said the hryvnia's rate depended on factors including the trade balance, currency regulations and the state of Ukraine's financial institutions.  

"It is for this reason that the Economy Ministry has worked out and tactically agreed on an average rate of 5.05 hryvnias per dollar in its 2006 macroeconomic forecasts," it said.  

"This takes into account that from 2007 the hryvnia will be pegged to the euro in accordance with the rules set down by the European Union." It gave no other details but the government has said that it wants the country to move closer to the EU before eventually joining the bloc.  

BASKET OF CURRENCIES?  

The Economy Ministry launched a debate earlier this year on whether Ukraine should change its policy by ending a rigid peg to the dollar and start targeting a basket of currencies.  

Teryokhin has also called on the central bank to raise the proportion of euros in its currency reserves.  

The central bank has said changes would depend on the structure of Ukraine's debt and trading obligations. Bank officials were not immediately available for comment on the ministry's statement.  

"Given the foreign trade structure of Ukraine and increasing Russian moves towards a EUR/USD RUB (euro/dollar rouble) basket, a Ukrainian move closer to EUR makes some sense, though a 100 percent EUR target would be extreme given the USD-linked nature of their exports," Bank Austria Creditanstalt said in a note.  

The central bank has failed so far to follow through on pledges to liberalise strict rules for market participants despite appeals from President Viktor Yushchenko, currency dealers and the International Monetary Fund.  

Analysts said the central bank had missed a chance to proceed with foreign exchange market liberalisation, given a recent spate of bad economic figures underscoring slowing growth and a worsening trade balance.  

"In the current situation, it is stupid to implement liberalisation. It is unclear what is going on. Macroeconomic data are bad, there are no signs of serious investments," said Glib Vishlynsky, senior analyst at GFk-USM.  

"Nobody needs currency volatility. Liberalisation will be delayed and the rate will be held stable."

title: UPDATE 2- Ukraine  cbank  intervenes , official says rate optimal
text:
(adds comments by top central bank official)  

KIEV, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Ukraine central bank on Thursday resumed purchases of dollars on the currency market it tightly controls and a top bank official described as "optimal" the rate of Ukraine's hyrvnia currency it has been defending.  

Anatoly Shapovalov, the bank's first deputy chairman, also predicted demand for dollars, now exceeded by supply, would soon pick up as autumn weather prompted energy purchases. He said the bank had enough reserves to prevent sharp currency movements.  

The central bank bought dollars at 5.0 hryvnias for the fifth consecutive session as it sought to uphold a competitive exchange rate for exporters.  

"Today we had what is now the standard situation," said one dealer. "Dollar supply exceeded demand and the central bank bought at 5.0 to the dollar."  

He said interbank deals were being struck at 4.97-4.995 -- as the market reopened after the Independence Day holiday.  

The central bank has long been committed to avoiding abrupt upward movements in the hryvnia. It oversaw a one-day three percent rise in late April, sapping market confidence, and has since intervened nearly every day to keep the hryvnia steady.  

Dealers said the central bank was only buying receipts from exporters. Other customers had to sell dollars more cheaply.  

Shapovalov told Reuters the central bank had concluded that it had found the right level for the currency.  

"There is pressure now but this is not coming from export earnings," he said.  

"We therefore look at the structure of inflows and conclude that this is the optimal rate. We look to see whether there is borrowing, credits, non-residents' funds. And there is no basis for a strengthening of the hryvnia."  

DEMAND FOR DOLLARS TO RISE  

Energy purchases in the autumn would "naturally push up demand. But I believe the reserves we have accumulated will be sufficient to prevent any sharp changes."  

The central bank launched trading with its now standard practice of issuing parameters for possible intervention at 5.0/5.06 hryvnias per dollar and set the indicative volume of intervention at $35 million. The market opened at 4.9740/4.9980.  

Some dealers say attempts to keep the hryvnia within certain limits would run up against a growing supply of dollars, particularly a probable influx of currency in response to plans to stage new privatisations of big industrial sites.  

The central bank has failed to make good on promises to liberalise market operations despite appeals from President Viktor Yushchenko, dealers and the International Monetary Fund.  

The central bank's former deputy head, Serhiy Yaryomenko, an advocate of tight market control who quit last week, told the daily Ekonomicheskiye Izvestiya that abandoning regulation would fuel inflation.  

"A rise in the hryvnia could stimulate inflation," he told the daily. "People will turn away from foreign currency on grounds that it has suddenly got cheaper and start buying property and durable goods."
