title: UPDATE 3-Ukraine C.Bank accuses banks of attacking hryvnia
text:
(adds more comment, fresh central bank intervention)  

KIEV, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank on Tuesday accused a number of banks with foreign capital of launching speculative attacks on the hryvnia currency and threatened to bar them from the market unless they stopped.  

The central bank, committed for months to avoiding abrupt upward movements in the hryvnia's value, intervened again on the market it closely controls, buying dollars at 5.0 -- a rate unchanged for four sessions.  

A central bank statement accused the banks of hatching a "plot" to destabilise the market by trying to sell unreasonable amounts of foreign currency on the market.  

But dealers dismissed the statement as groundless and unhelpful. Some described it as little more than bluster.  

"An analysis of events in recent months on the currency market shows that specific banks have been trying to conduct improper operations by offering to sell large amounts of foreign currency which they did not have available," the central bank said in the statement on its website  www.bank.gov.ua ("http://www.bank.gov.ua").  

"Unfortunately, such actions are mainly carried out by specific Ukrainian banks with foreign capital, in agreement with foreign banks," the central bank added. It did not name any banks.  

"This can be seen as a plot aimed not so much at benefitting from speculation but rather at driving the foreign currency market into instability and fuelling inflation."  

The central bank said it viewed these actions as "speculative attacks with the aim of deliberately destabilising the rate of the national currency".  

Out of an overall total of 163 banks in Ukraine, 22 have foreign capital including nine which are 100 percent foreign-owned.  

"This is a particularly heavy-handed way of verbally intervening," said Sonal Desai, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein in Milan. "There's an escalation in rhetoric, which is trying to prevent the inflows from occurring."  

ECONOMISTS BLAME CENTRAL BANK

Lars Christensen, senior economist at Danske Bank, said the central bank had no one to blame but itself.  

"The problems for monetary policy in Ukraine have not been created by 'the market' or 'speculators', but rather by outdated and untransparent policies of the central bank," he said.  

Sergei Voloboyev, emerging markets economist at CSFB in London was equally blunt: "This statement is an example of what the market would not want a central bank to do when it is under pressure. It is unfortunately not a constructive approach."  

Some dealers at banks in Ukraine with foreign capital were even more vocal in criticism.  

"What sort of crime is this?" said one. "Every investor wants to sell dear and buy cheap."  

"We are breaking no regulations," said another. "Perhaps it's aimed at intimidating someone or other."  

The central bank engineered a one-day three percent rise in the hryvnia in late April, sapping confidence in the market, and has since intervened nearly every day to keep it steady.  

It has bought dollars at 5.00 since last Thursday, a slight weakening of the hryvnia after intervening at 4.99 and 4.98. And the bank has since last week adopted a practice of announcing early in the session parameters for possible intervention.  

Some dealers said attempts to keep the hryvnia within certain limits would run up against a growing supply of dollars, particularly a probable influx of currency in response to plans for new privatisations of big industrial sites.  

The central bank has failed to make good on promises to liberalise market operations despite appeals from President Viktor Yushchenko, dealers and the International Monetary Fund.  

A government minister welcomed the resignation last week of a top bank official who wanted to maintain tight restrictions -- including a ban on buying and selling currency on the same day.  

(Additional reporting by Douglas Busvine and Meg Clothier in Moscow and Sujata Rao in London)

KIEV, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank on Wednesday on Wednesday intervened again on the currency market it closely controls, paying slightly more for dollars than before and sowing new confusion among dealers seeking clear policy guidelines.  

The bank bought dollars at 4.99 hryvnias, slightly higher than 4.98 at the previous three sessions.  

There was no explanation for the slight rise in the dollar against the Ukrainian currency a day after the resignation of the central bank's deputy chairman Serhiy Yaryomenko, an opponent of calls to liberalise the currency market.  

"Why did the dollar rise? This is a question troubling us all. It's difficult to understand -- perhaps this is what they wanted," said one dealer.  

Market participants expressed unease over the unpredictable nature of rates and the central bank's apparent reluctance to explain its policy.  

"Now that Yaryomenko is gone there is absolutely no clarity on what policy is to follow," said another dealer. "Everyone is waiting for the long-promised liberalisation of the market but so far there is no sign of any decision by the central bank."  

The bank intervened to buy dollars at 5.01 for several weeks beginning in late April after engineering a three percent rise in a single day that rattled confidence in the market. Last week, it bought dollars more cheaply, allowing the hryvnia to rise gently when it broke through the barrier of 5.0 per dollar.  

Dealers have expected central bank chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh to outline policy since President Viktor Yushchenko told him to draft proposals to ease tough restrictions on banks.  

WAITING FOR CLARIFICATION  

But there has been no sign of any impending statement. Stelmakh attended a fair in central Ukraine with Yushchenko on Wednesday with no indication of his programme in coming days.

title: UPDATE 2- Ukraine  rate hike,  intervention  has markets confused
text:
(Updates throughout after rate rise)  

KIEV, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank sent contradictory signals to the markets on Tuesday, resuming dollar purchases to stem a rise in the hryvnia currency while raising its key discount rate.  

A central bank statement suggested the rate hike was designed to curb inflation. But analysts say freeing the hryvnia is the only effective way of combating price pressure and that Tuesday's two decisions were likely to cancel each other out.  

"They have been consistent in their inconsistency. It is difficult to understand what they are trying to achieve," said Tim Ash, emerging markets economist at Bear Stearns in London.  

"What investors need is consistency across the board. But we are not getting a clear message."  

The hryvnia climbed to its highest since 1999 this week, breaking through the level of 5 to the dollar. Dealers said deals struck on Tuesday ranged from 4.90 to 4.96/97.  

The central bank ignored the rise on the interbank market throughout Monday and until the very end of trading on Tuesday. It intervened on the foreign exchange market after the session officially closed, buying dollars at 5.01.  

"Probably, the decision was very difficult," a currency dealer said. "Banks are queuing and the central bank is buying dollars at its usual rate of 5.01 to the dollar."  

The bank also raised its key discount rate to 9.5 percent from 9 percent from Aug. 10. Obligatory reserve requirements for commercial banks were raised to 8 percent from 7 percent from Sept. 1 on hryvnia and foreign currency deposits.  

A central bank statement said the rate decision was adopted "after analysing macroeconomic and monetary indicators and also taking into consideration increasing inflation pressures".  

Central bank officials declined requests for comment.  

TACKLING INFLATION  

Ukraine's central bank is facing a policy dilemma this year.  

The International Monetary Fund and government officials have singled out inflation as Ukraine's major macroeconomic problem. The IMF has urged the central bank to curb money supply growth and loosen its grip on the exchange rate.  

The central bank has for months been printing hryvnias to buy out dollars - about $5 billion this year. M3 broad money supply rose by 26.5 percent in the first seven months.  

But the central bank is unwilling to let the hryvnia appreciate too much as it will hurt exporters, a major driver of Ukraine's economic expansion.  

The pace of economic growth slumped to 4 percent in the first half in annual terms, its lowest level in five years.  

Inflation pressures are rising. Monthly inflation reached 0.3 percent in July, exceeding the government forecast. Annual inflation nearly doubled to 14.2 percent in seven months.  

"I think it is a step in the right direction that they want to do something about containing inflationary pressures," said Jens Nystedt, chief economist EMEA at Deutsche Bank in London.  

"But at the end of the day their main tool remains the hryvnia and we see this as the starting shot for the second appreciation step that we have been calling for ever since the first one. A significant appreciation is still in the cards."  

The central bank has intervened steadily to buy the dollar at 5.01 since late April when it allowed the hryvnia to rise by about 3 percent in a single day. The move, criticised by politicians and consumers, jolted market confidence.  

Analysts said freeing up the foreign exchange market was the ultimate solution for the central bank which acts a clearance house for the market as commercial banks are not allowed to buy and sell hard currency on the same trading day.  

"I think we should not expect currency market liberalisation this year," said Ihor Solntsev, first deputy chairman of Forum Bank. "In our country there is a lot of potential instability. Neither the central bank nor clients want to create more instability." (Additional reporting by Daniel Bases in London and Douglas Busvine in Moscow)

title: Emerging  FX -Euro decline buffets C.Europe, lira steady
text:
LONDON, June 1 (Reuters) - Sharp euro losses made for choppy trade in central European currencies on Wednesday, though they broadly held to established ranges as investors continued to mull the fallout from France's rejection of the EU constitution.  

The euro hit 7-1/2 month lows against the dollar <EUR=> around $1.2270 with another leg down coming on the back of media reports a possible failure of European Monetary Union was discussed at a high-level meeting of German officials.  

A German finance ministry spokesman later dismissed such talk as "absurd", though the market had already been in bearish mode on expectations the Dutch would join France in voting "no" to the constitution in a referendum on Wednesday.  

The impact of euro moves on central Europe was mixed, with the Polish zloty recovering some lost ground, while the Hungarian forint and Czech and Slovak crowns nudged lower.  

"The euro/dollar story is an important one, but it's tricky, the correlations go up and down," said Jeff Gable, emerging markets analyst at Barclays Capital.  

"By and large, I remain reluctant to bet for further central European strength in an environment of significant euro weakness."  

The zloty recovered some lost ground after tripping up on Tuesday on news of a sharp slowdown in Polish growth to 2.1 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, from 4.0 percent in the final quarter of 2004.  

"Polish GDP was disappointing, but there's no sign that its weak euro zone growth that is causing this...nothing in the data suggests the currency is at the wrong level or that weak German or Italian growth is causing the slowdown," said Gable.  

By 0847 GMT, the zloty traded at 4.1491 per euro <EURPLN=> from 4.1532 late on Tuesday and at 3.3778 per dollar <PLN=> from 3.3622.  

LIRA STEADY  

The Turkish lira held to tight ranges against the dollar, continuing to show resilience in the face of mounting uncertainty over its EU membership prospects following France's rejection of the constitution.  

EU officials have been quick to reassure Turkey that its accession talks, due to start on Oct. 3, would not be affected, but some analysts have still been surprised by the relatively calm reaction on Turkish markets.  

"Markets have effectively discounted the fact that come October the Turks are going to begin their accession talks. But I think there's a lot of potential noise surrounding the beginning of the talks," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America.  

"I expect the political parties in Germany to take quite a an anti-Turkish line ahead of the German elections. That comes a couple of weeks before the accession talks."  

The lira traded at 1.3640 to the dollar on the interbank market <IYIX=> from 1.3570 at Tuesday's close.  

Ukraine's central bank intervened to sell dollars for the first time in two months on Tuesday, to keep the hryvnia stable around 5.05 <UAH=>.  

The bank had been intervening to buy hard currency for most of May to stabilise the hryvnia after it allowed it to appreciate to 5.05, from 5.19 in a single day.  

Rising import demand had shifted the trend in favour of a stronger dollar in recent sessions, prompting the move from the central bank.  

The hryvnia traded at 5.0610 per dollar on Wednesday, according to Reuters data <UAH=>.

Tuesday's action was the first central bank intervention since April 5 to sell the dollar and prop the hryvnia.  

"Demand was big. Usually demand builds after the weekend. Besides our economy is relying on imports at the moment," a dealer said.  

The hryvnia currency <UAH=> is seen as undervalued due to a robust current account surplus, strong exports and a steady inflow of foreign investment into Ukraine's debt market.  

The central bank jolted the market last month by fixing the hryvnia at 5.05, up from 5.19 in a single day. It has since vowed to defend the new rate and regularly bought dollars at 5.01 hryvnias throughout May.  

But dealers said the trend had started to change in recent days due to rising imports.  

The government scrapped duties for oil product imports earlier this month to alleviate domestic fuel shortages and stabilise prices. It also cut import duties for meat products and some other foodstuffs.  

One dealer estimated demand was about $20 million higher than supply on Tuesday and the hryvnia was quoted at about 5.075/5.095 to the dollar. Deals were concluded at between 5.05 and 5.08 per dollar, dealers said.  

Dealers expected the market to calm down later in the week.  

Ukraine's foreign exchange market is rigidly controlled by the central bank. Banks are not allowed both to sell and buy currency on the same trading day.

title: WRAPUP 1-Ukraine's reformers spurn market in debt move
text:
KIEV/BELGRADE, May 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine acted on Monday to stave off a currency crisis by banning foreigners from buying short-term treasuries, making it harder for speculators to bet on gains by the hryvnia.  

The surprise decision followed a test of strength between the central bank, which allowed a sharp one-off gain in the hryvnia in April but wants to stabilise the currency, and the market, which is betting on appreciation.  

Capital has been sucked into Ukraine following last year's "orange revolution", which swept President Viktor Yushchenko to power promising to set the ex-Soviet state of nearly 50 million on a pro-western course.  

But, rather than embracing market reforms, Premier Yulia Tymoshenko's government has repeatedly resorted to interventionist measures to steady Ukraine's fast-growing but vulnerable economy.  

She has already had a bruising run-in with Russian oil firms over fuel shortages, and the government remains at loggerheads over how to deal with dodgy privatisations dating back to former President Leonid Kuchma's time in office.  

Yushchenko has promised to publish a final list this week of 29 companies whose privatisations will be subjected to review, but analysts say infighting is eroding the reformers' political capital ahead of parliamentary elections due in early 2006.  

"Maybe we were too optimistic," commented Jed Sunden, publisher of the Korrespondent and Kiev Post weeklies. "Sadly, the Yushchenko administration's impulses so far have too often been consistent with Ukraine's socialist past."  

KEEP OUT  

Non-residents hold $1 billion in domestic government debt -- or half the outstanding amount -- creating upward pressure on the hryvnia which persisted even after the central bank allowed the currency to spike by 3 percent on April 20.  

The central bank has fought to defend a new target rate for the hryvnia <UAH=> of 5.05 to the dollar with dollar-buying intervention on a near-daily basis, stoking inflation pressures.  

"A decision has been taken to set a limit -- a 365-day limit -- on non-residents' purchases. Non-residents do not have the right to invest in papers with 365-day or shorter maturities," said Halyna Pakhachuk, head of Finance Ministry debt department.  

Analysts said the decision appeared poorly coordinated, smacked of short-termism and failed to address the fundamental undervaluation of the hryvnia after it was pegged for five years to a weakening dollar.  

"They are simply trying to limit inflows of hot money," said Tomasz Balamut at WestLB in Warsaw.  

Analysts polled by Reuters see the hryvnia appreciating to 4.85 to the dollar by the end of this year.  

COORDINATION PROBLEM  

More serious is a rift between Yushchenko and the feisty Tymoshenko on a strategy for straightening out past privatisations and embarking on a fresh round of sell-offs.  

Yushchenko, who subordinates virtually every decision to his long-term objective of moving Ukraine out of Russia's shadow and closer to Europe, has promised a fast review of past sales made in questionable circumstances.  

He has promised this week to publish the hit-list of 29 companies whose sales will be reviewed -- but Tymoshenko has yet to even acknowledge its existence.  

"It is necessary to resolve (the privatisation issue) as soon as possible to declare an end to it and put businessmen's hearts at rest," Yushchenko said in a statement on Monday.  

Ukraine's business tycoons have nothing to fear if they pay fair value for assets sold to them on the cheap under the government of former President Leonid Kuchma, Deputy Prime Minister Olen Rybachuk said.  

"We are going to deal with them (business tycoons) very gently," Rybachuk said at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) in Belgrade.

title: POLL-Ukraine hryvnia seen firming to 4.85/dlr by yr-end
text:
LONDON, May 19 (Reuters) - The Ukrainian hryvnia will probably make modest gains against the dollar in the second half of the year as inflationary pressures prompt the central bank to loosen controls on the currency, a Reuters poll shows.  

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) stunned markets on April 20 by allowing the currency to jump three percent in one day, effectively abandoning a 5-year-old peg of 5.30 hryvnias per dollar. It has since intervened in the market to keep the hryvnia roughly around a new target level of 5.05. All but two of the 15 analysts surveyed May 16-19 expected the hryvnia to appreciate further this year. The median forecasts showed it at 5.03 per dollar <UAH=> at the end of June -- broadly unchanged from current levels -- but strengthening to 4.85 by the end of 2005.  

"The NBU should be able to hold its current peg for the next month or two, but with inflationary pressure building and the the currency massively undervalued at its current exchange rate, we expect a further appreciation later in the year," said Rory MacFarquhar at Goldman Sachs in Moscow.  

To curb the hryvnia's appreciation the central bank prints hryvnias to buy dollars on the foreign exchange market and bought over $4 billion in the first four months of the year.  

Analysts said it could not ignore the inflationary pressures of such active intervention, especially as Ukraine's new liberal government hopes to cut inflation to single digits this year from 12.3 percent in 2004.  

"We believe that unless there is a particularly good harvest, which induces a decline in inflation, the government hasn't done enough in terms of combatting inflation and there will be no option but to allow a certain additional appreciation of the hryvnia," said Sonal Desai at DrKW in Milan.  

FREE FLOAT FAR AWAY  

Although analysts expect the central bank to allow the hryvnia to firm in coming months, they do not think it will completely abandon the currency to market forces just yet.  

"Ukraine still has a long way to go before its financial system and markets mature enough to allow a full flotation of the hryvnia and it is not a given that the country will manage to stay the current pro-reform course all the way," said Tomasz Balamut at WestLB in Warsaw.  

Setting the hryvnia free would probably prompt a big rally. But with up to half of Ukraine's bank reserves held in dollars, a big appreciation of the hryvnia against the dollar could effectively slash the value of many people's savings.  

Five of the analysts said the hryvnia could be fully floating as soon as next year after parliamentary elections due in early 2006. Four said it could happen in 2007 or 2008, five said it would take longer and one gave no answer. Even with the forecast appreciation, the hryvnia is set to remain seriously undervalued, the poll showed. The median estimate put the hryvnia's current fair value at 4.00 per dollar.  

"Our view is that it is highly undervalued -- probably by as much as 30 percent. But the fair value is pretty hard to know given that we haven't had any time when we've had a free float," said Lars Christensen at Danske Bank in Copenhagen.  

The hryvnia was seen staying fairly stable against the euro in coming months. Medians showed it at 6.38 per euro <EURUAH=> at the end of June and at 6.35 at the end of the year, compared to 6.35 on Thursday.  

End year forecasts ranged from 5.70 to 6.86 hryvnias per euro and from 4.50 to 5.05 hryvnias per dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-Ukraine c.bank promises to ease  FX  market controls.
text:
(Wraps central bankers, intervention)  

KIEV, April 28 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank announced steps on Thursday to ease tight controls on the currency market after hefty capital inflows forced it to revalue the hryvnia last week.  

Volodymyr Stelmakh, head of the National Bank of Ukraine, told a news conference that new rules - including allowing market participants to buy and sell in a single session - would come into force after the holiday at the beginning of May.  

"The document has been already worked out. Tomorrow it will be submited to the Justice Ministry. I think it will take effect after May holidays," Stelmakh told a news conference.  

Predominantly Christian Orthodox Ukraine will celebrate Easter on May 1 and Victory Day on May 9.  

The central bank abandoned its longstanding peg of the hryvnia to the dollar last week. It allowed the hryvnia to rise by 3 percent against the dollar on April 20 after heavy bidding by foreign investors at a treasury bond auction.  

Since then Stelmakh has drawn a new line in the sand, vowing to defend a central rate of 5.05 to the dollar this year - up from the old rate of 5.30 which had been in force since 2000.  

Dealers said the central bank intervened again on the local market on Thursday, buying dollars at a rate of 5.01 hryvnias for the third day running.  

EASIER RULES  

Emerging markets investors zeroed in on Ukraine after the "Orange Revolution" swept a pro-reform leadership to power. Non-residents now hold 6 billion hryvnias ($1.2 billion) or about 50 percent of all outstanding government debt.  

That has strained the draconian currency market controls imposed after the 1998 financial crash in neighbouring Russia and the financial community has clamoured for the hryvnia to be allowed to float more freely.  

Valery Lytvytsky, Stelmakh's chief adviser, told Reuters earlier on Thursday the central bank may extend currency trading hours and allow market participants to buy second-tier currencies with hard currency.  

But the possibility of abolishing a 1.5 percent transaction tax on foreign exchange purchases, which goes towards the state pension fund, would depend on an improvement in Ukraine's budget situation. Non-residents are exempt but residents are not.  

"At the moment the situation is rather strained, but I would not rule out the possibility of abolishing this 1.5 percent tax for residents - if the budget balance turns positive," Lytvytsky said in an interview.  

Echoing Stelmakh, Lytvytsky said the central bank would allow small fluctuations of the hryvnia around its new target rate of 5.05 to the dollar, but would not tolerate major volatility.  

"I don't want this to be interpreted as a new fixed rate. We will in future observe the principle of flexibility," he said. "Fluctuations will be possible but the central bank will seek to prevent sharp moves from happening."  

Lytvytsky said the hryvnia remained fundamentally undervalued, but argued it was vital to move slowly to allow Ukraine's population - long used to a stable exchange rate - to adjust. Up to half of Ukraine's bank deposits are in dollars.  

(Additional reporting by Douglas Busvine).

title: Emerging  FX -High yielders broadly soft, zloty under pressure.
text:
LONDON, April 28 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty led a broadly soft tone for emerging market currencies on Thursday, with lower domestic interest rates and political jitters still applying downward pressure.   

 Global market uncertainty and nerves before first quarter growth figures in the United States at 1230 GMT kept the tone cautious in most high-yield currencies.   

 The zloty was anchored close to five-month lows against the euro, after falling the previous session on speculation, later confirmed, of a 50 basis point interest rate cut from the central bank which took the key rate to 5.50 percent.   

 Dealers said the market quickly refocused its attention on political risk in Poland with parliament due to vote next week on whether to dissolve itself, paving the way for early elections in June.   

 "We had a bit of a relief rally to 4.21 after the rate cut, but it was reversed very quickly. People still see significant political risk ahead of next week's vote in parliament and the referendums on the EU constitution," said one UK bank trader.   

 Investors are also concerned about a potential delay to the timetable for central European countries joining the euro if France and the Netherlands reject the EU constitution in upcoming referendums.   


By 0945 GMT, the zloty traded at 4.2550 to the euro  from 4.2350 late
on Wednesday and at 3.2928 to the dollar        from 3.2662.
  


"The zloty is about 10 percent lower against the euro since the
beginning of March, but there's still little appetite from foreigners
or domestic players to put fresh risk on the table," the trader added.
  


"In view of the current uncertainty worldwide, the risk reward does not
justify going long zloty," he said, pointing to the 4.29 level as a
potential near-term upside target.
  


The Hungarian forint also headed lower, weakening beyond 250 per euro
in line with the broadly softer regional tone. It traded at 250.40.
  


RAND EASES
  


The South African rand tracked the broadly softer tone in high-yield
currencies, but held inside established ranges before the U.S. growth
data later in the session.
  


The market shrugged off further evidence that inflationary pressures in
South Africa are picking up. March producer prices had a
higher-than-expected annual rate of 1.9 percent in March, up from 1.2
percent the previous month.
  


Analysts had already scaled back expectations for a rate cut at the
central bank's next policy meeting in June after March consumer price
data on Tuesday showed core inflation picking up from February's record
lows.
  


"The data confirms the trend that inflation has bottomed, but no
inflationary pressures are suggested to concern the central bank," said
Tania Kotsos, currency analyst at Royal Bank of Canada. "The 0.7
percent rise in imported prices was the highest since 2003 and a
reflection of rand weakness in March, but its still well below trend."
  


Kotsos said the impact on the rand was likely to be muted, with the
market more closely focused on the external environment and the
performance of the dollar. The rand was around 0.5 percent down at 6.08
to the dollar .
  

Ukraine's central bank intervened again at around 5.01 hryvnias per
dollar , according to Kiev dealers, in line with comments from a bank
adviser that it would look to keep the rate steady roughly around 5.05
in 2005.

title: Emerging  FX -Rand dips, eyeing Barclays, C.Europe soft.
text:
LONDON, April 26 (Reuters) - The South African rand slipped on Tuesday on investor concerns a big bank takeover might collapse, while the Polish zloty and Hungarian forint remained soft on global risk aversion and domestic political worries.  

The rand was pegged back versus the dollar on mounting concerns Britain's Barclays bank (BARC.L) might abandon its bid for a majority stake in South Africa's largest retail lender Absa (ASAJ.J) if minority shareholders demand a higher price.  

The rand had drawn strength from expectations of significant inflows into the country on the back of the deal, though analysts were optimistic the currency would not nose-dive if it did fall through.  

"The rand is going to stay in a 5.80-6.20 range against the dollar. I don't see much driving it out of that, even if the Barclays deal is off the agenda, it may go back to 6.20 but not much further," said Debbie Orgill, emerging markets analyst at ABN AMRO.  

By 0900 GMT, the rand traded slightly lower on the session at 6.07 per dollar .  

South African March inflation data failed to lift the mood, showing an upturn in the central bank-targeted CPIX indicator to an annual rate of 3.6 percent in March, compared with February's record low 3.1 percent.  

"It does signal a turn in the inflation cycle. The last few months have been below expectations, but now we're likely to see it heading up to 4 percent," said Orgill.  

Orgill added that an interest rate cut at the central bank's next policy meeting in June looked unlikely, but said there could still be scope for easing later in the year, depending on oil prices and wage developments.  

The bank rocked the market with a surprise 50 basis point cut earlier in April, taking key rates to 7 percent.  

FORINT, ZLOTY SOFT  

An uncertain global environment, coupled with ongoing domestic political jitters in Poland, continued to lend a soft tone to the Hungarian forint and Polish zloty.  

Some analysts also see a dovish interest rate bias across central Europe as potentially negative at a time when the Federal Reserve is mulling a faster pace of U.S. rate hikes.  

Hungary's central bank cut key rates by a modest 25 basis points on Monday, taking them to 7.5 percent, but did urge caution in future due to global investor risk aversion and the risks to the forint from the country's economic imbalances.  

"The decision did not have an impact on the currency, but the gradual erosion of the carry makes the forint more vulnerable to changes in sentiment," said Goldman Sachs analyst Istvan Zsoldos, in a research note.  

The forint traded was marginally down at 249.15 to the euro .  

Poland's central bank is widely expected to follow with a 25 bp cut of its own at two-day monthly policy meeting, which started on Tuesday, though seven out of 20 economists polled by Reuters said the bank may opt for a bigger 50 bp cut.  

Of greater concern for investors is the political atmosphere ahead of elections, which must be held by October. A poll at the weekend showing the euro sceptic Law and Justice party taking the lead from the centre-right Civic Platform.  

Another potential negative for the zloty would be a 'no' vote from the French in a referendum on the EU constitution next month - a result which could cause a substantial delay in Poland's timetable for joining the euro. The zloty was off 0.3 percent at 4.20 per euro .

Ukraine's President Viktor Yuschenko said he was unhappy about last week's shock move, saying it undermined stability, but still forecast further gains thanks to a steady inflow of foreign investment.

title: UPDATE 3- Ukraine  c.bank  intervenes  to stem hryvnia surge.
text:
KIEV, April 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on Thursday to rein in the country's soaraway currency only a day after unleashing it in a move that shocked markets and sparked anger and confusion among politicians.  

Wednesday's 3 percent jump caught Ukraine's new reformist government cold while parliamentarians summoned the central bank head and finance minister to explain the abandonment of a longstanding de facto currency peg.  

Dealers said the National Bank of Ukraine bought dollars at a rate of 5.02 hryvnias - a new five-year high - after stunning the market on Wednesday by letting the local currency rise strongly.  

Analysts saw more gains in store for the hryvnia, which they consider deeply undervalued, delivering a dose of anti-inflationary medicine which might have potentially harmful side-effects for Ukraine's export-led growth.  

The central bank said in a statement on Thursday the hryvnia's rise was a tool aimed at easing inflation pressure.  

"In its currency policy the central bank takes into consideration interests of all economic entities, in particular Ukraine's population with an aim to boost its consumer power," said the bank's First Deputy Chairman Anatoly Shapovalov.  

Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko wants a strong hryvnia to help bring down inflation, but her government sent mixed messages to a nation of 50 million wholly unprepared for the sudden move.  

"It is absolutely illogical to maintain an undervalued hryvnia rate artificially because its price should be formed by the market," Interfax news agency quoted Tymoshenko as saying.  

Economy Minister Serhiy Teryokhin warned the leap could sow panic among Ukrainians, who like many people in the former Soviet Union hold much of their savings in U.S. dollars and may rush to buy hryvnias.  

Parliament voted to summon Central Bank Chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh and Finance Minister Viktor Pynzenyk on Friday to explain what was going on. Both have been out of sight so far.  

"We had a storm warning today in Kiev," Mykola Noshchenko, one deputy, told parliament. "It snowed in some regions - but Ukrainian families only started worrying when they got the storm warning from the central bank. What will happen tomorrow?"  

Foreign exchange dealers said Wednesday's hryvnia move, to 5.05 to the dollar from 5.19 previously, came out of the blue.  

They said the central bank's strict control of currency trade - it acts as a market clearing house and players are not allowed to sell and buy in a single session - meant the jump had shaken market confidence.  

"Their reasons are unclear. It is impossible to make any forecasts," one dealer said.  

Teryokhin said he had asked central bank chief Stelmakh about the hryvnia's rise but received no clear answer. "The economy ministry and the finance ministry do not understand what the central bank is doing," he said.  

STILL UNDERVALUED  

Analysts said Ukraine's currency remained undervalued, in view of the weak dollar and bumper export earnings being raked in by key industries like steel which have widened the current account surplus to 11 percent of gross domestic product.  

"At the moment, the FX market is a one-way bet given the sheer magnitude of the external surpluses," said Sergei Voloboev, emerging markets economist at CSFB in London.  

Lavish spending by the government ousted in last year's "Orange Revolution" has pushed inflation up to 13.5 percent - providing another reason for the market to bet on appreciation.  

"Appreciation of 3 percent will have a very limited impact on inflation," said Lars Christensen, senior analyst at Danske Bank. "Appreciation of at least 15 percent is needed to bring inflation comfortably below 10 percent this year."  

Christensen noted that Russia and Kazakhstan - which like Ukraine have resource-based economies - had allowed their currencies to appreciate by around 15 percent against the dollar since 2002. Ukraine had held the hryvnia flat over that period.  

Hot portfolio inflows into Ukraine's domestic debt market may have provided the final trigger. A record $425 million in treasuries were snapped up at this week's auction - with up to 60 percent going to non-residents.  

Economic mismanagement could prove to be the undoing of Tymoshenko's three-month-old government, which faces a general election in early 2006, said Konrad Reuss, sovereign analyst at Standard & Poor's in London.  

"The way the Orange Revolution brought them in, the parliamentary election could sweep them out again," Reuss, just back from a visit to Ukraine, told Reuters.  

"Clearly there is a reform-minded government, but I am not really sure the government knows what it wants to do." (With reporting by Douglas Busvine in Moscow and Daniel Bases in Paris).

title: Ukraine's c.bank will allow stronger hryvnia-aide.
text:
KIEV, April 14 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank will allow a gradual appreciation of the hryvnia to curb rising inflation and support economic recovery, a senior adviser to the bank's chairman said.   

The International Monetary Fund believes the hryvnia, which trades at about 5.25 per dollar, is undervalued given a record current account surplus and strong exports.   

"We support a stronger hryvnia rate," Valery Lytvytsky told reporters late on Thursday. "But there will be no plunge in the dollar. The central bank will not stop intervening."   

The central bank rigidly controls Ukraine's foreign exchange market. It is a key buyer and seller of hard currency and sets the hryvnia rate by administrative means.   

The government, which rose to power amid street protests late last year, has also urged the bank to ease its grip on the market and let the hryvnia float more freely. The government sees a stronger hryvnia as a key measure against inflation.   

"A stronger hryvnia is not a panacea," Lytvytsky said. "The rate should not be blocking credits. The rate should not hinder exports and domestic production. It should help competition."   

Lytvytsky gave no level for the hryvnia rate by the end of the year. Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko said last month she expected the hryvnia to rise to about 5.0 per dollar by the end of the year.   

Ukraine is awash with hard currency due to booming exports of steel and chemicals and foreign fund inflows on the domestic debt market.   

The central bank has engaged in considerable intervention on the interbank market so far this year to buy hard currency. It has bought over $3.1 billion since the start of the year compared with $2.6 billion throughout 2004.   

Exporters had until this month been obliged to sell at least 50 percent of hard currency earnings on the interbank market but the measure was scrapped from April 1.

title: Ukraine cbank plans gradual freeing up of  FX  mkt.
text:
KIEV, April 9 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank is working on a plan to introduce a gradual liberalisation of the rigidly controlled foreign exchange market, a first deputy central bank chairman said on Saturday.   

Anatoly Shapovalov told reporters the central bank wants to allow commercial banks to buy and sell currency during one trading day and may extend the trading session by one hour.   

"We certainly need to remove market regulations to allow banks buy and sell the same day. This is a chance to become more flexible. The central bank will only appear on the market when it sees sharp volatility and then it will intervene," he said after a government meeting.   

Ukraine has one of the toughest currency regimes in the world. Commercial banks are allowed to buy or sell hard currency only under clients' orders. They can also either buy or sell hard currency during one trading day. The trading session lasts for about four hours.   

On Thursday, many currency dealers complained that the central bank, the dominant market player, did not buy dollars on the interbank market and banks failed to meet their obligations to clients.   

The central bank usually acts as a main seller or buyer of the hard currency. It also fixes the hryvnia rate to the dollar administratively.   

Ukraine's new liberal government, which rose to power on the back of the Orange Revolution, has repeatedly called on the central bank to free up the foreign exchange market and allow the hryvnia to float more freely.   

The restrictions were introduced in 1998 to battle consequences of a Russian financial crisis. Forex dealers and Western economists said the measures are now unnecessary given Ukraine's steady economic growth and a record current account surplus.   

One of the first steps in freeing up the market was a decision by the central bank and the government to scrap a rule demanding exporters sell at least 50 percent of their hard currency earnings on the interbank market.   

The rule was eliminated from April 1.   

Shapovalov said the central bank had set up a special working group which was working on how to change the software the central bank was using for the foreign exchange market.   

"Certainly, we need to give banks certain time to adjust," Shapovalov said. "But I think we will propose the changes in May."

title: UPDATE 1-Ukraine's Yushchenko sees hryvnia rising in '05.
text:
(Ccombines stories, adds quotes, details)  

KIEV, March 29 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko said on Tuesday the hryvnia currency would appreciate this year, but made no predictions on its future level.  

Yushchenko, who launched the hryvnia in 1996 during his six-year stint as head of the central bank, said the supply of dollars on the interbank market was "colossal" at the moment.  

"It is most likely that we can expect appreciation of the national currency," Yushchenko told a news conference.  

The hryvnia is currently traded at about 5.29 per dollar on Ukraine's interbank currency market. Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko has said the hryvnia could rise to about 5.0 by the end of the year.  

The central bank, which tightly controls the interbank market, is trying to curb any hryvnia appreciation and intervenes heavily to buy out dollars. Ukraine's economy is export-reliant.  

The central bank bought about $1.6 billion in the first two months of the year compared to $2.6 billion throughout 2004.  

The government has expressed concern that central bank dollar purchases might fuel inflation this year and last week ordered the rescinding of a rule requiring exporters to sell at least 50 percent of hard currency earnings.  

Ministers have urged the central bank to give its required consent to the change. But the central bank has so far been unwilling, saying financial stability remained fragile.  

A central bank spokeswoman, speaking by telephone, said Tymoshenko, accompanied by senior ministers, had met Central Bank Chairman Volodymyr Stelmakh on Tuesday to discuss currency policy. She gave no details.  

Yushchenko said the meeting was needed to clear up discrepancies between statements issued by ministers and the central bank in the past two months.  

"I think that after today's meeting of the National Bank head, the prime minister and the economy minister a position will at last be formed and publicly stated," he said.  

"I think the basis of these policies should be formed by the National bank taking account of the economy ministry's position."

title: IMF Warns Ukraine Of Rising Threat Of Overheating Economy
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The International Monetary Fund on Monday urged Ukraine's government to cut spending and raise interest rates to head off an overheating economy.  

Following several years of budget restraint, the government spent freely in the run-up to presidential elections, hiking the monthly pension bill by 36% in the remaining four months of 2004. Coupled with a booming economy and a strong inflow of foreign capital, the increase in public spending risks boosting inflation, the IMF said in a press summary of its regular annual review of Ukraine's economy.  

"The loosening of fiscal policy in 2004 increased the risks of overheating," the IMF said. It noted that, "although the surge in the deficit this year was largely financed through higher-than-expected privatization proceeds, the significant increases in recurrent government spending, particularly pensions, compromised the 2005 budget and placed public finances on a less firm footing."  

After expanding 12.5% in 2004, Ukraine's economy should grow around 6.0% in 2005, according to IMF forecasts.  

The IMF noted that Ukraine was unable to successfully complete a review of its one-year $627 million precautionary credit agreement, signed in March 2004, because of insufficient reforms. Some examples of problems were failure to end tax exemptions and arrears, a backlog of value-added-tax refunds, and some inaction on changes to lending rules.  

The inflows of foreign capital into the country has forced Ukraine's central bank to intervene in currency markets to maintain a peg to the U.S. dollar. The central bank should put a priority on fighting inflation, which has risen from a average low of 0.8% in 2002 to 8.8% in 2004, the IMF said. In September 2004, the consumer price index was up 10.7% and the producer price index rose 23.2%.  

"Given the choice between inflation and nominal appreciation...(the IMF) considered a move to a more flexible exchange rate regime more beneficial to Ukraine," the IMF said. The currency peg to the U.S. dollar is "exacerbating the challenge for the National Bank of Ukraine to achieve its inflation objective."  

Monetary policy remains inconsistent with the goal of reducing inflation to the single digits, the IMF added.  

In general, Ukraine must improve its investment climate if high growth rates are to continue, the IMF said. The IMF noted "governance problems remained widespread, ranging from tax collection and public procurement to law enforcement and divestment of public assets."  


 
  -By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9295; Elizabeth.Price@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 2-Ukraine budget gap soared $1 bln in run-up to vote.
text:
KIEV, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Ukraine's budget deficit jumped by $1 billion from almost nothing in the two months leading up to the political crisis triggered by November's disputed presidential election, official data showed on Tuesday.  

Although the data did not show how the money was spent, analysts said the deficit probably pointed to a spending spree by outgoing President Leonid Kuchma and Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovich to woo voters in the Nov. 21 presidential run-off.  

When Yanukovich was declared winner of the election, hundreds of thousands of protesters poured into the streets in support of opposition leader Viktor Yushchenko, bringing much of Kiev to a halt. The Supreme Court has declared the poll invalid and ordered a re-run for Dec. 26.  

Kuchma has repeatedly warned Ukrainians that the economy was on the brink of collapse, saying the protests were to blame. His remarks provoked a run on banks, drove up consumer prices and fuelled demand for dollars.  

But Tuesday's data released by the State Treasury Department showed the state budget started to suffer long before the political crisis erupted.  

The January-October deficit widened to 5.608 billion hryvnias ($1.06 billion) from 59.9 million hryvnias in the first eight months of the year, the statement said without elaboration.  

"Budget data for October shows massive pork-barrelling in the run-up to the presidential election by the Kuchma/Yanukovich administration," said Timothy Ash, emerging Europe analyst at Bear Stearns.  

"Whoever takes power after this debacle will need to rein in the budget, as a major priority," Ash said.  

By law, the 2004 deficit must not exceed 6.975 billion hryvnias.  

"We don't know what they spent it on right now. but yes, clearly the government was probably using the budget to gain favours here and there in the run-up to the election," Zsolt Pap, emerging market analyst at ABN AMRO in London.  

"The first round of the presidential election was at the end of October and we now have figures for the first 10 months. The deterioration (in the budget) happened in September and October, so it is reasonable to assume some of the spending is election related."  

Separate figures from Ukraine's central bank on Tuesday showed the country's gross hard currency reserves fell to $9.9 billion on Dec. 3 from $10.3 billion a week earlier, mainly due to higher market intervention.  

JPMorgan on Tuesday recommended investors cut exposure to Ukraine's sovereign debt to "marketweight" from "overweight" amid concerns that political instability would linger after the country's electoral crisis is resolved.  

"In our view, the main risks are that political uncertainty will continue even if Yushchenko wins the new elections," JPMorgan said in a note.  

The protesters have vowed to maintain a blockade of government buildings until they see Yushchenko inaugurated as president.  

TROUBLE TO COME  

Although official macroeconomic data has yet to show any major fallout from the crisis, economists warned the trouble could lie ahead.  

Kuchma's remark late last month that Ukraine's financial system could collapse "like a house of cards" may have triggered a fresh surge in consumer prices after inflation hit a record 2.2 percent in October.  

The comment came too late to affect November data, released on Monday, but could push December inflation above October's record.  

Analysts believe Ukraine, where the average monthly wage is the equivalent of about $100, can withstand the crisis until the end of December but warned investors that further turmoil could jolt the financial system.  

The central bank has repeatedly called on Ukrainians to remain calm and urged the government to take action to contain price rises. Analysts, however, say 2004 inflation could be far above the 12 percent forecast by the bank. (Additional reporting by Natalia Zinets, Greg Brosnan in New York and Sabyasachi Mitra and Daniel Bases in London).

title: UPDATE 1-IMF encouraged by Ukraine growth.
text:
WASHINGTON, Jan 19 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Friday said it was encouraged by economic progress in Ukraine and urged the former Soviet state to control its money supply to lower its inflation rate. 

 In its annual assessment of the Ukraine economy, the Washington-based lender forecast that inflation hit about 27.1 percent last year. On a more positive note, economic growth reached 4.2 percent in 2000, marking the first year of positive growth in almost a decade of independence. 

 The IMF's verdict on Ukraine was fairly upbeat, saying it, "welcomed the recent improvements in economic policy implementation and endorsed Ukraine's overall strategy based on a sound budget, tight monetary policy and supportive structural reforms." 

 The fund told Ukraine, which gained independence in August 1991, to stay the course of its program for economic stability and structural reforms, saying it was vital to help the former Soviet state make a successful transition to a market economy. 

 The IMF said the nominal exchange rate remained stable in 2000 but that inflation was higher than expected, eroding improvements in competitiveness achieved in 1999. With that in mind, the IMF urged the Bank of Ukraine, "Not to target any particular level of the exchange rate and to be prepared to accept greater exchange-rate flexibility in both directions." 

 Keeping monetary aggregates, or total money supply, under control would help lower inflation, the fund noted. 

 Some IMF directors were critical of the pace of privatization in Ukraine, noting that no large enterprise had yet been sold in an open and transparent bidding procedure. The IMF said it was essential Ukraine press ahead more rapidly with structural reforms to reduce the role of the state in the economy and bolster private sector confidence and investment. 

 The IMF said any privatization receipts above expected amounts should be used for debt reduction. It also said that efforts should be made to broaden the tax base before any tax cuts to make the overall effect on revenues neutral. 

 The lender said Ukraine's current account surplus will likely narrow in 2001, reflecting more moderate export growth and the full-year impact of higher energy imports. 

 The improved growth performance in 2000 stemmed largely from the real effective exchange-rate depreciation of the the national currency, the hryvnia, in 1999, better-than-expected growth in Russia and recovery in other export markets particularly in metals. 

 Ukraine's exchange rate was broadly stable in 2000 as it depreciated by 34 percent against the U.S. dollar. But intervention by Ukraine's central bank, which bought large amounts of foreign exchange in 2000, helped push inflation up to 27.1 percent from 19 percent in the previous year.

title: Ukrainian c.bank may  intervene  to prop up hryvnia.
text:
KIEV, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank may sell 5-10 percent of its $1.15 billion reserves to support the fragile hryvnia currency, a central bank official said on Thursday. 

 "If it is needed, we can sell 5-10 percent of the hard currency we have previously bought. We are obliged to do so to stabilise the market," Serhiy Yaremenko, currency regulation department head, told a news conference. 

 The hryvnia fell to 5.80-5.86 per dollar at street exchange booths from around 5.50 per dollar last week. 

 Its official rate, which lags the market rate by two days, was unchanged at 4.4397 per dollar on Thursday.

title: FOCUS - Ukraine floats hryvnia  currency .
text:
KIEV, Feb 21 (Reuters) - Ukraine will untie its hryvnia currency from a rigid trading band against the dollar and allow it to float freely, the central bank and government said on Monday in a statement which confirmed market expectations. 

 The more liberal currency policy meets demands of international lenders who have insisted on the abolition of administrative restrictions on Ukraine's forex market and confirms a de facto policy which began last year. 

 But the bank and government promised to intervene in the market to keep the hryvnia stable. 

 "Ukraine's cabinet of ministers and National Bank consider that under the current circumstances a floating rate will be the most realistic currency policy," the central bank and government said. 

 The move has largely been expected since it is an official acknowledgment of a policy in effect since the second half of last year, when the bank, short on reserves, let the hryvnia break the band at that time of 3.4-4.6 per dollar. 

 Some experts said the printing of large amounts of money by the central bank before last year's presidential election contributed to the fall. 

 On Monday the official rate was set at 5.5748 hryvnia per dollar and the government expects an average rate of 5.78 this year. 

 The central bank, whose reserves stood at just over $1 billion at the start of this year, became an active buyer of hard currency last year, purchasing more than $700 million. 

 On Monday authourites said they would intervene if the stability of the hryvnia was threatened. 

 "Ukraine's government and the National Bank intend to watch closely tendencies of economic development and events on the money market to defend the monetary system and...ensure the currency rate which helps economic growth," the statement said. 

 The government and central bank expected the floating rate to help Ukraine's integration into the world economy, support the competitiveness of domestic goods, raise the profitability of local companies and save currency reserves. 

 Cash-short Ukraine, which faces crushing foreign debt payments worth more than $3.1 billion this year, is seeking renewed financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund. 

 Ukraine introduced the hryvnia at 1.76 per dollar in September 1996 and the following year established a corridor. 

 ((Dmitry Solovyov, Kiev Newsroom, +380 44 244 9150 kiev.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Ukraine Bank Faces Hard  Currency  Choice As Polls Loom
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Pressure on Ukraine's currency, the hryvnia (UAH) has put the country's central bank in a quandary just three months before the Oct. 31 presidential election. 

 The hryvnia, down more than 7% against the dollar in recent weeks, is in peril of crashing out of its existing exchange-rate corridor, adding fuel to inflation during the sensitive run-up to the polls. 

 "Of course (the central bank) will continue to support the hryvnia," said central bank bank spokeswoman Lydia Mykhailova. The hryvnia "without a doubt" will remain within its current trading corridor of UAH3.9-UAH4.6, she said. 

 While offering support to its currency, however, the National Bank of Ukraine must ration its gold and foreign currency reserves to keep the country on track with the International Monetary Fund. 

 The timing and extent of the support will be crucial, analysts said. 

 The hryvnia began to plummet two weeks ago as Russia's gasoline shortage spread to its western neighbor. Ukrainian gasoline prices jumped by 100%, undermining the local currency in the process. 

 The hryvnia has fallen steeply, closing at UAH4.47-UAH4.55 in interbank trading Friday, more than 15% weaker than UAH3.92 on July 16. The dollar was quoted around UAH4.15-UAH4.50 in street kiosks, compared with UAH4.06 two weeks earlier. 

 "The hryvnia was slightly overvalued when it was at UAH3.94; that is why the National Bank of Ukraine was satisfied when it devalued to UAH4.10-UAH4.15," said an executive with a western bank in Kiev. "The pace of devaluation has decreased in the last few days but the pressure is enormous." 


                       IMF Rules



The National Bank also finds itself constrained by the terms of an
International Monetary Fund lending program that requires it to keep
reserves over $1 billion, limiting scope for intervention.



The margin isn't big. Ukraine's reserves rose by $100 million during
the first half of July to $1.29 billion, the National Bank of Ukraine
said on July 22.



By comparison, the government has $11.6 billion in outstanding foreign
debts, said Ivan Kompan, head of research at Wood & Co. brokerage in
Kiev, including $3 billion maturing next year.



With wage arrears at UAH7.1 billion, further depreciation of the
currency is to the government's advantage, he said.



And there are questions about the efficacy of central bank support for
the hryvnia. People often stash their savings, whether in dollars or
local currency, elsewhere than in the banking system.



The banks therefore cannot be sure when money is being spirited away
in panic and possibly changed into hard currencies, since it occurs on
the black market.



"A lot of money is in cash and people keep their money under the
mattresses, not in the banks," Kompan said. "It's difficult to say
whether interventions will help or not."



With the hryvnia fluctuating so widely, the bank will have be shrewd
about picking its moment if it does decide to prop up the currency.



If the bank chooses to intervene at UAH4.40-UAH4.50, just below the
ceiling of its trading corridor, investors are likely to call its bluff,
the western bank executive said. By contrast, if it enters the market at
the UAH4.20-UAH4.30, that would be taken as a sign for the market to
stabilize, he said.



But the central bank should be able to keep the hryvnia within its
corridor until the elections, the executive said. Ukrainian exporters
are obliged to sell 50% of their hard currency proceeds on local
exchanges, he noted. With the harvest season approaching, local
exchanges will see an influx of foreign currency from the country's
largest export, sugar, helping to relieve some of the pressure on the
hryvnia.



With gasoline prices likely to ease in the next few days, the hryvnia
is being largely influenced by "psychological factors," Mykhailova said.



Sergei Yaramenko, the head of the central bank's foreign exchange
department, said Friday that the bank is permanently monitoring the
foreign currency market to assess the need for intervention, the
Interfax news agency reported.



-By Andrea Chipman; 7095-974-8055; achipman@ap.org

title: Ukraine  Ctrl Bk May  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt-Interfax
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Ukraine doesn't rule out intervention in the country's interbank foreign exchange market, the Interfax news agency reported Friday, quoting a senior bank official. 

 Ukraine's currency, the hryvnia (UAH), has fallen steeply over the last two weeks. Early Friday, the dollar was officially offered at UAH4.21, more than 7% higher than UAH3.92 on July 16. The dollar was quoted around UAH4.25 in street kiosks, around 4.7% higher than UAH4.06 two weeks earlier. 

 The bank is permanently monitoring the foreign currency market to assess the need for intervention, said the head of the central bank's foreign exchange department, Sergei Yaramenko. 

 Referring to the rapid depreciation of the hryvnia, Yaramenko said the central bank "is working to prevent the hryvnia from falling," and he added that the Ukrainian currency would soon "be brought in order." 

 He said the National Bank might use stricter regulation in the foreign currency market, but he didn't elaborate.

title: INTERVIEW- Ukraine  c.bank mulls hryvnia  intervention .
text:
KIEV, July 29 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank is likely to intervene to support the weakened hryvnia but will not use administrative controls to limit dollar demand, a top central bank official said on Thursday. 

 "I will intervene, but when I will intervene I have not decided yet - I mean the central bank," the head of the bank's currency department Serhiy Yaremenko told Reuters. 

 "I mean that for now there will be no administrative restrictions...the necessity of intervention is being discussed," Yaremenko said. 

 The hryvnia has slipped by several kopecks in the past 10 days, sparking fears of a heavier fall among some traders and their clients after months of relative stability. 

 The official hryvnia exchange rate based on interbank trades of the previous two days eased to 4.1790 to the dollar on Thursday from 4.1569 on Wednesday and 3.9487 early last week. 

 Dealers said dollar bid/offer quotes had fallen to 4.55/4.60 hryvnias just before Yeremenko's comments from 4.33/4.37 at the open of interbank trade. There were hardly any deals. 

 "Central bank intervention is necessary, some kind of step in the right direction," said one dealer. 

 Dealers blamed last week's fuel crisis, which doubled the price of petrol over a week and exacerbated problems with the harvest, for sparking the first weakness in the hryvnia in the retail market, which spilled into the interbank market. 

 Some traders on Wednesday, noting increased dollar demand and no offers, said the market expected the hryvnia to fall further in closer proportion to the rise in fuel prices. They said psychological factors were also pushing the hryvnia lower. 

 Yaremenko said increased demand for dollars was coming from major fuel traders making large imports to replenish supplies. Central bank head Viktor Yushchenko said this week that fuel accounted for about 40 percent of imports. 

 "It is not that the currency market is destabilised but that there is higher demand for hard currency, which is connected with the need to purchase fuel," said Yaremenko. 

 Dealers said the bank needed to spend more now to balance the market than it would have done had it acted earlier. 

 "If the Bank had got involved back then, it would have been selling along with other big banks. But this way everyone's sitting on dollars," another trader said. 

 Yaremenko declined to say when the central bank was going to intervene or in what volumes but said the bank's board did not regard the situation as critical. 

 "I'm not saying that we're sleeping soundly but the bank's board does not see a critical situation for now," he said. Yushchenko said on Wednesday a fall in the the official rate of 4.3 percent in the last week was not a major move when compared to the rise in the price of fuel. 

 The hryvnia trades within a band of between 3.4-4.6 to the dollar, set by the central bank and government in agreement with the IMF until the end of the year. Yushchenko said the central bank would be able to support the band to the end of the year. (( Kiev Newsroom, +380 44 244 9150, e-mail:kiev.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: ANALYSIS-Ukraine c.bank in tough spot over ING bond.
text:
KIEV, June 18 (Reuters) - Ukraine has created a dilemma for its central bank by its restructuring proposal for an overdue $155 million ING Barings bond, analysts said on Friday, as a June 23 deadline for a deal edges ever nearer. 

 The Finance Ministry made an offer to investors in May to redeem 20 percent of the bond, which matured on June 9, and restructure the rest into three-year Eurobonds. 

 Some investors are insisting on 100 percent redemption, and the ministry says talks are continuing into the "remedy" period of 10 working days by the end of which the government must pay, reach agreement with investors or effectively default. 

 Analysts say default is unlikely. Top officials have also ruled out the possibility. 

 But the central bank said earlier this week redemption of 20 percent of the bond in cash would lead to serious difficulties in fulfilling promises to the IMF under Ukraine's $2.6 billion loan agreement. 

 The central bank said it was concerned for its foreign currency reserves, which the finance ministry would tap to buy dollars to pay ING. 

Central Bank head Viktor Yushchenko said this week gross foreign currency reserves, which the bank has been building to meet IMF targets, had risen to $1.28 billion from $1.18 billion last week. But the bank said it was still not in the clear. 

 "Intervention carried out by the National Bank of Ukraine on the currency market with the goal of replenishing international currency reserves for now does not permit confirmation that the problem of achieving the necessary volume of currency reserves is already solved," the bank's statement on the bond said. 

 Analysts differed over whether Ukraine's reserves allowed payment of $163 million, the ING bond's principal plus interest due. 

 But payment would in general endanger macroeconomic targets agreed with the IMF, said Ivan Kompan, Wood & Co. investment bank's research head, adding talks were likely to continue to the eleventh hour. 

 "Technically paying the loan is possible, the bank has enough reserves, but it would lead to non-compliance with IMF requirements and therefore IMF financing could be stopped," Kompan said. 

 "Ukraine would lose its only feasible source of financing. I don't believe Ukraine can afford to do that, on the other hand it has to pay its debts. They have to find some compromise." 

 Analysts said that in particular the finance ministry would have to sell new treasury bills to redeem any part of the bond. 

 That would effectively mean selling to the central bank, which has been the sole purchaser at primary auctions since commercial banks were scared off by the cash-strapped ministry's efforts to restructure their treasury bills portfolios. 

 But one analyst said the economic plan agreed with the IMF precluded further primary sales of treasury bills this month. 

 And Olexander Bazarov, head of Credit Suisse First Boston Ukraine said a new central bank regulatory law banned the bank from crediting the ministry at all. 

 "If the central bank makes an emission - because if it gives the ministry hryvnias that is essentially making an emission - then the central bank could fall outside the parameters approved by the IMF," he said. ((Kiev newsroom, +380 44 244 9150 email:kiev.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Ukraine c.bnk sees problems over 20 pct ING payment.
text:
KIEV, June 15 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Tuesday redemption of 20 percent of a $155 million bond issued through ING Barings could lead to serious problems fulfilling the terms of Ukraine's $2.6 billion IMF loan programme. 

 "Taking into account payments to the end of the month and the rate of growth of international currency reserves, the National Bank of Ukraine considers that payment of 20 percent of the ING bonds could lead to serious difficulties implementing the conditions of the EFF programme in June," a statement from the bank said. 

 Officials were unavailable to comment on the statement at both the central bank and the Finance Ministry, which in May said it had asked holders of the bond to agree to redemption of 20 percent of the bond. 

 The restructuring deal, which Finance Minister Ihor Mityukov told Reuters earlier on Tuesday was still under negotiation four working days after the bond matured on June 9, entails rolling over the remaining 80 percent into new three year Eurobonds. 

 One major bond holder told Reuters last week her company was demanding 100 percent redemption. Central Bank head Viktor Yushchenko told a news conference earlier in the day that gross foreign currency reserves, which must meet agreed targets under the IMF programme, had risen to $1.28 billion from $1.18 billion last Wednesday. 

 But the bank statement said the bank was still not in the clear. "Intervention carried out by the National Bank of Ukraine on the currency market with the goal of replenishing international currency reserves for now does not permit confirmation that the problem of achieving the necessary volume of currency reserves is already solved," the statement said. ((Kiev newsroom +380 44 244 9150 kiev.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: IMF's Camdessus meets Russian, Ukrainian leaders.
text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund's managing director held surprise talks on Wednesday with Russian and Ukrainian leaders on the financial crisis gripping Russia and fallout across the region. 

 An IMF spokesman in Washington said the fund's managing director, Michel Camdessus, was meeting with Russia's acting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma in Ukraine's Crimea peninsula, against the backdrop of the deepening crisis and plummeting currencies. 

 "The purpose of Camdessus's visit is to discuss recent developments in Russia and their impact on the region, especially Ukraine," the IMF spokesman said. 

 Last month Russia clinched a $22.6 billion rescue package with the IMF and other international lenders aimed at dragging Russia out of deep economic crisis. But conditions have deteriorated dramatically since that agreement was reached. 

 Russia stunned financial markets around the world a week ago by effectively devaluing the rouble and declaring a 90-day moratorium on repayment of some foreign credits. 

 Then Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Sunday fired the entire government of Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko, who had failed to stem a worsening financial crisis. 

 Yeltsin named as acting prime minister Chernomyrdin, whom he had fired in March in a quest for a premier who could inject new life into economic reforms. 

 But Chernomyrdin has been struggling to form a new cabinet, and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it was not possible for the IMF, the Group of Seven industrialised nations or the European Union to fix Russia's problems. 

 Russia's rouble plunged more than 40 percent against the German mark on Wednesday and the central bank declared it could no longer afford to intervene to support the currency. 

Ukraine, which is seeking a $2.2 billion loan from the IMF, has also been hit hard by the crisis. 

 Citing the knock-on effect of the crisis in neighbouring Russia, the IMF said on Tuesday it was reassessing economic conditions in Ukraine. 

 Once this reassessment is completed, the IMF was expected to consider Ukraine's loan, which would support a programme of tough economic reforms and help the former Soviet republic weather the financial crises gripping Russia and Asia. 

 Ukraine's hryvnia has taken a battering in the wake of neighbouring Russia's rouble devaluation. What happens in Moscow is critical for Kiev because Russia accounts for about 40 percent of Ukraine's foreign trade.

title: Ukraine  C.bank to  intervene  on t-bill market June.

KIEV, June 2 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank plans to participate actively on the former Soviet republic's primary and secondary treasury-bill markets in June, bank chairman Viktor Yushchenko said on Tuesday. 

 "We have reserved the possibility of conducting active operations on the secondary market in June," Yushchenko told reporters. "I think June requires detailed work from the central bank on the currency market and money market and we will be interested in working very actively with our portfolio." 

 He confirmed the central bank would purchase new treasury bills on the primary market in June, using money it had earned on the market so far this year. 

 Yushchenko declined to say how much money the bank would spend on the secondary market, where yields are higher than on the primary market. Three-month paper earned 57.73 percent and 12-month paper was at 53.30 percent at most recent primary auctions. 

 He said earlier this month the bank had sold 110 million hryvnias ($53.5 million) worth of paper on the secondary market between January and April this year.

title: Ukraine 's c.bank says  intervened  to help hryvnia.
text:
KIEV, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on the secondary interbank market to support the hryvnia currency once in recent days and may do so again, bank chief Viktor Yushchenko said on Thursday. 

 "The leadership reserves the right, depending on the situation on currency and Treasury-bill markets, to use such an instrument, possibly, on occasion," he told a news conference. 

 "Like any central bank we must guard our currency and we are fulfilling this function today." 

 Yushchenko announced in December 1996 that the bank would only work on the Ukrainian Interbank Currency Exchange this year. He confirmed in April that this policy had not changed. 

 But asked if this had changed recently, Yushchenko said: "This intervention did not happen several times but once a few days ago...In today's situation I cannot say that this was the Central Bank of Ukraine's one and only intervention". 

 He made clear he saw the problem with the currency as temporary and linked to financial market turmoil abroad. 

 "I do not think this (intervention) was enough by itself to calm currency and T-bill markets once and for all. Our thesis that the central bank does not consider it expedient to work on the secondary currency market is still actual," he said. 

 The hryvnia is being held within a range of 1.70 to 1.90 to the dollar this year, which is due to ease to 1.75 to 1.95 over the first half of 1998. 

 Yushchenko confirmed that the bank had dug into its reserves in September when markets were weak. A typical situation on the interbank exchange recently has been zero demand for hryvnias. 

 "We are in a controllable regime, but I cannot say we do not use the bank's reserves. Of course we use them...and it would be surprising if Ukraine was unaffected, when currency and stock markets all around it are having colossal problems costing billions of dollars," he added. 

 Dealers said the bank sold a big volume of hryvnias, but Yushchenko would give no details of the intervention. 

 In September and October the bank was forced to meet big demand for dollars on the Interbank Currency Exchange, where the hryvnia traded at 1.8770 to the dollar on Thursday. 

 Dealers linked this to the fact that foreigners' participation in the T-bill market had fallen back recently. 

 Yushchenko declined to say what reserves were. Ukrayinskiy Novyny said net reserves fell from $678 million on September 1 to $248 million a month later and had only recovered slightly by October 29 to $282.5 million. 

 "Since September, movement of central bank currency reserves has stabilised. We did not have any serious growth, but we had no serious losses," Yushchenko said.
