title: Talks on Ukraine $1.5bln hryvnya fund continue - IMF.
text:
KIEV, Sept 3 (Reuter) - Ukraine's request for a $1.5 billion currency stabilisation fund from the International Monetary Fund to back its new hryvnya currency is still under discussion, an IMF official said on Tuesday. 

 The hryvnya itself, introduced on Monday, was steady and bankers said it showed no immediate signs of weakening. 

 "The discussions are continuing," said resident representative Alex Sundakov. "It's hard to comment on any timetable." 

 The hryvnya replaces the interim karbovanets currency, introduced after independence in 1991, which will be taken out of circulation by September 16. 

 Sundakov would not comment on Ukraine's decision to launch the new currency, which at 100,000 karbovanets to one hryvnya, wipes five zeroes off prices. 

 But he said an IMF mission, which visits Ukraine regularly to review its economic performance under an $867 million loan agreement, will return to Kiev on September 16. 

 Ukrainian government and central bank officials say they are confident they will receive the stabilisation fund, but the issue was not settled when the last mission left Kiev in August. 

 The hryvnya was unchanged at 1.76 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange on Tuesday. Bankers and economists said this stability was to be expected. 

 "Many banks are not selling dollars for the hryvnya right now. They're waiting to see what the National Bank will do," said Ihor Davydenko of Ukrinbank. 

 He said the hryvnya was holding its own without central bank support. "That's keeping people calm," he said. 

 But Dmytro Kozmaty of Pravexbank said the central bank, whose $2.1 billion in reserves equals the amount of money circulating in Ukraine, was intervening to keep the hryvnya stable. 

 "They will probably keep doing that for two weeks, so that people don't panic," Kozmaty said. 

 Both bankers did not expect dollar demand to rise in the near future and predicted the hryvnya would remain at present levels or even rise slightly after mid-month when the karbovanets is removed from circulation. 

 "This change is denominational and there have been no changes in exchange rate policy, so it's normal that it's staying at the same level," said Rafal Antczak of the Harvard Institute for International Development. 

 The karbovanets had remained at about 176,000 to the dollar in the months running up to the hryvnya's introduction. 

 "Maintaining the level is a question of credibility, and it is a signal for enterprises, for exporters and importers," Antczak said. 

 Bankers said the shift to the new currency was not disrupting their work. 

 But the Ukrainian Stock Exchange, where share transactions reached into billions and trillions in the old currency, suspended its weekly trading session on Tuesday in order to revamp its accounting system. 

 "We have put off today's trading purely for technical reasons. We need to change the prices of shares and the starting capital of enterprises being privatised into hryvnya," said Viktoria Myasnykova, head of the exchange's accounting division.

title: POLL-Weakness in Ukraine's hryvnia seen short-lived
text:
LONDON, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Any weakness in Ukraine's hryvnia will probably be shortlived and should be over by mid-year, thanks to central bank intervention and a return of investor confidence after March general elections, a Reuters poll shows.  

The Reuters poll of 15 emerging market strategists showed the hryvnia <UAH=> at around 5.07 per dollar by end-June even as an increase in gas prices trims Ukraine's economic growth this year and nudges its current account into deficit.  

That is only slightly above the 5.05 level to which it was revalued last April and roughly where the central bank wants to keep the currency.  

It has bought hryvnias most days since the start of the year, resisting pressure for a weaker currency after parliament sacked the government over a contentious deal under which Ukraine is to pay more for imported Russian gas.  

Despite intervention, the hryvnia weakened to fresh nine-month lows of 5.19/5.20 per dollar on Thursday, with dealers saying the central bank had failed to cover all bids. But the hryvnia then regained ground after a top official told Reuters the bank was ready to continue interventions.  

"We expect (the central bank) to defend the loose dollar peg through this year's turbulent politics, to prevent any possible household panic from becoming self-fulfilling," said Rory MacFarquhar at Goldman Sachs in Moscow.  

A sharp weakening of the hryvnia versus the dollar could unsettle ordinary Ukrainians who tend to turn to the U.S. currency as a safe haven in times of political uncertainty.  

However, the 5.07 median forecast for end June and 5.05 for end-year could mask the potential for a weakening to 5.25 or 5.30 per dollar in the near-term.  

Some said intervention could pick up pace in coming weeks -- with currency reserves of over $19 billion the central bank can afford to be more aggressive.  

Even without bolder intervention, the hryvnia could strengthen once the March 26 parliamentary election is over and market attention returns to the currency's fundamentals.  

"Fundamentals relative to the pricing of the currency (suggest that) the hryvnia should be so much stronger -- about 15 percent at least," said Lars Christensen at Danske Bank in Copenhagen.  

ELECION OUTCOME UNCLEAR  

Strategists said the election would probably not result in an outright win for any party, but there was no clear consensus in the poll on the most likely coalition formation.  

Leading in opinion polls is the Regions Party of Viktor Yanukovich, the rival that liberal President Viktor Yushchenko defeated in the long, bruising 2004 presidential election.  

Lying second is a bloc led by Yulia Tymoshenko, Yushchenko's ally during 2004 "Orange Revolution" protests but dismissed as prime minister last September and now running against the president's allies. The pro-presidential Our Ukraine party is in third place.  

Despite differences, any two of these could form a coalition. Or whoever wins the most votes may join forces with smaller parties.  

"We are going to see fairly unstable governments for some time to come, but I don't think investor sentiment will necessarily be badly affected," said Sonal Desai at DrKW in Milan.  

One possible exception could be greater power for Tymoshenko, who has criticised the gas deal and favours policies such as higher social spending which please voters but can seem imprudent to foreign investors, strategists said. The results of the election could to a certain extent affect Ukraine's growth and current account outlook this year.  

Overall, the poll forecast growth of 2.5 percent this year -- fractionally up from a 5-year low of 2.4 percent posted last year and compared to 12.1 percent in 2004.  

That is based on Ukraine paying Russia $95 per 1,000 cubic meters of gas, up from $50 previously but still well bellow open market rates. Strategists said the gas deal would probably hold as there is little chance of Ukraine negotiating better rates.  

One risk, according to Tim Ash at Bear Stearns in London, is that Russia could push for even higher prices.  

"If the new government is seen in Moscow as being overly anti-Russia we could well see further attempts to renegotiate from July onwards," he said.  

The present deal will push Ukraine's current account into a deficit of 2 percent of GDP this year, the poll showed.  

But even if Ukraine had been allowed to continue paying old gas prices, the poll forecast modest growth of 4.5 percent this year and a current account surplus of just 1.0 percent of GDP.  

"Even without a natural gas issue, the low growth rate in net exports and low growth in fixed investments will provide low one digit growth rate of the economy," said Alexander Valchyshen at ING Bank Ukraine.  

Despite the negative effects on Ukraine's economy this year, the gas deal could eventually prove to be a positive.  

"In the long run, the sharp increase in gas prices is actually a positive for the country and holders of its longer-dated Eurobonds, as it improves the chances for an orderly transition to much higher prices for gas in about 5 years' time," said Sergei Voloboev at Credit Suisse in London.  

(Additional reporting by Natalie Harrison)

The hryvnia plunged to 5.1530/5.1670 to the dollar at 1035 GMT, its lowest point in nine months, compared with 5.1050/5.1150 at the opening.  

The central bank intervened, selling dollars at 5.06 hryvnias, the level it has been defending since last August.  

But dealers said, having failed to meet all bids, the bank and had paved the way for further weakness in the currency.  

"The central bank is imposing limits on dollar sales for no clear reason. It gives no explanation," one dealer said. "We are not demanding a hryvnia rate of 5.06 to the dollar. We want clear and transparent rules."  

Others said the repeated failure to cover dollar demand might unsettle Ukrainians, who tend to turn to the dollar as a safe commodity in times of political uncertainty.  

"Such central bank actions ... will fuel further demand and, inevitably, a sharp dollar rise on the cash market," said Serhiy Borysov, a deputy chairman at Finance and Credit.  

Economy Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk said there was no economic basis for the hryvnia to be subject to volatility given the central bank's robust reserves. The reserves grew to $19.4 billion at the end of 2005 from $9.5 billion a year ago.  

"We see no economic reasons for any currency volatility," said Yatsenyuk, who was deputy central bank chairman in 2004.  

"I am certain the central bank, as an independent body, has all instruments to uphold price stability via the stability of the currency rate."  

INTERVENTION NEARLY EVERY DAY

Dealers said the currency is also suffering from a sharp decrease in export revenues.

Ukraine's main industries are energy-intensive and prices for Russian gas have nearly doubled to about $95 per 1,000 cubic metres under the deal signed in the New Year.  

Political uncertainty is compounding the hryvnia's woes less than two months before a parliamentary election.

Yushchenko was chairing a meeting of the National Security and Defence Council on Wednesday. On Thursday, he and his prime minister are to attend a session of parliament.  

"The political turmoil is even greater than expected ahead of the election and I think the central bank is sitting half on the sidelines, just using the bare minimum of its reserves to maintain some kind of order," said Sonal Desai at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein.  

"I see the hryvnia bouncing around and maybe weaker in the intervening time but I do not see it going into freefall." (Additional reporting by Sujata Rao in London)

title: UPDATE 1-Fitch cuts Ukraine credit outlook on political row
text:
(Updates with analyst comment, background, fresh prices)  

LONDON, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Fitch Ratings lowered its credit rating outlook on Ukraine to stable from positive on Thursday but affirmed the ratings at 'BB-' after parliament voted this week to sack the government over a murky gas deal with Russia.  

Fitch's decision is the first negative sign on Ukraine's credit rating since the country agreed the pricing deal last week, doubling the price paid by Kiev after a standoff in which Moscow cut off supplies.  

"Fitch believes that the formation of the next government could be a prolonged affair and that the outcome may be a weak coalition vulnerable to splits," Sharon Raj, sovereign ratings analyst at Fitch in London, said in a statement.  

"Against this background, the outlook for progress with structural reform has worsened, while the risk of a slow or inappropriate policy response to the recent gas price or any future shock has increased," she added.  

President Viktor Yushchenko has refused to recognise Tuesday's no-confidence vote as legitimate and wants to keep Premier Yuri Yekhuranov in office until parliamentary elections due on March 26.  

Ukraine's benchmark sovereign dollar bond due 2013 fell on the Fitch news, losing about one point in price before clawing back to a loss of just 0.375 points at 106.625 to yield 6.589 percent <UAHGLB13=RR>.  

Ukraine's external bonds, which have a scarcity premium, are not expected to be hammered lower in any dramatic fashion as investors wait for clearer direction on domestic politics and the impact of the gas deal on the economy.  

Ukraine's sovereign debt traded at 192 basis points over U.S. Treasuries on the benchmark JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus <11EMJ> <.JPMEMBIPLUS>, five basis points wider on the day, indicating an increase in investor risk aversion.  

"I think there really are significant economic and political risks for certain but the credit continues to trade very tight," said Frank Gill, emerging markets analyst at IDEAglobal in London.  

The hryvnia currency, already weak, showed little reaction to the Fitch news. Ukraine's central bank intervened on Wednesday to sell dollars at 5.06 hryvnia <UAH=>, and said it would satisfy all bids at that level, after the local currency dropped to a nine-month low around 5.09.  

But on Thursday the hryvnia was around 5.095 in early trade before creeping back to 5.0805, a 0.40 percent loss on the day.  

SMALL DEBT  

Ukraine's relatively small debt to gross domestic product ratio and a tradition of current account surpluses, which supported its bonds and ratings, are now considered under threat as a result of the gas agreement.  

"Right now, potential investors are going to hold back until they can determine what sort of government is going to be voted in in March," Gill said.  

"If we see a lot of political gridlock, it is probably negative for foreign investment in the medium term."  

Rival ratings agency Standard & Poor's affirmed its Ukraine ratings on Wednesday and kept its outlook at stable. S&P rates Ukraine 'BB-', the same as Fitch, while Moody's Investors Service is one notch lower at 'B1'.  

S&P said despite relatively bleak economic prospects, Ukraine still enjoyed a fairly robust external position and low debt levels, giving the government flexibility with its budget.  

The parliamentary revolt was led by former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko and analysts said the opposition was using anger over the gas deal to undermine Yushckenko's supporters ahead of the March elections, which will bring broader powers to whoever has the majority.  

Fitch said the vote may have minimal near-term consequences for policy.  

"While Ukraine's long-term growth potential remains strong, 2006 will be a tough year and any ongoing political weaknesses will compound the economic challenges," the statement said.

title: UPDATE 4-Ukraine hryvnia hits 9-month low, c. bank steps in
text:
(Adds S&P report)  

KIEV, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market to sell dollars on Wednesday after the hryvnia slipped to its lowest level since April 2005 following parliament's sacking of the government.  

The intervention gave a lift to the currency <UAH=> which had fallen to 5.091/5.098 to the dollar in early trade compared with 5.075/5.0875 per dollar at the opening.  

Anatoly Shapovalov, first deputy central bank chairman, told Reuters the bank would cover all bids at a rate of 5.06 hryvnias to the dollar, the level it has defended for about 6 months.  

"The government resignation caused this jump (in the dollar)," Shapovalov said.  

"The central bank was selling hard currency. But certainly it was selling within its limits for each bank. Probably, some were still unable to cover all their bids," one dealer said.  

The hryvnia started to regain ground immediately after the central bank's announcement it would intervene, quickly reaching the 5.06 level.  

Standard & Poor's agency also provided some comfort, reaffirming its ratings on Ukraine, saying that despite relatively bleak economic prospects, low debt levels gave the government flexibility with its budget.  

Dealers expect the hryvnia to rebound further this week provided the central bank continues to support it.  

"I do not think the dollar will go higher than 5.07 hryvnias tomorrow. Many will wait for the central bank, including us," another dealer said.  

MARKET UNSETTLED  

The central bank keeps a tight grip on the currency and intervenes frequently, both selling and buying dollars, to keep the hryvnia within a target corridor of 5.00-5.06. But it stayed out of the market on Tuesday, unsettling dealers.  

Central bank officials have repeatedly said there were no economic reasons for the hryvnia to fall and vowed to prop up the currency when needed. The central bank's foreign currency reserves stood at $19.395 billion at the end of December.  

The average hryvnia rate is forecast at between 5.00-5.20 to the dollar for 2006.  

Shapovalov said some demand for dollars came from non-residents withdrawing funds after the finance ministry repaid some hryvnia-denominated government debt. He estimated the demand at about $36 million.  

"It is not a major factor and it was expected," he said. "The government resignation is an extraordinary event. The currency rate became the first indicator. (Banks) reacted in a similar way to previous resignations."  

Dealers said there was also demand for dollars from an unsettled population and from rising hard currency purchases by oil importers.  

Parliament voted on Tuesday to fire the government of Prime Minister Yuri Yekhanurov after Ukraine agreed to pay higher prices for Russian natural gas imports this year.  

It was the second government to fall in just over three months and since President Viktor Yushchenko took power after the 'Orange Revolution'.  

Yushchenko said the sacking was unconstitutional and said Yekhanurov would remain Ukraine's premier until the March 26 parliamentary election.  

Ukraine's internationally traded debt steadied on Wednesday after yield premiums widened by around 10 basis points a day earlier. Ukraine's section of the JP Morgan EMBI+ index <UKREMBIP=JPM> was steady at 183 ticks over U.S. Treasuries.  

The country's main PFTS <.PFTSI> stock index recovered some losses, inching up by 0.5 percent at Wednesday's close.

KIEV, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank said on Monday it may intervene on the foreign exchange market at a rate of 5.00/5.06 hryvnias to the dollar and set the indicative volume at $10 million.  

The central bank tightly controls the foreign exchange market and has been intervening nearly daily to prevent any sharp movements in the hryvnia currency. The hryvnia <UAH=> was quoted at 5.01/5.02 to the dollar in early trade on Monday, rougthly at the same level as on Friday.

title: Ukraine's c. bank buys dollars for fourth day
text:
KIEV, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Friday for a fourth straight day, buying dollars at 5.0 hryvnias, dealers said.  

The central bank, which tightly controls the foreign exchange market, has previously set the volume for intervention at $10 million.  

The hryvnia dipped slightly to 5.015/5.038 to the dollar on Friday after Thursday's sacking of Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, compared with 4.985/4.99 to the dollar on Thursday. Dealers said the slide was short-term.

title: UPDATE 1-Ukraine c.bank buys dlrs, mkt ignores govt sacking
text:
KIEV, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Thursday for the third day in a row, buying dollars at 5.0 hryvnias, unchanged from the previous session, dealers said.  

They said the market was steady and ignored President Viktor Yushchenko's decision to sack the government of Yulia Tymoshenko amid corruption allegations.  

"Nobody wants to take any risks today. Everybody is waiting to see what will happen. The market was hovering at its usual levels. Quotes were at about 5 hryvnias to the dollar," a dealer said.  

Ukraine's thinly traded dollar-denominated sovereign bonds held steady after news of the sacking.  

The thinly traded dollar-denominated sovereign debt due 2013 <UAHGLB13=RR> was unchanged on the day to bid 114.500, with the yield holding at 5.338 percent.  

Bonds due 2011 <UA018756480=> were off 0.46 points in price to bid 105.420, yielding 5.708 percent. The bond due 2007 <UAHGLB07=RR>, already slightly weaker on the day has held steady with a small drop of 0.063 points in price to bid 104.500, yielding 4.839 percent.
